News.title: UKHSA symptoms that mean unwell children should still go to school
News.content:
UKHSA symptoms that mean unwell children should still go to school

UKHSA has issued school absence advice to parents and carers on when to keep children off school if they are unwell

View Image UKHSA has issued new guidance to parents (Image: Ekaterina Goncharova via Getty Images)

As a new school year gets under way, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has issued clear guidance for parents and carers on when poorly children should be kept at home and when they are fit to attend school.

‌



The government body said now is an ideal opportunity to "familiarise ourselves with some of the common illnesses that can cause disruption to children's time in school during the colder months". UKHSA bosses say it is perfectly fine to send your child to school or nursery with a minor cough or common cold, provided they are otherwise well and free from a high temperature.

‌



However, if your child has a fever, they should remain at home until they are feeling better and the temperature has subsided. Children suffering from diarrhoea and/or vomiting must stay away from school for a minimum of 48 hours after their last episode.

‌



Routine COVID-19 testing for children and young people is no longer recommended unless advised by a healthcare professional. That said, if your child has tested positive for COVID-19, they should try to remain at home and limit contact with others for three days following the day they took the test.

Children and young people who attend school, college or childcare and live with someone who has tested positive for COVID-19 should continue to attend as usual.

Article continues below

Should your child display any of the measles symptoms listed below, and they have not received both doses of the MMR or MMRV vaccine, they must not return to school until four days after their rash first appeared.

Measles symptoms

The early signs of measles include a runny or blocked nose, a high temperature, a cough, sneezing, and red, sore, watery eyes. A rash usually appears several days later, starting on the face and behind the ears before spreading across the rest of the body.

The spots of the rash are sometimes raised and merge together to form blotchy patches, and they're not generally itchy. The UKHSA notes that it is highly unlikely to be measles if your child has received both doses of the MMR/MMRV vaccine or has previously had measles.

News.title: Middlesbrough - live: More arrests made after wrong-way A66 crash killed cops
News.content:
Cleveland Police announced more arrests on Friday as part of an operation against organised crime following the A66 crash - but said the deadly house fire in Grangetown was not linked to the collision

Police on Friday said seven more men have been arrested as part of an operation against organised crime following the A66 crash, which led to the deaths of two police officers and five young males.

It means Cleveland Police has now arrested 24 people since the collision between a marked police vehicle and a Volkswagen Passat near Middlesbrough last Saturday.

However, the force also confirmed detectives are not linking a fatal house fire which killed a seven-year-old girl and her aunt to last weekend’s deadly A66 crash.

On Wednesday, Valentina Foster, seven, and her aunt Natalie McDonald, 34, were tragically killed in a house fire in Grangetown on Teesside. Two men have since been arrested on suspicion of murder.

Following that, on Thursday morning a wall at a house in South Bank was allegedly rammed by a car. Some of the latest arrests relate to this incident.

It came as footage shared online showed a number of cars on fire in a field in Haswell, County Durham, as balloons were released at a memorial event for Michael Robert Cahill, 23, one of the five men in the Passat. It appeared the cars - including an £80K Porsche - were set ablaze as part of the event.

News.title: 97-year-old woman rescued after Nepali floods looked like 'a warrior'
News.content:
A 97-year-old woman pulled from flood debris in Nepal is recovering in hospital, according to her doctors.

Guna Maya Bohara's great-nephew, Dipak Bohara, has told BBC Nepali she looked like "a warrior" who had returned victorious from battle.

The operation to pull Bohara out of the rubble of her care home took four hours.

Bohara travelled from Kathmandu to help rescue his great-aunt.

Hundreds of people have been confirmed dead after Wednesday's flash floods, which scientists believe were triggered by a glacier collapsing in the Himalayan border region with Tibet.

Video produced by Mansi Kapur and Kamal Pariyar. Video edited by Suneth Perera, Jasmin Dyer and Andrew Webb.

More on this story here.

News.title: Christian festival 'devastated' as man dies after sign falls
News.content:
Organisers of a Christian festival say they are "devastated" after a sign fell at their event and injured seven people, with one man dying at the scene.

Sussex Police said it had been called to the Big Church Festival at Wiston Park, near Steyning in West Sussex, at about 15:38 BST on Friday.

It was later confirmed a 41-year-old man from Eastbourne in East Sussex had died.

The Archbishop of Canterbury said she was "sad and shocked" to hear about the fatal incident.

Dame Sarah Mullally said: "I pray for his family, friends and loved ones as they grieve. I pray for those receiving treatment, and the healthcare workers looking after them.

"And I pray too for the other festival goers, staff and event organisers as they come to terms with these tragic events.

"May the god of comfort and healing be with them all."

South East Coast Ambulance service said four of the six people injured were taken to local hospitals for further treatment, with two people having serious injuries.

The Big Church Festival, which describes itself as the UK's biggest Christian festival, was founded in 2009.

The festival began on Friday and was due to continue until Sunday, but a decision was made by organisers to cancel the remainder of the event after the incident.

"We are working with the emergency services, police and the Health and Safety Executive as they establish the circumstances surrounding today's incident," the organisers said.

"We are incredibly grateful to everyone who responded, and to our teams and community for the care they have shown one another."

News.title: Burnham's summer tour is over - now he has to prove himself in Parliament
News.content:
Andy Burnham is set to come under the most intense scrutiny of his political life when Parliament returns on Tuesday.

Since coming to power six weeks ago, the new prime minister has largely been free to set his own agenda.

The timing of Labour's leadership contest meant he walked into Number 10 after the House of Commons began its summer break, denying MPs the chance to question him and creating what some have seen as a honeymoon period.

Burnham has embarked on what Downing Street called a "summer tour" of the UK, appeared on podcasts and announced a series of eye-catching policies, mainly aimed at tackling the cost of living.

But things are about to get a lot tougher, with MPs finally getting a chance to grill the new PM when he makes a statement to Parliament on his priorities as PM.

He has taken questions from MPs in the Commons before, when he was a minister in Tony Blair and Gordon Brown's Labour governments.

But Tuesday will be his first appearance on the government front bench for 16 years.

News.title: Sarah Ferguson expected back in the UK 'shortly', source says
News.content:
Ferguson is expected to move into the six-bedroom home "imminently", which could be as soon as next week, the Sun reported, external.

It is believed she has been spending her time out of the public eye at an Alpine chalet in Verbier, Switzerland, since leaving Royal Lodge. Her belongings were collected from Mountbatten-Windsor's home in Sandringham this week, the newspaper added.

She had been keeping a low profile since losing her titles alongside Mountbatten-Windsor after she became mired in the scandal about her connections to Epstein, and faced calls to speak to US authorities after last year's release of millions of documents shed new light on their relationship.

In one email exchange from 2011, she appeared to privately apologise for her public rejection of Epstein, saying: "You have always been a steadfast, generous and supreme friend to me and my family."

A spokesperson for the duchess previously said the email was sent after Epstein had threatened to sue her for defamation - in an effort to convince him not to.

Another email suggested Ferguson took her daughters to see Epstein in the US days after he was released from prison for child sex crimes.

The emails do not indicate any wrongdoing.

Epstein was also ultimately the downfall of Mountbatten-Windsor, who was stripped of his titles by the King because of "serious lapses of judgment" over his friendship with the late paedophile. Mountbatten-Windsor has always denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.

Ferguson lost her courtesy royal divorcee title and reverted to her maiden name, and also lost the freedom of the city of York after councillors voted unanimously to remove the honour over the scandal.

Her expected return comes just days after the Duke and Duchess of Sussex came back to Britain with their children to begin a new life after six years living in the US.

News.title: We helped create UK emergency alert system - but question how government is using it
News.content:
The government's Cobra emergency committee met to discuss how to respond. After sign off from Prime Minister Andy Burnham's de facto deputy Louise Haigh, the alert was sent at 19:00 on 14 August.

It triggered a backlash on social media with some vowing to opt out of further alerts in their phone settings, domestic abuse charities and survivors saying victims with hidden phones were put at risk, and confusion about alerts sent multiple times.

Dowden's worry is that the wildfire alert was more like a public information campaign than an imminent threat to life across all of England and Wales.

"People need to know that when they receive an alert, it is a genuine imminent emergency," the Conservative MP says. "If that confidence is lost, people will simply ignore it."

A Cabinet Office report during trials in 2014 warned of this "cry wolf" effect, while pointing out there was strong support among the public for the alerts.

"Alerts should not be issued just because the government wants to be seen to be doing something," Dowden adds.

The National Fire Chiefs Council said the alert heightened people's awareness and public behaviour, while government insiders point out wildfire alerts are commonplace in many European countries.

"By following the guidance that was issued, people were able to take the necessary steps to keep themselves safe and front line services recorded a significant decrease in incidents in the following days," a government spokesperson said.

But Frazer Rhodes, who worked in government across a decade to help build the technology and devise high thresholds for the alerts, feels a review is now necessary to avoid future ones backfiring.

He was in a bar in Halifax, West Yorkshire, with his wife when the sound of pinging phones began echoing around.

"Everybody around was just going, 'what's this?' What's this?'" he tells us. "Then my wife shouted, 'he did that'."

His wife's joke aside, he said his "immediate thought" was whether it met the threshold for sending one. He explains: "At its heart are three criteria: urgency, severity and certainty. So, in simple terms, how bad, how soon, and how sure?"

Rhodes thinks the wildfire alert arguably met the bar for urgency and severity, but perhaps not for certainty of a threat to life.

"It should be very rare to get an alert," he points out.

News.title: Satellite images reveal scale of flood devastation in Nepal villages
News.content:
New satellite imagery has revealed the scale of the devastation along Nepal's Trishuli River caused by Wednesday's deadly flash flood, triggered by a glacier collapse.

Before-and-after images show how sections of the valley, where a torrent of floodwater and debris surged through, destroyed villages, bridges and hydroelectric power stations.

Hundreds of people have been killed and thousands more are missing, Nepalese officials say.

Among the worst-hit locations reviewed by BBC Verify was a key Nepal-Tibet border crossing, which was engulfed by a rush of floodwater and captured on camera.

The satellite imagery from US-based intelligence firm Vantor, shows the site has been almost entirely washed away. Shocking CCTV footage showed the moment as the deluge of water swept over buildings as people tried to escape.

News.title: What we know about the 33 British nationals missing in Nepal
News.content:
Families are flying out to Nepal to help the ongoing search for 33 British nationals still missing after deadly floods hit the country.

The brother of Neetu Goyal Tiwari, one of the missing Brits who has not been seen since Wednesday, has appealed to officials to locate his sister.

"Please help us find her", Naresh Goyal told the BBC as he struggled to hold back his emotions.

On Friday, Nepalese authorities named 573 tourists who are still missing in the country and despite fears of a second wave of flooding, search efforts have continued.

To help, the UK is deploying a rapid deployment team to Nepal to support British nationals affected in the region.

The specially-trained crisis response team is expected to arrive in Kathmandu on Saturday, a move that follows Prime Minister Andy Burnham's pledge of Â£5m worth of humanitarian support for relief and recovery efforts.

And as rescue efforts continue in the aftermath of the disaster which killed at least 538 people, details of the missing are slowly emerging.

News.title: Watch: Why rescuers fear new barrier lake could cause another Nepal-Tibet flood
News.content:
China has warned there is a "high risk" that a lake which formed after the recent landslide near the Nepal-Tibet border may breach its banks, causing a second flood downstream.

The warning comes after Wednesday's deadly flash flood in the same area which scientists say was triggered by the collapse of a mountain glacier into a river.

China correspondent Laura Bicker explains.

News.title: Strong winds and thunderstorms kick off the bank holiday weekend
News.content:
After weeks of scorching heat and drought the summer's swan song is set to be one of frequent downpours as well as gales for some.

Areas of heavy rain and showers are expected to sweep across parts of the UK on each day of the weekend, which is a bank holiday for many.

This could make for some soggy moments at many of the festivals taking place over the coming days.

Strong winds and gales may also cause problems for travellers and holidaymakers in southern parts of the UK.

News.title: The race to stop England running out of water
News.content:
England is already experiencing wetter winters, something climate models predict will continue. This prompts the question of whether we could just store more of this excess water for when we need it?

To do this, new reservoirs would be needed. But England has built no major new reservoirs for more than 30 years.

The reason for the lack of new storage sites has been hotly debated between water companies and campaigners, the latter saying there has been a lack of investment from the privatised sector, the former arguing they were not given permission to spend the money by the regulators because of the impact on water bills.

The government's landmark independent Cunliffe review into the water sector in 2025 accepted that both arguments were true.

Now 10 reservoirs are planned in England by 2050. But even with financial and political backing, building new reservoirs is not straightforward.

"Building enough reservoirs to hold all that water requires good places, which means places where the land is sloping, where we can find a valley," explains Dr Ross Woods, associate professor of water and environmental engineering at the University of Bristol.

"I don't think that's realistic countrywide."

One of the sites found to be suitable for a mega-reservoir serving 15 million people is near Abingdon.

This picturesque Oxfordshire town on the banks of the River Thames, was until recently, perhaps most famed for its bun-throwing traditions, but it is now at the centre of a national debate.

Public opinion on the reservoir has been split - some have objected to using the site for water, fearing high environmental costs from the destruction of ancient woodlands.

The government has now designated it and one other reservoir as Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects, bypassing some local decision-making processes.

But these designations do not overcome the environmental hurdles.

Reservoirs, as water bodies, have to achieve "good" status for water quality under environmental law - meaning it must be free from pollution such as from agricultural runoff and invasive species - which just 14% of bodies currently in England have achieved. The Environment Agency told the Cunliffe Review that "the treatment costs of meeting 'good' may render the new reservoirs infeasible".

News.title: Disorder at balloon release unacceptable, says MP
News.content:
Serious disorder at a balloon release for one of the young men who died in the A66 car crash is "unacceptable", an MP has said.

Durham Police said a large crowd gathered on a privately owned field near Haswell, County Durham, on Thursday evening where five vehicles were set on fire and balloons, flares, and fireworks were released.

Redcar MP Anna Turley said it put lives at risk, while Assistant Chief Constable Jon McAdam said the force condemned "anyone who would use that tragedy as an excuse for disorder".

In an update on Friday afternoon, Cleveland Police ACC Dave Sutherland said the force was not currently linking the A66 crash to a house fire which killed a woman and a seven-year-old girl.

It had previously said it could not rule out a link to organised crime in relation to the house fire and the crash.

Earlier this week 17 people were arrested in connection with the investigation into the crash which killed PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38,

Seven more men have also been arrested, bringing the total number of arrests to 24.

Turley said the police force had been "at pains to say we shouldn't think that these are all connected, and we shouldn't be jumping to conclusions".

The BBC understands the King has written to the families of two officers killed in the crash to express his deepest sympathies for their loss.

Meanwhile Middlesbrough FC said it would ask supporters to pay their respects to the officers before Saturday's fixture against West Bromwich Albion.

"We are also showing our appreciation for the dedication and hard work of both men, and to Cleveland police force in protecting and supporting our local community," the club said in a statement.

Seven people, including PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough, died in the crash near Middlesbrough on Saturday. Two people were arrested on suspicion of murder following the house fire in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, on Wednesday.

With regards to Thursday night's disorder, Labour Home Office minister Turley said it "put lives at risk" and left residents "frightened and angry in their own communities".

She added: "People have a right to grieve and to pay their respects - but people also have a right to feel safe in their own homes and neighbourhoods."

News.title: Mountain of broken fridges growing across England and Wales
News.content:
A mountain of broken fridges is building up in waste centres across England and Wales, the Local Government Association (LGA) has warned.

This year's multiple heat waves have increased the numbers of white goods such as fridges and freezers breaking down and needing to be scrapped at specialist sites.

Dozens of councils have been forced to stop collections of white goods due to a major backlog, which has built up due to a national shortage of specialists needed to safely process the appliances.

Earlier this month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced the latest crackdown on illegal waste dumps - and the LGA is now calling on the government to take urgent action on dealing with white goods too.

LGA Neighbourhoods committee chair Councillor Arooj Shah called on the government to force white goods companies to pick up the burden, help councils with the cost of extra storage, and prevent the same problems recurring in future.

"The backlog of defunct white goods is getting bigger by the day â they're at risk of becoming a mountain," he said.

"It is not right that residents who are trying to do the right thing can't take old or broken appliances to their local recycling centre due to failures elsewhere in the system."

Councils from Bradford to Gloucestershire, Durham and Nottinghamshire are among 26 to have suspended fridge collections this month.

A Department for Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) spokesman acknowledged the capacity issues and said short-term storage was being set up.

He said: "Our priority is to minimise disruption to household collection or proper disposal of fridges and other cooling equipment, and we are pushing producers of these items to take all necessary steps to achieve this and resolve any collection delays."

News.title: UK soldiers could get paragliders to drop behind enemy lines
News.content:
British soldiers could soon be given powered paragliders to enable them to fly up to 200 miles behind enemy lines.

The backpack-sized gliders mean Royal Marine and Parachute Regiment troops could fly into hostile areas during the night without the need to drop from aircraft.

Manufacturer Blakcro, which is based in Wiltshire, say the machines can be assembled in eight minutes and launched on foot.

The Ministry of Defence is spending Â£6m on the system, with trials set to begin "in the coming months".

Defence Minister Luke Pollard said the government was building a "more resilient, homegrown defence supply chain and ensuring our armed forces receive the pioneering equipment that can give them the edge on the battlefield".

The paragliders, which have a range of up to 200 miles, can carry body armour, night vision equipment and weapon mounts.

The manufacturers say the titanium-framed machines can be used to enter hostile territory covertly as they are more difficult to detect by radar or sound than traditional aircraft.

The gliders will be powered by a fan but pilots will be expected to launch them on foot.

The technology is currently being used by other Nato member countries.

Blakcro, which employs 11 people, was founded in 2023 and has received government support for two other projects.

The company also works with the US Department of Defense.

The government has said it wants to spend more on UK-made defence equipment and bring smaller companies into the supply chain.

Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to increase defence spending after he resigned from Sir Keir Starmer's government in protest at its investment plans.

As defence secretary, he accused Starmer's government of having no clear timetable to reach the target of spending 3% of the UK's national income on defence.

He is expected to increase spending further - but will not be setting out any plans in his first Budget in October.

Instead, a revised defence plan will be set out as part of a wider government spending review in the spring.

A government spokesperson said: "The first duty of government is to keep its citizens safe.

"The prime minister and chancellor are committed to fully funding the defence investment plan.

"At the spending review we will set out a pathway to meet our NATO commitment of 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 and will set a target date to hit 3% on that path."

News.title: I couldn't reach Yr Wyddfa's summit because people jumped the queue
News.content:
When Helen Pacey and her family booked a trip on the Snowdon Mountain Railway, they were looking forward to touching the summit marker at the top of Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon.

But after spending 30 minutes waiting in a queue at the top of Wales' highest mountain, 58-year-old Helen ran out of time and had to get the return train back down.

"I've had both my hips replaced, so there was no way I could have gone up the rocky side of it," said Helen, from Hull in Yorkshire.

"Because people were pushing in, we missed out. That is not fair."

Scores of visitors have climbed Yr Wyddfa this summer, but there have been reports of people waiting more than an hour to reach the mountain's highest point, at 1,085m (3,560ft).

Earlier this week, we reported on arguments breaking out between queue-jumpers and those waiting in line at the top. Dozens of readers subsequently got in touch to share their views on the issue.

News.title: Four plead guilty to arson attack on Jewish community ambulances
News.content:
Four men have pleaded guilty to destroying four Jewish community ambulances in an arson attack causing Â£1m of damage in north-west London.

Hamza Iqbal, 20, Rehan Khan, 19, Judex Atshatshi, and Saif Ali, both aged 18, pleaded guilty at the Old Bailey to a charge of destroying or damaging property being reckless whether life would be endangered.

The attack, which took place in the early hours of 23 March, saw four vehicles operated by the charity Hatzola set alight in Golders Green.

Prosecutors had said they believed the incident was a targeted attack against the Jewish community.

The court heard three of the men set fire to the fully stocked ambulances, while a fourth had waited in a nearby car.

After the ambulances were set alight, gas canisters exploded inside the vehicles.

As well as destroying each of the Â£250,000 vehicles, the fire damaged four electrical charging stations and cables costing approximately Â£5,000 each.

Leo Seelig, prosecuting, told the court that the Crown Prosecution Service would be arguing that the four men should be sentenced on the basis that the arson attack was related to terrorism.

Mrs Justice Cheema Grubb said she would not rule on the question of terrorism at this stage - with defence counsel arguing that there was no evidence for such a connection.

The judge said that the four would be sentenced following the outcome a trial of a fifth man, Subhan Ahmed, who has denied assisting an offender.

Iqbal and Khan, of Leyton, Atshatshi, of Dagenham, and Ali, of Walthamstow, were remanded into custody.

Run by volunteers, Hatzola has served the north London community of Golders Green, which has a large Jewish population, since 1979.

Hatzola, the Hebrew word for save or rescue, is a large non-profit, Jewish-led organisation that provides a free emergency medical response and transportation to hospitals regardless of faith by volunteer medics.

Community Security Trust, a charity working to protect British Jews from terrorism and antisemitism, welcomed the pleas and said the four's actions "caused immense shock and distress across the Jewish community".

"This was an appalling antisemitic act against a volunteer ambulance service providing emergency medical assistance to people of all backgrounds across north London, simply because those ambulances belonged to a Jewish charity," a spokesperson added.

News.title: Stadium closures for Old Firm over fan disorder
News.content:
Celtic and Rangers have both been ordered to play their next home Scottish Cup matches behind closed doors after last season's quarter-final was marred by fan disorder.

Both clubs will also have to pay Â£100,000 to the team they are drawn against in that fixture.

The two clubs could also face a second home match without fans if there is a further incident of either side's supporters engaging in "unacceptable conduct" in a Scottish Cup fixture.

Celtic progressed to last season's semi-finals by beating Rangers on penalties at Ibrox, after which fans of both teams spilled on to the pitch.

The sanctions are likely to come into force when both sides enter this season's Scottish Cup in January.

Meanwhile, Rangers say they will provide Celtic with 300 tickets for next month's Scottish League Cup quarter-final at Ibrox.

Celtic had been given 8,000 tickets for the 8 March Scottish Cup tie.

News.title: Olivia Rodrigo and Nicole Kidman are dating finance bros. But should you?
News.content:

Are you looking for a man in finance?

For years, the finance bro has been one of dating’s most maligned archetypes: the entitled, emotionally unavailable man in a quarter-zip, working punishing hours and measuring his success in salaries, status and expensive watches. He’s ambitious, competitive and, according to the stereotype, more interested in closing deals than opening up about his feelings.

However, a recent string of high-profile relationships has fans questioning whether something has shifted in the dating equilibrium. Nicole Kidman has been seen spending time with private equity investor Michael Reinstein, just months after filing for divorce from her husband of 19 years, country singer Keith Urban. Meanwhile, Olivia Rodrigo has been linked to Julian Croonenberghs, a private equity associate, following her split from British actor Louis Partridge.

When Rodrigo’s relationship came to light this summer, some fans were less than impressed. Some dismissed the romance as an “embarrassing” dating mistake of your twenties, while others questioned whether dating a man in the corporate world was at odds with the singer’s progressive image.

While some see finance bros as a dating no-go, experts insist that most men in the industry actually lean more towards Richard Gere’s romantic businessman in Pretty Woman than Leonardo DiCaprio’s ruthless Jordan Belfort in The Wolf of Wall Street.

open image in gallery Dating expert Jaime Bronstein says men in finance don’t always behave like Leonardo DiCaprio’s character in ‘The Wolf of Wall Street’ ( Rex Features )

“Just because a man is smart, successful and good-looking doesn’t mean he’s going to treat you badly,” Jaime Bronstein, a licensed relationship therapist based in Chicago, tells The Independent. “They can be nice, they do exist,” she added, noting the importance of a “good mentor and positive influences.”

Bronstein argues that daters should look beyond the stereotypes and judge the individual, rather than making assumptions based on their profession.

“As long as both parties are willing to have empathy toward each other and have the willingness to understand each other and not judge their differences, then it can absolutely work,” says Bronstein.

Just because a man is smart, successful and good-looking doesn’t mean he’s going to treat you badly Jaime Bronstein, relationship therapist

“I believe the best relationships have no judgment and just love each other unconditionally,” she continues. “They may not have an interest in what the other person [does] but if they show an interest, it’s fun to learn from each other.”

Why Hollywood creatives are dating men in finance

When it comes to understanding why Hollywood women might be drawn to men in finance, Bronstein believes the “opposites attract” theory may offer part of the explanation.

“In the Hollywood world, [celebrities] date each other, but this makes so much more sense because in a relationship, opposites attract,” Bronstein said.

open image in gallery Olivia Rodrigo and Nicole Kidman are both dating men who work in private equity ( Getty Images )

Bronstein hypothesized that just as introverts are drawn to extroverts, free-spirited artists might be attracted to more structure and analytical thinking in a partner.

This can be especially alluring if those traits are in direct contrast to the ones they found in past relationships.

For example, in a June podcast appearance, Rodrigo told the host about her new relationship: “There’s something nice about a nice, normal boy... I like it when people don’t know a ton about my job.”

“Novelty is an aphrodisiac,” New York-based relationship and sex therapist Georgina Vass explained. “We’ve learned from our experiences...it would make sense that they try something alternative with the hope it would yield different results.”

High-profile artists and professional money managers have more similar lifestyles than one might think — which could be the secret to a lasting relationship.

For a start, they can afford to be in the same VIP circles. “It’s a different field, but the outcome in terms of status and perks are similar, so maybe there’s that to bond over,” said Vass.

open image in gallery In the 1990 rom-com ‘Pretty Woman,’ Richard Gere’s character is a wealthy businessman who falls in love with Julia Roberts’s Vivian ( Rex Features )

As much as romantics might try to tiptoe around it, money matters in a relationship. Who earns more, who puts down their card at dinner, and who grew up wealthier can all shape important power dynamics in a partnership.

Taking this dynamic into account, it makes sense that people with the resources would be inclined to skip potential financial imbalances — and avoid future resentment — by dating someone with a comparable income and similar privileges.

“Evolutionarily, if we look at our roots, a lot of people want to seek partners who have comparable or higher socioeconomic or physical status,” Vass said. “That was true before because [women] needed resources, but that’s particularly true for those women, perhaps because it’s familiar.”

Can a finance bro offer more than financial security?

But what if you’re not a rich celebrity – or simply have no interest in building a fortune? Is there still an advantage to dating someone whose career is centred on money?

According to Vass, the appeal may have less to do with a finance bro’s bank balance and more to do with the qualities it takes to succeed in the industry.

“These people would have very high standards to get to this point,” she said, suggesting that someone who is highly driven and motivated may also be willing to put that same effort into maintaining structure and healthy communication in their personal life.

The pressures of the job may also cultivate qualities that are useful in a relationship. Investment bankers, traders and dealmakers are routinely required to solve problems on the fly, make high-stakes decisions and stay composed under pressure – traits that can come in handy outside the office, too.

And while long hours might mean accepting a later dinner reservation, dating someone in a demanding but established profession can offer a different kind of stability to a relationship with someone whose career is more unpredictable. “Not even just in a financial way, but they’re not waiting for their next acting job or music gig,” Bronstein said, noting that they may also spend less time travelling for work than an actor on location or a musician on tour.

There is, perhaps, also something to be said for playing the long game. A finance bro who is rarely home because he’s working towards his next promotion, deal or bonus may eventually reach a point where he has more freedom – and, ideally, more time to spend with the person he’s been working so hard for.

Plus, Brontein says, “a man in a suit always looks good.”

News.title: I swapped the Med for a long summer weekend in Stockholm’s archipelago
News.content:

More fool me, but Stockholm had never made it onto my holiday hitlist – let alone my summer one. When a 24-hour work trip stretched into a long weekend exploring the city and its surrounding archipelago, I came home convinced it’s one of Europe's most underrated summer destinations.

I’m clearly not alone in falling for Stockholm's seasonal charm. As Southern Europe swelters through increasingly punishing summers, travellers are looking north. For those seeking cooler climes, Scandi tourism is having a moment.

Sweden recorded a record 7.58 million guest nights in June 2026, while Norway saw foreign guest nights rise 17 per cent from July 2024. With temperatures in the Med regularly climbing into the mid-30Cs, Sweden’s gentler 20-25C summers – coupled with long daylight hours – are increasingly seductive.

And there’s plenty to fill those long, light days. Hike through the lush island landscapes of Grinda, cycle past castles and colourful wooden houses, island-hop by ferry or kayak through the archipelago’s glassy waters. Stockholm is encircled by a coastal labyrinth of some 30,000 islands and islets stretching out into the Baltic, making it a rare capital where a city break can so easily become a seaside escape.

open image in gallery Postcard-perfect Vaxholm is the historic capital of the archipelago ( Daisy Lester/The Independent )



On a guided boat trip to Vaxholm, the historic capital of the archipelago, we cruised past scarlet wooden cottages, grand archipelago “mansions”, dense pine forests and smooth granite shorelines that rival Croatia or Italy. The public ferries make exploring wonderfully easy, while those with a little more nautical ambition can hire a boat and set their own course.

Vaxholm itself is a pure summer postcard: 19th-century pastel houses, a 16th-century fortress and rocky swimming spots for plunging into the Baltic (as baltic as you’d expect). At Hembygdsgårds, a cafe created from a local resident’s former home, the fika offering is near-theatrical, with a towering self-service cake table. After salty sea dips and a stroll through the protected nature reserve, we ended the afternoon at Magasinet, an old smithy transformed into an idyllic waterfront cafe and bar.

Closer to the city, Fjäderholmarna – Stockholm's nearest neighbour – can be explored in a morning, while Djurgården deserves considerably longer. The island is home to some of the city’s best museums, from pop royalty at the ABBA Museum to the extraordinary Vasa Museum, where a remarkably preserved 17th-century warship dominates the gallery. Onwards to Skansen – the world’s oldest open-air museum and zoo – where Sweden’s past is brought to life across 150 historic buildings, alongside Nordic animals.

If the rise of the “coolcation” has taught us anything, it’s that Scandinavia doesn’t need to compete with the South on the South’s terms. Stockholm is creating its own version of the beach club, with hotels such as Ellery House offering three outdoor pools, a sea-view wooden sauna and a full suite of spa facilities. It’s become as much of a social haunt for locals as a retreat for visitors.

open image in gallery Ellery Beach House boasts outdoor pools and a laidback vibe, while Yasuragi is home to thermal bathhouses ( Daisy Lester/The Independent )

Wellness here embraces ancient Nordic traditions of nature, sauna and cold water therapy. The latest “Viking wellness” trend is less concerned with elaborate pampering than with getting back to basics. Yasuragi, nestled among pines in the Stockholm archipelago, is where Swedish bastu rituals combine with Japanese-inspired interiors.

The hotel’s outdoor and indoor bathhouses are as much social spaces as places for restoration, with guests and locals lingering in thermal pools over wine, beer and tea as the evening beneath the stars stretches on. Sea air and water therapy sent me back to Stockholm with a spring in my step.



Back in the city, the hotel scene reflects the city’s world-famous design sensibility, from townhouse hideaways to waterfront institutions. At the top of your list should be Ett Hem, Ilse Crawford’s celebrated 1910 townhouse, where Swedish craftsmanship, contemporary design and a residential feel make it more like staying in an impossibly chic private home. Villa Dahlia brings a more playful, Italian-meets-Scandi sensibility to Vasastan, with a buzzy rooftop bar, curated art and softly furnished rooms flooded with light.

Hotel Diplomat offers classic Art Nouveau glamour with a distinctly Swedish polish on elegant Strandvägen, while At Six puts art and modernist design centre stage, with a striking Brutalist-inspired interior and museum-worthy collection. And then there’s Grand Hôtel, Stockholm’s grande dame since 1874, where historic glamour, waterfront views and contemporary touches make it the city’s most classic luxury stay.

open image in gallery Svenskt Tenn is must-have for design lovers, while fashion fans must pay a visit to the Acne Studios’ archive store ( Daisy Lester/The Independent )

A city that birthed Acne Studios, H&M and Toteme is naturally a stylish one. Don’t miss these labels’ flagship or archive stores – and their discounted prices – but be sure to shop vintage too, from the hidden gems found at Nitty Gritty on Södermalm island, to Broadway & Sons, a military surplus store, and the Our Legacy workshop. For design lovers, Svenskt Tenn is a must-visit. Founded in 1924, the design company’s showroom is like wandering through a time capsule – even if you leave empty-handed, you’ll have more interior inspiration than you know what to do with.

Stockholm’s distinctive food identity isn’t limited to meatballs (though Restaurant Tradition, Pelikan and Tennstopet are essential spots). Mornings can be spent savouring pastries and cardamom buns at bakeries such as Lillebrors Bageri and the viral Stora Bageriet, while lunchtime calls for a wander through Östermalms Saluhall, a magnificent market hall serving the city since 1888. As in Copenhagen, people spill out onto waterfront terraces and bars come evening, with summertime favourites including Norr Mälarstrand, Angbatsbryggan, Strandbryggan and Loopen.

The day after I landed back home, my parents were coincidentally setting off to Sweden for their summer holiday: a road trip up the west coast and into Norway, taking in its spectacular mountainous scenery. I know what’s next on my Scandi hitlist.

How to get there

Flights from all major UK airports – including London Heathrow, London Gatwick, London Stansted, Manchester, Birmingham, and Edinburgh – take around two hours 30 minutes to Stockholm Arlanda Airport. Once arrived, the Arlanda Express shuttle train can get you into the city centre in less than 20 minutes, while taxis take around half an hour. Stockholm’s public ferries run year-round from central docks such as Strömkajen and Nybroviken to thousands of islands in the archipelago.

After a miserable winter, Stephen Retford thought things were looking up. How wrong he was.

The retired police officer, 70, has lived on the Henfold Estate in Tyldesley, Greater Manchester, for 40 years – moving into this quiet slice of suburbia as soon as it was built.

For almost all of those four decades, the garden of his house backed onto fields and he enjoyed the views over them.

But that came to an abrupt end last year with the construction of the Astley Business Park, made up of four hulking warehouses – up to 60ft tall, on that land, just over his garden fence.

Distraught residents told The Independent of their anger over the construction of the four warehouses, claiming that the process was damaging their homes, while the views from their windows were blocked by the massive structures which now tower over them.

Construction completed in January 2026 and distribution firm Whistl became the first organisation to operate from one of the warehouses, setting up shop last month.

open image in gallery The huge warehouses now dominate the estate ( Getty )

Now, the locals claim that Whistl is working through the night and the noise of its operations, in particular its heavy goods vehicles, in such close proximity to their homes is making their lives a misery.

Mr Retford’s home is directly opposite the firm’s service yard and he says the noise means he cannot sleep.

“The noise is 24/7. It is constant throughout the night”, Mr Retford told The Independent.

“Given the hot weather we've been having, if you have your window open, it's like sleeping on a motorway service station – in the heavy goods vehicle part.”

Mr Retford remains incredibly frustrated that Wigan Council allowed the construction of the warehouses that now tower over his home. But he believes the granting of a licence to Whistl to work overnight has added insult to injury.

“Not only did they build these warehouses right on top of our homes, but they then granted a 24/7 operating certificate for them”, he said.

open image in gallery The view from Mr Retford's back garden, with one of the warehouses now towering over it ( supplied )

“If you ever want to crush a community, build them in the first place, and then give the occupants a 24/7 operation permit.”

Mr Retford is part of local action group Astley Warehouse Action, which has brought together residents from the various housing estates surrounding the business park.

The group was formed to oppose the development and is demanding that overnight operations are stopped immediately.

They met with representatives from Whistl and Wigan Council on Wednesday, and a spokesperson for the distribution firm said it put forward a proposal to address their concerns. The local authority welcomed that and added it would “assess whether the steps taken have the desired effect and, if necessary, to explore other potential options”.

John Peters, 72, who has lived on the estate for more than 30 years, is among the leaders of the campaign group. He said that what residents are enduring now is proving to be even more challenging than the construction phase.

He told The Independent: “It's probably worse than we ever imagined because we didn't realise the volume of a national logistics company operating metres away from your house – the volume and the impact that would have on the local residents, especially the ones that live on the border.”

“People always talk about traffic and noise pollution and whatever, but the actual working noises on a 24/7 basis, so close to bedrooms at 2:00 or 3:00 in the morning, is having a real severe impact on local residents who live near it.”

Mr Peters counts himself lucky that, due to the location of his home on the estate, the biggest personal impact on him is the loss of a view from his house. But he will keep fighting with more of the warehouses to be filled by other firms.

“We have an awful visual impact that obviously can't go away”, he added.

open image in gallery The Astley Warehouse Action group opposed the development from the get-go ( Astley Warehouse Action )

“But as a group of residents, we're sticking together with the people that are now affected [by noise], and because there are a whole group of people who don't know they're going to be affected, as there are two more warehouses sitting brand new but empty at the moment.

Sound monitoring at the business park found that noise from Whistl’s operation is having a “significant adverse impact” on neighbouring residents at night.

Murray Acoustics monitored noise continuously for four nights at the closest home to the warehouse yard using a sound meter and synchronised audio recording.

When assessed against the British Standard for industrial and commercial noise the warehouse noise exceeded the existing night-time background level by between 18 and 26 decibels once the character of the sound was taken into account, the action group said.

While there is no single fixed decibel limit the standard says a difference of around 10 decibels from the existing background level is likely to indicate a significant adverse impact.

The findings led the group to demand Wigan Council’s environmental health department to force Whistl to stop operating at night until it resolves the issues with noise.

An acoustic fence, designed to block out some of the noise, has proven to be futile, according to Mr Retford.

“You cannot believe how difficult it is to live here right now”, he said. “It's almost impossible to live here.

“We've got an acoustic fence there that's about 16 feet high, supposed to kill all the sound. Let me tell you, it stops absolutely nothing.

“It's just a big, ugly wooden fence that we believe hasn't been constructed correctly. It's unbelievable, we thought it would be bad, but we didn't think it would be this bad”, he added.

A spokesperson for Whistl said: “During a meeting on Wednesday 26 August between Whistl, Wigan Council, and the Astley Warehouse Action Group, Whistl put forward a proposal to address local residents’ concerns about nighttime noise from its operations at PLP Astley.

“This proposal is now being considered by local residents, and we hope to soon reach agreement on further nighttime noise reduction actions we can take now while Whistl, Wigan Council, the site’s owner PLP, and Astley residents work together towards a long-term solution.

“In the meantime, our existing measures to monitor and mitigate noise levels remain in place and under daily review.”

open image in gallery Houses are now dwarfed by the nearby warehouses ( Getty )

“At the same time, we are on-the-ground reviewing the site’s operations on a daily basis to monitor our activity and put in place immediate measures to address residents’ concerns as they are raised by them to us.”

A Wigan Council spokesperson said: “We welcome Whistl’s commitment to working with residents to mitigate the impact of their operations at Astley Business Park.

“We will continue to work with them to assess whether the steps taken have the desired effect and, if necessary, to explore other potential options.

“We take the concerns of residents very seriously and have again met with the Action Group this week to discuss the present situation as part of our ongoing engagement with the local community.”

Liverpool host Nottingham Forest as Andoni Iraola takes charge of his first Premier League game at Anfield.

Iraola’s side required a late Dominik Szoboszlai penalty to rescue a 2-2 draw at Newcastle last time out, while Oliver Glasner’s reign at Forest has started with back-to-back defeats to Leeds United in the Premier League and Carabao Cup.

Japan's government has updated its assessment of the country's earthquake risk, with one densely-populated western region now facing as much as a 60 per cent chance of a major quake within the next 30 years.

Active faults in and around the Kinki region, which includes Osaka, Kyoto and Kobe, could trigger an earthquake of magnitude 6.8 or larger, with a 50 to 60 per cent probability over that period, Japan's Earthquake Research Committee said on Friday.

The probability stood at 30 per cent for active faults in the region's northwestern part, 40 to 60 per cent for those in the central area known as the Kinki triangle, and 7 per cent for the Kii Peninsula. The assessment is based on 45 active faults in and around the region.

The Kinki region has an unusually high concentration of active faults, largely because of the expansion of the Sea of Japan during the formation of the Japanese archipelago. The committee said the region's earthquake risk is now comparable to that of the Kanto region, which includes Tokyo.

The updated figures are part of a wider, ongoing review. The committee has already published long-term assessments for 114 major active faults across Japan, covering the Kyushu, Kanto, Chugoku and Shikoku regions, with assessments for the Chubu, Tohoku and Hokkaido regions still to come.

Kobe, in the Kinki region, was devastated by the magnitude-7.3 Great Hanshin earthquake in January 1995, which killed more than 6,000 people and remains one of Japan's worst recorded disasters.

This latest update comes against the backdrop of a far larger, long-feared threat facing Japan as a whole – a megaquake along the Nankai Trough, an 800-kilometre undersea trench running along the country's Pacific coast.

Damages in the aftermath of the Japan earthquake ( AFP/Getty )

Last year, Japan’s earthquake investigation panel had increased the probability of that megaquake happening, rating it as 80 per cent probable within the next 30 years.

A megaquake is an earthquake of magnitude 8 or higher, capable of causing more damage than a typical quake, especially when it occurs close to the surface or in densely populated regions.

Megaquakes have struck along the trough roughly once every 100 to 150 years, with the last occurring in 1946. In a worst-case scenario, the government has estimated a Nankai Trough megaquake and the tsunami it would trigger could kill up to 298,000 people and cause economic losses of around 292 trillion yen (£1.3trn).

Japan, one of the most earthquake-prone countries in the world, has heavily invested in early warning systems and infrastructure upgrades, but officials say more preparation is needed to protect communities from a disaster of this scale.

EasyJet passengers were left stranded for hours in Manchester and Milan after their pilot cancelled their flight 10 minutes before it was set to depart for Turkey on Friday.

After being stuck at Manchester Airport for more than four hours, passengers finally boarded their plane to Antalya, but were told while in the air that it was diverting more than 1,200 miles away to Milan.

Flight EZY2141 had been due to depart Manchester at 7.45am, but customers were made to return to the terminal because of traffic control restrictions caused by adverse weather across Europe, the airline said.

EasyJet said the delay would have pushed the crew to exceed their legally permitted hours, so a stop in Milan was arranged to replace the crew and refuel.

Passengers faced more delays at Milan airport, arriving just after 2pm local time, and not leaving for Antalya until 8.30pm. They were given €25 food vouchers while they waited for their new crew to arrive.

open image in gallery Easyjet has apologised to its customers ( Reuters )

An easyJet spokesperson said: “We are sorry for any inconvenience this will have caused and did all we could to minimise the impact of the disruption. The safety and wellbeing of our customers and crew is always easyJet’s highest priority.”

It did not say whether passengers were entitled to compensation or a refund.

James Lanson, who had been travelling with his wife and two-year-old daughter, described the situation as a “sh**show”.

Speaking from Milan, he told Manchester Evening News: “I used to work as a prison officer and the prison that I used to work in kept the prisoners in better condition.”

open image in gallery The flight arrived in Antalya after midnight on Saturday ( PA )

He added: “We were due to get there at 12pm. We thought we'd get there nice and early and have a full day there today. So it's a great start to the holiday, which was meant to be seven days and is now going to be six days.

“It's a sh**show. We've been told the crew that are coming to fly our plane to take us to Antalya are coming from Manchester. No one's given us any information. All they've done is given us a voucher.”

Manchester airport declined to comment.

A couple has warned other travellers to check their passports before booking trips after being refused boarding on a Jet2 flight to Greece, causing them to lose £500.

Celia Jenkins, 78, and her husband Rees, 82, were due to fly to Kefalonia from Bristol airport last week for a six-month stay at their property on the Greek island.

Despite travelling the route frequently, the couple were caught out by a passport rule that applies to British travellers since the UK left the European Union.

UK passport holders are now seen as “third-country nationals” by the EU, meaning entry rules to Schengen area countries have changed.

Travel to Europe requires that passports must be less than 10 years old, regardless of when the document expires.

When Ms and Mr Jenkins arrived at the departure gate for their flight, Jet2 staff told them that their passports were 10 years and three days old, meaning they were just over the threshold, which would result in them being denied entry into Greece.

Ms Jenkins said: “We were escorted out through border security because technically we had no passports suddenly. We felt like criminals.”

She added that the couple recognise that they had missed the fact that their passports would not be valid, but feels like the rules have not been made clear by the government nor the airline.

“We accept that our passports are three days outside the 10-year rule,” Ms Jenkins said. “We accept that. But we weren't informed clearly enough by anybody at any time. We didn't get it because we saw the expiry date rather than the date of issue as being a problem.”

Rees Jenkins, 82, and Celia Jenkins, 78, were due to fly out to Kefalonia when the incident occurred ( Celia Jenkins )

She also suggested that airlines could do more to inform customers during the booking and check-in process whether or not their passport is within the 10-year rule.

Usually customers do not have to enter passport numbers and expiry dates until checking in to flights. However, you can upload your passport details on your Jet2 account ahead of check-in.

Once Ms Jenkins arrived home, she immediately applied to renew her and her husband's passports, but is not holding out hope for the new documents to come in time to meet their family in Kefalonia.

The couple’s children and grandchildren are due to travel to the island for a week-long holiday at their Greek property, but Ms and Mr Jenkins will now likely arrive after their family leave.

After paying for a night at an airport hotel and the flights, along with bus and taxi fares, Ms Jenkins predicts that she and her husband lost £500 after being denied boarding.

Despite the new passport rules applying to UK citizens since 2021, people are still getting caught with the 10-year rule as their travel documents edge closer to expiry, especially those still with burgundy EU passports.

Ms Jenkins and her husband are not the only ones who fallen foul and been turned away at the gate.

James Luton recently missed out on celebrating his 50th birthday in Portugal after Jet2 staff found he had an invalid passport issued over 10 years ago, he told BBC News in May. Last year, a ground handler for Norwegian Air at Gatwick airport claimed he was turning six people away a day for passports that did not comply with Schengen rules.

Celebrated children’s author Michael Rosen recently missed an awards ceremony in Italy for also having an out-of-date passport.

There have also been cases where passengers have presented the correct documents, but were still denied boarding due to confusion around the rule. Airlines have misinterpreted the rules and denied passengers from boarding flights.

British Airways staff turned away a couple last October after claiming that passports were not valid beyond nine years and nine months after the date of issue, yet this has never been the case.

Ms Jenkins gives advises anyone travelling out of the UK: “Don't go to the airport unless you've double-checked, because the airlines are not picking it up.”

Under post-Brexit rules, the passports of UK travellers to the European Union must meet two conditions:

Issued not more than 10 years before the date of entry to the EU.

At least three months remaining on the intended day of departure from the EU.

A spokesperson for Jet2.com told The Independent: “As part of our pre-departure communications, we always remind customers to check the validity of their passport, in line with Government advice. We also point them to our Travel Help Hub page on our website, where they can find more information on how to ensure that their passport is valid, in line with Government guidelines.

“Our team have explained to the customer that it is not possible for an airline to verify the validity of their travel documents until they are physically examined at the airport.”

News.title: Cherki magic helping Maresca to step out of Guardiola shadow
News.content:
Rumours of Manchester City’s supposed demise without Pep Guardiola appear to be much exaggerated.

They swept past Crystal Palace at Selhurst Park with a style of play under new manager Enzo Maresca that was just as swashbuckling as under his predecessor, with Rayan Cherki playing the role of chief architect. The Frenchman’s two goals included a captivating mazy dribble, which will long be remembered by those who had the fortune to see it.

City created enough space for themselves through clever movement. With Cherki zigging one way and Phil Foden zagging the other, they created even more by dribbling past a mesmerised Palace back three that became a back five at times and still could not cope.

Erling Haaland also scored twice. Even with the creative and unpredictable talents of those behind in a four-man attacking City midfield, Haaland remains irreplaceable with his ability to convert chances.

However, this night belonged to Cherki. Guardiola chided him publicly after he set up a City goal with a “rabona” cross last season. The thrust of Guardiola’s comments were that Cherki was not Lionel Messi. Of course not, but he possesses a genius all of his own, which Maresca would surely be foolish to rein in.

The jaw-dropping splendour of Cherki’s first goal drew a collective intake of breath at Selhurst Park.

Collecting a Foden pass, he attacked the Palace area on a diagonal path, slaloming between Jaydee Canvot, Takehiro Tomiyasu and Chris Richards, before having the spatial awareness and technique to flick his left foot at the ball to send it rolling on a perpendicular trajectory past Dean Henderson.

News.title: England light years ahead of lamentable Pakistan
News.content:
Who needs Ben Stokes? Actually, it is hard to think of any side that would need him against this Pakistan team.

After just five days of cricket, and despite their own limitations with the bat, England are on the cusp of a series victory at Lord’s with a 261-run lead and power to add thanks to the prowess of a seam attack that has emerged quickly from the shadow of its former captain.

It will take longer to feel the full effects of Stokes’s absence. When England need a spinner in the side, they will miss the seam-bowling all-rounder to balance the XI. There will be times when they are up against it on a flat deck on a boiling day and be desperate for Stokes’s sheer will to win. It is still hard to think he will not play some part in the Ashes next summer.

For the final two years of his career it was Stokes’s bowling that was top class, his batting having become ordinary. But with bowlers of the quality of Ollie Robinson, Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson gelling, England are more than making up for Stokes’s retirement. This bowling attack against Pakistan’s batting was a complete mismatch.

Joe Root has stepped into Stokes’s shoes confidently, laying down the law off the field and tactically he has been spot on, although Pakistan have hardly stretched him. The only stir they have made since arriving was the stink they kicked up over Sky Sports’ interview with Imran Khan’s sons.

Conclusions are impossible to draw with any confidence against such poor opponents. Sri Lanka and West Indies two years ago put up a stronger fight in the first two Tests of their series. Tamim Iqbal scored two hundreds as Bangladesh at least landed some blows in 2010. Pakistan have managed one fifty in three innings and were bowled out for 171 and 135 at Headingley and a lamentable 110 here.

They were a batsman down at Lord’s because of a calf injury to opener Imam-ul-Haq, but only reached three figures because England dropped top scorer Azan Awais on eight; he went on to score 46.

England’s batting is hardly firing, but with a 180 first-innings lead, they could afford to be 13 for two without panic spreading. Losing Root for 24 kept Pakistan interested, but Emilio Gay toughed it out in the gloom to reach stumps unbeaten on 30; England 81 for three, light years ahead in the game.

Robinson’s astonishing figures of 13-6-11-4 set him on the way for a probable third man-of-the-match award in a row and continued his unexpected resurgence. Rarely did his pace go above 78mph, he just landed the ball time and again on a length and let movement off the seam do the rest.

News.title: I’ve lived in Norfolk for more than 30 years. Here’s how to explore England’s windswept east
News.content:
Norfolk’s vast sandy beaches are its chief draw for visitors: even on the busiest summer day there is always space for games, kite-flying or a family picnic in the dunes. Boating, crabbing, digging for cockles and wading in creeks provides hours of entertainment for all.

But there’s much more to Norfolk’s coast than its beaches. It’s also a landscape of dense pine forest and large expanses of salt marsh, which flush purple with sea-lavender in August. Birdlife is astonishingly rich, and wildflowers include yellow-horned poppies and lilac-flowering sea pea.

Inland, the undulating countryside and sleepy flint-built villages are perfect for gentle cycling, walking or touring by car. Grand stately homes make enjoyable days out, and almost every village has a sublimely beautiful medieval church at its centre.

Lively Georgian towns such as Burnham Market and Holt offer quirky shopping – and, wherever you are, you’re never far from an atmospheric pamment-floored pub serving local ales, or an excellent delicatessen selling the region’s specialities. Look out for pungent cheeses, smoked fish and salt-marsh flavoured honey.

News.title: Telegraph Fantasy Football tips: Game Week 2

As the Telegraph Fantasy Football season heads into 2026-27, the award-winning experts at Fantasy Football Hub ccontinue to bring you the very best in fantasy football knowledge, tips and tools to help you rise up the ranks and win your mini-leagues.

Join the Hub and get access to all their great resources and expert tips.



Welcome back

We would like to start by thanking everyone for playing Telegraph Fantasy Football for the 2026-27 season.

If you are a new player, we really hope you enjoy the game. Telegraph Fantasy Football has been running for over 30 years and is widely regarded as the purest form of fantasy football. No captains, no wildcards and no gimmicks.

For the returning players, we apologise for the delay with getting the game live. We had to rebuild it from scratch following the World Cup and, in order to have a game ready in time for the new season, several features are still being worked on, including updated iPhone and Android apps.

Please be aware that there are ongoing issues with the android app that will not be fixed until later in September. Instead use a web browser on these devices. You can also try adding a shortcut to your homescreen for quick and easy access.

Rest assured we are working through the site improvements and, if you have any feedback, please use the Contact Us chat on site.



Telegraph Fantasy Football: last week's insights

Champions open with a win

Mikel Arteta’s side kicked off the new campaign in perfect fashion: three goals, a clean sheet and three points in north London. Captain Martin Odegaard (£5.2m) netted and looked back to his best, but it was the full-backs Riccardo Calafiori (£4.4m) and Ben White (£4.1m) who really stood out with a clean sheet and an assist each.



Tigers humble Manchester United

Many TFF managers started with Red Devils’ assets with the Manchester club opening up with back-to-back fixtures against newly promoted teams, but they were duly shocked as Hull City outfought and at times outplayed the 13-time Premier League champions. Ollie McBurnie (£2.9m) is one to keep an eye on for when the Tigers’ fixtures turn.



Chelsea attacking flair

A fully fit Cole Palmer (£6.2m) has sparked TFF managers to rethink their set-ups, as his 11-point haul on Monday night has put non-owners on red alert. The Blues’ talisman returned a goal and an assist, and an injury-free season should have the ex-Manchester City midfielder challenging at the summit of the points scoring charts.

Telegraph Fantasy Football Tips: Game Week 2



The Telegraph Fantasy Football player list has been analysed ahead of the upcoming games, and these look like the best players to transfer in:



1. Christos Tzolis (£4.0m)

Despite not delivering any attacking returns in his first game, the Gunners’ summer recruit impressed onlookers and Arsenal fans alike with his performance. The price point, the Monday night entry point and the fixture itself all point to the 24-year-old being an astute acquisition.



2. Marcus Tavernier (£3.1m)

The midfielder netted at the Etihad on Sunday, and forms part of an attractive Cherries attacking line-up that should continue to score many goals this season. It’s home comforts this weekend for their No.16 and he could be a great option to transfer in for any newly injured players in your starting XIs.

3. Enzo Le Fée (£3.3m)

The Black Cats underwhelmed in their opener, but with Fulham looking defensively vulnerable on Monday night, the French penalty-taker could take advantage this weekend.

News.title: England return to proper Test cricket with gritty batting performance
News.content:
Cox unfurled some fine drives and assessed conditions like a veteran, scoring quickly to a run-a-ball 38 but only six more from his next 48 as Pakistan knocked over partners at the other end. It was vital Cox stayed in to stabilise the innings. It is the job of a No 3 to attack or defend; calibrate their game to what is required at the time. Cox, when he played briefly for England in New Zealand two winters ago and before injury cut short his tour, looked to be a player drunk on the Bazball fumes. He was out in a warm-up match against a New Zealand XI in Queenstown hooking and flailing at the ball. This was his second mature performance in a row, an innings of 55 to follow his 73 at Leeds and this was made in much harder circumstances.

Pakistan were better after their Headingley horror show. Mohammad Abbas must feel more at home on a dank London day than he does in Sialkot, and can earn a place on the honours board if he nicks the last England wicket after taking four for 56. Mohammad Ali bowled some jaffas, and some rubbish, for three for 67 and spinner Usman Ali kept it tight and found some turn before losing control as Smith went after him. England still scored at 4.4 an over a reflection of some of the wasted deliveries by Pakistan and 10 no-balls.

Inevitably they were a mixed bag in the field. Three dropped catches were redeemed by a run out and a world-class grab at slip by Salman Ali Agha – captain last week, left out here – to dismiss Cox when he lost his shape trying to hit the ball too hard.

News.title: Ebola response shifts to Congo’s river network
News.content:
Stacked with logs and crammed with hundreds of passengers, the giant barges are nudged day after day along one of Africa’s greatest waterways.

The weeks-long voyage looks sedate, but the tugs are pushing their heavily-laden charges along an unstoppable aquatic superhighway.

Sharing the Congo river with these trade behemoths are canoes, fishing boats and smaller wooden cargo ships.

The river connects the wild east of Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to the capital Kinshasa, in a vital economic artery and transport corridor nearly 1,100 miles long.

The waterway is a lifeline for passengers, timber, produce and goods. Roads are rare and unreliable, and airfares are far too expensive for most.

Now there are concerns the river risks becoming a conduit for something else heading to the capital of nearly 18 million people: the deadly Ebola virus.

News.title: Great British fry-up implicated in Salmonella outbreak
News.content:
The outbreak, which involved packets of chicken-flavoured instant dried noodles, was traced back to a manufacturing plant near Kyiv, according to an assessment issued by the European Centre for Disease Control (ECDC) in June.

“Epidemiological investigations have found that cases in Denmark, Estonia, Germany, Latvia and Lithuania had consumed flavoured noodle products from the same brand. Investigations have linked the products, which were distributed in several countries, to the same producer in Ukraine,” the ECDC said in a statement at the time.

Another outbreak, which lasted from 2021 to 2024, sickened 174 people in the UK and killed one. It was linked to frozen, steam-cooked chicken breast fillets produced in Ukraine.

Although it is not known if the latest outbreak is linked to Ukraine (the UK also imports eggs from countries including Poland, Spain, and Belgium ), Ukraine sits outside of the EU and Salmonella contamination is common in many of the country’s poultry farms.

A senior figure investigating a connected outbreak of Salmonella in the Netherlands told The Telegraph that the “working hypothesis” among British health officials is that the contaminated products have come from Ukraine.

“In Ukraine, thousands of salmonellosis cases are reported each year. The highest incidence is observed among children,” said a study published in the academic journal Advances in Animal and Veterinary Sciences earlier this year.

“The main sources of the pathogen are eggs, chicken meat, and meat and dairy products. Analysis shows that frequent outbreaks are associated with poor food storage conditions [...] predominantly in the southeastern regions of Ukraine,” added the authors from the Institute of Laboratory Diagnostics and Veterinary-Sanitary Expertise in Kyiv.

Britain’s egg consumption has boomed over the last two decades, with 209 eaten per person on average every year compared to roughly 163 per person in 2000.

The rise is thought to have been driven by a spike in baking during the pandemic, the rise of brunch culture and the rise of a focus on diets rich in protein among the young, according to experts.

Sports.title: Transfer news LIVE: £123m Barcola to Liverpool imminent, Man Utd offered Chelsea deal
Sports.content:
The latest transfer news from the Premier League and further afield, including updates on Arsenal, Manchester United, Liverpool, Tottenham Hotspur and many more

Welcome to Mirror Football's transfer blog for Saturday, August 29.

Bradley Barcola's seemingly imminent transfer from Paris Saint-Germain to Liverpool has continued to dominate the headlines, as one of the most exciting sagas of the summer is set to come to an end. It is claimed that an agreement has been reached between the two clubs, and that the Reds will pay a total of £123million for the 23-year-old winger.

That's broken down into a guaranteed £106m, as well as £17m in add-ons. A move to Anfield is expected to be formalised in the coming days. Barcola isn't the only talent that could bolster Andoni Iraola's first-team in the coming days, however.

The Reds are also reportedly setting their sights on Crystal Palace's Ismaila Sarr, with Nicolo Schira claiming that an agreement in principle over a contract running to 2031 has been met between Liverpool and the player. A new bid is expected to come, after Palace rebuffed an initial offer of around £51m.

In the English capital, meanwhile, Arsenal are still chasing Julian Alvarez's signature, with his future with Atletico Madrid up in the air. The 26-year-old centre-forward has missed training thrice this week, albeit, citing illness as the reason for his absence, as the Gunners prepare to table a £130m bid to secure his signature.

Manchester United's search for a new left-back also runs on, having seemingly ditched their pursuit of Lews Hall as a result of Newcastle United refusing to sell the 21-year-old. While Alejandro Balde was considered an ideal candidate, the 22-year-old has now told Hansi Flick that he wants to fight for his place at Barcelona.

Sports.title: Arsenal given hours to convince Julian Alvarez as Atletico Madrid issue final transfer ultimatum
Sports.content:
Arsenal given hours to convince Julian Alvarez as Atletico Madrid issue final transfer ultimatum

Arsenal are in a race against time to sign Julian Alvarez, with Atletico Madrid demanding a decision from the Argentina international with the transfer deadline looming

View 2 Images Julian Alvarez doesn't have long to earn a move (Image: NurPhoto, NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Atletico Madrid have given Julian Alvarez until Sunday to make a decision over his future. That leaves Arsenal with just hours to convince the forward over a return to the Premier League, after being denied the opportunity to move to Barcelona.

‌



The 26-year-old made no secret at the start of the summer that he was desperate to swap the Wanda Metropolitano for Barcelona. The drawn-out saga has sparked a bitter row between Barca and Atletico, and Alvarez looks set to miss the weekend fixture against Sevilla after sitting out training sessions this week through illness.

‌



Arsenal have been looking to capitalise on the dispute between the two Spanish clubs to lure Alvarez to the Emirates. Alvarez has notched 49 goals in 107 appearances since arriving at Atletico in 2024 following his £81.8million departure from Manchester City, and established himself as a star.

‌



It is understood that the Gunners are firmly interested in securing Alvarez, but will only pursue a deal if the player himself is fully on board.

With the transfer deadline rapidly approaching, time was already running short, but Sky Sports report that Atletico's hierarchy are demanding a decision by Sunday.

‌



Manchester City have also been touted as potential suitors for their former striker. However, Alvarez is said to have reservations about returning to England.

Atletico are demanding a guaranteed £128.4m to release their prized frontman, though carefully managing his return to the fold will be crucial after the club dashed his ambitions. Alvarez has faced a backlash from supporters following his stance this summer.

In June, Alvarez said: "I spoke with the people at [Atletico] I needed to speak with, and the best thing for everyone is a transfer.

‌



View 2 Images Julian Alvarez has little over a day to make a decision (Image: Irina R. Hipolito/Europa Press via Getty Images)

"I want to fulfil my dream. It's ‌not the time ‌to talk about this. But I also can't ‌hide it. I try to be an honest person."

Atletico Madrid have made their position abundantly clear on numerous occasions — they will not do business with Barcelona.

‌



"The members of Atletico Madrid's Board of Directors have unanimously expressed their full support for the club's decision not to negotiate the transfer of Julian Alvarez to FC Barcelona," Atletico said in a statement.

"The members of the Board of Directors are aware that: Atletico Madrid is open to negotiations that are part of the transfer market, but always in an ethical and professional manner and with respect between clubs.

"We fully support the position previously communicated by the club that FC Barcelona have not met these requirements and, as a result, there have been no negotiations, nor will there be any negotiations with them regarding the transfer of Julián Alvarez."
