World.title: East Africa: Red Sea States Seek Stronger Maritime Security Cooperation As Threats Rise
World.content:
Nairobi — Countries bordering the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden are seeking to strengthen maritime security cooperation as threats including piracy, human trafficking and disruptions to commercial shipping continue to grow.

Maritime security officials from Somalia, Ethiopia, Yemen and Djibouti met in Nairobi this week for a two-day meeting focused on addressing emerging threats in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, among the world's most important shipping routes.

The meeting, facilitated by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), with support from the European Union, INTERPOL, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), focused on strengthening regional cooperation and information sharing.

Officials agreed that the security challenges facing the region could not be effectively addressed by any single country and stressed the need for closer coordination among maritime security and law enforcement agencies.



They also discussed improving the sharing of intelligence on suspicious and potentially dangerous activities to help authorities identify and prevent threats before they affect commercial vessels and international trade.

The meeting comes as security tensions in parts of the Middle East have disrupted commercial shipping and raised concerns over the safety of vessels navigating the Red Sea.

The Red Sea and Gulf of Aden connect the Indian Ocean with the Suez Canal, making security in the region crucial to global trade and supply chains.

World.title: Uganda: Court Gives DPP Nod to Extradition of Ugandan Katungi to the U.S.
World.content:
Kampala — The Buganda Road Chief Magistrates Court has committed a former UPDF soldier, Michael Katungi Mpeirwe, to Luzira prison pending a decision by the Minister of Justice and Constitutional Affairs on his extradition to the United States of America.

Katungi is "wanted" in the US to face trial on charges of cocaine trafficking, illegal firearms possession and providing material support to a Mexican drug cartel and a designated foreign terrorist organization.

In a ruling delivered on Friday through the Judiciary's online system dubbed the Electronic Court Case Management Information System, Chief Magistrate Ritah Kidasa Neumbe has dismissed all the preliminary objections raised by Katungi and ruled that the Ugandan government had established the legal and evidential threshold required for his committal under the Extradition Act.

Katungi is wanted before the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia on three counts arising from an alleged international drug-trafficking and weapons conspiracy. The first count accuses him of conspiring to distribute and possess with intent to distribute five kilograms or more of cocaine, knowing or intending that the drugs would be unlawfully imported into the United States.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The second count alleges a conspiracy to possess firearms, including a machine gun and a destructive device, in furtherance of a drug-trafficking crime. The third count alleges conspiracy to provide material support or resources to a designated foreign terrorist organisation. The United States' extradition request identifies the organisation as Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generación and alleges that Katungi and his co-accused attempted to supply, or agreed to supply, military-grade weapons in connection with narcotics trafficking.

Katungi was first produced before the Buganda Road Chief Magistrate's Court on June 29, 2026, after a warrant for his arrest was issued under Section 8 of the Extradition Act at the request of the United States government.

He objected to the extradition and, through his lawyers, including Macdusman Kabega, Frank Kandiho and Medard Lubega Sseggona, raised a series of preliminary challenges questioning the procedure used to commence the case, the authority of government officials involved in processing the request, his entitlement to diplomatic immunity, the admissibility of an affidavit filed by a United States official and the authority of the Director of Public Prosecutions to conduct the proceedings.

Objections dismissed

The court dismissed all the objections that remained for determination. On the procedure used to commence the case, Katungi's lawyers had argued that the Extradition Act does not specifically provide for the use of a notice of motion supported by an affidavit.

They also challenged inconsistencies in the case numbering and filing records on the Electronic Court Case Management Information System.

However, Chief Magistrate Kidasa ruled that Section 10 of the Extradition Act gives the presiding magistrate discretion on the manner in which an extradition hearing is conducted, subject to the general framework of criminal procedure.

The court found that Katungi had suffered no prejudice because he had been served with the evidence relied upon by the prosecution, had cross-examined the government's witness at length and filed detailed submissions on both the preliminary objections and merits of the extradition request.

The magistrate also found that inconsistencies in the ECCMIS case numbering were administrative and did not amount to a jurisdictional defect.

The court has further rejected an argument that the Minister of Justice and Constitutional Affairs had acted without authority by processing the request. According to Katungi's lawyers, since the allegations involved narcotics, the request ought to have been channelled through the Attorney General under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (Control) Act.But the court has disagreed with them and found that that extradition is governed by the Extradition Act and is different from mutual legal assistance in criminal investigations.

The magistrate said the provisions of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (Control) Act relied upon by the defence relate to assistance between countries in investigations, including obtaining evidence and documents, rather than the surrender of a person to face trial in another country.

The court has also found no illegality in the involvement of the Solicitor General, noting that the Interpretation Act permits the Solicitor General, in prescribed circumstances, to exercise the powers and perform the duties of the Attorney General.

Diplomatic immunity

The court has also rejected Katungi's claim to diplomatic immunity. His lawyers had argued that he was previously a deputy head of mission, most recently in Nigeria, and was therefore protected from the extradition proceedings.

The court found that diplomatic immunity under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, as incorporated into Ugandan law through the Diplomatic Privileges Act, primarily protects diplomatic agents from the jurisdiction of the receiving state.

The magistrate held that Nigeria was the relevant receiving state in Katungi case and that neither Uganda, as the sending state, nor the United States, to which he had not been accredited, was a receiving state for purposes of the claimed immunity.

The court therefore ruled that there was no diplomatic immunity capable of preventing Uganda from exercising jurisdiction over him or from considering the United States extradition request.

Another issue in this case was the involvement of the Director of Public Prosecutions to institute and conduct extradition proceedings. Katungi's lawyers had argued that extradition proceedings are a special category of proceedings rather than ordinary criminal proceedings and therefore do not fall within the DPP's constitutional mandate. The defence had noted that no Ugandan police file, station diary reference or crime report book number had been opened against their client in connection with the alleged conduct.

The court rejected the argument, holding that Article 120 of the Constitution gives the DPP powers to institute and conduct criminal proceedings, while Section 10 of the Extradition Act requires extradition hearings before a magistrate to be conducted, as nearly as possible, in the same manner and with the same jurisdiction and powers as criminal proceedings.

According to the Magistrate, the Constitution and the Extradition Act, read together, give the DPP authority to conduct the judicial phase of extradition proceedings on behalf of the Republic of Uganda. The absence of a Ugandan police file, the court said, did not affect the DPP's standing to conduct proceedings concerning the surrender of a person to answer a foreign indictment.

As such, the Court has found that Katungi's identity was not in dispute and that the United States warrant and extradition documents had been properly authenticated under Sections 24 and 25 of the Extradition Act.

Kule's cross-examination

The court has relied on the extradition request, indictment and arrest warrant submitted by the United States, together with the surviving evidence of Detective Assistant Superintendent of Police Kule Yona of the Criminal Investigations Directorate. Kule told the court that he personally received and processed the extradition request in Uganda, participated in tracing and arresting Katungi , verified his identity and caused him to be produced before court.

During cross-examination, however, Kule acknowledged that he had not participated in the United States investigation and had no personal knowledge of whether Katungi had conspired to traffic narcotics, possess firearms or provide support to a terrorist organisation. He also confirmed that no Ugandan police file had been opened against Katungi over the alleged conduct.

The magistrate ruled that the authenticated United States documents could independently be relied upon under the Extradition Act and did not require the personal attendance of every foreign official involved in preparing them. The court has also found that the principle of dual criminality has been satisfied. Under this principle, the alleged conduct must amount to an offence in both the requesting and requested countries, even if the offences do not have identical names or statutory wording.

Close 

The court found that the alleged cocaine trafficking corresponds to offences under Uganda's narcotics legislation; that the alleged firearms conspiracy corresponds to offences under Uganda's firearms, conspiracy and narcotics laws.

U.S. prosecutors allege that Katungi was part of an international criminal network that conspired to supply military-grade weapons, including rocket launchers, grenades, sniper rifles, anti-personnel mines, anti-aircraft weapons and surface-to-air missile systems, to Mexico's Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generación (CJNG), which the United States has designated a foreign terrorist organisation.

He is also accused of participating in a conspiracy to distribute at least five kilograms of cocaine, knowing the drugs would ultimately be smuggled into the United States.

According to the indictment, Katungi allegedly worked with Bulgarian national Peter Dimitrov Mirchev, Kenyan national Elisha Odhiambo Asumo and Tanzanian national Subiro Osmund Mwapinga to obtain fraudulent End-User Certificates intended to conceal the true destination of the weapons.

Prosecutors say the certificates were used to facilitate the export of a test shipment of 50 AK-47 rifles and ammunition from Bulgaria, as the group allegedly planned to supply weapons worth about €53.7 million (roughly US$58 million) using falsified documentation. Court records further allege that Mirchev had previously been linked to convicted international arms trafficker Viktor Bout.

Katungi has been on remand in Luzira prison since June 29th, 2026.

Meanwhile, Katungi had challenged his extradition process in the Constitutional Court. But following today's decision, it implies that the pending constitutional petition will remain in the system for only academic purposes.

World.title: Kenya: US Launches Sh930m Initiative to Modernise Kenya Police Training
World.content:
Nairobi — The United States has launched a Sh930 million ($7 million) initiative to support Kenya's efforts to modernise police training and strengthen the professionalism and effectiveness of the National Police Service.

The initiative was launched on Friday at the Kenya Police Training College in Kiganjo, where the US Embassy said well-trained officers were essential to protecting citizens and creating a secure environment for businesses.

The embassy said the programme was part of Washington's continued support for Kenya's pursuit of a modern and professional police service.

"We believe well-trained officers can best protect and serve their fellow citizens," the US Embassy in Nairobi said.



It said security was also critical to the operations of both Kenyan and American businesses, linking effective policing to a safe and prosperous economic environment.

The launch coincided with the graduation or commissioning of a new cohort of police officers, with the embassy congratulating the newest recruits as they begin their service.

The US Embassy said it remained committed to supporting efforts aimed at enhancing security in Kenya, emphasising the importance of professional policing in protecting citizens and supporting economic activity.

The Sh930 million investment comes as Kenya continues to face scrutiny over police accountability, professionalism and the need to strengthen public confidence in the security services.

The National Police Service has in recent years been under pressure to improve training, discipline and adherence to human rights standards while responding effectively to emerging security challenges.

The US has historically supported Kenya's security sector through training, equipment and institutional capacity-building programmes, particularly in areas including counterterrorism, law enforcement and professional development.

The latest initiative places police training at the centre of those efforts, with the Kiganjo college serving as a key institution in preparing officers for service.

The embassy said the partnership reflects Washington's broader commitment to a secure Kenya, where citizens and businesses can operate safely.

"Congratulations to the newest officers! We remain committed to a safe and prosperous Kenya," the embassy said.

World.title: Fox Hollow coroner reveals why he doubts suspected serial killer acted alone in hunt for answers
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Nearly 30 years after thousands of human bones and bone fragments were unearthed at the sprawling estate of suspected serial killer Herb Baumeister, new questions are being raised about the mystery of what really happened at Fox Hollow Farm.

The coroner leading the renewed investigation claims a key figure in the case has not been fully forthcoming with investigators.

"I have had an opportunity to speak with Mark Goodyear a couple of times," Hamilton County Coroner Jeff Jellison told Fox News Digital.

FOX HOLLOW FARM SERIAL KILLER'S 10TH VICTIM IDENTIFIED: CORONER

"The first question I would ask him is, ‘Are you ready to be honest with me?’ Because in the conversations we’ve had, he’s not been honest. I’ve asked him questions that I knew the answer to, and he didn’t pass that test. So for me to sit down with Mark Goodyear, he’s going to have to be willing to be honest in this conversation. I don’t have time to sit down with somebody that tells lies, untruths."

Jellison appears in the ABC News Studios true crime documentary "Return to Fox Hollow: New Victims, Darker Secrets," which explores new theories about potential accomplices, overlooked evidence and witness accounts in the case of Baumeister, a suspected serial killer believed to have murdered numerous men in Indiana. It's a follow-up to the 2025 docuseries "The Fox Hollow Murders: Playground of a Serial Killer."

Jellison said he wants to determine whether Goodyear knows something that could help investigators identify the remaining victims and determine how they died.

Goodyear has never been charged with any crime related to the case and has repeatedly denied any involvement in the disappearances.

"If we move forward in that conversation, certainly I want to know any information I can gather to help identify these remains," said Jellison. "Were you familiar with anybody? Things that would focus more around identification and how these people died."

"Mark Goodyear knows a lot about this case," Jellison said.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Jellison also shared that Goodyear knew many people through gay nightclubs and could help investigators identify some of the remains.

Goodyear, who participated in the first docuseries, has described himself as Baumeister's only known survivor. The film detailed how investigators believed Baumeister may have filmed his victims with a secret camera hidden in an air vent in his basement. Goodyear said he was forced to watch some of the tapes in 1994. He said the video was so "bad" it made him scream.

"It was like having a camera right up against something," Goodyear said. "You're not going to be able to tell what's going on, but the minute you got a flash of what was going on, it made you scream."

The previous documentary examined how Goodyear's account of his relationship and encounters with Baumeister has changed over the years. At the time, Jellison told Fox News Digital it was unlikely those tapes, if they exist, would ever be recovered.

Fox News Digital reached out to Goodyear for comment but did not receive a response.

Goodyear initially agreed to another interview for the follow-up documentary but did not appear for the scheduled interview, according to the film.

SIGN UP TO GET THE TRUE CRIME NEWSLETTER

About 10,000 burned and broken human bones and bone fragments were recovered from the 18-acre estate that once belonged to Baumeister. Before investigators could arrest him in 1996, Baumeister was found dead of a self-inflicted gunshot wound in Ontario, Canada. He was 49.

Investigators believe Baumeister frequented gay bars in Indianapolis, lured men to his home while his family was away, killed them there and disposed of their remains on the property.

Baumeister's son discovered a human skull in the woods at Fox Hollow Farm in 1994, but, according to reports, investigators did not search the property until June 1996.

Goodyear said he first encountered Baumeister at an Indianapolis gay bar in 1994, where Baumeister introduced himself as "Brian." Goodyear later told investigators that he went home with Baumeister and described what he said was a disturbing sexual encounter.

Goodyear's account eventually helped advance the investigation. After encountering Baumeister again the following year, Goodyear helped investigators obtain information that led them to identify Baumeister.

While Jellison has questioned Goodyear's account, he also made clear in the documentary that Goodyear was not a suspect.

GET REAL-TIME UPDATES DIRECTLY ON THE TRUE CRIME HUB

"There are very strong indications there is another suspect, and it wasn’t Mark Goodyear," Jellison said in the film.

Jellison said there are still more than 9,000 bones and bone fragments yet to be examined. Investigators believe at least 25 people fell victim to Baumeister, according to WRTV.

The scope and placement of the remains have also raised another question for Jellison: whether Baumeister could have carried out the crimes alone.

"I was always convinced that there was more than one," Jellison said. "There were a lot of people that lost their lives in this incident, and just the placement of the evidence alone. How does one man pull this crime off? And how does one man get ... deceased individuals from his residence to potentially 200 yards through very dense woods? I think it would've been a very difficult task."

Jellison is determined to put names to the unidentified victims. He believes some families may still be unaware that a loved one vanished or that the person's remains may have ended up at Fox Hollow Farm.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Jellison compared the scale of the investigation to the recovery effort at the World Trade Center.

"Some of these folks did not have close family connections, and they were somewhat marginalized," he explained. "So there may be families out there not even knowing that their loved one went missing, much less consider that person was a victim at Fox Hollow."

GOT A TIP?

"Thirty years have passed since these remains have been recovered," he reflected. "So potentially, mom and dad could be deceased, and maybe they had no brother or sister. So we’re reaching out further down the lineage to cousins. And a cousin may not even know that they had a family member that even went missing."

Jellison said identifying the Fox Hollow victims presents a unique challenge.

He contrasted the case with the World Trade Center investigation, where records and missing-person reports gave investigators a clearer idea of who they were looking for. At Fox Hollow, investigators started with remains but few clues about their identities.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"I really believe that this investigation is more complicated in some ways than the World Trade Center," he said. "With Fox Hollow, we’ve recovered these remains, but we have no idea who it is that we’re looking for."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

Jellison is urging anyone who believes a missing loved one could be connected to the case to contact his office. After the original documentary aired, his office received approximately 500 emails, phone calls, text messages and social media messages, Jellison said.

SEND US A TIP

"Come forward," he said. "If you don’t know what to do or you don’t know who to call, call me. I’ll get you going in the right direction."

World.title: Trump’s tougher round-two birthright citizenship strategy hinges on key legal distinction, experts say
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Conservative legal experts say President Donald Trump’s latest attempts to narrow birthright citizenship and crack down on birth tourism may have stronger legal footing than his first effort.

After the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in June that children born in the United States to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present are citizens at birth under the 14th Amendment, Trump issued two new executive orders taking narrower approaches to citizenship and birth tourism.

The first, signed Aug. 6, directs federal agencies to withhold documents recognizing citizenship from certain children born when neither parent is a U.S. citizen, including some whose parents are members of designated foreign terrorist organizations, foreign-government employees or participants in transactions or fraud intended to obtain birthright citizenship.

Experts from the Manhattan Institute, America First Legal and the America First Policy Institute, all right-of-center organizations, argued that Trump’s new order is narrower than his first and is built around longstanding exceptions to birthright citizenship that they believe could apply here.

TRUMP SIGNS EXECUTIVE ORDERS TARGETING BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP, BIRTH TOURISM AFTER SUPREME COURT SETBACK

"The Supreme Court has long recognized that there are exceptions to the 14th Amendment's birthright citizenship clause for the aliens who are considered children of invading armies or the children of ambassadors," America First Policy Institute senior fellow Chad Mizelle, who previously served as the Justice Department’s chief of staff, told Fox News Digital. "So in a situation where you have a terrorist here contrary to the laws of the United States … who is looking to do harm … That has long been recognized by the Supreme Court, and basically going back to the history of our country, as recognized exceptions to any sort of claim of birthright citizenship."

United States v. Wong Kim Ark, decided by the Supreme Court in 1898, recognized exceptions to birthright citizenship for children of diplomats and children of alien enemies born during a hostile occupation. Trump’s order argues that members of foreign terrorist organizations can fall within that enemy exception.

TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP FIGHT COMES ROARING BACK WITH ‘INVADERS’ PLAY AFTER KAVANAUGH ROADMAP

"The Supreme Court ruled that you can't restrict birthright citizenship to kids of people in the country temporarily or illegally," Manhattan Institute director of constitutional studies Ilya Shapiro told Fox News Digital. "But what the new executive order does is it goes to one of the classic exceptions to birthrights citizenship, two of the classic exceptions, those who owe an allegiance to a foreign government, meaning employed by a foreign governing diplomats otherwise, and those who are invaders of foreign armies and terrorists, members of foreign organizations hostile to America, certainly qualify in that category."

David Bier, the director of immigration studies at the libertarian Cato Institute, however, argued that the president’s attempt to redefine what constitutes an alien enemy without going through Congress puts the administration on legally shaky ground.

"Congress ultimately establishes what it means to be subject to U.S. jurisdiction," Bier told Fox News Digital. "There's this very limited exception for accredited diplomats and everyone else in the United States is subject to U.S. laws so the idea that the president himself on his own authority can decide who is subject U. S. jurisdiction and U.S. laws is really a radical expansion and assertion of executive power and really would be unprecedented in the history of the United States."

JACKSON ACCUSES THOMAS OF ECHOING INFAMOUSLY RACIST COURT DECISION IN BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP CLASH

"I really do think this case is testing a different proposition from the earlier case," Bier added, explaining that the issue at hand has more to do with executive power than birthright citizenship. "And I think it's a lot more questionable as well."

Amanda Frost, a professor at the University of Virginia School of Law, pointed out that United States v. Wong Kim Ark specifies that only children of enemies "occupying" some portion of the country are barred from citizenship at birth, meaning that Trump’s order would not apply to terrorists simply residing within the country. She said the Trump administration could potentially expand who is legally defined as a diplomat to preclude more people from birthright citizenship, but explained such a move would make it difficult to prosecute individuals for criminal offenses, a concern shared by Bier.

Frost and Bier both believe the new executive order should be ruled unconstitutional.

Some have floated the issue of standing as a potential problem for those looking to challenge Trump's order. Legal standing requires plaintiffs to show they suffered or imminently face a concrete injury caused by the defendant that a court can remedy.

"It's going to be interesting to see who actually does have standing to challenge this order," America First Legal co-founder and president Gene Hamilton told Fox News Digital. "Is there somebody who thinks that they're going to swept up in the definition of a foreign terrorist organization? And if so, it would be kind of fun to see them try to sue the government or have someone sue on their behalf."

Trump’s new order is already facing legal resistance.

TRUMP TO ASK SUPREME COURT TO REHEAR BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP CASE AFTER 'INSANE DECISION'

The same groups who challenged his initial order are now arguing that his new one unlawfully creates exceptions to birthright citizenship that conflict with the Supreme Court’s June ruling. The order remains on the books but is not scheduled to take effect until Sept. 6, with a Maryland judge scheduled to hear an injunction request Aug. 28 and a related motion still pending in New Hampshire.

Issued on the same day as the first new executive order, the second order directed the State Department and the Department of Homeland Security to deny travel visas to or pursue removal actions against individuals believed to be in the country for the purposes of birth tourism. Birth tourism is a process through which noncitizens enter the United States while pregnant and give birth in order to secure citizenship for their child.

Hamilton described this second order as being on "sound, solid legal footing."

"It relies and invokes Section 215(a) of the INA to impose conditions and delegates authority of the Secretary of State … to ensure that we are not granting visas and allowing people to remain on visas who may be engaged in birth tourism," he explained. "It is the sovereign right and province of all governments across the world, and certainly the United States is no different, to determine who should be able to receive a visa and who shouldn't. There's no entitlement to a visa. There's no constitutional right to a visa."

SEN ERIC SCHMITT SEEKS TO END BIRTH TOURISM, REVOKE CITIZENSHIP FOR BABIES OF FOREIGN DIPLOMATS

Critics also argue that the administration already had tools to combat birth tourism. Since 2020, State Department rules have directed consular officers to deny visitor visas when they have reason to believe an applicant’s primary purpose is traveling to the United States to give birth and obtain citizenship for the child.

"No new executive orders are required for the federal government to go after birth tourism operators or deny fraudulent visa applications," Center for American Progress senior director of immigration policy Debu Gandhi told Fox News Digital. "Americans should take note that from day one, the Trump administration has tried to evade the Constitution's clear and unequivocal language on citizenship and unilaterally decide who is born an American."

If the administration’s latest effort fails, supporters of further limits on birthright citizenship could turn to Congress or pursue a constitutional amendment, which would require approval by three-fourths of the states.

Shapiro says that the administration is on "solid ground" but noted that "if they had proceeded originally in this more targeted, narrower way" then the Supreme Court may not have ruled against them originally.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The White House did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Wednesday.

World.title: GOV JEFF LANDRY: SpaceX bets on Louisiana as America’s next frontier takes off in the South
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

For generations, Americans looked west when they thought about opportunity. Today, they should look south.

Louisiana has always powered America. We fueled the nation with energy, fed it through our farms and ports, built ships that defended it, and manufactured the products that helped it grow.

Now, we are helping lead America’s next frontier: space.

NASA AT 68: AMERICA MUST LEAD ON THE MOON, MARS AND BEYOND—OR CHINA WILL

With SpaceX choosing Louisiana for its newest chapter, our state is taking its place at the center of the economic and technological race that will define the 21st century. This is more than a win for Louisiana. It is a win for America.

For many years, Louisiana saw transformative investments land somewhere else. We watched other states attract the industries of the future while too many of our own left in search of opportunity.

Not anymore.

SpaceX did not choose Louisiana by accident.

THE RED-STATE WINNERS IN THE CLIMB TO BECOME AMERICA’S NEXT ECONOMIC POWERHOUSE

It chose Louisiana because we made a deliberate decision to compete.

Over the past two years, we have cut taxes, reduced bureaucracy, modernized economic development, strengthened workforce training, and created an environment where major employers know they can build and succeed.

THIS RED STATE HANDS REPUBLICANS FRESH AMMUNITION IN THE FIGHT OVER AMERICA'S ECONOMIC FUTURE

The results speak for themselves.

Louisiana has secured more than $250 billion in announced private investment. Meta is building one of the largest artificial intelligence data centers in history in North Louisiana. Hyundai Steel is investing billions in advanced manufacturing along our River. And Louisiana continues to solidify its position as America’s energy powerhouse through transformative LNG investments — including Woodside’s $17.5 billion Louisiana LNG project, Venture Global’s $18 billion expansion, and Commonwealth LNG’s $13 billion facility.

HOW AMERICAN ENERGY HELPED BUILD 250 YEARS OF FREEDOM AND OPPORTUNITY

Together, these projects are creating thousands of jobs, strengthening American energy security, and cementing Louisiana’s role as a global energy leader.

Louisiana is not betting its future on a single industry. We are building an economy that leads in energy, manufacturing, technology, and now aerospace.

INNOVATION IS KEY TO AMERICA STAYING A SUPERPOWER. BUT IT IS MISSING AN ESSENTIAL PIECE

SpaceX is the latest chapter in that story.

Some will see rockets. I see what they make possible.

ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM

I see high-paying jobs for Louisiana workers. I see engineers, welders, electricians, fabricators, software developers, and skilled tradespeople building the future right here. I see students who once believed they had to leave Louisiana to pursue careers in technology and innovation realizing they can build those careers at home. I see communities gaining investment, growth, and optimism. Most importantly, I see Louisiana becoming a state that attracts talent instead of exporting it.

That matters because the greatest challenge facing our state has never been a lack of resources. It has been a lack of opportunity.

For decades, Louisiana was known for what we were losing. Today, we are becoming known for what we are gaining.

The proof is already visible.

Louisiana recently recorded population growth for the second consecutive year. Young adults accounted for most of that growth. Our labor force participation rate recorded one of the largest increases in America as thousands more Louisianians entered or reentered the workforce.

People are choosing Louisiana again.

SpaceX did not create that momentum.

It confirms it.

This project joins a growing list of investments that send the same message to the country and the world: Louisiana is open for business, ready to compete, and prepared to win.

For too long, Louisiana was told to think smaller. We were told the industries of the future belonged somewhere else.

SpaceX proves otherwise.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The same state that helped America reach the moon through generations of aerospace manufacturing is now helping shape the future of space exploration itself. That should make every Louisianian proud.

More importantly, it should make every American optimistic.

Because when companies choose to build in Louisiana, they are choosing to build in America.

The future of American energy, artificial intelligence, manufacturing, and now space exploration is being written in places willing to compete for it. Louisiana is competing.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Louisiana is winning.

And if SpaceX’s decision proves anything, it is that America's next frontier runs straight through Louisiana.

World.title: Appeals court delivers unsettling ruling — and says Supreme Court left it no choice
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A federal appeals court says decades-old Supreme Court precedent forced it to protect the in-home possession of AI-generated child sexual abuse material, as judges warned that rapidly advancing technology has complicated legal lines drawn nearly 25 years ago.

The ruling exposes a widening gap between Supreme Court precedent and rapidly advancing artificial intelligence. The Seventh Circuit said it was bound by a 2002 Supreme Court decision that rejected restrictions on sexually explicit depictions of fictional children when no actual child was involved in their creation. But two judges warned that modern AI can now generate images virtually indistinguishable from material depicting the abuse of real children.

"Indeed, in Free Speech Coalition, the Supreme Court addressed the scope of First Amendment protections for virtual CSAM, but that was nearly twenty-five years ago, and the image-generation technology available today was likely unimaginable back then," Judge John Lee wrote. "Given the relentless advancement in artificial intelligence models, we have some concerns about the lines these cases draw, but we are not free to redraw them ourselves."

WORKER AT SWANKY COUNTRY CLUB ACCUSED OF USING AI TO CREATE EXPLICIT PHOTOS OF TEEN: POLICE

The Seventh Circuit affirmed a lower court’s dismissal of one of four charges against Steven Anderegg, who investigators said had hundreds of AI-generated sexually explicit images depicting children on devices seized from his Wisconsin home.

Anderegg was charged with producing and distributing the AI-generated material, transferring it to a minor under 16, and possessing it. A federal district court dismissed only the possession charge on First Amendment grounds, leaving the other three charges intact.

The Justice Department appealed that dismissal, arguing that the government should be permitted to prohibit possession of obscene virtual child sexual abuse material even when no actual child was involved in its creation. But the Seventh Circuit sided with the lower court.

The government generally cannot criminalize the private possession of obscene material inside someone's home, but it can prohibit possession of child sexual abuse material involving real children because its creation exploits actual victims.

However, the Supreme Court complicated that distinction in 2002 when it struck down restrictions covering sexually explicit images of fictional children created without using actual minors. The justices reasoned that the government's overriding interest in protecting children from exploitation did not apply in the same way when no real child was involved.

AOC OFFERS RARE PRAISE TO LATE SEN GRAHAM FOR BACKING AI PORN BILL NOW STALLED IN HOUSE

Hans von Spakovsky, a senior fellow with Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital that the appeals court "had no choice but to uphold the dismissal under the First Amendment" because of the Supreme Court's ruling.

But von Spakovsky agreed with the concurrence by Lee and Judge Joshua Kolar, who warned the Supreme Court that the rapid growth of AI technology could require the justices to revisit precedent.

"Unforunately, AI-generated images are now virtualy indistinguishable from the real thing and some of these images be created based on real child sexual abuse material," von Spavosky said. "Technology may have overtaken and overwhelmed the reasoning used in those prior decisions."

NEW YORK MAKES HISTORY WITH FIRST-OF-ITS-KIND LAW REGULATING AI-POWERED COMMERCIALS

The Supreme Court previously ruled in Free Speech Coalition that taking images of real children and "morphing" them into sexually explicit poses would not be protected under its ruling on the possession of child sexual abuse material depicting fictional children because the practice involves the interests of real children.

Justice Department lawyers have warned that the rise of AI-generated child sexual abuse material could bog down investigators trying to identify real victims, as increasingly realistic artificial images become harder to distinguish from depictions of actual abuse.

HAWLEY CHAMPIONS GUARD ACT AS HEARTBROKEN FAMILIES SAY AI CHATBOTS ALLEGEDLY PUSHED TEENS TO SELF-HARM

Judges Lee and Kolar raised another concern in their concurrence, citing research that found hundreds of child sexual abuse material images in a major dataset used to train image-generating AI. The judges suggested that could create a link between AI-generated material and the exploitation of real children, though they stressed that the government did not raise the issue in this case and that the record was insufficient to resolve it.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Justice Clarence Thomas anticipated the dilemma more than two decades ago, warning in the Supreme Court’s 2002 ruling that advancing technology could eventually make virtual depictions indistinguishable from child sexual abuse material involving real victims.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"If technological advances thwart prosecution of ‘unlawful speech,’ the Government may well have a compelling interest in barring or otherwise regulating some narrow category of ‘lawful speech’" to enforce laws against material produced through the abuse of real children, Thomas wrote.

World.title: Jewish AG’s convention boycott exposes deepening Israel fault line among Michigan Democrats
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

LANSING, MI - Michigan Democrats gather Saturday in the battleground state's capital city to hold their 2026 state nominating convention amid controversy over recent antisemitic harassment and open hostility within the party over U.S. support for Israel.

Democratic Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, who is Jewish, recently announced she wouldn't attend the confab due to security concerns, after anti-Israel party activists shouted down pro-Israel speakers, including Rep. Haley Stevens, at a prior convention in April.

This weekend's convention comes as a growing number of Democrats push for cutting military aid to Israel, amidst the Israeli government's ongoing war against Hamas terrorists in Gaza.

The convention is also being held just a few weeks after Abdul El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel who describes their military actions as "genocide," narrowly edged Stevens to win the Democratic Senate nomination for a crucial seat the Democrats must hold in the midterm elections.

DEMOCRATIC MICHIGAN AG ACCUSES HER PARTY OF 'ABSOLUTELY NOT' DOING ENOUGH TO COUNTER ANTISEMITISM

"I don’t feel safe going. I feel like my presence isn’t going to be welcome. I don’t want to get chased around. I don’t want to get harassed. I don’t want to get yelled and screamed at. I don’t want to get booed off the stage, irrespective of what I’m saying," Nessel said during a roundtable discussion last month. "I believe that if I go, that is what will happen because it’s been happening to me."

Responding, the Michigan Democratic Party said it is "committed to ensuring party-hosted events are safe and secure environments for all attendees."

"We reject antisemitism, Islamophobia, and all forms of hateful conduct. We are working diligently with stakeholders, elected officials, and party membership to prepare for our August convention and look forward to welcoming Michigan Democrats to the Lansing Center on August 29," state party spokesperson Derrick Honeyman said in a statement.

CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POLL IN MICHIGAN'S BLOCKBUSTER SENATE RACE

Joan Lowenstein, endorsement chair of the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus, told Fox News Digital she hasn't "talked to anybody who thinks they will be unsafe at this convention."

But Lowenstein, who also sits on the Michigan Democratic Party Central Committee, added, "Some people think it will be unpleasant and why should they bother."

But other Jewish Democrats in Michigan are very concerned.

"People are traumatized from the previous convention. Many people I talked to, many super progressive people, are really traumatized by the way they were treated, and the way Haley Stevens was booed, and the way other candidates were treated," Rabbi Asher Lopatin told Fox News Digital last week.

Lopatin, who was interviewed after joining Republican Senate nominee former Rep. Mike Rogers at a campaign event to unveil Democrats supporting Rogers, referred to Nessel's decision not to attend the convention and said "it just shows how terrible these extremists are that they're intimidating even the attorney general of our state."

WHAT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM RACES SHOW

But Lopatin emphasized, "We got to be strong. We got to be proud. We got to be courageous. The Jewish community cannot cower."

Stacy Gittleman, a lifelong Democrat who is supportive of Israel, attended the April convention.

"I saw more Palestinian flags than American flags on the floor," Gittleman, a writer who published her observations at the convention on substack, told Fox News Digital this week.

Gittleman said the jeers and what she highlighted as a "lack of decorum and disrespect" were signs to her of "how far left our party is drifting."

The convention is being held as some Jewish leaders in Michigan are circulating an open letter urging Jewish Democrats and independents in the state to sign their names in support of Rogers. The news was first reported last week by the Jewish Insider and confirmed by Fox News Digital.

"This is sort of a do-or-die moment," a person involved with the letter who asked to remain anonymous to speak more freely told Fox News Digital. "There are many lifelong Democrats who are feeling homeless. ... It’s not just a leftward drift but has turned into an anti-Jewish drift as well."

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Lowenstein, who doesn't support the petition, said those behind the letter "feel it’s an existential issue, and I think that represents a lot of people. And, so, they have to do what they have to do."

"It’s sort of 50/50," she added. "Half the people I talk to say, ‘I could never vote for Abdul El-Sayed because of things he’s said about Israel and, consequentially, the Jewish community. And the other 50% say ‘it is so important for Jews as Americans to have an Democratic Senate that I could never vote for Mike Rogers.'"

Rogers and El-Sayed are running to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. The race is among a dozen that will determine if the Democrats win back the Senate majority from the GOP.

Rogers, in an interview last week with Fox News Digital, reiterated that he's not asking Democratic voters to become Republicans. And he highlighted concerns he's heard from Democratic Jewish voters in Michigan.

THESE 12 MIDTERM RACES WILL DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE SENATE

"I've talked to two young women who were at University of Michigan who were afraid to walk to class. They couldn't display their Star of David. To say that they're afraid is probably an understatement," he said.

Rogers said "the violent rhetoric ... is going to make a difference" in the general election.

El-Sayed is a former Wayne County Health Department director who, if elected in November, would make history as the nation's first Muslim senator. The epidemiologist who unsuccessfully ran for governor as an insurgent candidate in 2018 has made support for Medicare for all a major component of his campaign and has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

But it's El-Sayed's stance and comments on Israel that have angered some Jewish people in Michigan, a state that also has a large Arab and Muslim population.

El-Sayed used the word "bloodthirsty" to characterize Israel's military moves in Gaza in an MS NOW interview this month. He has argued against unconditional U.S. military aid to Israel, as have other progressive politicians. And El-Sayed has repeatedly declined to directly answer whether Israel has the right to exist.

World.title: Comedian finds the secret to surviving boomer parents: Put them in your act
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

"How much do you weigh?"

This question, asked of comedian Jared Freid by his father while on vacation in Delray Beach, Florida, became the inspiration for his new hour of stand-up covering family, body issues, adulthood and the strange closeness between millennials and their boomer parents.

He also justifies why, at 41 years old, he chooses to remain on the family cellphone plan.

Aptly titled "Family Plan," Freid's second special will drop on Netflix Sept. 1. The comic is known for giving dating advice on his long-running podcasts, "The JTrain Podcast" and "U Up?" and most recently in his new book, "Walking Red Flag."

Freid sat down with Fox News Digital to talk about his new special and unpack his parental relationships, from some of his "most horrific memories" involving his mother arguing with other moms over beach chairs to the grave realization that he has the exact same body as his father.

For all his jesting complaints about his loud, Jewish family, Freid described them as "the main driver" of his material. Frustration is where a lot of his jokes originate, he said, and few people frustrate him with as much precision as his own kin.

"We [millennials] have a weird relationship, that's okay to acknowledge, with our parents," Freid said.

B.Y.O. Boomer: Fun for the whole family

"Millennials are incredibly insecure and notice everything. Boomers are incredibly confident and unaware. And what a horrible combination," the comedian said.

"Millennials might be living in hell on earth, considering that combination. Our parents are the most confident and unaware generation, and we have to deal with them every day and we love them," he continued.

"So that takes an incredible amount of restraint and empathy from our end, because the enraging part about parents is they're always 10% right."

Freid, who clarified that he uses the word "boomer" with love, made the case that millennials have a uniquely intertwined relationship with their parents, in part because many millennials are worse off financially than the generation before them, which comes with certain entanglements (like staying on the family phone plan or attending a family vacation paid for by mom and dad).

JEFF ARCURI REVEALS HOW 'BACHELORETTE' WIFE’S CANCER FIGHT TRANSFORMED HIS COMEDY — AND THEIR MARRIAGE

He said "Family Plan" is exactly the type of comedy he wants to do: an hour of material, unified by the through-line of the Freid family beach trip, that people can watch with their own families, be it their parents or "that cousin that they go and smoke weed with during Thanksgiving."

That approach has already shaped his next hour. Freid said his current material grew from another parental indignity: his father offering him Ozempic at dinner.

"Should I be embarrassed to leave the house? Do I look that horrific that you have to offer me your prescription medication?" Freid wondered.

Rather than repeat the jokes from "Family Plan" — Freid made it clear that his parents provide no shortage of material — he will try to repeat its form, starting with a moment of anger and letting it expand into something larger.

I'll be your mirror

The specifics of the set are his, but the emotional dynamic is widely recognizable, and fans have told him so.

"People would come up to me and go, 'That's my parents! You're talking about my dad, that's my mom. My parents ask me about my weight and are obsessed with my body and I'm on the family plan.'"

Beyond merely cracking jokes at boomers' expense, Freid aims to create a humorous mirror that allows audiences to recognize their own loved ones. He is careful about where he points the joke.

"I only talk about myself," he said. "I want to make fun of people I know and love."

COMEDIAN DES BISHOP ON HOW AMERICA MADE HIM FUNNIER AND HIS 'HEALTHY COLLABORATION' WITH WIFE HANNAH BERNER

His material seems to resonate especially powerfully with Jewish crowds.

"I have Jews come up to me, and they go, 'Does anyone else get it?' And I'm like, 'You were in the room, everyone was laughing!'" he said.

"Being Jewish, to me, is a culture of discussion and love and empathy and [getting] annoyed, and all of those things. And that's all in this... I do believe stand-up is our Jewish sport, you know? We created the art form. When I do shows for Jews, I'm representing the whole culture."

The boomer-parent material is contemporary, but Freid sees himself working inside a much older tradition of turning aggravation into laughter. And it doesn't stop at his own family.

The Atkins Diet

Freid performs an extended bit in "Family Plan" roasting Rob Lowe for serving as the face of Atkins, a pairing he found especially absurd as someone who has struggled with body issues himself.

"There is nothing as transparent as we're gonna put Rob Lowe in our commercial so that chubby me will believe that if I eat Atkins foods, I can become Rob Lowe," Freid told Fox News Digital.

Then he actually met Lowe.

Freid encountered the actor at a Netflix golf tournament and nervously introduced himself, explaining that he had been doing a joke about him onstage every night for two years.

Lowe immediately knew which one.

"Atkins?" Freid recalled him saying. "I heard about the bit. I heard it's hilarious. Can't wait to see it."

DAVID CROSS DOESN’T 'GIVE A F---’: THE ACTOR-COMEDIAN ON HIS NEW SPECIAL, SOCIAL MEDIA AND ‘TERRIFYING’ AI

"I melted," Freid said.

The moment forced Freid to live up to his own self-imposed standards of conduct.

"I only make fun of people I could meet," he said.

'Stand-up is the love of my life.' (Don't tell his girlfriend.)

Freid made it this far on his own terms. He said Hollywood never regarded him as an obvious star.

"No one was going to come knock on my door to say, 'Jared, you got the goods. You're so good looking, we need to put you on TV.'"

NATE BARGATZE REVEALS FAMILY-FOCUSED VISION BEHIND $350M NASHVILLE THEME PARK AHEAD OF HIS FIRST MOVIE RELEASE

That forced him to build direct relationships with audiences through podcasts, social media, books and touring. He's been pursuing stand-up for 16 years, describing it as the love of his life. Everything else has been in service of making it into a career.

"That's why I do a lot. You know, two podcasts, and the book, and stand-up. It's always been like a little bit of a desperation," Freid laughed.

The comic graduated from Penn State with a degree in economics before moving to New York City. He thought he would sell insurance and annuities, but it wasn't for him.

The best part of his day was writing emails, he said. Specifically, he enjoyed making friends and colleagues laugh on group email threads or over Google Chat.

"It made me feel amazing, so I was like, 'How do I do that all the time? How do I take that drug?' And that turned into me doing open mics and sketch class and improv class and eventually, you know, becoming a comedian."

Nobody has it figured out

Freid, known for dishing dating advice, has this year entered a relationship of his own.

Asked if his position as a prominent voice in the online dating discussion creates any pressure to have his own situation figured out, Freid replied simply, "No."

"I don't think good advice comes from people who have it figured out. I think good advice come from vulnerability and admitting your faults," he explained.

DAN GAINOR: GEN Z IS RIGHT TO BE ANGRY, BUT BOOMERS ARE NOT THE REAL ENEMY

The instinct to carve his own path and be authentic carries over from his comedy philosophy into his dating work and new book, which he named after himself.

"It's called 'Walking Red Flag' because I'm the red flag. I'm not trying to be a hero. I'm telling you how I felt, the emotional things I was going through, because I am 10% away from any guy someone's dating."

He warned against trusting people who market themselves as finished products.

"If anyone says they've figured it out, they're a liar trying to make money off you."

For better or worse, Freid has people in his life who have no problem pointing out his perceived flaws.

There's no stopping Jewish mothers

For all the frustration Freid mines from his family, he doesn’t seem particularly interested in escaping it.

Asked what advice he would give Jewish mothers whose sons have started dating, Freid laughed off the premise.

"They're not going to listen to me," he said.

"Keep bothering your sons. Keep giving them crap. They love you for it," Freid continued. "It actually calms them."

FROM SOUTHERN CLUBS TO NETFLIX: HOW CLEAN COMIC DERRICK STROUP IS STOPPING AUDIENCES IN THEIR TRACKS

He described the familiar barrage from his own mother: When are you coming home? When are you leaving? Why are you eating that? Eat, you haven’t eaten anything. Stop eating. Take. Eat. Drink. What are you drinking for? You drive so fast. You drive like an old lady.

For Freid, that running commentary is less a nuisance to be solved than a kind of family soundtrack.

"That is like a Jewish man’s white noise machine," he joked.

Fortunately, it is also an endless source of material.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

After 16 years in stand-up, Freid has learned that the people who can get under his skin most effectively are often the same people who make for his best stories. His parents may never stop asking questions, offering opinions or telling him what he should be doing differently.

At this point, Freid probably wouldn’t want them to.

World.title: Crackdown on critical tech could open Americans to a new national security threat
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Americans' sensitive information could increasingly be processed overseas if restrictions on artificial intelligence data centers slow construction in the U.S., a data privacy advocate and industry executive warned.

The warning comes as states and local governments weigh new restrictions on the rapidly expanding data center industry amid concerns over electricity costs, grid reliability and other impacts on surrounding communities.

Brittany Kaiser, CEO of Alpha Compute, said state moratoriums and restrictions on new data centers could push American companies to seek computing capacity in other countries as demand from AI continues to surge.

"One of my top concerns as a top data protection and privacy advocate is that with data center moratoriums being passed in the United States that it will force Americans and American companies to send our data to be processed abroad in other countries," Kaiser told Fox News Digital.

"American companies are going to still run their AI," she added. "They're still going to be purchasing data center space in other countries, and it means our sensitive information will be sent abroad and shared with companies and organizations that might not have America's best interests at heart."

FROM NETFLIX TO GPS: 10 WAYS THIS HIDDEN TECH INFRASTRUCTURE QUIETLY POWERS MODERN LIFE

Data centers are large facilities filled with servers and computing equipment that process, store and transmit information behind many everyday technologies. They support everything from email, social media and internet searches to online banking, streaming services and AI platforms. As demand for AI grows, companies are building increasingly powerful data centers that require vast amounts of electricity, advanced chips and high-speed network connections.

Kaiser said the facilities have become critical infrastructure for the digital economy, making decisions about where they are built and who controls the data they handle a matter of growing economic and national security concern.

Artificial intelligence, however, requires significantly more computing power, fueling a rapid expansion of data center construction across the country.

That growth has sparked pushback in some communities over concerns about electricity costs, water consumption, noise and environmental impacts. Kaiser acknowledged those concerns and said companies should be subject to "common sense regulation" designed to protect communities.

"Not all companies are doing it [building data centers] in the same way," she said. "Some are more responsible than others."

Kaiser said responsible developments can use closed-loop water cooling systems and generate power independently rather than increasing demand on the existing electrical grid.

Alpha Compute, she said, is pursuing projects designed to operate "off-grid, behind the meter," meaning the facilities would generate their own power rather than relying on electricity supplied through the local grid. Kaiser said that approach is intended to prevent the massive energy demands of data centers from straining existing infrastructure or contributing to higher electricity costs for nearby residents.

ONE MONTHLY BILL AMERICANS CAN’T AVOID IS QUIETLY SURGING THANKS TO EMERGING INDUSTRY

The company is developing a project in Pennsylvania, where Gov. Josh Shapiro recently imposed new requirements on large data center developments. Kaiser said Alpha Compute plans to comply with the regulations and welcomed provisions promoting cleaner energy.

Pennsylvania is among a growing number of states confronting the rapid expansion of data centers. In Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott has pushed data centers to provide more of their own power and shoulder infrastructure costs as development accelerates across the state.

Other governors have gone further. Democratic New York Gov. Kathy Hochul imposed a one-year moratorium on new hyperscale data centers as states grapple with concerns over electricity costs, grid reliability and the pace of development.

ONE OF AMERICA'S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS SAYS AI IS CREATING JOBS — NOT REPLACING THEM

But she cautioned that policies that significantly restrict domestic development could have broader consequences for America's position in the global AI race.

"Compute power has now become nearly a utility," Kaiser said, comparing the need for domestic computing infrastructure to energy independence.

"We want to have the right to compute," she said. "We want to be able to process data within our own borders as a national security priority, but also for our own intellectual property to make sure we're not sending our data abroad."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Kaiser has launched a campaign called "Right to Compute," advocating for domestic data center development alongside sustainability standards and regulation.

"We should have the right to both energy independence as well as compute power," she said, "so that Americans and American companies can process all of our sensitive data within our own borders."

World.title: ICE arrests far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos
World.content:
Milo Yiannopoulos, a self-described libertarian and professional internet troll who became known for his controversial right-wing political views, is in ICE custody.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News that ICE arrested Yiannopoulos, a United Kingdom national, on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Kenner, Louisiana.

The DHS spokesperson said Yiannopoulos legally entered the U.S. on May 14, 2019, through New York City, but then “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws.”

Yiannopoulos was taken into ICE custody Thursday after “failing to show up for his immigration hearing” on July 22, prompting an immigration judge to issue a final order of removal against him, according to the spokesperson. “He will remain in ICE custody pending removal,” the spokesperson added.

TMZ first reported Yiannopoulos’ ICE arrest.

Yiannopoulos has ties to Kanye West, known now as Ye, and previously served as the rapper’s chief of staff when Ye tried to run for president in 2020 and 2024. He also worked at Ye’s clothing brand Yeezy, but resigned from that job two years ago after the singer announced he was launching an adult entertainment studio under his Yeezy brand, TMZ reported.

Ye is scheduled to perform in Louisiana Friday night at the New Orleans Caesars Superdome. It’s unclear whether Yiannopoulos was in the state to attend the concert.

A former editor for Breitbart, the conservative internet publication President Donald Trump once considered one of his favorite news sources, Yiannopoulos resigned from the role in 2017 amid backlash to his reported comments about teens and sexual abuse.

The DHS spokesperson said that the Trump administration is “working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.”

World.title: White House teleprompter operator ordered to pay $172K for placing bets on speeches
World.content:
A teleprompter operator for President Donald Trump who made online prediction trades based on information from upcoming speeches has been ordered to pay $172,000, a federal agency said Friday night.

Gabriel Perez used “material, nonpublic information” he obtained through his job to place “trades” on a prediction market, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission said in a news release.

Perez was ordered to pay the money he made in profits, $107,539.02, as well as a civil penalty of $65,000.

He’s also banned from trading on prediction markets for three years, the CFTC said.

Perez made the trades through Kalshi. The CFTC said Kalshi assisted in the matter.

“A Kalshi surveillance investigation caught a White House staffer engaging in prohibited trading activity. Today this individual was subjected to penalties by the CFTC and by our exchange,” Bobby DeNault, Kalshi’s lead lawyer, said in a post on X.

“It doesn’t matter who you are: violate our rules or federal law and you will face the consequences,” he added.

The White House did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Friday night. Perez could not be reached for comment.

The CFTC called it a case of insider trading, adding that Perez traded “presidential mention market contracts, which are event contracts reflecting words or phrases the President may use during his speeches.”

Perez was a technical assistant to the president who had served as a teleprompter operator for Trump since 2016.

The CFTC cited what it called Perez’s “exemplary cooperation” in the case when announcing the fine and penalties Friday.

Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt in July called the online trades a breach of ethics, and “deeply unfortunate and frankly a disgrace.”

Perez was placed on leave in July and Leavitt said at the time that “this individual will no longer be here.”

World.title: Death toll climbs to more than 600, with 2,400 still missing as rescue efforts continue
World.content:
The death toll from catastrophic flash floods and mudslides in Nepal rose to at least 626 on Saturday, as more than 2,400 people remained missing in the country, including around 90 Americans.

Rescuers have struggled to reach devastated communities along the Nepal-Tibet border, with the scale of the disaster coming into view four days after the torrent of water, ice and debris swept through Himalayan valleys, destroying homes, bridges and other infrastructure.

As families wait for news about their relatives, damaged roads, power outages and fears of further flooding have hampered rescue efforts.

China has separately reported seven deaths and 554 people missing in its Tibet region, including hundreds of foreigners. It is unclear how much overlap there is between the Chinese and Nepali missing-person counts.

00:30 House nearly engulfed by Nepal floodwaters 00:00 00:00

The disaster began Wednesday when a massive chunk of ice and rock dozens of times larger than the Empire State Building broke off a mountaintop and triggered the catastrophic flooding, geologists said.

Videos from the hardest-hit border regions showed people running as the debris flow swallowed buildings and vehicles, devastated towns and settlements, and severed roads, power and communications. The suspected collapse of a melting glacier shook the ground so violently that seismic monitors initially registered it as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake.

The State Department said it is not aware of any confirmed American deaths, but the large number of U.S. citizens still unaccounted for has added to the growing uncertainty surrounding the disaster.

Among the missing are Murphy, Texas residents Raghu Rajan and Archana Suresh. The pair were expected to cross the China-Nepal border Wednesday morning when the floods hit. Their phones last pinged that morning near a bridge that washed away.

“We know the severity of it, but still, you know, there’s a ray of hope for us to find our loved ones,” Rajan’s sister-in-law Divya Chandrashekar told NBC Dallas-Fort Worth.

Deepak and Madhu Ahuja, Plano, Texas business owners who have been married for 34 years, were in the area for a religious journey to Mount Kailash, a sacred site for both Hindus and Buddhists. Their family is now desperately trying to find them while holding out hope that they survived.

“My first reaction was, ‘That cannot be true,’” Deepak’s brother Sushil Ahuja said. “They went there for a good cause, right? This cannot happen to them.”

The State Department has urged U.S. citizens “currently in, or recently traveling through Rasuwa or another affected area” to get in touch via KathmanduACS@state.gov.

A spokesperson said relatives seeking information about family members in Nepal “should call 1-888-407-4747 toll-free from the United States and Canada, or 1-202-501-4444 from other locations.”

On Saturday, helicopters resumed operations in Nepal’s flood-hit Nuwakot district after poor weather temporarily halted efforts.

Some helicopters arrived loaded with boxes and bags of aid, including clothes, instant noodles, crackers and rice, while others returned from the flood-hit areas carrying survivors, among them several babies from the nearby community of Trishuli.

An Army personnel carries out an elderly woman from a helicopter during a rescue operation in the aftermath of Nepal-Tibet flash floods at Trishuli camp in Nuwakot district on Aug. 29. Arun Sankar / AFP via Getty Images

Scores of bodies recovered along the banks of the Trishuli and Narayani rivers have been brought to the city of Pokhara on Phewa Lake in central Nepal for identification.

At the Western Regional Hospital in Pokhara, a crowd of families gathered Friday outside the facility’s morgue as they anxiously waited to see if their loved ones might be among the dead being brought to the medical facility.

Inside the hospital, a digital display could be seen being set up to show photographs of the faces of some of the victims, in hopes that their loved ones might be able to identify them.

The display was set up by police, with authorities saying some of the bodies recovered from the floods were in an advanced state of decomposition, making physical identification difficult.

Meanwhile, rescuers are working “day and night” to search for survivors amid challenging conditions, a U.N. official said.

“The government has established a relief fund, and already the World Bank, India, China and the U.S. have committed to pledge $229 million to support,” Lila Pieters Yahia, the U.N. resident coordinator in Nepal, said, adding that the U.N. is also providing $2 million from its humanitarian relief fund for immediate assistance.

Nepal may need $4 billion to $5 billion to rebuild following the disaster, the country’s finance minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters on Saturday.

Lights out, Instagram off? The changes to Meta for teens could be a big deal

toggle caption Manuel Arias Duran/Moment RF/Getty Images

Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.

The social media company Meta has agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion in a settlement in a federal lawsuit alleging the company's social media platforms have harmed children and teens. The company denies the allegations, but has agreed to make a suite of changes to its social platforms — Facebook and Instagram — to make them less compelling and potentially dangerous to minors.

This comes at a time when healthcare providers are increasingly seeing symptoms of social media addiction among youth, says psychologist Mitch Prinstein, who is the Co-Director of the Winston Center on Technology and Brain Development at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill.

"We know that about 50% of kids are reporting at least one symptom of clinical dependency on social media," he says. "We know that kids who are having a difficult time getting off social media are also reporting more depression, loneliness, anxiety, even suicidality over time."

Sponsor Message

While Meta denies the allegations that it designed its social platforms to be addictive for kids, child safety advocates and researchers have welcomed the settlement as a major development in holding tech companies accountable.

"This settlement isn't perfect, but I do think it's a critical first step in making sure platforms are safer for our children and that our kids can grow up healthy," says Julie Scelfo, founder of the grassroots organization Mothers Against Media Addiction.

The changes Meta will have to make are intended to reduce the addictiveness of Facebook and Instagram. For example, it will have to give minors the option of having a non-personalized feed, where it doesn't use an algorithm to tailor content based on individual preferences to keep kids scrolling. The changes are detailed in a press release from California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led a coalition of 50 states and territories and the District of Columbia that settled with Meta.

The other reforms Meta has agreed to for people under 18 include:

a default daily time limit of two hours for minors, with only parents having the ability to opt kids out.



a default block on nighttime use from midnight to 6 a.m.



a default block on notifications to minors – both overnight, and from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. during the school year.



a ban on showing minors how many likes or reactions their posts receive.



a ban on cosmetic procedure image filters.



a better system for teens to report potentially harmful content and a commitment that Meta respond to 90% of those reports within six hours.



Sponsor Message

Meta is also promising to do a better job of verifying users' ages and has agreed to report regularly to an independent auditor.

Meta is calling on other social media companies to make the same changes, and has negotiated that $5 billion of the settlement will be paid to states if other companies join the effort. Texas negotiated an additional $1 billion settlement with Meta.

"This framework will only work if all our peers join us," Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement. "Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution. We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away."

Enthusiastic reception from experts

"It is very exciting to see that a lot of the changes that are written into the settlement are very similar to what we saw scientifically," says Prinstein, who was scheduled to testify next week in the case brought by the states.

For example, he says, studies show why the design elements of Facebook and Instagram are particularly addictive for teens and pre-teens.

"By the time a kid turns around ten or 11, the part of their brain that makes them suddenly super interested in things like popularity and who sits at the lunch table are really showing a hypersensitivity to social signals," he says. And so, when kids encounter constant notifications about followers, likes, and dislikes on social media accounts, it easily leads to time spent on these platforms.

"We saw kids unable to stop themselves on these platforms," explains Prinstein. "They would tell us, 'I have tried to quit and I can't. It's interfering with my daily roles and routines.'"

So turning off notifications during school days and overnight should help lower problematic use by minors, he adds.

Making sleep a priority

Similarly, the block on nighttime use could make a big difference to teen mental health, says Dr. Jason Nagata, a pediatrician and researcher at the University of California, San Francisco.

Sponsor Message

His analysis of the longitudinal Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, where researchers have followed thousands of children as they grow up, shows that a big proportion of teens are using their cell phones between midnight and 4 a.m.

"The most used app category during this period was social media," says Nagata. "So I think that it is likely that most of these teenagers are … on social media and getting the notifications and kind of distractions that are impairing their sleep."

And sufficient sleep is key to teen brain development and mental wellness.

Implementation will be important

But Nagata and Prinstein also caution that it remains to be seen whether these changes required by the settlement actually will have the desired effect on kids' experience of social media and their mental health.

"I do think that the details of the implementation are really important," says Nagata. "What we have found, even in some of the testimony during this case, is that it's actually very hard to get some of these things to work."

He is referring to some of the changes Meta had already made on its apps, like the "Take a Break" feature on Instagram, which reminds teen users to close the app after they have been on it for a certain length of time. As Instagram head Adam Mosseri testified in court, the feature wasn't as effective as they had hoped.

"We really need to know how this is going to be implemented," says Nagata, "and then I do think that this needs to be rigorously evaluated. It's not just like we're going to make some changes and then that's it."

Prinstein agrees. "We still need research to make sure that these changes are actually helping, and they're not in some ways making kids worse or kids are finding sneaky ways around them," he says. "So we still have some work to do."

Sponsor Message

The settlement does include an agreement from Meta "to maintain, review, and improve existing teen content safety measures" and to "create enhanced parent supervision tools."

World.title: Trump cuts to science advisory boards have long-lasting consequences, researchers say
World.content:
Trump cuts to science advisory boards have long-lasting consequences, researchers say

toggle caption Lucy Lu for NPR

Netia McCray recalls how excited she was to join the federal advisory committee on long COVID in 2025. She had been diagnosed in the early days of the pandemic — and symptoms such as fatigue, heart palpitations and shortness of breath had become a frustrating but inescapable part of life.

By joining this group of doctors, researchers and other experts advising on the disease, McCray, 36, had hoped to channel her years of experience as a long-COVID patient into "something that could benefit so many individuals like myself and my community," she says. The work, she felt, could make her part of the solution for a debilitating condition that impacts millions of Americans.

toggle caption Lucy Lu for NPR

But McCray had only been on the committee for a few months when she received an email notice that the group was terminated, "effective immediately."

Sponsor Message

McCray's advisory group is one of more than 100 science-focused federal committees that have been terminated under the second Trump administration, according to a news analysis in the journal Nature. As of March of this year, more than a quarter of the country's healthcare-related committees have been shut down, according to the advocacy group Public Citizen.
