A source has previously told CBC News that the U.S. wanted Canada to apply sectoral tariffs, primarily on steel and aluminum, to its trading partners, and countries that have a free trade deal with Canada would face tariffs on imports above 2025 levels.

Where does Canada go from here?

Charette said as it stands, Canada's "pens are down, but the door is open."

"We're prepared to go and work with the United States on a deal that would be in the economic interest of Canadians, as long as it doesn't impact Canadian sovereignty," she said.

As for whether Canada can trust the U.S. as negotiating partners, Charette said that remains to be seen.

"Trust is earned, and trust is earned through the fine print of a trade agreement that was under negotiation right up until those final moments in the night on Friday."

WATCH | Canada won't accept U.S. attitude that we're a 'subsidiary,' Carney says: Canada won't accept U.S. attitude that we're a 'subsidiary,' Carney says | Duration 1:24 Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Monday that Canada would return to the negotiating table with the U.S. if the Americans come with the 'right attitude.'

Greer has said there are no open channels right now, but he has a good relationship with Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc. Meanwhile, Lutnick has claimed Canadian negotiators will kickstart talks again once the Quebec election and Alberta referendum are complete.

The Canadian government is bracing for a long fight. On Tuesday, it announced it will match U.S. President Donald Trump's new 50 per cent tariffs on hundreds of Canadian goods by tariffing $27.6 billion of comparable U.S. goods.

The Liberal government is also rolling out $7.5 billion to help workers and businesses weather the U.S. tariffs. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has said that the federal government will continue its support for "as long as it takes."

Asked how she feels about where everything stands now, Charette said she's proud of the work the Canadian team did.

"We didn't leave anything, we put it all out on the field. There was no stone unturned, we did everything we thought we could," she said.

World.title: Cancer survivor fights to axe the U.K.'s sunscreen tax. Should Canada do the same?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Interview with skin cancer survivor Jessica Zbinden-Webster : As It Happens 6:31 Skin cancer survivor wants the U.K. to axe the tax on sunscreen

When Jessica Zbinden-Webster was diagnosed with skin cancer at the age of 26, it upended everything she thought she knew about sun safety.

"I had always mistakenly assumed that skin cancer was a disease that exclusively affected older people and people who had used sunbeds to excess and who had sun bathed to excess," the West Sussex, U.K., woman told As It Happens guest host Paul Hunter.

"And now, of course, I'm living proof that it can happen to anyone at any time."

Now recovered, Zbinden-Webster is on a mission to convince the U.K. government to scrap its 20 per cent tax on sunscreen. Canadian cancer organizations told CBC this country should also consider making sunscreen tax-free.

"Affordability is particularly important because effective sun protection is not a one-time purchase. Sunscreen needs to be applied generously and reapplied at least every two hours during sun exposure," Falyn Katz, CEO of Melanoma Canada, said in an email.

"For families, outdoor workers and people spending significant time outdoors, the cost can add up quickly. Those costs can create an additional barrier for lower-income Canadians."

An unexpected diagnosis

Zbinden-Webster's cancer journey began in 2018, when she developed what she thought was an unsightly pimple beneath her right eye.

"I had a lot of pimples growing up and that extended into my 20s," she said. "I thought, 'Oh goody, another one to deal with.'"

But several months passed, and the pimple didn't go away.

"One morning, I was sat at my desk and I rubbed the skin on my eye, where the pimple was, and it began to bleed. And that was my red flag. That prompted me to visit my doctor the following day," she said.

"To my surprise, he diagnosed me with skin cancer on the spot."

She had infiltrative basal cell carcinoma, an aggressive, but highly treatable, form of skin cancer that is often hard to detect, but can burrow deep beneath the surface.

Zbinden-Webster was diagnosed with infiltrative basal cell carcinoma at the age of 26. (Submitted by Jessica Zbinden-Webster)

The Canadian Skin Cancer Foundation recommends using sunscreen with an SPF of 30 or higher on any exposed skin any time you're outside.

"I actually only used sunscreen the way most Brits use sunscreen, which is as a seasonal product. I would use it during the summer months and I would also use it more frequently when on holiday," Zbinden-Webster said.

"But I most definitely did not regard it as an everyday essential."

Daily sunscreen is expensive

That's changed. Now that she's cancer-free after a successful surgery, Zbinden-Webster uses sunscreen every day.

It's a healthy habit, she says, but also an expensive one.

Non-prescription sunscreen in the U.K. is classified as a cosmetic product, and subject to a 20 per cent value-added tax (VAT).

"Not only does this send a damaging message about the importance of sun safety to our public health, but it prices the poorest out of skin cancer prevention," Zbinden-Webster said.

People apply some sunscreen on an Ottawa beach in 2024. The Canadian Skin Cancer Foundation recommends all Canadians wear sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher when outside, and re-apply every two or three hours. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

Zbinden-Webster's online petition, "Tell the Government to axe VAT on Sunscreen," has garnered more than 100,000 signatures.

She's not alone in her mission. Several U.K. skin health organizations, including Melanoma Focus are also calling for the government to remove VAT from sun protection products with an SPF of 30 or higher.

A 2026 report from the U.K. parliamentary UV Safety Inquiry recommended the same.

CBC was not able to reach the U.K. government for comment, but a spokesperson told the BBC : "As part of our 10-year plan to reform the health service, and through a national cancer plan, we will fight cancer on all fronts, from prevention, to diagnosis, treatment, and research."

What about Canada?

In Canada, sunscreen is regulated as a health product.

However, like many health-care products, it is subject to the five per cent federal Goods and Services Tax, as well as provincial sales taxes, which vary from five to 15 per cent.

"From our perspective, there is therefore a disconnect between recognizing sunscreen as a regulated health product and an important cancer-prevention measure, while continuing to tax it as an ordinary consumer purchase," said Katz of Melanoma Canada.

Lindsay Timm, executive director of the Canadian Cancer Survivor Network, says she welcomes any effort to make sunscreen more accessible, including making it publicly available in parks, outdoor pools and hiking trails.

"We believe that making sunscreen more affordable/accessible is an excellent goal for all countries, including Canada," she said in an email.

WATCH | Sunscreen use declining in Canada: Canadians are spending more time in the sun – but many are ditching sunscreen | Duration 1:48 Some experts say while sun exposure is on the rise in Canada, sunscreen use is losing popularity. Skin cancer rates are also growing. In Quebec, the incidence of melanoma per 100,000 people, jumped by more than 430 per cent in the last three decades, according to Statistics Canada.

Health Canada referred questions about the sunscreen tax to the Department of Finance Canada.

"Applying the GST/HST to a broad base of goods and services helps keep the tax more efficient, simpler, and lower," Finance Canada said in an emailed statement.

A handful of basic necessities — including prescription drugs, medical devices, menstrual hygiene products and some groceries — are tax-free in Canada.

Asked whether the government would consider adding sunscreen to that list, the department said: "The government is continually reviewing the tax system to ensure it is both effective and efficient and will continue to do so."

Zbinden-Webster says it's easy to get bogged down in the bureaucracy.

But then she remembers Australia, where sunscreen with an SPF of 15 or more has long been exempt from the 10 per cent Goods and Services Tax .

"There is hope," she said. "It has been done, and it can be done again."

World.title: NASA is launching the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Here are just a few of the wonders it will reveal
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

If all goes to plan, at 7:26 a.m. Sunday morning, a new space telescope will blast off from Cape Canaveral, Fla., on top of a Falcon Heavy rocket, ready to reveal new wonders about our universe.

The highly anticipated Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is named after NASA's first chief astronomer, also known as the "mother of the Hubble Space Telescope." Once launched, it will orbit 1.5 million kilometres away, at a point called L2 where gravitational forces balance to keep satellites in a steady orbit. It is a five-year mission, with the possibility of extension.

But why bother adding a new telescope to the arsenal of telescopes already in orbit, like the Hubble Space Telescope or the James Webb Space Telescope?

Because each telescope is equipped with different instruments, and Nancy Grace Roman is no different. While it has a mirror that is roughly 2.4 metres across, similar to Hubble, it also has a coronagraph that can block out starlight to reveal planets orbiting distant stars. It also has its Wide Field Instrument that is just as sensitive as Hubble's but has the ability to image an area 100 times larger. It's like going from looking through a pinhole to something the size of a golf ball.

Teams inside the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida encapsulate the agency's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope within the payload fairing on Aug. 21, ahead of connecting it to a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket. (Sydney Rohde (Rocz)/NASA)

Its camera will be able to resolve billions of stars, allowing for all different types of sky and stellar surveys.

So, what makes Nancy Grace Roman so special? Let's take a look at just some of the highly anticipated discoveries astronomers are hoping this telescope will make.

The search for other planets

While we don't know of any other planets with life, astronomers are continuing to investigate other stellar systems to find out what makes our solar system so unique. Or perhaps it's not that unique.

To date, more than 6,300 exoplanets have been confirmed, mostly from the Kepler Space Telescope.

There are a few ways to look for exoplanets. The most popular is the transit method, where a telescope looks at a star for an extended period of time. If there's a planet that crosses — or transits — in front of it, the light of the star dips ever-so slightly. And that's what Nancy Grace Roman will do as well. But on a much bigger scale.

WATCH | Everything you need to know about NASA's Roman Space Telescope:

"It's just going to be crazy how much more we're going to learn because right now you know we've got Kepler, which I guess we looked at, like, 200,000 stars or something like that, and then with Roman we're going to look at 100 million stars and we're going to go from 10,000 planets to 100,000 transiting exoplanets," said Kelsey Hoffman, a co-investigator on one of the observing programs with the telescope and a researcher at Bishop's University in Sherbrooke, Que.

"So that increase in numbers, it's… I can't even imagine what we're going to learn."

But the telescope will also use another method to search for exoplanets — something called microlensing, which allows astronomers to peer even deeper.

"If you have a distant star that you like to call a source of light, and then a star with its planets moves precisely right in front of it, that mass of the star and the mass of the planet act as two lenses, and causes the light that's coming from that distant star to bend a little bit, which we observe as a magnification event," explained Jason Rowe, who is also part of a Nancy Grace Roman observing program and is a professor in the department of physics at Bishop's University.

He's particularly excited because this type of observation will allow scientists to look for more Earth-like planets.

"We've discovered previous planets with microlensing, but we're going to kind of blow the doors open and now discover a very large sample of them," he said. "And microlensing is very sensitive to planets at longer periods, including those that have masses about Earth's size, about Earth masses."

Dark matter and dark energy

What we are able see makes up only five per cent of what exists in the universe. Roughly 27 per cent is dark matter, a sort of invisible glue that holds the galaxies and the stars within them together. The other 68 per cent is dark energy, also invisible, and something that is believed to speed up the expansion of our universe.

Astronomers have been trying for decades to figure out exactly what dark matter is, and Nancy Grace Roman will look for dark matter within galaxies and within beautiful globular clusters, a collection of thousands to millions of stars that are all tightly gravitationally bound.

The globular cluster Omega Centauri is seen in this image from the European Southern Observatory's La Silla Observatory in Chile. (ESO)

The mission will measure the locations and amount of dark matter, as well as normal matter, in hundreds of millions of galaxies.

"Normally with surveys, you have this trade-off where you decide, am I going to stare out one little patch for a very long time? Or am I gonna scale across the sky?" said Nicole Drakos, an astrophysicist at the University of Hawaii, Hilo, who is also part of a Nancy Grace Roman observational program. "With Roman, you can stare at one patch on the sky, but you still have an enormous area.

"So you can see these distant galaxies, but also see where they live. You can see their environment. You can map out the dark matter structure around them, the gas around them."

WATCH | Nancy Grace Roman's ultra-deep field:

The telescope will also investigate dark energy, which, like dark matter, is invisible. But in this case, dark energy is causing our universe to expand rather than slow down.

"I'm, you know, involved with the deep field stuff, so I'm obviously interested in that. But, you know, in my heart, I am a cosmologist; I really love the cosmology," Drakos said. "Getting a better handle of things like the expansion of the universe, I think, is really cool."

World.title: Canada's economy has found its footing. But is it enough to survive the U.S. trade war?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's surge in growth in the second quarter of this year couldn't come at a better time.

Data from Statistics Canada show the economy grew at its fastest pace since 2004 . Gains were seen in roughly 90 per cent of the economy. Energy exports led the way, but even the heavily tariffed auto industry saw major gains.

Put it all together, and you can see Canada's economy has carved out a small cushion to help weather the next blows from the trade war with the U.S. And economists say Canada needs every inch of it.

"This is genuine resilience, but not immunity from a trade war," says David-Alexandre Brassard, the chief economist with Chartered Professional Accountants of Canada.

Statistics Canada also revised the first quarter's growth figures from 0.0 per cent to 0.1 per cent. As such, Canada's economy did not contract in back-to-back quarters and thus officially avoided even a "technical recession."

"While the economy was weak at the turn of the last calendar year, it wasn't in a recession," wrote Michael Davenport, senior economist at the research firm Oxford Economics.

The numbers had been anticipated by both the statistical agency and most economists in the country.

Douglas Porter, chief economist with BMO Capital Markets, says the boost shows the Canadian economy was turning a corner of sorts after a wildly volatile 18 months.

He says an economy is made up of millions of decisions made every day by consumers and businesses.

"What these numbers are telling us is that a lot of these decisions had started to turn positive through the spring," Porter told CBC News.

However, not all that momentum is going to carry into the third quarter. The preliminary estimate from Statistics Canada is that growth in July was flat.

The latest round of tariffs will only target about five per cent of Canadian exports. But much like the first tranche of tariffs, where they hit, they will hit hard.

And once again, uncertainty will weigh more heavily on the economy than the tariffs themselves.

Transport trucks cross the Ambassador Bridge from Windsor, Ont., into the U.S. on Aug. 22. (Dax Melmer/The Canadian Press)

World wants what Canada sells, analyst says

But not all sectors are equally exposed to tariffs.

Canada's energy sector is booming due to an increase in oil prices. As that industry thrives, you can see its benefits fan out across the country.

Machine and equipment manufacturers in Quebec and Ontario see a rise in demand. Financial firms, lawyers and consultants on Bay Street benefit. Marine logistics companies in B.C. pick up business as exports increase.

Crude oil tankers docked at the Trans Mountain Westridge Marine Terminal in Burnaby, B.C., where oil from the expanded Trans Mountain pipeline is loaded onto tankers, pictured in June 2024. (THE CANADIAN PRESS)

Energy analysts say the resource sector is poised to continue driving Canada's economic growth.

"The big money is still to come," said Heather Exner-Pirot, director of energy, natural resources and environment at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute think-tank.

She says the last few months have underscored the point that the world wants what Canada sells. Demand for critical minerals, fertilizers and energy products puts Canada in an enviable position.

"The broader point is we are clearly moving into a commodity cycle upswing, and Canada is particularly attractive this time around," Exner-Pirot told CBC News.

She says Canadian producers will export more and see new investment in resource and energy infrastructure.

But none of that growth is guaranteed, she warns.

"It's extremely important that we don't rest on our laurels. We will do well. But if we have ambition and high expectations, we can do tremendously," Exner-Pirot said.

That difference would matter at any juncture for the economy. But as Canadian businesses weather this next wave of the trade war, it will be especially important to find ways to boost growth in areas less exposed to tariffs — because those areas getting hit are facing very real pain.

World.title: Economists have some ideas about how to Trump-proof the economy
World.content:
Article content

Solving that dilemma was a signature piece of Carney’s economic plan. Ottawa has for the most part done what it can on this front as the federal barriers — which were never really the big problem — have largely been removed. But the broader goal of free trade within Canada, despite today’s trade challenges and a Constitution that says products from one province shall “be admitted free into each of the other provinces,” governments continue to reject the benefits of economic union.

World.title: Finance minister presents Colombia’s $203B budget proposal
World.content:
Colombia’s Finance Minister Miguel Gomez presented a budget proposal of COP634.9 trillion ($203 billion) for the coming year, a 14% increase compared to last year.

Much of the increase is due to the government’s debt obligations, which went up 55% to 155.4 trillion ($49.8 billion), almost a quarter of the entire budget.

At a presentation, Gomez told press that an earthquake that left tens of thousands homeless in western Colombia earlier this month also forced the administration of Abelardo de la Espriella to increase spending.

In a video, the finance minister also said that the government “has taken deci

The budget bill, a revision of the one that was presented by the former government of former President Gustavo Petro, will have to be approved by Congress before October 20 or be issued as a decree.

The government will also present a Finance Bill, which determines how the government plans to pay for its spending, before December.

World.title: Colombia claims killing eight suspected EMBF guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella said Thursday that Colombia’s armed forces killed eight guerrillas of FARC dissident group EMBF in a joint operation.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said that the military offensive targeted “camps used by structures of the Jorge Suarez Briceño Block,” a unit of the EMBF, in a rural part of El Retorno in the Guaviare province.

In a precision airstrike followed by an operation carried out by our commandos, the preliminary tally shows that 8 terrorists have been killed so far, 11 rifles and 5 machine guns have been seized, along with a large amount of logistical supplies. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that “Colombia must know we are going on the offensive” against organized crime and illegal armed groups that are all deemed “narco-terrorist” organizations by the government.

“Major ringleaders and their criminal organizations will find no hiding place or sanctuary anywhere in the country,” the president added.

De la Espriella took office earlier this month, vowing to end peace negotiations with illegal armed groups and go on a military offensive with the help of the US military instead.

One of the groups that was negotiating peace with the administration of former President Gustavo Petro was the EMBF, led by former FARC commander “Calarca.”

The group, together with FARC dissident group EMC, controls large swathe of territory in southern Colombia and along the border with Venezuela.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.

World.content:
