World.title: García Luna corruption case wins $5.8M for Guerrero schools: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

💰 García Luna case yields $5.8M for Guerrero schools : UIF chief Omar Reyes Colmenares said Mexico received US $5.8 million this week from its civil suit victory over the Weinberg family — ex-Security Minister García Luna’s alleged frontmen — in a Miami-Dade court. Sheinbaum said the funds will go to schools in Guerrero’s disadvantaged Montaña region.

: UIF chief Omar Reyes Colmenares said Mexico received US $5.8 million this week from its civil suit victory over the Weinberg family — ex-Security Minister García Luna’s alleged frontmen — in a Miami-Dade court. Sheinbaum said the funds will go to schools in Guerrero’s disadvantaged Montaña region. 🇲🇽 Mexico is ‘Doing very well,’ Sheinbaum says ahead of second report: Sheinbaum declared Mexico is “doing very well” almost two years into her six-year term. Her positive assessment of the current state of affairs came ahead of the presentation of her second annual government report next Tuesday.

Sheinbaum declared Mexico is “doing very well” almost two years into her six-year term. Her positive assessment of the current state of affairs came ahead of the presentation of her second annual government report next Tuesday. 🚣 Gold for rower Kenia Lechuga: Sheinbaum congratulated Nuevo León native Kenia Lechuga on her gold medal in the women’s lightweight sculls at the 2026 World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam, saying that as a former rower herself she felt “special affection” for the win. Mexican rowers also won gold in the women’s lightweight double sculls and bronze in the men’s lightweight sculls.

Why today’s mañanera matters

Today’s mañanera was significant as the federal government was able to demonstrate that its successful civil suit against former Security Minister Genaro García Luna — now imprisoned in the United States — is reaping monetary rewards.

Also of note was President Claudia Sheinbaum’s positive assessment of the current state of affairs in Mexico almost two years into her six-year term. Her favorable evaluation of the prevailing situation came four days before she is scheduled to present her second annual government report (segundo informe de gobierno) in a speech in Mexico City.

Sheinbaum: US $5.8 million recovered in García Luna case to go to schools in Guerrero

Omar Reyes Colmenares, head of the federal government’s Financial Intelligence Unit (UIF), told reporters that on Tuesday of this week, Mexico received US $5.8 million in funds recovered in the case involving García Luna, who in 2024 was sentenced to 38 years in prison in the United States after he was found guilty of collusion with the Sinaloa Cartel.

He noted that the UIF filed a civil suit in Florida aimed at recovering public money that was diverted out of Mexico in a corruption scheme involving García Luna and members of the Weinberg family. Members of the Weinberg family have been identified as frontmen for García Luna, who served as security minister during the 2006-12 government led by former President Felipe Calderón.

Reyes highlighted that a court in Miami handed down a ruling in May in favor of the Mexican state and against the Weinberg family. As part of the ruling, Judge Lisa Walsh in Miami-Dade County ordered members of the Weinberg family and related companies to pay US $578.5 million in damages to the Mexican state for losses incurred as a result of their involvement in corruption schemes.

“As a result of this process,” said Reyes, “the Mexican state received US $5.8 million on Aug. 25, 2026.”

The UIF chief said the money was obtained from the recovery of a surety bond and “the liquidation of 12 properties located in Florida, United States, and linked to the Weinberg family.” He noted that Mexico is awaiting the liquidation of other assets in order to recover additional funds diverted out of the country by García Luna.

Later in the press conference, Sheinbaum said that the $5.8 million in recovered funds that Mexico received this week would be allocated to schools in the Montaña region of the southern state of Guerrero.

“It’s around 100 million pesos that is going to be used in [one of] the most disadvantaged areas in the country,” she said.

Mexico is doing ‘very well,’ Sheinbaum says ahead of her second annual report

A reporter reminded Sheinbaum that in her first annual report speech — delivered at the National Palace on Sept. 1, 2025 — she said that Mexico and her government were “doing well” and would do “even better.” He subsequently asked the president how her administration is doing 12 months later.

“Mexico is doing better, Mexico is doing well,” Sheinbaum said.

“We’re doing very well — with the difficulties that any country can face, but we’re doing well,” she said.

@Claudiashein afirmó que México progresa positivamente en economía, reducción de la violencia y bienestar social, rumbo a su Segundo Informe de Gobierno. Algunos spots de campaña serán difundidos en radio, televisión y redes sociales. Las piezas muestran sus giras de… pic.twitter.com/pu8YEMBrT4 — Nota Central (@notacentralmx) August 28, 2026

Sheinbaum said she is “very optimistic” about Mexico’s economy and declared that Mexicans’ quality of life is improving. She also pointed out that violence has declined — a statement supported by a 30.8% annual reduction in homicides in the first seven months of 2026.

Sheinbaum subsequently spoke about her government’s raison d’être, saying that the reason why “we’re here” is to “create well-being for the people of Mexico.”

On Wednesday, the president presented economic data that she said was indicative of the strength of the Mexican economy. She highlighted the record foreign direct investment Mexico received in the first half of 2026, quarter-over-quarter economic growth of 1.4% in the second quarter of the year and the USD:MXN exchange rate, which at the time was below 17.

Sheinbaum congratulates world champion rower

The president congratulated Mexican rower Kenia Lechuga, a Nuevo León native who on Thursday won gold in the women’s lightweight sculls at the 2026 World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam, Netherlands.

“Many congratulations,” Sheinbaum said, adding that as a former rower herself, she reserved “special affection” for a victory by a Mexican rower.

Lechuga, who had previously won silver and bronze medals at World Rowing Championships, wasn’t the only Mexican rower to win gold in Amsterdam on Thursday. Aylin Ibarra and Melissa Márquez won the women’s lightweight double sculls, while Aléxis López placed third to secure the bronze medal in the lightweight men’s sculls.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: How Mexico City can solve its 400-year water crisis
World.content:
Following a bout of heavy rains in September 1629, water rose through the streets of Mexico City and did not recede. The city had just spent 22 years digging a drainage channel through the mountains, the Desagüe de Huehuetoca, meant to solve a problem the closed, mountain-ringed basin had faced for centuries: nowhere for excess water to go.

The project failed. Parts of the city stayed flooded for years and more than 30,000 people died, mostly from disease in the standing, sewage-laced water.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by ABC News (@abcnews)



The city kept making the same trade for four centuries after that: draining the water to survive and turning every success into a new, worse problem.

A city that traded its lake for a sinking foundation

Before the Spanish conquest, Tenochtitlán sat on an island in Lake Texcoco, its neighborhoods built with the lake rather than against it. Colonial and then Porfirian-era engineers kept draining it instead, culminating in the Gran Canal del Desagüe around 1900. Draining the lake solved flooding and erased the city’s water supply at the same time, so the city turned to pumping the aquifer beneath the old lakebed’s soft, clay-rich sediment.

Pumping that aquifer releases the pressure holding the clay open. The clay compacts, causing the ground to drop. A 2021 study published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth measured subsidence near 50 centimeters a year in the worst areas, and found the sinking no longer tracks current pumping rates: It is now driven by decades-old compaction that cannot be undone, even if every well stopped tomorrow.

That uneven sinking has warped the Gran Canal itself, leaving stretches of the drainage system sloping the wrong way. Mexico City has sunk roughly 30 feet across the lakebed zone, and engineers now run pumping stations just to lift sewage back up to where gravity can take over — the same 1607 trade, repeated at greater cost.

The newest version, the Túnel Emisor Oriente, finished in 2019 after 11 years of digging, carries wastewater 62.5 kilometers (39 miles) to Hidalgo state, where it irrigates the Mezquital Valley. Only about 36% of the city’s wastewater gets treated at all; the nearby Tula Valley region now draws 90% to 100% of its own aquifer from decades of Mexico City’s former runoff.

What survives to reach a kitchen tap

Mexico City’s water is treated properly at the source. What happens after is where the system fails.

Official figures from Mexico City’s water agency, the Sistema de Aguas de la Ciudad de México (SACMEX), put network-wide leak loss at roughly 40%, while researchers studying intermittent, low-pressure water systems in general have documented exactly how contamination gets in through a leaking network: a crack or joint, a nearby contaminant source, and a pressure gradient pulling inward.

Rooftop reservoirs, also known as tinacos, exist precisely because city pressure is not continuous, and a small pilot study in Guadalajara found contamination rates more than double after water sat in a home’s storage tank versus straight off the network.

Water contamination

Two boroughs carry a documented, more specific version of this.

In Iztapalapa, two named SACMEX/UNAM wells have shown arsenic and heavy-metal levels exceeding Mexico’s own drinking-water standard since they opened; separately, UNAM researchers found microplastics, Giardia muris and E. coli in the borough’s water.

SACMEX’s own 2020 data recorded arsenic violations across 28 wells in Tláhuac, Tlalpan, Coyoacán, Iztapalapa, Iztacalco and Azcapotzalco, signifying a documented national pattern: Only 1 in 10 Mexican treatment plants is even equipped to remove arsenic or fluoride.

Stressing the system

Meanwhile, large companies are also extracting from the same stressed basin. CONAGUA’s public registry shows Coca-Cola FEMSA holds a well concession in Cuauhtémoc, where it extracts 1.13 billion liters a year. PepsiCo’s bottler holds another in Iztacalco, extracting 511 million liters.

Nationally, Coca-Cola and PepsiCo’s Mexican bottlers have extracted roughly 14.7 billion and 25.7 billion liters, respectively, since 1994.

What none of the public record shows is what becomes of the 15% to 30% of that water any industrial reverse-osmosis system inevitably rejects as concentrate, a limit set by the physics of the membrane itself.

Where the hope is

The subsidence side of this cycle has already been broken elsewhere.

Tokyo sank roughly 4 meters before two laws, the 1956 Industrial Water Law and the 1962 Law on Regulation of Groundwater Use in Office Buildings, made new wells prohibitively expensive to drill while the government subsidized cheaper surface-water infrastructure as the replacement. Groundwater pumping in the city’s 23 wards peaked in 1964 and has fallen since; subsidence in the most heavily regulated districts was brought close to zero.

Venice stopped pumping groundwater entirely and now draws its drinking water from the Italian mainland instead, sinking at about 1 millimeter a year, down from a rate that once threatened the city outright.

Neither city undid the damage already on the books. Both proved the mechanism itself can be stopped, and both did it with a law, not a technology.

Legal remedies vs. a household fix

The legislative move mirrors Tokyo’s. Sustained public pressure on regulators, not new technology, is what got its fix passed. Here, that looks like contacting a local representative directly, and backing investigations like “Veneno en mi agua,” or “Poison in my water,” that keep this issue on the public record instead of letting it fade after one news cycle.

A household’s own move is smaller and immediate: A fix goes under the sink.

An ultrafiltration membrane, at roughly 0.01 microns, physically blocks the bacteria and parasitic cysts responsible for most water-borne illness here, the exact risk documented above. It runs on the building’s own water pressure: no pump, no electricity and a 100% water recovery rate, so there is no reject stream at all. The water that enters the membrane is the water that leaves the tap, only cleaner. That combination — no pump, no electricity, no wasted water — also makes it the cheapest of these options to buy and run.

Reverse osmosis, run at home, sends roughly 3 liters down the drain for every liter it produces, a smaller version of the same tradeoff bottlers make at industrial scale. Given how much of this city’s wastewater exits the basin rather than getting treated and returned, that reject water is likely gone from the Valley of Mexico’s own water cycle for good, unlike ultrafiltration, which never enters that path at all.

Ultrafiltration

Garrafón delivery carries its own documented risk: Independent testing found the majority of samples in one Mexico City study contaminated with coliform bacteria, and nearly a quarter with E. coli, in an industry that grew 85% between 2012 and 2018.

Ultrafiltration is the one choice in this entire chain that does not ask the aquifer for anything extra to keep a household safe. It does not fix the leaking network, the sinking ground, or the four centuries of trades that got the city here. It is the one piece of the cycle a single kitchen can opt out of today, without waiting on a General Water Law that has been stalled in Congress for eight years, or a recharge program that exists as exactly one working pilot against a documented crisis.

Andrew D. Daily lives in Roma Norte, where he runs a water filtration company and mexicocitytravel.com, a simplified guide for visitors. Before meeting his wife and relocating to CDMX, he worked 11 years in Los Angeles, CA, as a television Production Manager on shows like Shark Tank, The Voice, and Miss Universe.

World.title: Meet Jacinto Canek, the Maya rebel who rose against Spanish rule in Yucatán
World.content:
The people of Cisteil were tired. After years as a Spanish district, they depended heavily on the municipality of Yaxcabá, located in what is now the state of Yucatán. Despite being a relatively small town, it had a fiery population that wanted to free itself from the Spanish yoke.

Cisteil lasted no more than eight years under this abusive regime. Little did the Spanish know that this small Yucatecan town would spark a major Maya anti-colonial uprising, led by a Maya man named Jacinto Canek.

From student and Maya physician to revolutionary leader

Long before Miguel Hidalgo began the Mexican independence revolts in Dolores, in what is now the Bajío region, southeastern Maya communities were already seeking to rid themselves of Spanish invaders.

Despite his standing as a prominent figure of Maya resistance, little is known about the early life of Jacinto Uc de los Santos Canek. Born in the 18th century, he led the “most important Maya rebellion in Yucatán during the colonial era,” according to the Great Maya Museum in Yucatán.

Documentary evidence shows he was born around 1731 to a poor family in the southeastern state of Campeche. Historical records indicate he studied Latin, history and Christian doctrine at the Convento Grande in Mérida before being expelled for his rebellious nature. Canek had a strong knowledge of Christian doctrine, joined a religious organization in his hometown of San Francisco de Campeche and practiced traditional Maya medicine learned through oral tradition.

After the 1761 rebellion, “Jacinto Canek chose a name of historical significance for the Maya,” according to a study by Robert W. Patch from the University of California, Riverside. He proclaimed himself king of the movement to reclaim “political and religious domination of the Yucatán Maya.”

Thousands of Indigenous people recognized his authority and viewed him as an incarnation of Kukulkán, the sacred serpent of the Maya pantheon. Researchers note the movement sought to revitalize Maya culture after two centuries of colonialism, with revolutionaries believing the days of Spanish rule were numbered.

Jacinto Canek: Kukulkán and Christ, embodied in a Maya revolutionary

No other significant anti-colonial movement had taken place in present-day Mexico to this point. However, as a review of a criminal trial resulting from the rebellion emphasizes, “it was a highly serious rebellion, with a strong anti-colonialist content.”

Beyond establishing stronger trade ties with former Maya chiefdoms, the people of Cisteil wanted to reclaim their culture, traditions and religion. “The Maya continued to believe in a cyclic version of history,” the study points out, “which led them to think that one day in the future they would overthrow the Spaniards.”

Canek took a name sacred to two religious traditions: Maya and Christian. From 1761 onward, he was known as Jacinto Uc de los Santos Canek Chichán Moctezuma. He embodied the man-god myth of Mesoamerican tradition, presenting a syncretic Maya-Christian figure blending Jesus Christ and Kukulkán. Under that name, he summoned the highest rulers of Cisteil to wage revolution.

How the Maya remember Jacinto Canek

Yucatán Governor José de Crespo y Honorato ordered the arrest of the revolt’s leaders to quell the movement. Spanish forces captured Canek and took him to Mérida, where he was condemned to be “broken alive” — having his limbs broken with iron bars — before being executed on Dec. 14, 1761. His body was burned to ashes after his death.

Many followers were killed alongside him. Following the execution, Spanish commanders suppressed the rebellion before it could spread beyond central Yucatán.

The Spanish then launched a campaign to delegitimize the revolutionaries, framing the event as a “drunkards’ riot,” according to UNAM records. Among the Maya, however, it remained “a noble uprising against colonial exploitation.”

Today, Canek is remembered as “one of the most significant figures in the history of Yucatán” and as someone who “lives in the hearts of the women and men of the Maya people.”

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

Zacatecas closes August with its most spectacular tradition: the Morismas de Bracho, a three-day, citywide reenactment that has run for nearly two centuries.

Morismas de Bracho: Mexico’s Grand Reenactment

The Morismas de Bracho are Zacatecas’ deepest-rooted cultural tradition: since 1836, the city has honored San Juan Bautista with a theatrical reenactment of the battles between Moors and Christians, passed down through generations of families.

More than 10,000 people take part in costume — from babies carried by their parents to elders who have marched for fifty years — making it as much a act of devotion as a spectacle.

What Happens Each Day

The celebration unfolds over three days between the Historic Center and the Lomas de Bracho hills, where the battle simulations play out with horses, rockets and full period costume.

The grand parade through the city’s main streets is the emotional peak: entire battalions of ‘Moors’ and ‘Christians’ march past the pink-quarry cathedral and the UNESCO-listed streetscape.

Why Zacatecas Is Worth the Trip

Zacatecas’ historic center is a UNESCO World Heritage site — a silver-era city of pink stone, home to the Mina El Edén, a cable car crossing the city and one of Mexico’s strongest museum scenes.

The Morismas weekend is the most atmospheric moment of the year to visit: the whole city becomes a stage, and visitors are welcomed into the spectacle.

Practical Notes for Visitors

The best free viewing is along the parade route in the historic center; arrive early on the main days for curbside spots near the cathedral.

Zacatecas sits at 2,400 meters — late-August days are warm but evenings turn cool; bring a layer for the night events in the hills.

GOL Caracas Flights: The Return Schedule

GOL Caracas flights re-enter the airline’s booking system with a clear structure: G3 7230 leaves Guarulhos at 5:15 p.m. on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sundays, touching down at Simón Bolívar International at 10:20 p.m. local time.

GOL pulled out of Caracas after the earthquakes that battered Venezuela, joining a list of carriers that paused operations to the country amid the emergency.

The airline had only relaunched the route in 2025 — its first Caracas service since 2016 — making the September 15 return the second comeback for the link in just over a year.

What It Means for Brazilian–Venezuelan Travel

The resumed route restores the only nonstop Brazil–Venezuela link from São Paulo, critical for the large Venezuelan community in Brazil and for business ties between the two countries.

GOL is also studying a fourth weekly frequency before the end of the year, which would restore the full pre-suspension schedule.

A Wider Regional Reopening

The GOL move lands amid a broader normalization of Venezuela’s air links: other carriers have been restoring service to Caracas as the situation stabilizes.

For expats and nomads in São Paulo, Caracas becomes reachable again with a single evening flight — and onward Venezuelan connections via local carriers reopen with it.

World.title: Bolivia Files Illicit Enrichment Charge Against Adviser Cerimedo
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Bolivia · JUSTICE

Key Facts — Declaration Cerimedo told prosecutors on 28 August 2026 he earns close to US$1 million monthly.

— Charge Prosecutors filed a formal illicit enrichment case against the Argentine consultant on 28 August.

— Seizures Five raids on 20 and 21 August produced cash, telephones and documents.

— Palace Paz says Cerimedo never had authorization to represent the Presidency, government or family.

— Same man The attempted femicide detainee of 18 August is Cerimedo, not another adviser.

Prosecutors in Santa Cruz filed a formal charge hours after the Argentine consultant described his monthly earnings.

Fernando Cerimedo told Bolivian prosecutors on 28 August 2026 that he earns close to US$1 million a month. Hours later Bolivia’s Public Prosecutor’s Office moved the illicit enrichment case against him from inquiry to formal charge.

The Plaza Murillo in La Paz. The presidency says there was never a contract.

What Cerimedo told prosecutors in Santa Cruz

Fernando Cerimedo gave a statement to Bolivian prosecutors on 28 August 2026 in Santa Cruz de la Sierra. He answered as a formally accused person, not as a witness.

The session took place where he is already held, at the Palmasola prison complex. Prosecutor Miguel Cardozo said afterwards that many of his answers were evasive.

Cerimedo told investigators he earns close to US$1 million a month from work outside Bolivia. He said the money comes from companies he owns with his wife.

He also confirmed that President Rodrigo Paz was his main contact inside the government. Asked what he did after the election, he said the question had nothing to do with the case.

The million-dollar figure and what it covers

The figure refers to company revenue rather than a declared personal salary. Bolivian outlets reported the sum as close to US$1 million a month during 2025.

He named Numen Group Inc in the United States and Numen de Publicidad in Argentina. He also cited a training academy and an audiovisual production firm held with his wife.

Not every outlet reported the same number, and the discrepancy is unresolved here. Some Argentine media put the figure at more than half a million dollars a month instead.

Prosecutors have not accepted the explanation as proof that the money was lawful. They argue his assets grew out of proportion during 2025 and 2026, which is the core allegation.

Who Fernando Cerimedo is

Cerimedo is an Argentine media operator who founded La Derecha Diario, a right-wing outlet. He built it into a network with editions in several countries.

In 2023 he worked as a digital strategist for Javier Milei’s La Libertad Avanza. He had earlier built ties to Brazil’s Bolsonarist circles during the 2022 campaign there.

After Brazil’s 2022 vote he promoted claims of irregularities in the voting system. Brazil’s electoral court rejected those claims, and federal police examined the networks behind them.

He then moved much of his work to Bolivia and taught at his own marketing academy. He advised during the 2025 election and joined the runoff effort behind Rodrigo Paz.

How the inquiry became a formal charge

The inquiry began as an ex officio investigation opened by the departmental prosecutors in La Paz. Bolivia’s Public Prosecutor’s Office is itself the complainant in the file.

Investigators raided five properties linked to Cerimedo on 20 and 21 August 2026. They seized more than Bs 500,000 (US$41,900 at the Banco Central de Bolivia rate of Bs 11.92 on 29 August 2026).

Officers also removed dollars, euros, telephones and what prosecutors described as a small bot farm. A La Paz authority issued an arrest warrant against him on 26 August 2026.

That warrant cited Article 226 of Bolivia’s Code of Criminal Procedure. The offence is illicit enrichment by private individuals affecting the state, which is distinct from official corruption.

On 28 August the prosecution said the charging resolution would be filed within hours. Bolivian outlets reported the same day that it landed, moving the illicit enrichment case past its preliminary stage.

What the Palacio Quemado says

President Rodrigo Paz addressed the affair in a message distributed by the Presidency on 26 August 2026. He said Cerimedo never had authorization to represent him, the Presidency, the government or his family.

Paz added that there was never a contract and therefore never a direct working relationship. He said institutional representation runs through ministers, vice-ministers or a presidential delegate.

He did acknowledge that contact was made for the 2025 runoff campaign. Paz described Cerimedo as a strategist of worldwide recognition who worked on that second round.

The presidential spokesman has accepted that Cerimedo gave digital communication advice after the vote. The Palacio Quemado denies that this ever amounted to a formal post inside the state.

The evidence that cuts against the denial

Prosecutors say a search turned up business cards naming Cerimedo as principal adviser to the president. The cards carried an official presidential email domain, according to case material cited in Bolivia.

Testimony in the file says he helped draft at least two supreme decrees and one law. Nadia Beller, his former partner, has stated that he joined cabinet meetings.

None of these claims has been tested in court, and Cerimedo rejects all of them. They remain allegations inside an active file rather than findings of fact.

He has called the whole matter an attempted coup against the Paz government. His defence says it will ask for the illicit enrichment case to be placed under reserve.

Two cases, one man, not two advisers

Bolivia is pursuing Cerimedo in more than one file, and the names can be confusing. The attempted femicide case and the illicit enrichment case involve the same person.

On 17 August 2026 gunmen shot the lawyer Nadia Beller outside a hotel in Santa Cruz de la Sierra. She survived, and her complaint named Cerimedo as the person behind it.

Police detained him at Viru Viru airport the next day, on 18 August 2026. A court then ordered 180 days of preventive detention at the Palmasola prison.

The financial inquiry grew out of the searches carried out in that first case. There is no second Paz adviser behind these headlines, only one man facing separate charges.

What happens next

Prosecutors say they will seek six months of preventive detention in the enrichment file. They want him moved to Chonchocoro, the maximum security prison on the altiplano near La Paz.

A precautionary measures hearing has already been rescheduled once, and no new date is confirmed. Until a judge rules, the six-month request remains a request and nothing more.

For Paz the political cost is the harder problem, less than a year into his term. His government took office in late 2025 promising a break from the previous administration.

Foreign investors tracking Bolivia’s currency and fuel troubles now have a governance question too. The illicit enrichment case tests how far the courts will follow money into the president’s circle.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Fernando Cerimedo the same adviser detained in the attempted femicide case? Yes. The man detained on 18 August 2026 in Santa Cruz is the same Fernando Cerimedo now facing the illicit enrichment case. What exactly did Cerimedo say about his income? He told prosecutors his companies outside Bolivia bring in close to US$1 million a month. He named firms in the United States and Argentina held jointly with his wife. Has a Bolivian court convicted him of anything? No. He is charged and held in preventive detention, and no verdict has been issued in either case.

World.title: Panama Canal Transit Slot Sells for Record US$5.3 Million
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Panama · CANAL

Key Facts — Record bid SK Gas paid US$5.3 million for a single crossing on 1 September.

— Previous mark US$4.6 million, set earlier in August by a sister gas carrier.

— Normal price A winning bid sat near US$55,000 before this year’s shipping disruption.

— Capacity cut Daily transits fall from about 36 to 34 on 3 September.

— Canal revenue US$4.8 billion in the nine months to June 2026, up 17%.

Drought and diverted energy cargo have turned a leftover reservation into a seven-figure asset.

A South Korean gas carrier, the G. Spirit, paid US$5.3 million at auction for the right to cross Panama on 1 September 2026. It is the highest price ever paid for a Panama Canal transit slot.

A Panama Canal lock. The auction is separate from the published toll tariff.

What the record bid actually bought

SK Gas paid US$5.3 million for a Panama Canal transit slot in the waterway’s daily auction. The result was reported on 25 August 2026.

The ship is a liquefied petroleum gas carrier of about 54,502 tonnes deadweight, operated by SK Shipping. Its northbound crossing is booked for 1 September 2026.

The previous record was US$4.6 million, paid earlier in August by SK Shipping for a near-identical gas carrier. That bid had beaten a mark of roughly US$4.2 million set earlier in 2026.

Before this year’s disruption a typical winning bid sat near US$55,000. The new figure is close to one hundred times that level.

How the daily auction works

The Panama Canal Authority (ACP) sells reservations in booking periods, and unsold capacity feeds a daily auction. Between three and five slots reach that auction on a normal day.

Those slots come mainly from cancelled bookings rather than from positions in the queue. The authority says a Panama Canal transit slot bought at auction was already counted for that day.

Chief financial officer Victor Vial has rejected the idea that bidders jump a line. He said the auction gave the winner a slot that was already accounted for.

A confirmed reservation remains the only way to guarantee a specific transit date. Ships without one wait their turn, and lately that has meant days rather than hours.

The canal publishes its booking tariffs and auction results, so bidders can see recent levels. Those published levels have risen sharply through 2026.

Why prices climbed this fast

Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz pushed more energy cargo onto routes through the Americas. Asian buyers of liquefied petroleum gas have been paying for speed.

Auction prices ran near US$385,000 in March and April 2026. By the middle of August a single Panama Canal transit slot was fetching millions.

Vessels without reservations have faced waits of up to eleven days this month. Administrator Ricaurte Vásquez put the recent average nearer 8.5 days.

Owners weigh a bid against charter costs and a delivery window they cannot miss. Vásquez has drawn the obvious conclusion, saying that everyone has to book.

The drought behind the squeeze

Panama declared a national state of emergency in late August over El Niño. The measure runs to June 2027.

Vásquez expects the pattern to last around eight months. He has warned of very low precipitation ahead and drier soils across the watershed.

The canal reported in July that the chance of a severe El Niño had reached 81%. That warning followed almost two years without any draft restrictions.

Gatún Lake feeds the locks and also supplies drinking water to much of the country. Every crossing sends fresh water out to sea.

Advisory A-29-2026, issued on 20 August 2026, set out the response. It trims daily capacity and reorganises the auction that prices a Panama Canal transit slot.

How many crossings Panama will offer

From 3 September the canal offers nine Neopanamax and 25 Panamax reservations each day. Panamax slots fall again to 23 on 15 September.

Daily transits therefore move from about 36 now to 34, and then to 32. The drought of 2023 and 2024 had pushed that number down to 22.

A maximum authorised draft of 14.63 metres was postponed to 2 September. A further step down to 14.48 metres was postponed to 1 October.

The Panamax locks take the older and smaller ships, while the Neopanamax locks take the largest. The reductions fall on both sets of chambers.

Fewer crossings mean fewer reservations, and a scarcer Panama Canal transit slot at auction. Every cancelled booking becomes more valuable to whoever needs it next.

New booking rules from 30 August

The authority announced temporary booking changes on 28 August 2026. They take effect on 30 August and apply to bookings from 13 September.

Neopanamax customers may now hold several reservations for the same date or for consecutive dates. Vessel swaps are allowed where the replacement carries equal or greater capacity.

The canal offers 63 Neopanamax reservations a week, including long-term and NetZero allocations. Minimum allocations per booking date protect container, gas and vehicle carrier traffic.

Full container ships get at least five reservations a day, while gas carriers get three each. Bulkers, vehicle carriers and other segments share three a week.

What the squeeze means for Panama’s revenue

Canal revenue reached US$4.8 billion in the nine months to June 2026, a rise of 17%. Net income climbed 19% to US$3.6 billion.

Transits over that period totalled 10,726, up 5.2%, carrying 389.96 million tons. Auction income sits on top of the ordinary tolls.

Panama’s other maritime earner is growing on the quays rather than in the locks. The Panama Maritime Authority counted 488,567 cruise passengers between January and July 2026.

That was 21.6% more than a year earlier, on 143 ship calls against 119. Colón 2000 on the Atlantic and the Amador terminal on the Pacific handle most of them.

The next cruise season opens in October, when the tighter transit rules will already apply. The canal has not said how the cuts will affect cruise crossings.

The reservoir meant to fix this

Panama is planning a US$1.6 billion reservoir on the Río Indio to add fresh water. Vásquez has said the geology found on site may delay it by six to eight months.

Panamanian reporting puts rainfall deficits on the Pacific side near 60%. Eleven watersheds are described as under stress, a count the canal has not itself published.

Until the reservoir exists, the canal manages scarcity with draft limits and fewer bookings. That is the mechanism now pricing a Panama Canal transit slot in the millions.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a Panama Canal transit slot? It is a confirmed reservation to cross on a set date. The canal sells them in booking periods and auctions leftover capacity each day. Which ship paid the record US$5.3 million? The gas carrier G. Spirit, owned by SK Gas and operated by SK Shipping. Its northbound crossing is booked for 1 September 2026. Will these prices last? That depends on El Niño and on demand for gas cargoes heading to Asia. Daily crossings fall from 3 September, which keeps every reservation scarce.

Colombia’s fashion industry has turned solidarity into a bidding war — and every peso goes to families hit by this month’s earthquake.

Ponemos Auction Medellín: How It Works

The Ponemos auction in Medellín runs online at Subastasycomercio.com until Monday, August 31 — anyone can bid on donated designer pieces, artworks and experiences from their phone.

The grand finale is a live ascending-bid auction on Monday from 5 to 9 p.m. at the Makeno store in Medellín, where the top lots go under the hammer in person.

Who Is Behind It

The initiative was convened by Centro Democrático senator María Clara Posada together with Paola Betancur and Manuela Rubio of Makeno and Tuti Barrera and Lorenzo Márquez of Huevos y Escobas.

They rallied a who’s who of Colombian fashion: Johanna Ortiz, Silvia Tcherassi, Juan Pablo Socarrás, Faride Ramos, Maygel Coronel, Beatriz Camacho, Hernán Zajar, Paula Mendoza, Baobab, Specia, Tania, Agua by Agua Bendita and Sea & Salt, among others.

Where the Money Goes

Every peso raised goes to Fundación Presentes, which channels the funds to families and rebuilding efforts in the areas hit by the recent earthquake: Suroeste Antioqueño, Montenegro and Quimbaya.

The earthquake destroyed homes, businesses and savings in the region — organizers frame each lot as a direct, traceable contribution.

Why It Matters for Expats

For foreigners living in Medellín, Ponemos is a rare chance to buy into Colombian design culture and help the region that hosts them at the same time.

The online format means you do not need to be in Medellín to bid — only Monday’s live finale requires showing up at Makeno.
