World.title: Belize City man fined $1,500 for taking common-law wife’s money and wounding her but somebody beat him up and sent him to court with ‘batty eye’
World.content:
Belize City man fined $1,500 for taking common-law wife’s money and wounding her but somebody beat him up and sent him to court with ‘batty eye’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man has been spared jail but ordered to pay a $1,500 fine after pleading guilty to wounding his common-law wife during a domestic dispute on Central American Boulevard. He showed up to court on Friday with two “batty eye” local slang for both his eye being swollen from an apparent beating.

Thirty-four-year-old construction worker Alton Nicholson appeared unrepresented before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison in Court #6 on Friday, where he pleaded guilty to wounding his 51-year-old common-law wife.

The charge arose from an incident on Tuesday, August 25, 2026.

According to the police account, the woman was on Central American Boulevard at around 11:45 a.m. when Nicholson approached her while she was with a friend and asked for $10. She reportedly gave him a $20 bill, expecting him to return with her change.

When he did not return, the woman went looking for him. She told police that when she found Nicholson, he accused her of having a sexual relationship with one of his friends and threatened to hurt both of them.

Nicholson allegedly began dragging her toward an abandoned house. She managed to break free and run, but Nicholson chased after her and she fell, sustaining injuries.

Police arrived and later escorted the woman to the hospital, where a doctor classified her injuries as wounding.

Nicholson was also observed with swelling around both eyes and reportedly told police that he had been beaten by another man during the incident.

At his arraignment, Nicholson admitted to the offence and asked the court for leniency, telling the magistrate that he is the sole provider for his family.

As a first-time offender, Nicholson was spared an immediate prison sentence and fined $1,500 plus $5 cost of court. He has until December 31, 2026, to pay the fine or face six months in prison in default.

World.title: Free after 92 days: Trinidadian says failed Belize job arrangement left him with $11,470 Golden Bay Hotel bill
World.content:
Free after 92 days: Trinidadian says failed Belize job arrangement left him with $11,470 Golden Bay Hotel bill

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Trinidadian national Rubindra Dale Rampersad walked out of the Belize City Magistrate’s Court a free man on Friday after spending 92 days behind bars over an unpaid $11,470.24 hotel bill, and is now telling his side of the story.

The 46-year-old had been charged with making off without payment after allegedly leaving Golden Bay Hotel on May 29 without settling the bill accumulated during a month-long stay.

On Friday morning, a representative of Golden Bay Hotel confirmed to the court that the outstanding amount had been paid in full. Following a criminal mediation agreement, the charge against Rampersad was dismissed.

Rampersad, who appeared with attorney Kimberly Wallace of Lavenders Chambers, emerged from court shortly after midday and began his first interview as a free man by apologizing to our court reporter, whom he had treated disrespectfully during two previous court appearances.

He then sought to explain how he ended up in Belize and ultimately behind bars.

Rampersad said he travelled to Belize expecting to work in connection with the Millennium Challenge Account-Belize (MCA-Belize) programme. According to him, he had been promised approximately US$5,000 along with reimbursement of expenses, including his travel to Belize, but said the arrangement did not materialize as he had expected.

“I am no scam,” Rampersad said, maintaining that he travelled to Belize intending to work but found himself stranded without the financial support he expected.

His account is consistent with claims he made earlier in the case. News 5 reported in June that Rampersad alleged a procurement-related work arrangement included up to US$5,000 in relocation support, but that after he arrived he was told the reimbursement was not guaranteed. Police, meanwhile, said Golden Bay Hotel reported that a credit card used for the stay repeatedly failed and that Rampersad was intercepted at the airport after leaving the hotel without settling the bill.

MCA-Belize is the independent entity established to implement Belize’s US$125 million Millennium Challenge Corporation Compact, which focuses on education and energy. The organization has been publicly recruiting personnel for various positions throughout 2025 and 2026.

Rampersad was initially denied bail because the court considered him a flight risk, citing his lack of established ties to Belize. At subsequent hearings, the Chief Magistrate indicated bail could be considered if he secured a Belizean surety and confirmed prepaid accommodation, while his attorney, Darrell Bradley, pushed for the matter to be resolved through criminal mediation.

That mediation eventually succeeded, with Golden Bay agreeing to the settlement once its outstanding bill was paid.

Rampersad said he believes some of his constitutional rights were violated during his lengthy detention, though no court finding to that effect has been made.

Despite describing his incarceration as a difficult experience, Rampersad also spoke warmly about Belizeans and the people he met inside the Belize Central Prison.

“There are great people in prison,” he said, adding that he made friends during his more than three months behind bars and remains grateful to those who treated him well.

Rampersad leaves the ordeal without a criminal conviction in Belize and says he is simply happy to be free after 92 days in custody.

World.title: Police await CCTV after 77-year-old woman killed crossing Philip Goldson Highway
World.content:
Police await CCTV after 77-year-old woman killed crossing Philip Goldson Highway

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are awaiting surveillance footage as they investigate Thursday’s fatal traffic accident that claimed the life of 77-year-old Burrell Boom resident Erlene Gillett.

The accident occurred shortly before 11:30 a.m. on August 27 in the vicinity of Mile 2 on the Philip Goldson Highway.

Police say Gillett was attempting to cross the highway when she was struck by a Dodge Caravan being driven by a man whose name has not been released.

The vehicle has since been impounded as part of the investigation, while a sample was obtained from the driver and he was served with a Notice of Intended Prosecution.

During Friday’s police press briefing, Assistant Superintendent Stacy Smith said investigators have received assurances that surveillance footage from an establishment in the area may have captured the accident. That footage is expected to help police establish the exact circumstances surrounding the collision, including whether other motorists may have stopped to allow Gillett to cross.

Smith urged pedestrians to use designated crossing areas where available, but stressed that motorists also have a responsibility to remain alert, even when travelling within the speed limit.

Local media reports say Gillett was crossing the highway in front of My Lights when she was struck by a southbound minivan.

The investigation continues.

World.title: Police indicate inmate has died following apparent suicide attempt while in police custody
World.content:
Police indicate inmate has died following apparent suicide attempt while in police custody

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have indicated that an inmate who reportedly attempted to take his own life while in custody has since died, though police say further details on the case are still being gathered.

The matter arose during Friday afternoon’s police press briefing when reporters sought an update on the condition of the inmate.

Assistant Superintendent Stacy Smith indicated that her understanding was that the inmate had died, but said she had not yet received a complete briefing on the investigation.

Smith also indicated that a post-mortem examination was expected and said police hope to provide additional information on the matter by Monday.

Reporters raised concerns about the circumstances because the deceased was in the custody of the state at the time of the incident, placing a duty of care on the institution responsible for him.

Police did not provide the inmate’s identity, the facility where the incident occurred, or further details surrounding the apparent suicide attempt during Friday’s briefing.

The investigation remains ongoing.

World.title: International News: Missing persons near 2,000 in Nepal flood disaster
World.content:
International News: Missing persons near 2,000 in Nepal flood disaster

By Zoila Palma: The number of people reported missing after devastating flash floods in Nepal has surged to 1,924, according to the country’s disaster relief agency, as rescue teams continue searching areas devastated by a massive flood wave.

At least 517 foreign nationals are among those reported missing, although authorities have issued varying figures as the situation continues to develop, BBC reports.

Nepal’s reported death toll has risen to 579, while at least five people have died in Tibet, where 558 others are reported missing. Information from Tibet remains limited, with reports largely coming from Chinese state media as rescue and recovery operations continue near the Nepal-Tibet border.

The disaster has left widespread destruction in its wake, with one rescue worker describing the scene near the border as “nothing but ruins.”

Rescue teams are now working in extremely difficult terrain near Gyirong Port, where roads have been destroyed and dense forests and steep cliffs have hampered access.

China’s state broadcaster CCTV reported that firefighters from Tibet and Sichuan reached the area on Friday, including six Tibet fire and rescue personnel, 15 members of a Sichuan rescue team and a rescue dog.

World.title: Belize and regional partners strengthen Agricultural Disease surveillance
World.content:
Belize and regional partners strengthen Agricultural Disease surveillance

By Zoila Palma: Belize and other member countries of the International Regional Organization for Agricultural Health (OIRSA) have agreed to strengthen regional surveillance and coordination to protect agricultural production and trade from emerging diseases and pests. The agreement was reached during the 97th Extraordinary Meeting of the International Regional Committee for Agricultural Health (CIRSA) held today in Guatemala City.

The meeting brought together Ministers of Agriculture and other senior representatives from Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama and the Dominican Republic.

Belize was represented by Luis Alex Balona, Minister of State in the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries. The meeting was chaired by Guatemala’s Minister of Agriculture, Livestock and Food, María Fernanda Rivera.

Among the major agricultural health threats discussed were African Swine Fever, Fusarium Wilt Tropical Race 4 and Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza. Regional authorities noted that these diseases can cross borders and cause significant impacts on agricultural production and international trade. To address the risks, countries agreed to maintain constant surveillance and strengthen standardized prevention and response protocols, particularly at borders, ports and airports.

The meeting also examined the growing impact of extreme weather events on agricultural health. Changes in rainfall patterns and rising temperatures can create favourable conditions for the emergence and spread of pests and diseases, making regional cooperation increasingly important. Authorities emphasized that coordinated action is essential to protect farmers and the communities that depend on healthy and resilient agricultural systems.

CIRSA members also reviewed efforts to strengthen OIRSA as a regional institution, including progress toward approving its 2026–2036 Strategic Plan, a new Investment Policy and updated organizational regulations. These measures are intended to improve the capacity of member countries to detect, prevent and respond to agricultural health threats while protecting food production and regional trade.

World.title: Belize hosts regional Fruit Fly meeting as 50-year Medfly Control programme reaches milestone
World.content:
Belize hosts regional Fruit Fly meeting as 50-year Medfly Control programme reaches milestone

By Zoila Palma: Belize hosted the XII Meeting of the Fruit Fly Commission on August 27, 2026, in Placencia, bringing together senior representatives from the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), Mexico’s SENASICA, Guatemala’s MAGA, the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries (MAFSNGI), and the Belize Agricultural Health Authority (BAHA).

The annual meeting serves as a key platform for regional coordination under the Trinational Agreement between the United States, Mexico and Guatemala to prevent and control the spread of the Mediterranean fruit fly (Medfly) into North America.

Commissioners reviewed achievements, assessed emerging risks and priorities, and agreed on the joint work programme and budget for 2027, with the continued protection of the Medfly-free areas of Belize and Petén, Guatemala remaining a priority.

This year’s meeting also marked the 50th anniversary of the regional Medfly programme and Belize’s national programme, which began in 1976 with support from the USDA.

Over the past five decades, BAHA’s plant health teams have maintained Belize’s Medfly-free status through ongoing surveillance and rapid response efforts, helping protect agricultural production and preserve access to international markets for commodities that are hosts of the pest.

The milestone also provided an opportunity to recognize BAHA officers whose technical expertise and dedicated fieldwork have contributed to the programme’s success, with staff receiving awards for their service.

The meeting concluded with Chief Executive Officer Servulo Baeza signing the 2027 Cooperative Agreement between Belize and the United States, securing continued technical and financial support for the country’s Medfly prevention and control efforts.

World.title: Ministry of Agriculture and FAO train officers to protect Coconut Industry from pests and disease
World.content:
Ministry of Agriculture and FAO train officers to protect Coconut Industry from pests and disease

By Zoila Palma: The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), in partnership with the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries (MAFSNGI), has concluded a five-day Training of Trainers Workshop focused on coconut pest and disease management.

The training, held in Belmopan, forms part of FAO’s technical cooperation programme supporting the revision of Belize’s National Rural Development Strategy, with a specific focus on the coconut sector.

The initiative also supports the global “One Country One Priority Product” (OCOP) initiative, which promotes green enterprise and sustainable development within Belize’s growing coconut industry.

Participants included members of the Ministry’s fruit tree programme team, district extension officers and officers from the Caribbean Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI) involved in coconut production.

During the first four days, participants received technical training on integrated pest management strategies for major threats to coconut production, including the coconut weevil, red mites and red ring disease. The sessions covered pest and disease identification, host recognition and modern management techniques to strengthen the ability of agricultural officers to diagnose problems quickly and provide farmers with appropriate guidance.

The workshop concluded with practical field and laboratory exercises, where participants identified mite infestations and signs of fungal diseases in coconut plantations and learned laboratory techniques for confirming red ring disease in infected plant tissue.

The trained officers will next take these practices to farmers across the country, with district-level training sessions scheduled for September and October 2026 as Belize works to protect smallholder livelihoods, strengthen sustainable farming and build climate resilience in the coconut sector.

World.title: Cooper’s Pen pledge
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness (second left) in dialogue with Cooper’s Pen resident Debbie Lewis (second right) during a tour of the community on Friday. Looking on are (from left) minister of state in the Office of the Prime Minister Senator Abka Fitz-Henley; Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett; and Member of Parliament for Trelawny Northern Tova Hamilton. Photo: Horace Hines

COOPER’S PEN, Trelawny — Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness has given a commitment to “personally oversee” the relocation of residents of Cooper’s Pen whose houses were demolished during a dispute over privately owned land, saying he may have to invoke emergency powers to get the process started by December.

Residents will be provided with a relocation grant to replace belongings damaged during the eviction, but they will have to pay for the land and utilities once they are resettled. Two sites within Trelawny are being contemplated for the subdivision which will house them.

Holness — who on Friday toured the community alongside Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett, Trelawny Northern Member of Parliament Tova Hamilton, and state minister in the Office of the Prime Minister Abka Fitz-Henley — said his intention is to move eligible residents into a properly planned community instead of shifting them from one informal settlement to another.

“My wish is that by December we could start the process of the relocation,” Holness told residents.

He cautioned, however, that the December timeline was not a firm commitment, given the number of factors involved, including the need for contractors and infrastructure works, as well as possible delays caused by weather.

“It means that I may have to use emergency powers to address some of the situation,” he said.

The prime minister also pointed out that of the two sites being contemplated, the one closer to Cooper’s Pen may not be large enough.

“I don’t believe we can accommodate all the legitimate claims that are here,” Holness said, explaining that by legitimate he meant individuals who had been acknowledged as squatters on the land before the court action and orders.

The lots will be surveyed and pegged, there will be roads, water, and electricity, and land titling will also be part of the plan.

But Holness was emphatic that the land would not be free.

Options available to residents, based on their circumstances, include long-term leases, outright purchase, and social housing arrangements for those assessed as unable to afford the cost.

Some residents who contribute to the National Housing Trust (NHT), he noted, could access their contributions to assist with acquiring the property.

For those found to have little or no means, the prime minster said there could be fully or heavily subsidised lots, with some contribution from residents through “sweat equity”.

“Government’s role is to make it affordable,” Holness said, adding that the objective was to put residents on a legitimate path to property ownership rather than perpetuate what he described as a “freeness” mentality.

He also explained the rationale behind the relocation grant.

“The Government couldn’t take up public taxpayers’ money and pay for damage caused by a private action,” he said, adding that the distinction was important to avoid setting a legal precedent that would lock the Government into being held responsible for similar circumstances in the future.

Holness framed the Cooper’s Pen saga as a pivotal moment in the country’s long-running battle with a culture of squatting.

“I see Cooper’s Pen as the watershed. This is the incident that must change Jamaica’s spatial settlement for the better,” he argued.

The prime minister said a social survey is already being conducted to determine who should benefit from the relocation programme. The Ministry of Housing has interviewed about 70 per cent of the occupants, he said, while the survey team is being augmented by the Social Development Commission along with the Ministry of Labour and Social Security.

The combined exercise, he said, will provide a clearer picture of the households, families, and vulnerable people in the community and help determine who qualifies for assistance.

Holness also warned that people who had not been living in the community before the demolition should not attempt to move in to take advantage of the Government’s response.

“I want to make it clear that anybody [who is] trying to scam the system, it won’t work!” he said.

“Bear in mind that we don’t have limitless resources, so the more people we have to accommodate, is the less you get,” he told residents.

He also reiterated that his Government does not condone or encourage squatting, adding that he has tasked Minister with Responsibility for Land Titling and Settlements Robert Montague to review the Government’s policies for dealing with squatter settlements and return with a broader proposal on regularisation and relocation.

Holness used the occasion to criticise previous administrations which, he argued, encouraged people to occupy land informally with the expectation that their status would eventually be regularised.

“The answer can’t be to acquire property illegally. The answer must be to create a process through which all Jamaicans — regardless of your colour, your class, your place of birth, your religion, your status in society — you have a fair opportunity to acquire property,” he said, adding that he was determined not to repeat those missteps.

Still, the prime minister struck a sympathetic tone with the displaced residents, saying the Government recognises the difficult circumstances in which they now find themselves.

“I don’t want any of you to feel as if the State has abandoned you. I don’t want you to feel shame, and I don’t want you to see the Government as your enemy,” he said.

“The fact is that you are also a victim of history and a victim of bad government policy… My objective is to make all of you here property owners,” he added.

World.title: ‘A master of the craft’
World.content:
Former Calabar Head Boy Dervan Malcolm, on one of the many outside broadcasts he did for Power 106.

THE Jamaican media fraternity lost one of its most distinctive voices on Thursday with the passing of veteran broadcaster Dervan Malcolm after a long illness.

Members of the media, political, business, and Diaspora communities were effusive in their tributes to Malcolm who entered the media landscape in 1993 at the now-defunct

Power 106 while still serving as head boy of Calabar High School.

Leading the tributes was Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness, who remembered Malcolm for his “calm, distinct and trusted voice”.

“Through his work at Power 106 and especially his programme, Both Sides of the Story, he created space for meaningful conversations on the issues that matter to Jamaicans at home and in the diaspora.

“Dervan was a consummate communicator who used his platform to inform, educate, and empower. His commitment to public discourse, road safety, child protection, entrepreneurship, and the Jamaican Diaspora reflected a deep desire to make a positive difference,” said Holness as he expressed condolence to Malcolm’s family, friends, colleagues and the wider media fraternity.

“Jamaica has lost a respected broadcaster and a distinctive voice whose contribution will not be forgotten,” added Holness.

In the meantime, Opposition spokeswoman on information Nekeisha Burchell described Malcolm as “a super talent and a master of the broadcast craft”.

“Dervan Malcolm was blessed with a powerful, silky voice, but his gift went far beyond the quality of his voice. He was poised, controlled, and totally unruffled behind the microphone, with a signature style that was unmistakably his own.

“He was among that early generation of broadcasters who helped to shape Power 106 and define it as an informative, accessible, middle-of-the-road station where Jamaicans could engage seriously with the issues of the day while still being entertained,” said Burchell.

“Under the leadership of Newton James, Dervan and others helped to establish the character of the station. Even in his earliest programmes, his talent was evident. There was something wonderfully Jamaican about the call-in programmes he hosted. Each exchange felt familiar and authentic, while remaining respectful and entertaining. Dervan could connect with people from every walk of life without ever losing his composure or command of the programme,” added Burchell.

She said Malcolm’s extraordinary range distinguished him even among accomplished broadcasters.

“He was an adept voice impersonator who could portray characters with remarkable ease and precision, and his command of Spanish was another dimension of his talent. He would weave Spanish effortlessly into his broadcasts, never boastfully or simply for effect. You could leave his programme having learnt something new, sometimes even in another language. That was Dervan: Informed without being overbearing, confident without being boastful, authoritative without being disrespectful. His versatility reflected the breadth of the man and his mastery of communication,” said Burchell.

For his part, veteran journalist and head of Nationwide News Network Cliff Hughes said, with Malcolm’s death Jamaica has lost one of its most talented exponents of the art of broadcasting

“Blessed with a rare ability to communicate flawlessly, Dervan distinguished himself as a hard-working professional, a dedicated pro who evolved as an advocate of the diaspora community,” said Hughes.

The Press Association of Jamaica (PAJ) also paid tribute to Malcom, noting that he “was a respected and influential voice in Jamaican broadcasting whose career spanned more than three decades”.

“He dedicated 31 years of service to the Independent Radio Company, building a reputation as a consummate professional, a trusted journalist, and a passionate advocate for public education and national development,” the PAJ said.

The PAJ pointed out that Malcolm’s journey into broadcasting was rooted in his success in the performing arts, including his participation in the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission’s Festival of the Performing Arts.

“Dervan represented the very best of Jamaican broadcasting and journalism. He understood that journalism is not simply about reporting what is happening; it is about helping people understand the issues that shape their lives,” PAJ President Dashan Hendricks said.

“His work with the diaspora is particularly noteworthy. We will remember Dervan for his professionalism, warmth and commitment to public service, all of which earned him the respect of colleagues and audiences alike,” Hendricks added.

The PAJ said that throughout Malcom’s “distinguished career”, he served in several key roles, including news presenter and editor, sportscaster, talk show producer and executive producer of programmes.

“In 2007, he launched and hosted Both Sides of the Story on Power 106 FM, a programme that became synonymous with informed and balanced public discourse. Through that platform, Dervan sought to educate, empower, and enlighten listeners while championing entrepreneurship and civic engagement,” the PAJ said.

It added that Malcom’s impact extended well beyond the studio as he was a strong advocate for road afety, child protection, and issues affecting Jamaicans living overseas.

“His dedication to the Jamaican Diaspora earned him numerous accolades, including the Union of Jamaican Alumni Associations’ Diaspora Ambassador in Media Award and the Team Jamaica Bickle Award for his service, journalism and commitment to Diaspora-related issues. His work was also recognised by the City of Los Angeles and the Jamaica Awareness Association of California,” the PAJ said, adding: “His voice may be silent, but his contribution to Jamaican journalism and public service will not be forgotten.”

World.title: Holness to tighten eviction rules
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness is welcomed by head of the Trelawny Police Division Superintendent Velonique Campbell during his visit to Cooper’s Pen, Trelawny, on Friday. (Photo: Horace Hines)

TRELAWNY, Jamaica — Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness says he will move to tighten rules governing security-force involvement in evictions after displaced Cooper’s Pen residents complained about the conduct of police and soldiers during the early-morning demolition of their homes on privately owned land.

Holness said he will take the matter to the National Security Council to establish clear rules for how security forces should operate when supporting evictions.

“What is clear is that the operation, as it was executed, needs policy guidance,” Holness told residents during a tour of the community on Friday.

“That is where I come in as your prime minister, to make sure that subsequent operations are done according to the law, and with respect for your dignity and your rights,” he added.

Holness was responding to complaints from residents that members of the security forces had detained men from the community before the August 11, 2026 demolition which was carried out on a court order.

The action sparked questions about whether the Government knew the operation was going to take place.

On Friday, Holness reiterated that he had no prior knowledge of the demolition as he was neither informed nor consulted about when it would be carried out.

“Nobody wrote to me or advised me of it,” he said.

He also rejected suggestions that the operation was directed by his Administration, stressing that there is a separation between the Government and the police when it comes to police operations.

“No prime minister or minister of national security can direct police operations, and I want that to be clear,” Holness said.

He explained that while the Government is responsible for setting policy, it does not interfere with operational decisions by the police.

Holness said the police have a duty to maintain peace and may act preventively where there is a risk of loss of life or destruction of property.

“So yes, the police are in the right to support the eviction, to give support to the eviction process,” he said.

But the prime minister suggested that the authority of the security forces to support an eviction must be distinguished from the manner in which the operation is carried out.

It is that aspect of the process, he said, that will form part of the policy discussion with the security forces at the National Security Council.

Holness also accused some critics of using the Cooper’s Pen controversy for political gain, saying he is often blamed when problems arise.

“I represent the source of solutions, and equally, if solutions don’t come, and you need somebody to blame, it’s ultimately me,” he said.

“But I think it is being used in a political way to gain political advantage, and when it reaches that, then I have to stand up and say ‘No, it is not true’,” he added.

World.title: Vincent Chen eulogised as a man of quiet strength
World.content:
Vincent George Chen (Kasey Williams)

MANDEVILLE, Manchester — The patriarch and co-founder of SuperPlus Food Stores, Vincent George Chen, was on Thursday eulogised as a man of few words with a strong measure of work and worth evident in his legacy through his children.

Chen, the father of SuperPlus Chairman Wayne Chen and husband of the late Hyacinth Gloria Chen, died on August 17 at age 96.

Together the couple raised nine children — NCB Chairman Michael Lee-Chin, Wayne, Charles, Jody, Lisa, Bobby, Collin, Jeremy, and Richard.

“Dad was the product of two people — Edward, the frustrated scholar who came across an ocean from a small village [Ten Sim Wui in China] to start a life in a strange place, and Iris, who came from a small village [Kilmarnock in St Elizabeth], the descendant of rebellious and freed former African slaves. [They] came to Port Antonio,” Wayne Chen told congregants during the thanksgiving service held at Saint Paul of the Cross Cathedral in Mandeville.

He explained that there was strong economic activity in Port Antonio, which pulled many people there to settle.

“Port Antonio was the most prosperous town in Jamaica in the 1910s and the 1920s; it was the birthplace of the global fruit trade. The banana industry was king. People were making fortunes…” he said.

According to Chen, his father was sent to Kingston to learn the Chinese language, but left after two years.

“He felt bullied. He felt targeted and discriminated against. He said there was one particular housekeeper that, if anything went wrong… [said] he must be at the centre of it,” said Wayne Chen.

The elder Chen then went to Titchfield High for two years where he completed school.

“He… never sat the final exams. By the time it came around to pay exam fees [his father] didn’t have any money so fees were never paid, and there ended dad’s formal education,” said Wayne Chen.

From a young age Chen worked in grocery stores at Snowhill, St Margaret’s Bay, and Port Antonio.

While working in Port Antonio he met Hyacinth Gloria and got married. Life then quickly transitioned in what would become the growth and moving of their family and the building of many businesses.

“They started their own dry goods store (named Chen’s) on West Street in Port Antonio. My dad also worked as a projectionist in the Delmar Theatre. He became a salesman at the Singer sewing machine company and travelled all over [Portland],” said Wayne Chen.

In 1967 the family moved to Priory, St Ann, when Chen was promoted as regional manager at the company.

“In 1968 he was again transferred, this time to Mandeville, to be regional manager for the southern region. Mandeville became our home,” said Wayne Chen.

In 1969 Chen left the company and joined his wife at her toy and baby store, Humpty Dumpty, at Manchester Shopping Centre.

“In 1973, amidst the shortages and lack of import licences, they sold the toy and baby business and bought a supermarket in Christiana. In 1978 they sold it and were planning to immigrate to the United States. They stayed home for a year,” said Wayne Chen.

The couple then bought another supermarket in Mandeville, called L & M, at Park Crescent in the town centre.

“I won’t get into the long history of the grocery business,” Wayne Chen said in moving on to speak personally about his father, whom he described as a gentleman who was gracious, quiet, patient, iconic and a man of few words.

“Mom was the more voluble, outgoing partner. More people knew mom. She was the one everybody saw and heard first and most often,” he said, adding that his dad was the ying to his mom’s yang.

“They formed a strong and successful partnership that raised a large family and built a business,” said Wayne Chen.

“He worked very hard at it for decades in the business. Six days a week, very long hours — oftentimes working a second job after the shop had closed to provide for this large and growing family — but he always still found time for the Sunday drives,” said Wayne Chen.

The elder Chen was described as being very artistic.

“Mom used to say if dad had completed his education properly he would have been an engineer, but in hindsight… he may well have been an artist because he had a very natural talent for drawing, and his handwriting was unique and brilliant right up to the end,” said Wayne Chen.

Thursday’s thanksgiving service was attended by hundreds of people, among them business, health, education and civic leaders.

World.title: WATCH: PM says he has no power to keep Cooper’s Pen residents on land
World.content:
Prime Minister Andrew Holness speaking to residents in Cooper's Pen, Trelawny on Friday, August 28, 2026. (Photo: Horace Hines)

TRELAWNY, Jamaica – Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness told residents of Cooper’s Pen in Trelawny, whose houses were demolished earlier this month, that he has no power to keep them on the land.

He made the revelation to the residents during a tour of the community Friday, accompanied by Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett and Member of Parliament for Trelawny Northern, Tova Hamilton.

Before beginning the tour of the demolished area, the prime minister spoke with residents and told them he would meet with them again after the tour.

He said he would announce possible solutions following the tour.

On August 11, some 20 houses were demolished in the community, leaving roughly 20 families homeless and affecting approximately 40 families overall.

Since the demolition, residents have staged two separate demonstrations calling for the prime minister’s intervention and assistance.

– Horace Hines

World.title: Courage under fire
World.content:
Firefighters battle the inferno at Super Parts Limited on Hagley Park Road on Thursday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Employees of Superior Parts Limited and a taxi driver battled to save millions of dollars worth of motorcycles and cars on Thursday as a raging fire tore through the company on Hagley Park Road in St Andrew, while firefighters were hampered by a lack of water amid the severe drought that has triggered water restrictions in sections of the island.

Although firefighters from seven stations in Kingston and St Catherine responded, the majority of the stock was destroyed in the midday inferno that sent thick black smoke into the air and created traffic snarls on Hagley Park Road and adjoining thoroughfares.

In the midst of the chaos and destruction, 71-year-old Leroy Terlon used a forklift to remove numerous wooden boxes from the premises and placed them on the road.

“I had to put out the energy and the effort to get certain things saved. I have been here for 20 years and I helped to build the company to where it is now, with labour and loyalty. This event shouldn’t have happened,” Terlon told the Jamaica Observer as he sipped a cold beer at a nearby gas station following his heroics.

He said he was cooling off after his exposure to the intense heat.

“This hurts me. This company is like mine. If I talk about it, tears will come to my eyes. I have been there for so long. It hurts me. I don’t have liquid cash in the business, but I have years of service,” he added as he received congratulatory messages from friends for his bravery.

Other employees also rushed to move stock from the building, while taxi operator Kemal Dunn used his car to tow motor vehicles from a car mart adjoining the burning property.

“I just saw it and said I had to help. I knew it would spread because Superior has a lot of boxes,” he told the Observer.

“I was just driving past. My uncle owns a car dealership up the road. This car dealership just started. For a trying man, I decided to just assist him as best as I could,” Dunn explained.

“Only one car got damaged out of more than 30 that were there. I helped them rescue a good 20 of them. I used my car to pull out some. We used a wire to jump-start others because they were parked for a good while and they had no power to start. I am glad I helped them to minimise the loss.

“I was just watching the electric wire. The fire, you just have to know how to stay a good distance because you are going to feel the heat. The wires were sparking and gashing.”

“I love to help a person and he can pass it on to a next person. I am not going to take my phone and video when I can help,” he added, taking an apparent jab at the many onlookers who stood recording the fire with their cellphones.

Dunn said he banged on the windows of neighbouring houses to ensure that no humans were inside.

“All of these things are material things that can be replaced. A lot of people won’t have a job tomorrow, but they still have life,” Dunn reasoned.

As the fire raged, people in a number of adjoining residential and commercial premises moved out as many supplies and furniture before the flames spread.

One Superior Parts employee, who wished to remain anonymous, speculated that welding sparked the blaze.

“There was welding going on around the back. The fire started around that side. Nobody is allowed to smoke on property, so we believe it started with the welding. We don’t see any other way the fire could have started,” the worker said.

Amid the devastation wrought by the fire, police were kept on their toes by onlookers who wanted to get close-up shots to post on social media. Cops were heard repeatedly telling them to remove from the area for their safety.

Other onlookers were heard venting that the motorbikes were being destroyed and the police did not allow them to go in and grab one for themselves.

Throughout the ordeal, power lines caught fire, sending sparks flying and forcing people to take cover. At the same time, numerous loud explosions were heard coming from the premises.

Three firefighters were reportedly injured during their attempt to put the blaze out.

The Observer was told that the Jamaica Fire Brigade had received a call alerting it to the fire at 12:08 pm. Units from Trench Town initially responded, but according to a firefighter who requested anonymity because he was not authorised to speak to the media, the magnitude of the fire was so great that units had to be requested from other stations.

“There were units from York Park, Half-Way-Tree, Rollington Town, Port Royal, Stony Hill, Portmore, and Spanish Town,” the firefighter said, while pointing to the difficulty they experienced accessing water at the scene.

“The water challenges were expected because of the drought conditions. A lot of the hydrants have no water or low water pressure and it was a massive fire,” he added.

Up to 6:00 pm, the fire had not been fully extinguished.

World.title: Sandals Foundation head Heidi Clarke honoured with 2026 Skift IDEA Trailblazer Award
World.content:
CLARKE... I believe the success of any business should also be measured by the opportunities it creates for others to rise, empowering generations and strengthening communities

IN recognition of her far-reaching impact, Sandals Foundation Executive Director Heidi Clarke has been selected to receive the prestigious ‘Trailblazer Award: Women Shaping the Future of Travel,’ as part of the 2026 Skift IDEA Awards.

The Skift IDEA Awards are the travel industry’s way of recognising excellence in design, creativity, and innovation with winners being a beacon of where the industry is heading.

Presented in partnership with Women Leading Travel, the Trailblazer Award honours a woman whose career demonstrates exceptional leadership, resilience, and influence in shaping the future of travel.

Clarke, who heads the philanthropic arm of Sandals and Beaches resorts, has harnessed the power of tourism to strengthen communities and expand opportunity across the Caribbean.

Since the launch of the not-for-profit Sandals Foundation in 2009, Clarke has led initiatives that improve lives across the Caribbean, with a focus on education, community development, and environmental conservation in the nine islands where Sandals and Beaches resorts operate.

Under her care, the foundation has touched more than 1.8 million lives, supporting more than 2,600 schools, close to 200 large-scale conservation initiatives, and mobilising more than 32,500 volunteers across the region, among other extraordinary projects.

“It is truly an honour to be recognised, and I am immensely proud of what our team, together with our incredible partners, has made possible,” said Clarke.

“I believe the success of any business should also be measured by the opportunities it creates for others to rise, empowering generations and strengthening communities. Tourism has an extraordinary footprint, and when we harness that reach with purpose it can be a tremendous force for positive change across our Caribbean region,” added Clarke.

Her work has championed tourism as a force for positive, lasting change, bringing together communities, governments, non-profit organisations, businesses and travellers to address local needs and strengthen the destinations that sustain the industry.

Born and raised in Jamaica, she has spent nearly two decades developing programs that strengthen communities, expand economic opportunity and advance environmental stewardship throughout the Caribbean.

“Heidi is a true champion for the Caribbean and has dedicated her career to creating opportunities for its people and building a stronger future for the region,” said Adam Stewart, executive chairman of Sandals and Beaches Resorts and president of Sandals Foundation. “She leads with tremendous heart and purpose, and with an unwavering belief in the potential of our Caribbean communities. Her work through the Sandals Foundation is at the heart of who we are at Sandals Resorts and Beaches Resorts, and reflects our deep and enduring commitment to the region we call home. This recognition is incredibly well-deserved, and we could not be prouder of Heidi and the contributions she continues to make,” added Stewart.

The Skift IDEA Awards are now in their eighth year. The 2026 winners were evaluated through an initial review by the Skift Editorial Team, followed by an independent judging panel of travel and business leaders representing top hospitality organisations.

World.title: Dancehall gets recognition from the JUNO Awards
World.content:
2025 JUNO nominee Skystar.

AHEAD of the 2027 staging of the JUNO Awards, Canada’s equivalent to the Grammys, the Canadian Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences (CARAS) has introduced a series of category and eligibility updates.

These updates, according to CARAS in a press release shared with the Jamaica Observer, are designed to better reflect Canada’s music community and to provide clear, meaningful pathways for artistes to have their work recognised.

The category Reggae Recording of the Year has been renamed Reggae/Dancehall Recording of the Year. The reggae category was first instituted in 1985 as Best Reggae/Calypso Recording. For the 1994 staging, the category was renamed Best Reggae Recording, with the name Reggae Recording of the Year coming into effect in 2003.

Canada-based dancehall artiste Phenique is pleased with the evolution of the JUNO Awards.

“I’m excited to see the JUNO Awards continuing to evolve and recognise the diversity within today’s music. I think these changes create more opportunities for artists across different genres to have their work recogniSed and celebrated. It’s definitely a positive step forward,” Phenique told the Jamaica Observer on Tuesday.

Recording artiste, broadcaster and curator of the weekly Reggae North Canadian Reggae/Dancehall Top 20 chart, Tony Anthony, believes that the inclusion of dancehall is long overdue.

“The inclusion of Dancehall in the JUNO Awards’ Reggae/Dancehall Recording of the Year category is a significant and long-overdue step forward for our community. Industry professionals and supporters within the reggae and Dancehall community have advocated for Dancehall to be properly recognised on one of Canada’s biggest music stages. This announcement is not just a change in the name of a category—it is an acknowledgment of the cultural impact, creativity and contribution that Dancehall has made to Canadian music and to the broader music industry. This is an important milestone, but also a reminder that our community must continue to advocate for both genres and ensure that its artists receive the respect, visibility and opportunities that come with being recognized as a vital part of Canada’s music industry,” Tony Anthony disclosed.

2025 JUNO nominee dancehall artiste Skystar, who is originally from the Kingston 20 area, sees the revamping of the reggae category to include dancehall as a step forward.

“I’m excited to see the JUNOS expanding the conversation to officially recognise dancehall. Reggae is deeply rooted in Jamaican culture, but Dancehall has grown into a powerful global movement that continues to influence music, fashion, language and youth culture around the world,” he noted. “For artists like myself who represent the next generation of Jamaican music here in Canada, this recognition matters. It tells us that the sound, culture and evolution of our music are being seen and valued. I believe this is a great step forward, and I hope we continue creating space for the many different sounds and generations that make Reggae and Dancehall so powerful. Respect to the JUNOS for recognising the culture.”

However, Carrie Mullings, former chair of the Reggae Committee for the JUNO Awards, says dancehall music was always submitted for consideration.

“During my time with the JUNO’s (17 years, 12 as a chair) the category already consisted of dancehall submissions when you read the category description. As much as it is nice for the word Dancehall to be included in the category title it was never excluded. I feel these small steps are good but the bigger conversation in my opinion is the fact that an album body of work and a single can be submitted in the same category. We should be addressing the reason the category has not been split into 2, 1 for Reggae/Dancehall Recording of The Year (for single submissions) and 1 for Reggae/Dancehall Album/EP of the Year. As our music grows, collectively we should express our needs for expansion and recognition. Reggae/dancehall has walked the JUNO Red Carpet since 1985, please acknowledge our culture’s growth and award it accordingly,” said Mullings.

Other category changes for the 2027 JUNO Awards include:

Rap: Melodic Rap Recording of the Year and Rap Recording of the Year will replace Rap Album/EP of the Year and Rap Single of the Year.

Electronic/Dance: Electronic/Dance Single of the Year and Electronic/Dance Album/EP of the Year will replace Electronic Album of the Year and Dance Recording of the Year.

Contemporary Christian/Gospel: Contemporary Christian/Gospel Recording of the Year will replace Contemporary Christian/Gospel Album of the Year, with singles, EPs and albums now eligible.

The submission for awards and songs for consideration for the 2027 staging of the JUNO Awards will open on September 21 with November 5 being the final submission date.

The 56th annual JUNO Awards will be broadcast live from Canada Life Centre in Winnipeg, Manitoba, on Sunday, April 4, 2027. JUNO Week runs from April 1 to 4, 2027.

World.title: Trump-shaped ecstasy pills can be fatal, Dutch drug institute warns
World.content:
The tablets are shaped like the U.S. commander-in-chief’s head, researchers say.

An ecstasy pill shaped like the head of U.S. President Donald Trump is potentially lethal and should not be taken “under any circumstances,” a Dutch drug institute has warned.

The pills come in different colors, are shaped like the commander-in-chief’s head and are stamped with the words “Trump” and “NL,” according to a red alert issued by the Trimbos Institute, a drug and addiction research center based in Utrecht, on Friday.

It's currently not possible to know how many of the pills are in circulation, but "multiple" drug-testing locations have received them, Anniek Groothuis, a spokesperson for the institute, told POLITICO. Testers have previously encountered pills shaped like Superman logos or featuring car brands, Groothuis said.

World.title: Germany plans to blame Russia for Leipzig attack as tensions with Putin escalate
World.content:
One of the officials familiar with the matter said that in response to the Leipzig drone incident, it was no longer enough to expel individual Russian diplomats or close the Russian House in Berlin. Tougher measures were needed, such as intensified sanctions or even more extensive arms deliveries to Ukraine. The three officials declined to provide further details on which precise measures Merz plans to announce.

It is unclear to what extent Berlin plans to hold individual Russian actors or the Russian government itself responsible for the attempted drone attack. Berlin is already preparing for a sharp counter reaction, as the officials said that Germany must prepare for punitive measures by Moscow.

The planned move lands amid high tension with Russia, amid a spate of incidents on European soil that top officials have described as "hybrid warfare." On Tuesday, CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a surprise trip to Moscow where he warned the Russian government against escalating tensions with NATO. But the timing of Merz' expected announcement is also domestically sensitive. On Sunday next week, elections will take place in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, followed by elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin two weeks later. In Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — known for its pro-Russia stance — is leading in the polls.

Merz had already announced Tuesday that there would be severe consequences for the Leipzig incident, though without naming any specific party.

“The drone attack in Leipzig, among other things, shows that we are also facing very real threats,” he said. “The federal government is making the perpetrators of hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for this.”

In response to questions from POLITICO about Germany's plan to hold Russia directly responsible, a government spokesperson said: “The Chancellery does not engage in speculation. The only thing that matters is the official attribution made by the federal government at its own discretion and after weighing all the results of the investigation.”

World.title: Russia kills 27 as drone hits ammo warehouse near homes in Ukraine
World.content:
The warehouse appears to have been storing ammunition; Zelenskyy referred to a detonation after the drone strikes, and to a police investigation into why ordnance was stored close to residential properties, which is prohibited. Criminal proceedings on charges of negligence have also begun. “Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions,” he said.

Russia is bombarding Kyiv with “virtually nonstop attack from jet-powered drones,” Zelenskyy added. In a separate video address Friday evening, he admitted Ukraine needs to “significantly accelerate” production of interceptors capable of taking down the Iranian-designed, jet-powered Shahed drones.

In response to Russia’s increased attacks, Ukraine plans to launch 1,000 long-range drones into Russia every day, up from a current average of 300. There “must be more” strikes, Zelenskyy said Friday night.

Kyiv’s use of long-range drones — striking deep into Russia, disrupting its economy, logistics and bringing the reality of the war to ordinary Russians previously shielded from it — has in recent months improved Ukraine’s position in the conflict. One Ukrainian commander has described them as “our most important card in this war.”

While noting Kyiv's priority is to strengthen defenses against jet-powered drones, sending more long-range drones into Russia will make it “feel even more responsible for its choice to continue this war,” Zelenskyy said Friday night.

In the same address, he also pointed to signs that Russia’s economy is ailing, including the fact that it is now importing gasoline, an unusual step for one of the world's largest oil exporters.

Zelenskyy also said American representatives briefed Ukraine on the recent unexpected visit to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe, who warned Russian officials not to escalate conflict with America’s NATO allies. Zelenskyy thanked the U.S. for the "necessary tone of the conversation with Russia."

World.title: Ein Spaziergang mit Manuela Schwesig
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Strand, Sonne und ein erbitterter Kampf um das politische Überleben. In Rostock-Warnemünde begleitet Gordon Repinski Manuela Schwesig auf einem Spaziergang durch den Wahlkampfendspurt in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Die SPD-Ministerpräsidentin will ihr Land unbedingt gegen den erstarkenden AfD-Herausforderer verteidigen.

Um die Menschen an der Ostsee zu überzeugen, schlägt Schwesig ihren ganz eigenen Weg ein und geht auf maximale Distanz zur Bundespolitik. Sie attackiert den wirtschaftlichen Kurs von CDU-Kanzler Friedrich Merz schonungslos und fordert einen staatlichen Preisdeckel für Sprit. Die arbeitende Mitte dürfe in diesen Zeiten nicht länger die Hauptlast tragen, ist ihr Mantra.

Neben scharfen Angriffen in der Rentendebatte zeigt sich Schwesig beim Spaziergang aber auch von der persönlichen Seite. Sehr offen reflektiert sie ihre überstandene Krebserkrankung und wie dieser Schicksalsschlag ihren politischen Fokus verändert hat.

World.title: Ousted Ukrainian defense chief Fedorov takes advisory role with Italy
World.content:
Fedorov, who called for wartime elections after being pushed out of government in President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s latest reshuffle, also stressed that he is not decamping to Rome. “My main focus remains unchanged,” he wrote, adding he will continue working in Ukraine on projects to strengthen the country’s defense and attract international resources.

Crosetto first offered the position in July, saying he called Fedorov the day after his dismissal and asked: “When would you like to come to Rome to work with me as an adviser?” He praised Fedorov as an innovator who had “completely changed the rules of the game on the battlefield.”

The former minister was dismissed in mid-July after roughly six months at the helm of Ukraine's defense department amid tensions with the country’s military leadership and policy disputes. His removal triggered rare wartime protests.

He has since sharpened his criticism of President Zelenskyy, calling for elections earlier this month despite Russia’s ongoing invasion and warning that Ukrainians “cannot endlessly live” without understanding how major decisions are made.

Zelenskyy has rejected the idea, warning that wartime elections could “destroy” the country.

World.title: Climate and AI to loom large in von der Leyen’s State of the Union
World.content:
During Friday's discussion with the cabinet chiefs, Seibert linked the expected focus on climate to the damage caused by floods and wildfires over the summer, according to the two officials, who were briefed on the gathering. They were granted anonymity to discuss the closed-door talks.

The climate focus comes as von der Leyen’s Commission tries to defend its 2040 emissions-cutting target while responding to mounting pressure from industry and national capitals to limit the economic cost of the green transition.

The discussion also touched on how to present AI’s impact on jobs. Von der Leyen’s team has asked the Commission’s relevant policy units, in particular DG Connect, to provide fresh statistics for the speech on the number of jobs likely to be lost and created as AI adoption spreads, according to one of the officials.

Seibert also raised migration as a likely topic in the address, referring to the crisis in the Spanish autonomous city of Ceuta, according to one of the officials. The Commission is expected to revamp the mandate and operations of EU border agency Frontex, a third official said.

The Commission president's speech is expected to include references to social policy around the 10th anniversary of the European Pillar of Social Rights next year, alongside Ukraine and enlargement, according to one of the officials. But the topics have yet to be finalized.

The meeting was the second major opportunity for commissioners to get their priorities name-checked, with their cabinets having already submitted two- to three-page pitches to Seibert. The Commission's policy units, known as the directorates-general, also submitted documents outlining the topics they want von der Leyen to cover.

World.title: What it’s like to live through Kyiv’s constant air raids
World.content:
Kyiv has survived more than 20 air raid alerts since Thursday night. Some were an hour long, while others lasted for up to 10 minutes.

Indeed, every alert, as Russia continues its persistent destruction of millions of books, food warehouses and liquor factories, also means everything has to stop until we hear the words: “Air raid alert is over.” Dozens of trains are delayed, and businesses shut down and wait, losing customers and money.

But “survivors must still go to work,” as we like to joke bitterly. People are still expected to commute, even though Kyiv’s subway has stopped running between the left and right banks of the River Dnipro. Sleep-deprived civilians need to walk for hours, squeeze themselves into buses, or get stuck in traffic on bridges, just to get to work and back home. Transport chaos overground means even more danger for people stuck in large groups all around the city.

But our wartime economy, on which we need to rely more and more due to the slowing of foreign aid, cannot afford to stop.

“The country’s defense spending is constantly growing, and this requires maximum mobilization of domestic resources,” said Hlib Vyshlinsky, the executive director of the Center for Economic Strategy think tank based in Kyiv. “The policy of zero tolerance for the risk to the life and health of civilians under constant missile and drone strikes becomes irrelevant, because the state is still not able to protect them at 100 percent.”

As a Kyivan, I can tell you that this terror sends your mental stability into a spiral.

World.title: Indian PM Modi expected to attend December European Council
World.content:
Narendra Modi shakes hands with António Costa prior to a meeting in New Delhi on December 19, 2019. | Prakash Singh/AFP via Getty Images

Participation would enable signing of EU-India trade deal, which opens up market of 2 billion people.

BRUSSELS — Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is planning to attend the EU summit in December, according to two officials familiar with the discussions.

The visit would come after the EU and India concluded negotiations on a free-trade agreement and signed a security and defense partnership in January.

"We are working on it," said one of the officials when asked to confirm that Modi would join leaders in Brussels on Dec. 17-18 for the European Council’s final scheduled meeting of the year. The visit hasn't been officially confirmed and plans may change.

World.title: Heavy gunfire in Niger capital as clashes reported at presidential palace
World.content:
Gunfire rang out across parts of the Niger capital of Niamey overnight amid reports of an attack on the presidential palace.

 

The cause of the shooting was not immediately clear.

Bana Wagana Ibrahim, a member of Niger's Consultative Council, shared a statement on Saturday saying: "In light of current events, let us remain calm and avoid sharing unverified information."

"Our defence and security forces have been mobilised for the defence of the homeland," the statement read.

Ibrahim had earlier condemned what he called "another cowardly attack" on the Base 101 military airbase but added that the situation was "under control."

"Once again our defence and security forces have risen to the challenge," he wrote in a post on social media.

It comes as a security source told the AFP news agency that Niger's presidential guard had fought off "insurgents from within the armed forces" who attempted to make their way into the presidential palace in Niamey on Saturday.

The west African nation's state TV was also off air on Saturday, locals told AFP, with a black screen showing in place of regular programming.

One local said they had heard "heavy gunfire and explosions" at Base 101. Several other witnesses corroborated the report.

Another resident said he heard "bursts of gunfire" at around 7 am local time.

"I went to get credit for my phone. I saw a military vehicle heading towards the base that had to turn back," he added. "The weapons we're hearing are not the kind that terrorists on motorbikes can carry. The fighting has been non-stop since last night."

A military junta has ruled Niger for three years but has struggled to contend with jihadist violence.

Jihadists have already targeted Niamey airport twice this year. The Islamic State in the Sahel group attacked in January, before the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims attacked in June.

World.title: Nepal flood highlights growing risk of glacier disasters in the Alps
World.content:
Authorities in Nepal suspect that the recent devastating flash flood was triggered by a glacial lake outburst or a glacier collapse in the Himalayas - something experts say could also threaten the Alps.

 

A torrent of water, mud and debris surged almost 170 kilometres through southwest Tibet and into central Nepal earlier this week, killing hundreds of people.

Such disasters are also possible in Europe, particularly in the Alps, explains glaciologist Olaf Eisen, a professor at the Alfred Wegener Institute for Polar and Marine Research and at the University of Bremen.

As an example, Eisen cites an incident in the Swiss village of Blatten in May 2025, where a rock and glacier collapse occurred. The village had been evacuated beforehand, but a 64-year-old man was killed.

However, Eisen considers it unlikely that such an event in the Alps could reach the same scale as in Nepal.

"The disaster in Nepal was, in terms of the volume of the avalanche, around 10 to 20 times larger than Blatten, according to current estimates," Eisen said.

"Europe is among the continents warming the fastest, driven by human-made climate change. Rapidly retreating glaciers and thawing permafrost are destabilising high mountain regions," he added.

The areas most at risk are those at about 2,500 to 3,000 metres, including parts of France, Italy, Austria and Switzerland.

"In combination with extreme weather events such as heatwaves or heavy rainfall, similar natural disasters are becoming more likely there too," Eisen continued.

Risk of glacier collapse in Switzerland

Around 1,000 glaciers have disappeared in Switzerland since 1850. In total, an area of about 1,000 square kilometres has lost its ice cover, according to SRF.

One glacier that has been monitored for years is Weisshorn East, which saw three small glacier collapses earlier this week.

"This glacier has been monitored for years and there are repeated movements – sometimes more, sometimes less," Frederic Imboden, the mayor of Randa, the municipality bordering the glacier, told SRF.

Several hundred thousand cubic metres could potentially break away from the glacier. While there is no danger for local residents at present, according to Imboden, hiking trails and cycling routes have nevertheless been closed.

Causes of glacier collapses

There are several causes of glacier collapses: on the one hand they can be normal, cyclical processes, Eisen told Euronews.

Increasingly, though, they are being driven by human-induced climate change.

Glacial lake in Zermatt, Switzerland, 19 September 2025 © KEYSTONE / JEAN-CHRISTOPHE BOTT

The situation is particularly critical in regions that have historically remained permanently below freezing.

These contain so-called permafrost, ice that has stayed frozen continuously for at least two years.

"As temperatures rise, permafrost begins to thaw and a glacier starts to melt at its base. As a result, it no longer 'sticks' as firmly to the ground," Eisen says.

"In some cases, the formation of a pocket of water has been observed beneath a glacier that was still frozen at its snout," he continued.

During heatwaves or rainfall, this pocket can exert such intense pressure that the still-frozen front of the glacier gives way.

That would then cause the entire ice mass to be released in one go, Eisen explains.

Such an incident occurred in 2022 on Italy's Marmolada glacier in the Dolomites, when a huge block of ice broke away from the glacier, killing 11 mountaineers.

"Climate protection is glacier protection. Every tenth of a degree less counts. If average temperatures were to fall again, glaciers could adapt and grow," Eisen says.

Mechanical protection would only have a short-lived effect and is used solely in certain ski areas, requiring a great deal of energy and labour.
