World.title: Hollywood's 'Odyssey' craze turns eyes to Turkey: Did Homer compose his epics in an Izmir cave?
World.content:
Nestled along the olive-strewn hillsides outside Izmir, a moisture-dampened cave in the Bornova Valley has long held a sacred place in local lore.

 

Generations of residents have passed down the belief that it was inside this very cavern that the ancient poet Homer sat down to compose "The Odyssey".

As Christopher Nolan’s film adaptation The Odyssey has become one of this year's biggest hits both critically and at the global box office, a global frenzy has reignited an age-old literary mystery: Where was literature’s seminal text actually written?

For Turkish archaeologist Prof. Aylin Ümit Erdem, an expert at Ege University, the cinematic craze offers a vital opportunity to re-examine the historical, linguistic, and physical realities connecting Homer to ancient Smyrna, modern-day İzmir.

"When we evaluate Homer, we are dealing with the accepted author of the Iliad and the Odyssey," Prof. Erdem said in an exclusive interview with Euronews. "Scholars have long debated how an 8th-century BC poet could depict the Trojan War - an event that occurred 400 years earlier - with such vivid detail and tragic depth. Some credit a 400-year continuous oral tradition, while others view the epics as a compilation of stories by various bards."

Regardless of authorship debates, Prof. Erdem emphasizes that ancient sources overwhelmingly point toward Izmir.

"From the 5th-century BC historian Herodotus to the 1st-century BC geographer Strabo, ancient authors explicitly claimed Homer was from Smyrna. While candidates like Chios or Cyme were raised, Smyrna has stood since antiquity as one of the strongest contenders."

The Smyrna connection

According to Prof. Erdem, the primary scientific arguments linking Homer to Izmir lie within the language of the texts and the urban geography of the 8th century BC.

"The epics were written predominantly in the Ionic dialect, but they contain significant Aeolic vocabulary and archaic Greek terms," Prof. Erdem told Euronews. "Geographically, 8th-century BC Smyrna -located at Bayraklı Höyük- sat directly on the boundary separating the Aeolian region to the north from the Ionian region to the south. Bayraklı was founded as an Aeolian settlement before joining the Ionian League. A bard composing in this specific hub would naturally utilize this unique dual-dialect vocabulary."

Furthermore, Erdem underscores that Bayraklı Höyük represents the only active, fortified urban center in the İzmir basin during the 8th century BC, making it the primary historical setting where Homer would have lived.

However, addressing popular claims of direct physical traces, Prof. Erdem maintains strict scientific caution, drawing a clear line between late ancient reverence and direct 8th-century BC proof.

"We must be clear: we do not yet have direct, concrete archaeological evidence explicitly proving Homer lived or wrote in Smyrna," Prof. Erdem emphasized to Euronews. "Direct 8th-century BC artifacts inscribed with Homer's name have not been unearthed at Bayraklı, largely because those deep early strata have not yet been fully exposed across wide excavation areas."

Prof. Erdem notes that later artifacts, such as Hellenistic coins minted in Smyrna bearing Homer’s portrait or the seated cult statue found at the nearby sanctuary of Klaros, reflect how later generations claimed the poet as a native son rather than providing proof from his actual lifetime.

"Sustaining archaeological excavations with the support of our Ministry of Culture and Tourism and local authorities is vital," Prof. Erdem added. "If a direct finding linked to Homer is ever to emerge, it will come from digging deeper into these layers."

While academia awaits definitive excavation results, local enthusiasm in Izmir has reached a peak, fed by centuries of folklore.

Along the hillsides outside the city, a damp cavern in the Bornova Valley has long been revered by locals as the site where Homer composed his masterworks. Ancient texts frequently referred to the bard as Melesigenes ("born of the Meles"), referencing the river flowing beside Bayraklı.

"Preserving Homer's legacy is a duty we owe to humanity," Bornova Mayor Ömer Eşki told AFP, detailing municipal plans to restore the cavern for international cultural tourists. "The stories he tells belong to this landscape."

Local researchers also point to ancient reliefs mirroring the physical contours of the Bornova cave.

"This place was always called Homer's Valley. For me, there's no doubt he is from these lands," Turkish researcher Altan Altın explained to AFP, adding that the poet's legacy bridges regional histories. "Homer is 2,800 years old, while modern borders are just a century old. Homer is Greek. Homer is Anatolian."

Archaeologists like Mehmet Akif Erdem also noted that coins and statues prove ancient residents viewed Homer as their own. Yet, as Prof. Erdem highlights for Euronews, while historical and linguistic paths consistently lead back to ancient Smyrna, the ultimate physical proof still rests beneath the earth.

World.title: Bundeswehr expands 'Schakal' fleet for NATO's eastern flank
World.content:
The Schakal is more than just a new armoured vehicle. It is a key component of the German army's so-called Medium Forces - a new category of troops designed to be rapidly deployable while also offering substantial firepower.

 

This capability is particularly important in the context of NATO's eastern flank.

Rapid forces for the eastern flank

The current security situation in Europe has fundamentally changed the demands placed on the Bundeswehr.

The central question once again is how German units can be quickly moved to an area of operations in the event of a threat, and how they can then hold their own there against a heavily armed opponent.

For NATO, the eastern flank is of particular importance.

Since Germany plays a key role within the alliance in reinforcing and defending this region, the Bundeswehr needs units that can cover large distances quickly.

This is precisely where the Medium Forces come in. They are intended to fill the gap between light, highly mobile units and heavy armoured troops.

The Schakal is the key combat vehicle for this task, with the Bundeswehr describing it as the "backbone" of the Medium Forces.

Germany had originally ordered 150 Schakal infantry fighting vehicles, but a further 35 are now being delivered. The contract not only covers the vehicles themselves, but also additional services for logistics, training and operations.

The timing is noteable. At the same time, the Bundeswehr is pursuing a number of other major procurement programmes. New main battle tanks, artillery systems, air defence systems and additional protected vehicles are being acquired in an effort to close capability gaps that have developed over the last few decades.

Why the Schakal?

Why is the Bundeswehr not relying solely on heavy tracked vehicles for this mission?

The answer lies in mobility.

The Schakal is based on the GTK Boxer, an eight-wheeled armoured vehicle, and unlike a heavy tracked tank, it can cover long distances on roads relatively quickly. It is precisely this combination of protection, firepower and mobility that is crucial for the Medium Forces.

The basic idea is simple: a unit should be able to move to a different theatre of operations at speed, and without having to depend on extensive transport capacity for every major redeployment.

With the new vehicle, the Bundeswehr is trying to close a gap between different vehicle classes.

On one side are heavily armoured tracked vehicles, such as the Puma infantry fighting vehicle, which offer high levels of protection and combat power but are less suited to rapid redeployment over long distances.

Related How a NATO essay contest won a Lithuanian schoolgirl a ride in a Bundeswehr tank

On the other are lighter vehicles, such as the Dingo, which are more mobile but do not have the same firepower as an infantry fighting vehicle.

The Schakal is intended to sit between these two - heavy enough for combat but mobile enough for rapid operations.

The Schakal uses the Boxer chassis and has an unmanned RCT-30 turret derived from the Puma infantry fighting vehicle. Its main weapon is a 30-millimetre automatic cannon.

This enables the vehicle, among other things, to engage lightly and moderately armoured targets. It also has capabilities for countering drones and aircraft, as well as the integrated MELLS guided missile system for engaging heavily armoured targets.

German Bundeswehr soldiers in 2024. Copyright 2024 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Ordering the vehicles is just the first step. It does not mean the new formations will be operational overnight.

Soldiers have to be trained, spare parts and ammunition provided, logistics structures set up and the new units fully established.

The first Schakals are scheduled to be delivered from the end of 2027, but it will be longer before the entire fleet and the supporting structures are fully in place.

The expansion of the Schakal fleet is therefore a long-term project, but it also highlights the direction in which the German army is heading - towards a force once again capable of deploying larger formations for a potential conventional conflict in Europe.

World.title: At least 27 killed after Russian strike sparks major fire and explosions at a warehouse in Bucha
World.content:
At least 27 people were killed after a Russian drone strike caused a major fire and explosions at a warehouse overnight, according to local authorities.

 

Tymur Tkachenko, the head of the Kyiv Oblast Military Administration, said at least 42 people, including four children, were also injured in the attack on the village of Myla, with 381 people evacuated from the area.

"The attack caused a large-scale fire. The fire also spread to private residential buildings. Fires in 5 houses and a catering establishment have already been extinguished," Tkachenko wrote in a post on Telegram.

He added that the fire was "accompanied by explosions."

Emergency and rescue teams are continuing to work at the scene.

Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office said it has since launched a pre-trial investigation into possible "negligence" surrounding storage conditions at the warehouse.

"In particular, the legality of the placement and storage of explosive objects and materials on the territory of the enterprise, the availability of the necessary permits and approvals, as well as the actions of officials who made the relevant decisions will be checked," it said in a statement.

Video footage circulating on social media, seemingly taken near the scene, shows a huge explosion and fireball rising into the night sky.

Russian strikes kill one in Kherson

On Saturday, a man was also killed following a Russian drone strike on Kherson in southern Ukraine. A 44-year-old also suffered a blast injury and shrapnel wounds to their chest in the attack on the city.

Another two people were injured in an attack on Kyiv's Sviatoshynskyi district, per local authorities.

Ukraine's air force said Russia had launched one Onyx anti-ship missile, one Iskander ballistic missile, and 267 drones at Ukraine since 6 pm on Friday.

Local air defences had shot down or "neutralised" 233 of the drones as of Saturday morning, it added.

Moscow and Kyiv have been ramping up long-range strikes in recent months, particularly targeting logistics and energy facilities.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called on his forces to further "step up" their deep strikes on Russia, setting a target of 1,000 drone launches a day.

"Right now, we average over 300 of our long-range sanctions - there must be more," he said in a video address on Friday evening.

World.title: ‘I’m free’: How VR therapy helped a schizophrenia patient silence 27 years of voices
World.content:
For 27 years, Vibeke Andersen heard voices telling her she was worthless.

 

The 53-year-old was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia and heard voices for 27 years, which had her repeatedly going in and out of psychiatric hospitals. The voices controlled what she said and did, and sometimes told her that even her family could not love her.

“They told me that I was not worth living as a human being. Nobody cared about me,” Andersen told Euronews Health.

Then, in 2020, she was offered an experimental treatment that asked her to do something that might seem counterintuitive. Instead of trying to distance herself from the voice, she would confront a virtual version of it face-to-face.

Confronting symptoms inside virtual reality

Therapists working with the VIRTU research team used specialised software to create an avatar based on Andersen’s description of the dominant voice she heard, adjusting its appearance and sound until it resembled her experience.

Once Andersen put on a virtual reality (VR) headset, the avatar appeared in front of her while her therapist repeated the kinds of things Andersen normally heard, using voice-transformation software to make the voice sound similar.

“They engage in this conversation, talking back and forth, standing up against the voice, reclaiming the power and control over it,” Louise Birkedal Glenthøj, head of the VIRTU research group and associate professor at the department of psychology at the University of Copenhagen, told Euronews Health.

Screenshot of an example of a VR therapy session for an eating disorder patient VIRTU

The process became so difficult that around her fourth or fifth session her therapists considered ending the treatment.

“They told me that I better drop off this treatment,” Andersen said. “I was still stubborn and I thought, ‘No way. I'm going to do this treatment to the end.

Towards the end of the intervention, Andersen went into a forest and began screaming at the voice.

“F**k off,” she remembers shouting. “I don't want these voices anymore. They had to get out of my life. They had to leave me, leave my mind, and I had to be free as a person.”

A ‘safe and tolerable’ treatment

Andersen was part of the CHALLENGE project led by doctors and scientists at the VIRTU Research Group at Copenhagen University Hospital’s mental health services.

The trial included 270 people with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders and persistent auditory hallucinations. Those assigned to the VR therapy received seven sessions, while the comparison group received standard care with additional supportive counselling.

The results of the study, published in The Lancet Psychiatry in 2025, found that VR therapy significantly reduced the overall severity of auditory hallucinations after 12 weeks compared with the control group, while patients also heard voices less frequently at both 12 and 24 weeks.

“We were very surprised. This was a very experimental study. Could it actually work? Was it feasible? What would the patients think of going into this simulated reality and confronting their symptoms?” Glenthøj said.

The wider VIRTU research programme now involves around 1,000 participants across studies of several mental health disorders, and some of its VR treatments are now being used in Denmark’s psychiatric services, according to Glenthøj.

The conditions covered by the research affect millions of people worldwide. Schizophrenia affects around 23 million people and eating disorders around 16 million, while anxiety disorders affect about 359 million. Around one in 127 people globally are autistic, according to the World Health Organization.

“What is very rewarding now is to see that we can actually achieve quite a change by very short-term interventions,” Glenthøj said.

While participants in the trial received a set number of sessions so researchers could compare the results, Glenthøj said the treatment can be more flexible when offered to patients outside a research trial, depending on how much preparation and therapy an individual needs.

The confrontational approach may also not be suitable for everyone.

“For some, it is very overwhelming,” Glenthøj said. “You might experience a deterioration or increasing symptoms for a period, but that will pass, and then you will hopefully have greater control over the symptoms.”

“We try to adjust individually also how we pace the therapy in terms of the anxiety response,” she added, saying some patients may need other therapy or more preparation before starting. Overall, she said their research has found the treatment to be “safe and tolerable”.

Researchers are still trying to understand exactly why confronting a simulated voice can have such an effect. One hypothesis is that turning something experienced only inside the patient’s head into something they can see, hear and respond to gives them greater control over it, a process researchers describe as ‘externalisation’.

“With VR, we can kind of bridge patients’ daily life and therapy,” Glenthøj said. “We can bring daily life into the therapy room.”

VIRTU is now studying VR across psychosis, eating disorders, social anxiety, autism and depression, adapting the virtual experience to different symptoms.

For people with eating disorders, for example, an avatar can represent the critical “eating disorder voice” some patients experience, while other projects recreate social situations to work with paranoia or anxiety.

When the voice disappeared

By the time Andersen arrived for what would have been her final session, the voice had disappeared.

“I came to my last treatment after Christmas and I said, ‘I don't have to say goodbye to something which is not there’. So I left the session. I said, ‘I think I'm cured’,” Andersen said.

At a six-month follow-up, she was still not hearing voices, and five years later she says they have not returned.

“I'm free. I'm living my life as I always have dreamt of,” Andersen said.

Since then, she says she has started studying to become a social worker.

“I felt some meaning in my life for the first time in my life. I was a human being. I was just not a number in a system. I was not seen as a diagnosis, a paranoid schizophrenia,” Andersen said.

The next step is AI

Glenthøj said one goal is to incorporate artificial intelligence (AI) into some of the interventions.

“We can't give therapy to all these patients that actually need it,” Glenthøj said. “So if we can use AI safely and ethically for some of these purposes, that would be very helpful.”

One idea is to develop an AI-supported virtual therapist that patients could access outside the clinic.

After completing face-to-face treatment, they might use an app at home to practise coping strategies, reinforce what they learned in therapy and remind themselves how to respond when symptoms return.

The group is also experimenting with generative AI in the construction of virtual environments. Patients can describe a scenario from their past and researchers use text-to-image AI tools to help recreate aspects of it in VR.

But Glenthøj stresses that using AI with people experiencing severe psychiatric symptoms will require careful clinical and ethical safeguards.

World.title: 60 years of Notting Hill Carnival: 10 essential songs chosen by its veterans
World.content:
This weekend, Notting Hill Carnival returns to the streets of west London for its 60th anniversary - six decades since a small community celebration grew into one of the world’s biggest street festivals. Each year the two-day event is a joyous and physical reminder of the enduring influence of Afro-Caribbean culture on London. Its roots lie in the Windrush generation and the sound system culture brought over from Jamaica, against a backdrop of the racial tensions and violence that gripped Notting Hill in the late 1950s. Following the 1958 race riots and the 1959 murder of Antiguan carpenter Kelso Cochrane by a gang of white men, local social worker Rhaune Laslett organised a children's street party in 1966 in the hopes of bringing the divided community together. And when Trinidadian steelpan player Russell Henderson and his band took to Portobello Road, the foundations of Carnival were laid. By the 1970s, sound systems had become central to the festival, with organiser Leslie Palmer introducing more Caribbean masquerade and live music. As he put it himself: "The sound systems were the voice of the youth." Since then the soundtrack of carnival has continually evolved - from calypso, reggae, dub and soca to jungle, drum & bass, hip-hop, grime and UK garage. So for carnival's big 6-0, we rounded up ten people who've lived and breathed Carnival - from Channel One legend Mikey Dread to Seduction City's Lady Banton, to costume designers and photographers - and tasked them with picking one track that for them epitomises Notting Hill Carnival. Mikey Dread (Channel One) Mikey Dread of Channel One at Notting Hill Carnival Credit: Ruby Bevan Notting Hill Carnival wouldn't be the same without Mikey Dread. He co-founded the illustrious Channel One Sound System and has been behind the decks since 1983. A serious legend. Don't miss him this weekend - he'll be playing out his collection of conscious reggae and exclusive dubplates for all to enjoy on the corner of Westbourne Park Road. Mikey's track selection - 'Guess Who's Coming To Dinner' - Black Uhuru (1979) We choose this tune because it’s what Channel One is about. Roots, Rastafari, heavyweight bass and unity from Jamaica to London, we’ve carried that message at Carnival for over 40 years. Mikey Dread Wayne Crichlow Wayne Crichlow Credit: Wayne Crichlow (IG) Crichlow is a London-based documentary photographer who has spent more than 15 years immersed in Notting Hill Carnival. He's recently released Carnival of Resistance, a photobook made with Wayne Campbell, documenting the festival’s sound systems, Mas, dancers, community and spirit of resistance. Wayne's track selection - 'Warrior Charge' - Aswad (1980) I was never really a soca or calypso guy growing up - my musical world was much more reggae, hip-hop and, later, jungle - but 'Warrior Charge' takes me straight back to my early years at Notting Hill Carnival.

I remember standing around sounds like Aba Shanti-I and Jah Observer, physically feeling that deep, rolling bass, with those huge brass lines sounding almost like a chant of resistance. You didn’t just hear that music at Carnival - you felt it through your body.

For me, that sound captures something fundamental about Carnival. Beneath the colour and celebration, there has always been resistance, identity, community and the assertion of Caribbean culture in Britain. That connection has stayed with me and is very much reflected in Carnival of Resistance, the book I’ve co-authored with Wayne Campbell. Wayne Crichlow Linett Kamala Artist and DJ Linett Kamala attending Notting Hill Carnival Credit: Linett Kamala Linett broke into London's sound-system culture as a teenager, becoming one of the first women ever to DJ at Notting Hill Carnival. She's now a Notting Hill Carnival Board Director and has spent decades promoting music, art and making sure the next generation of women get their rightful turn behind the decks. Linett's track selection - 'Rum & RedBull' - Beenie Man, Future Fambo, Seanizzle Absolute Notting Hill Carnival timeless anthem. It's a guaranteed crowd pleaser, which completely sums up the vibes, because Jamaican dancehall classics like this being pumped out of a giant sound system speaker is unsurpassed! Linett Kamala Oxman (Greensleeves HiFi) Oxman attending Notting Hill Carnival Credit: oxmanreggae The primary host and selector of Greensleeves Hi-Fi, the sound system project carrying the name of one of reggae's most iconic labels. This Carnival weekend he'll be on deck duties with Becca D and YNG CPTN at The Hoxton in Shepherd's Bush. Oxman's track selection - 'Police and Thieves' - Junior Murvin (1976) The soundtrack to a time where it felt as though the song was penned for that specific event. A bittersweet feeling of enjoying the carnival but being weary of the police at the same time. Oxman Lady Banton (Seduction City Sound) Lady Banton (pictured left) on decks at Notting Hill Carnival Credit: Lady Banton A Carnival veteran. Lady Banton is the force behind Seduction City Sound, a Carnival institution she founded over 30 years ago. Seduction City became the first all-female-led sound system at Notting Hill Carnival. Three decades on, she's still behind the decks, and this Sunday she'll be doing what she does best on Telford Road. Lady Banton's track selection - 'Three Little Birds' - Bob Marley & The Wailers (1977) This track always creates a sense of community of all nations to sing along to on our sound system during the event. Seduction City Sound System Ras Sherby (Channel One) Ras Sherby attending Notting Hill Carnival Credit: Ras Sherby One of Channel One’s legendary resident MCs. Mikey Dread's trusted right-hand man with more than 20 years experience at Carnival. Ras' track selection - 'Live In Love' - Ras Sherby (2024) I am going to be a bit selfish and choose my own song released on the Channel One Sound System record label titled 'Live In Love'. It was created from my experiences of Carnival, which I see as a melting pot where people of different cultures and races come together in one big celebration of our Caribbean culture and all its elements.

Notting Hill Carnival reminds us that we can all come together in love and unity. It can be a blueprint for greater togetherness and bigger causes, but most of all, I love seeing people happy together. It’s much better than disharmony! Hope I haven’t gone on too much! Ras Sherby YNG CPTN Chris Reid attending Notting Hill Carnival. Credit: Chris Reid A London-based DJ known for blending reggae, dancehall, Afrobeats, jungle, garage and house. A regular on London’s Carnival and sound system circuit. This Carnival Sunday, he’ll be busy shelling out at both the Notting Hill Arts Club and The Hoxton. YNG CPTN's track selection - 'Soul Rebel' - Gappy Ranks ft. Nereus Joseph I picked this track because without the rebels who stood up against racism and oppression following the racially motivated attack that killed Kelso Cochrane, we wouldn't be able to experience Carnival as the celebration we know it today.

The original Soul Rebel is by Bob Marley, but I choose Gappy Ranks' version as he's from North West London.

Ultimately, the song represents standing up for who you are, what you believe in, and refusing to accept oppression. YNG CPTN Helen Davenport Award winning artist and Carnival costumier Helen Davenport Credit: Helen Davenport For 27 years, Carnival costumier Helen has been helping make Carnival look as wild, colourful and larger-than-life as it does. She’s also passionate about passing the craft on, running workshops for people of all ages, cultures and abilities. Helen's track selection - 'Savannah Grass' - Kes (2019) I love this song. It’s infectious. It’s Carnival. Helen Davenport Jamie Rodigan West London-born DJ Jamie Rodigan Credit: Jamie Rodigan West London-born DJ Jamie Rodigan grew up immersed in reggae, thanks in part to his father, legendary broadcaster Sir David “Ram Jam” Rodigan. His sets draw on everything from reggae and dancehall to jungle, garage and house. He'll be bringing the sound to the Notting Hill Arts Club afterparty on Sunday along with YNG CPTN. Jamie's track selection - 'Promised Land' - Dennis Brown I’ve chosen this song as it brings back memories from my youth attending Carnival. The song always resonated with me on two levels - the incredible production by west London’s own Aswad and the subject matter. I was fascinated by the connection with Ethiopia and Jamaica and the fact that Emperor Haile Selassie provided a land grant for Rastafarian people to repatriate and settle in Shashamane. A true Carnival anthem! Jamie Rodigan Roachee Roachee Credit: Roachee A certified barrer. East London MC and former member of pioneering crew Roll Deep, joining the collective in 2004. A product of the youth-club and pirate-radio scene that birthed grime. Roachee's track selection - 'Who Am I' - Beenie Man For me, going to the carnival back in the days it was always the Rampage stage I would visit, that's where it would always be going off, and one song that sticks out that used to beat through the sound systems was 'Who Am I' by Beanie Man.

I will just never forget the weight of the baseline and how it made everybody dance. It was vibrational. Not only was the place vibrating but I mean it was spiritual too. I can't explain it - it was just mental.

Big up Beanie Man and the producer because that instrumental is phenomenal work. Roachee The Notting Hill Carnival takes place over the August bank holiday weekend with parades and sound systems from Sunday 30 to Monday 31 August 2026.

World.title: Russian strike on warehouse near Kyiv kills dozens
World.content:
Hundreds were also forced to evacuate after a Russian attack on a warehouse near Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, sparked a huge fire and explosions.

A Russian drone strike on a warehouse near Kyiv late Friday has killed at least 37 people, Ukrainian authorities said.

"Unfortunately, the death toll in the Bucha district has risen to 37," Kyiv region governor Tymur Tkachenko said in a post on Telegram on Saturday.

Among those killed was Taras Didych, head of the Dmytrivka community, who was one of the first to rush to the scene to rescue people, Tkachenko earlier said.

It had previously been reported that more than 40 people had been injured.

In recent months, Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes, increasingly hitting civilian infrastructure such as logistics warehouses and oil and port facilities. These attacks have resulted in more civilian casualties.

What else do we know about the Russian drone attack near Kyiv?

The strike sparked a major fire and explosions at the warehouse in the Bucha district, close to the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv, forcing more than 370 people to evacuate the region.

In a statement on X, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that "a warehouse was struck, followed by a detonation," and that nearby infrastructure suffered "significant damage."

He also said that criminal proceedings had been opened on charges of official negligence.

"There are regulations in place — ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas," Zelenskyy said.

Kyiv under jet-powered drone attacks

Friday's drone attack followed ​two days of constant air raids aimed at the Ukrainian capital and the surrounding region.

"Kyiv is under virtually nonstop attack from jet-powered drones. Ukraine cannot be left alone in finding solutions to defend against such strikes," said Zelenskyy.

It's been more than four and a half years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbor.

World.title: Germany news: Fire at Berlin refugee home sparks evacuations
World.content:
08/29/2026 August 29, 2026 Study: Germany's sick leave wage bill doubles in 15 years

The average number of sick days taken by German workers has risen sharply Image: Sergey Mironov/Zoonar/IMAGO

The total amount of wages German firms paid in sick and maternity leave has more than doubled over the past 15 years, a study from the Cologne-based German Economic Institute (IW) shows.

IW estimated that German companies paid a record-high €85.6 billion ($111 billion) in wages to employees who were out sick last year.This compares to €36.9 billion in 2010.

Of the larger figure, €72.5 billion represented gross wages, while €13.1 billion was earmarked for social security contributions.

IW said several factors have contributed to the rise, including wage hikes and inflation in other employee costs.

The institute said the total number of employed people has also grown since 2010, meaning more workers are eligible for sick leave.

IW, however, said it had noted a "significant" rise in recorded sick leave since Germany moved to electronic medical certificates in 2022.

Separate research by the Berlin-based IGES Institute in January showed that German workers now take an average of 19.5 working days as sick leave per year, a noticeable increase from about 13 days in 2018.

In an effort to stem the rise, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government will from January ban patients from receiving sick notes from doctors by phone.

In Germany, employers are generally required to pay workers' salaries for up to six weeks before the statutory health insurance fund takes over by paying sickness benefits.

World.title: US, Ecuador forces strike alleged drug smuggling boat
World.content:
Tackling drug trafficking in Latin America is a key priority for Washington. In March, Ecuador joined a US-led coalition to combat the drug trade in the region.

The US military said on Friday it had destroyed an alleged drug trafficking boat in a coordinated operation with Ecuador.

In a post on X, US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said that its forces intercepted a vessel "operating as a floating refueling station" in the Eastern Pacific.

According to SOUTHCOM, the vessel was operating "in support of the Los Choneros violent narco-terrorist organization," referring to one of Ecuador's most powerful criminal gangs, which Washington has designated as a Foreign Terrorist Organization .

"Working together with our Ecuadorian partners, our coalition dealt a decisive blow to a narco-terrorist operation responsible for moving significant amounts of drugs through the region," SOUTHCOM said.

US, Ecuador combat drug cartels

In March, Ecuador joined President Donald Trump's "Shield of the Americas" — a US-led coalition focused on combating drug trafficking across the region.

Ecuador's strategic location between Colombia and Peru — the world's two largest producers of cocaine — makes the country a key transit hub for drug-trafficking gangs.

The US military launched Operation Southern Spear in September 2025 as part of a fight against drug trafficking in the region.

The Trump administration, however, has not presented definitive evidence that the vessels targeted in its operations were carrying or transporting illegal drugs.

World.title: Death toll from Nepal-Tibet floods rises to over 600
World.content:
Heavy rain is complicating an already difficult rescue effort, as hundreds remain missing three days after deadly flash floods hit the Nepal-Tibet border region.

The latest death toll from the devastating flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border was reported on Saturday to be over 600, as frantic rescue operations to search for hundreds of missing people entered a fourth day.

According to Nepal's disaster agency, the death toll in Nepal now stands at 626, with 2,426 people — including foreigners — still missing.

Across the border in Tibet, China's state news agency, Xinhua, has confirmed seven deaths and reported 554 missing individuals.

A glacial collapse on Wednesday sent rock, ice, mud and debris surging through the Himalayan mountain river systems below.

The flood swept through areas near the Chinese border, ravaging entire towns and damaging hydropower plants.

What is the status of rescue efforts in Nepal?

Rainy weather conditions are hindering aerial rescue operations in Nepal.

Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told the media on Saturday that helicopter operations were on hold until the weather improved.

Rescuers are battling thick layers of mud in the affected areas, which is making it difficult for helicopters to land and take off.

Tunnels in the mountainous region are also a challenge, Basnet said.

The army has located people trapped in a tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project in Nepal's Rasuwa District. Over 100 people are believed to be inside the tunnel filled with mud.

Basnet said that rescuers were struggling to locate the entry points of the tunnel and had made use of baskets and ropes to reach some people. There are also limited places for helicopters to land in the area.

Members of the Nepal Army load relief material as a helicopter containing relief supplies takes off Image: Athit Perawongmetha/REUTERS

On Friday, Nepal's Army shared visuals of some people being rescued from the tunnel. The survivors were seen stuck in the mud, while officials crawled through the sludge and held out their hands to them.

Nepalese authorities said that the bodies of many flood victims have also been found dozens of kilometers from the disaster zone in Chitwan District in southern Nepal, which borders India.

Meanwhile, Indian authorities said they recovered the bodies of seven people who were swept downstream from Nepal and believe them to be flood victims.

More than 1,000 believed missing after Nepal flash floods To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Nepal needs help in technical areas, says foreign minister

Late on Friday, Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told the Reuters news agency that his country needed equipment, along with technical knowledge in tunnel rescue operations.

Khanal also told Reuters that Nepal did not need help with search and rescue operations but needed assistance in opening transport and communication lines in places where bridges were destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storage of bodies for a longer timeframe.

"We have already made requests for such ⁠specialized ​services and technical assistance in areas where we don't have enough expertise and technical know-how," ​Reuters quoted Khanal as saying.

Nepal's Foreign Ministry had on Friday declined foreign involvement in search and rescue.

Nepal's post-flood rebuilding estimated at $4-$5 billion

In another Reuters interview, Nepal's Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle said that the Himalayan nation may need $4 billion ⁠to $5 billion ⁠to rebuild after the flood.

The estimate is equivalent ​to nearly a tenth of Nepal's economy.

"The initial estimate is ​between $4-$5 billion. Just an estimate," Wagle told Reuters, adding that the bill would be much less than what was needed in reconstruction after the disastrous 2015 earthquake — Nepal's worst ‌ recorded disaster.

"Loss and damage is being assessed," he said.

People carry salvaged belongings from damaged houses following the flash floods and mudslide Image: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

What do we know about rescue operations in Tibet?

In Gyirong, one of the hardest-hit areas in Tibet along the China-Nepal border, Beijing had temporarily halted its rescue efforts due to the risk of renewed flooding before announcing that the threat had waned.

China's Xinhua agency reported on Saturday morning that two villagers had been rescued in the Gyirong area.

Rescue workers operate excavators and loaders to repair a damaged road leading to Gyirong Port Image: China Daily/REUTERS

The glacial collapse on Wednesday led to the formation of a barrier lake upstream due to debris dams. Experts warned that the lake had started to overflow.

On Saturday, Chinese authorities announced that the lake had begun to shrink.

China's state broadcaster, CCTV, cited the Ministry of Water Resources as saying that satellite imagery of the surface area of the lake in the Tsangpo River basin on Saturday morning showed a reduction of around 21,000 square meters compared to images from Thursday.

Authorities have also identified a larger body of water at the bottom of the glacier collapse.

"We estimate its area to be over 120,000 ⁠square ​meters, but its depth is currently unknown," Reuters quoted Chen Hongqi, a senior engineer at ​the Ministry of Natural Resources' Geological Disaster Technical Guidance Center, as saying.

Reuters also reported an official of Nepal's Disaster ​Management Authority as saying that flood risks will remain until the two lakes have fully drained.

World.title: South Korea leans toward military conscription for women
World.content:
Facing a population decline, fewer potential service members and calls for social equality to be extended to national military service, Korea is inching closer to breaking the taboo on women on the front line.

Nearly 60% of South Koreans are now in favor of young women serving mandatory military service alongside their male counterparts, according to a recent survey, representing a significant shift in the long-held taboo against women being obliged to defend the nation.

Thousands of women already serve in the South Korean armed forces on a voluntary basis, but the debate over mandatory service has always been delicate.

Now, for a series of reasons that include a falling birth rate and shrinking number of recruits as well as an insistence that social equality means that women should also serve, the issue has re-emerged ahead of a reform of the national defense plan scheduled to be released this autumn.

Yet, there are still those who insist women should be kept away from the front lines and, instead, that South Korea should invest more in drones and other advanced technologies.

"South Korea's male-centered conscription system has long been closely connected to traditional gender roles," said Hyobin Lee, a professor at Sogang University in Seoul.

"Men were generally expected to protect the country and the family and to fight in wartime, while women were expected to take primary responsibility for childbirth, childcare and the household," she told DW.

A second factor is the intensifying debate about gender equality, a debate in large part driven by young men, she said.

Warfare moves beyond the physical

"South Korean men generally perform their military service in their early 20s, which interrupts their education, employment or early career development," Lee said.

"At the same time, gender equality has become an increasingly important social value, and women's opportunities in education and employment have expanded."

"As a result, some younger men ask a very simple question: If society expects equality in rights and opportunities, why does one of the country's most significant civic obligations — military service — still fall only on men?"

South Korea proposes talks to officially end war with North To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Another contributing factor is the change in the nature of the military itself, with a shift away from physically demanding combat roles that were perceived as being more suited to men and the emergence of a national defense more heavily reliant on technology.

This includes unmanned systems, cyber capabilities, information and communications technology and others that do not require physical strength.

What does the study show?

According to the study, carried out by the Reform Institute, the policy research arm of the conservative-leaning Reform Party, and published on August 20, almost 60% of the respondents were in favor of changing the law to require women to undergo national service. Just 34% were opposed to the idea.

Nearly 65% of men were in favor — a figure that rose to 71.7% among men in their 20s and 30s — with 54.5% of women across all age groups similarly supportive.

At present, all able-bodied men are required to complete a minimum of 18 months and up to 21 months of service and can be called back into service in the event of a national emergency, such as war breaking out on the tense Korean Peninsula.

The latest figures highlight, however, personnel shortages that have affected South Korea's armed forces.

According to the Defense Ministry, around 332,000 men were eligible to perform mandatory military service in 2019. That number fell to 257,000 men in 2022 and is forecast to shrink to just 120,000 men in 2043.

While Hyobin Lee is strongly in favor of equality throughout South Korean society, she fears that obliging women to serve the same military terms as men may turn out to be a negative because so many other elements in society still lag.

Women's traditional responsibilities remain unchanged

"Women in South Korea still bear a much greater share of the responsibilities associated with pregnancy, childbirth and childcare," she underlined.

"Having a child can still lead to career interruption or withdrawal from the labor market, and women's responsibilities for caregiving have not declined to the same extent that their participation in education and employment has increased," Lee added.

Korean 'comfort women' memorial angers Japan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"If women were also required to complete military service, the cumulative burden across their life course could become even greater," she pointed out.

"In a country that is already experiencing an extremely low birth rate, it is also possible that this additional compulsory obligation could further delay or discourage marriage and childbirth."

Lee comes from a family with a strong military background, with a grandfather an admiral in the navy and her father serving in the same branch of the military.

But she would have had reservations in completing mandatory service herself.

"If someone chooses a military career, that is completely different from compulsory service," she said.

"Eighteen months in your 20s is a very significant period in a person's life. It is a time when people are studying, beginning their careers, and making important personal choices. Having to put all of that on hold because the state requires it is a substantial burden," she said.

"Personally, I would have found it extremely difficult to give up 18 months of my younger years in that way."

Song Young-Chae, a Seoul-based academic and human rights activist, completed two years in the infantry as a younger man, when periods of service were longer. He is opposed to mandatory service for women.

"The defense of the nation is traditionally the responsibility of men, and I do not believe that there is such an urgent need to conscript women into front-line service," he told DW.

Need to invest in modern technology

"I served along the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) with North Korea, and it was a hard posting," he added. "I believe that we should be investing far more in drones, robots and other advanced military technologies to protect our borders."

How China's rise is shaping Trump's strategy in Asia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The South Korean government set up a task force in 2025 to revise the nation's basic defense plan, with troop modernization and an overhaul of the conscription system — introduced in the 1950s — high on the agenda.

In an interview with the Yonhap News Agency on August 9, Military Manpower Commissioner Hong So-young admitted that the nation faces a "demographic cliff" and that reforms are urgently required. Those include potentially reducing the number of people exempt from service and requiring foreign-born people who have taken South Korean nationality to also serve.

Hong made no comment about mandatory service for Korean women, but said the system needs a "fundamental" overhaul.

Edited by: Shamil Shams

World.title: This extremely successful author polarizes German readers
World.content:
She's young and she says what she thinks: Caroline Wahl is topping Germany's bestseller lists with her novels. But she has also faced public backlash.

Caroline Wahl, 31, has published three novels to date. All three shot to the top of Germany's fiction bestseller lists.

Now, her fourth book is set to be released on August 28: "1999 Meter über dem Meer" (1999 Meters Above Sea) tells the story of a young woman who takes on a false identity to mingle among the high society in St. Moritz, Switzerland.

It is one of the most anticipated new books of the summer in Germany.

So what is the secret to Caroline Wahl's success?

Debut with a bang

Caroline Wahl's breakthrough came with her first novel, from 2023: "22 Bahnen" (22 Lengths) sold more than a million copies in German-language editions.

The story of the young student Tilda, who has to navigate everyday life alongside her alcoholic mother and her little sister, was praised by critics for its straightforward, modern writing style.

What's more, the novel managed to fascinate readers across generations: It includes references to contemporary pop culture as well as to classic literature.

"The many references make the novels both diverse and ambiguous," says Matthias Schaffrick, a research associate at the Collaborative Research Center "Transformations of the Popular" at the University of Siegen, who recently organized a two-day symposium on Wahl's works.

"What stands out most is how she experiments with different narrative styles and questions them, instead of simply telling a story," Shaffrick tells DW. "This opens up a literary space with multiple possibilities, enabling different interpretations and certainly contributing to the appeal of her novels for many readers."

Polarizing ambition

The success led to the media becoming interested in the young author, and quickly showed that Caroline Wahl does not care much for conventions: She speaks her mind freely and doesn't mind facing backlash. "I enjoy being polarizing," she told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper last weekend. "I like that there's no gray area, people either hate me, and then they really hate me (...). Or they like me."

In the podcast "Hotel Matze," she said she wanted to become one of Germany's most famous authors. Her words quickly created a stir, but Wahl didn't mind: "I'm really not up for false modesty. It's not wrong to state your goals ambitiously," she said on the arts and culture TV show "Twist" on the Arte channel. "For young women in particular, it's more extreme than for men — people get irritated when a young woman says, 'I want to be the best.' I want to change that with my attitude."

A passion for fast cars

Part of that is openly speaking about enjoying her newfound wealth. In an interview with SZ-Magazin, she said: "It's not only the writing that is enjoyable, but also being successful. Financial success is also important." She loves fast cars, drives a convertible and bought a camper van she likes to park somewhere with a view of the sea to work.

On social media, she faced a lot of criticism. She has been accused of making money off the literary depiction of poverty in "22 Bahnen," despite never having lived an impoverished life herself. It's an age-old discussion about whether authors are only allowed to write about things they have experienced themselves. Wahl replied to this criticism on the Deutschlandfunk radio station, explaining that above all, writing to her means "exploring spaces that I don't know and feeling empathy for people who live a different life than mine."

No fan of false modesty: Caroline Wahl Image: Felix Hörhager/dpa/picture alliance

But even without the debate on her credibility, a young woman who speaks openly about material success still seems to be unsettling for many people in Germany — men and women alike — as the many negative reactions show. To Wahl herself, the debate is misogynist.

On Instagram, she wrote a caption for a photo of her light blue BMW: "I find it weird and don't quite get why it's cool for rappers or other men to show off their AMGs, etc., but when a woman author wants to buy a sports car (and can afford to do so!!!), people advise her not to do it and more importantly, not to show it in public."

Author and influencer

"What happens when something becomes very popular?" asks literary scholar Matthias Schaffrick: "The popularity starts being scrutinized, which you can observe in Caroline Wahl's case. And we can see what it means to be a popular author. It's not only her novels that play a role, but also the persona she creates for herself as an author."

By being active on Instagram, where she has even tested energy drinks, she also taps into the role of an influencer, says Matthias Schaffrick. "It makes her even more popular and offers new topics for conversation. At the same time, the public debate shifts the focus away from her literature, which is what's actually interesting about the Caroline Wahl phenomenon."

Wahl herself admits that the intensity of the backlash and criticism has hurt her. In an interview with the SWR TV channel, she explained that social criticism is not necessarily her intention. "I'm not trying to change anything with my stories. Above all, I want to tell stories."

'22 Lengths' on school curricula

When it comes to best‑sellers, opinions always differ among German literary critics: Is this entertaining literature, or serious literature with high artistic aspirations? The arts and feature sections of numerous newspapers come to different conclusions on whether Caroline Wahl's novels can be classified as part of the latter. In an interview with Spiegel, Wahl said she finds "drawing a line between entertaining and serious simply annoying."

So far, Wahl's novels have not been nominated for the German Book Prize, Germany's highest literature award. In 2024, the writer voiced her disappointment in typical fashion on Instagram: "I'm sad and angry that I have not been included on the longlist, even if I somehow knew this would happen. Too successful, says my agent."

Back then, her debut novel could have been included on the list — a book that was quickly added to school curricula and has now been made into a film.

Likewise, on this year's longlist, Wahl's novel "Die Assistentin" (The Assistant) has not been included. A literature critic from Frankfurter Rundschau had this to say about the decision: "Why is good literature always supposed to hurt before it can be deemed 'valuable'? (...) The fact that an author like Wahl has been ignored, simply because her captivating writing fascinates millions of readers, makes me really angry."

Presumably, Caroline Wahl's fans will ensure that her new novel becomes another bestseller — even without the German Book Prize.

World.title: Serbia: Keeping EU, Russia in play ahead of key election
World.content:
As Serbia heads towards an uncertain election, President Aleksandar Vucic is balancing ties with Russia and EU ambitions. But growing geopolitical tensions and pressure at home are narrowing his room to maneuver.

Smoke from the wildfires still hangs over parts of Serbia, but as the flames slowly recede, another debate is taking shape in their wake — one that has less to do with firefighting and more with politics.

In early August, wildfires swept across Serbia, affecting more than 3,500 hectares (8,600 acres) in the Deliblato Sands Special Nature Reserve alone. For days, firefighters, soldiers and helicopters battled the flames.

Serbia turned to Russia for help in fighting wildfires in the Deliblato Sands Special Nature Reserve Image: Marko Dimic/ZUMA/picture alliance

Then a Russian Ilyushin Il-76 firefighting aircraft arrived in the southern city of Nis. Serbia had turned to Moscow for help, making Russia the first foreign country it asked to provide a firefighting aircraft. Pro-government media greeted its arrival with celebratory coverage, dubbing the aircraft the "Russian beast."

"Considering that there are no firefighting aircraft of this capacity available within the European Union, the arriving Russian aircraft will significantly strengthen our capacities to fight the fires," said Luka Causic, head of the Serbian Interior Ministry's Department for Emergency Situations.

A pragmatic choice between EU, Russia — or a political signal?

The episode, however, was already being viewed through a geopolitical lens, as Serbia had sought Russian assistance before activating the EU's emergency mechanism.

When it did, the response was swift. Brussels mobilized four helicopters from its strategic rescEU reserve, based in Czechia, Romania and Slovakia, along with ground firefighting teams from Germany and Romania.

Emergency services, including German firefighters, were on hand to help Serbia battle wildfires Image: Feuerwehr Bonn/dpa/picture alliance

Vucic rejected the idea that turning to Russia first was a foreign-policy decision or a sign of Serbia's political alignment with Moscow.

"As far as equipment and resources are concerned, we are a European giant. The helicopters we received from Europe to fight the fires are less capable than ours and have a lower carrying capacity than our own," Vucic said during a visit to the Deliblato Sands.

Zelenskyy in Belgrade

The wildfire episode came less than two weeks after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy made his first official visit to Serbia.

The two presidents reaffirmed their support for each other's territorial integrity, which is particularly significant for Belgrade because Ukraine does not recognise Kosovo's independence.

But Vucic is also trying to keep the other side on board, says Vuk Vuksanovic , a political scientist and foreign-policy lecturer at King's College London.

Vuksanovic argues that Vucic's engagement with Zelenskyy must therefore be portrayed in Moscow not as a fundamental shift in Serbia's relationship with Russia, but as a response to Western pressure and Serbia's own interests.

"Vucic is now trying to make sure that neither the West nor Russia becomes an open opponent during the election campaign," said Vuksanovic.

"Zelenskyy was primarily received so that the ruling coalition could present itself to Europeans as a great friend of Ukraine. In the same way, Vucic is trying to present himself to the Trump administration as a great friend of Israel, primarily to ensure that neither the European Union nor the United States becomes an opponent of the ruling party during the election campaign," Vuksanovic added.

Vucic's room for maneuver is shrinking

The problem is that the room to maintain these relationships may be shrinking.

The deeper the confrontation between Russia and the West becomes, the harder it is for Serbia to remain close to both without facing pressure to choose.

The European Union increasingly expects candidate countries to align their foreign and security policies with those of the bloc. Serbia's refusal to impose sanctions on Russia remains one of the most visible obstacles to closer alignment.

But Moscow, too, has reasons not to take Belgrade's loyalty for granted, Vuksanovic said. He argues that Russia does not fully trust Vucic, even as Moscow continues to support his narrative about "color revolutions" — a reference to anti-government protests, in this case the student-led protests in Serbia that started last year, which Vucic and Russia portray as Western-backed attempts to destabilize the government.

For Vucic, however, the longer-term question of Serbia's ties with Russia can wait. The more immediate question is whether he will survive the election, tentatively scheduled for October, and remain in a position to preserve that delicate balance himself.

Edited by: Rob Mudge

World.title: Iceland holds knife-edge referendum on EU membership talks
World.content:
The Nordic nation shelved earlier plans to join the EU over fishing rights, but geopolitics, including Trump's threat to seize Greenland, has prompted a rethink.

Iceland holds a national referendum on Saturday on whether to restart negotiations to join the European Union.

The Nordic nation has spent the better part of two decades wrestling with the question of becoming the bloc’s 28th member.

Iceland's left-leaning government, elected in 2024, originally vowed to hold a vote next year but brought it forward because of rising geopolitical tension over Russia's war in Ukraine and Greenland.

Iceland debates joining EU amid Trump's Greenland interest To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What do we know about Iceland's referendum?

As they head to one of hundreds of polling stations, voters will be asked a simple yes/no question:

Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?

The question relates to a previous attempt by the Icelandic government to join the EU in 2009, at the height of the global financial crisis that devastated the local economy. The accession plan was later shelved.

Saturday's vote is described as too close to call, with a Gallup poll on Friday suggesting a narrow majority of Icelanders oppose reopening talks. Other recent polls suggest a narrow lead for the yes vote.

Although Iceland has never been an EU member, it is already closely integrated with the bloc.

It is a member of both the European Economic Area (EEA) — which gives access to the EU's frictionless single market — and the Schengen Area free-travel zone.

Of Iceland's roughly 400,000 population, around 265,000 are eligible to vote.

Saturday’s referendum is too close to call Image: B. Niehaus/snapshot/IMAGO

What are the deciding factors among voters?

Voters have grown increasingly concerned about geopolitics, including the threat from Russia and US President Donald Trump's threats to seize nearby Greenland from Denmark.

Icelanders, who gained independence from Denmark in 1944, have been asking whether they could be next.

"We can't really trust the US anymore," said Hildur Knutsdottir, a horror fiction writer who plans to vote in favor of EU membership.

Arctic nations sit at the center of a growing contest for the polar north, as the United States, Russia and China jostle for influence over sea routes, natural resources and security.

The left-leaning Icelandic coalition believes EU membership could help counter Trump's ambitions in the North Atlantic.

"The international order that underpinned our security and prosperity for decades is under serious pressure," Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Gunnarsdottir told Reuters last week.

"In times like these, small nations need to ​think carefully about where they stand and who stands with them," she added.

Is the US driving Iceland to join the European Union? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Fishing, interest rates and national identity

The last attempt to join the EU was shelved in 2015 largely over concerns about joining the bloc's common fisheries policy.

Icelanders have been living off hefty cod and haddock catches for centuries and are loath to open the chilled Arctic waters to Spanish, Dutch and other EU trawlers, which is a requirement from Brussels.

The government has said it could try to negotiate a full opt-out from the policy.

Some economists think Icelanders, who have struggled under high inflation and interest rates, could benefit financially from EU membership and possibly the adoption of the euro.

National identity is another driver of voting, with opponents of EU membership noting how Iceland enjoys all the benefits of European integration without being a full member.

"For a country like ours with our small economy, it's very important to maintain our sovereignty and not to transfer more power than we would have to do to the EU," former Prime Minister Katrin Jakobsdottir said at an ​event in Reykjavik ‌on Thursday.

What happens if Iceland votes to restart EU talks?

A yes vote would trigger a negotiating process with the EU's executive branch, the European Commission.

This would involve discussions on 35 areas, from the economy to human rights.

A foreign ministry memo estimates accession talks could start by the end of the year and take 18 to 24 months.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

World.title: La tragedia de Nepal alerta sobre un peligro creciente: 15 millones de personas viven bajo la amenaza de los lagos glaciares
World.content:
El mapa global de riesgo por inundación repentina tras el desborde de estas lagunas, un fenómeno conocido como GLOF, se ha multiplicado por seis en un siglo, impulsado por el cambio climático

La monstruosa riada del Tíbet y Nepal, que ha causado centenares de muertos y miles de desaparecidos, ha puesto de actualidad el riesgo de vivir en cordilleras con glaciares, ya que todo indica que una de estas masas de hielo colapsó y desencadenó la tragedia. El fenómeno se conoce como GLOF (siglas en inglés de glacier lake outburst flood), una inundación repentina provocada por el desborde de un lago glaciar. El cambio climático y su aumento de las temperaturas están impulsando estos eventos: las riadas se han multiplicado por seis en el último siglo. Las grandes cadenas montañosas como el Himalaya, los Andes o los Alpes concentran los lugares donde más ocurren este tipo de riadas, a las que viven expuestas 15 millones de personas en todo el mundo, la mitad de ellas en Perú, India, China y Pakistán. Monitorizar glaciares y lagunas no es sencillo —sobre todo en países en desarrollo—, pero salva vidas: el año pasado, un pueblo de Suiza fue evacuado dos días antes de que otro glaciar colapsara.

“Los glaciares están retrocediendo desde 1950, y desde 1990 lo hacen de una forma acelerada. Los últimos cuatro años están entre los cinco que más pérdidas han tenido de la serie histórica, mientras que en los 25 años del siglo XXI el retroceso se ha duplicado respecto a los 25 anteriores”, explica Juan Ignacio López, experto en glaciares del Instituto Pirenaico de Ecología (IPE-CSIC). “El Himalaya no se escapa, sino que es uno de los puntos calientes de pérdidas de hielo a nivel global”, advierte. Al ser un retroceso general, “queda claro que no se debe a factores locales, sino al incremento térmico impulsado por el cambio climático de origen humano”.

Esta regresión tiene muchos efectos sobre el sistema climático y los ecosistemas, pero además está aumentando los lagos glaciares —que retienen el agua de deshielo—, que han crecido un 50% en número y superficie desde la década de 1990. “El agua no está tras una presa sólida, como las construidas por los humanos, sino por morrenas [lomas de hielo y sedimentos] o bloques de hielo, que son muy inestables. Cuando se desestabilizan por cualquier motivo, se desencadena una avenida repentina o GLOF”, apunta Jesús Revuelto, que estudia este fenómeno en el IPE-CSIC. Esto, unido a la mayor presión demográfica en las montañas, genera riesgos para millones de personas en esos lugares.

El mapa global de riesgo de GLOF, publicado en 2023 en Nature Communications, muestra que las zonas que más pueden sufrir este tipo de riadas están en Asia Central (sobre todo China, Nepal, India y Pakistán, que comparten el Himalaya y otras cordilleras), los Andes (Perú, Bolivia, Chile y Argentina) y los Alpes (Suiza, Italia, Francia y Austria). Otras regiones serían el noroeste de Norteamérica, Islandia y Escandinavia, aunque con muchas menos afecciones.

Paisaje de desolación en Nepal tras la monstruosa riada causada por el colapso de un glaciar hace tres días. Rajesh Kumar Singh (AP Photo)

En esos lugares viven alrededor de 15 millones de personas, según el mismo trabajo. De ellas, la mitad están en áreas montañosas de Perú, India, Pakistán y China. López resume: “Más de la mitad de la población del mundo expuesta a riesgos de glaciares vive en el Himalaya y en otras montañas altas de Asia. Otro punto muy complicado son los Andes, sobre todo en Perú, donde ha habido muchos accidentes en el siglo XX, pero precisamente por eso se ha invertido mucho en tomar medidas para reducir el riesgo de la población y se ha reducido la mortalidad”.

Desde comienzos del siglo XX hasta la década de 2010, la media anual de GLOF documentados se ha multiplicado casi por seis, pasando de los 7,6 anuales de la primera década del siglo XX a los 43,7 de los 2010. Revuelto lo analiza: “Por un lado, la población mundial se ha incrementado y hay más posibilidades de tener vídeos de estos eventos, que a veces ocurren en lugares remotos. Por otro, el cambio climático aumenta las temperaturas, lo que hace que se funda más hielo de los glaciares que desemboca en estas lagunas y puede desestabilizarlas, romper las presas naturales y generar grandes deslizamientos o riadas”.

Más de 3.100 riadas glaciales

La base de datos histórica de GLOFs elaborada por la Universidad de Viena ha identificado 3.151 riadas glaciares desde el año 850 hasta el 2022 ocurridas en 27 países. La mayoría se ha concentrado en Norteamérica (833), Asia Central (569), los Alpes (443) y los Andes (337). Hay que tener en cuenta que en las áreas más remotas —como los Andes y el Himalaya— los GLOFs han sido más difíciles de confirmar hasta la reciente llegada de las imágenes por satélite. De hecho, todavía no está claro qué laguna se desbordó tras el colapso del glaciar del Tíbet.

Precisamente por ocurrir en zonas apartadas, muchos de estos fenómenos no causan víctimas, aunque el trabajo ha constatado que 44 riadas glaciares mataron al menos a 3.636 personas —no se cuentan las de los últimos cuatro años—. Una de las más catastróficas ocurrió en 1941 en Perú, cuando un trozo de un glaciar cayó en una laguna, generando una ola que rompió el dique y creó una riada que arrasó Huaraz, donde causó la muerte de más de 1.800 habitantes. Este jueves, el Instituto Nacional de Investigación en Glaciares y Ecosistemas de Montaña peruano advirtió de que al menos 58 lagunas de los Andes están en riesgo “muy alto de desbordamiento”.

El pueblo suizo de Blatten, arrasado en 2025 tras el colapso de un glaciar en los Alpes. Michael Buholzer (AP/LaPresse)

¿Cómo evitar futuras catástrofes? Revuelto responde: “Suiza lo hizo el año pasado en Blatten. Monitorizaron el glaciar y las laderas con sensores, elementos de sismicidad… Constataron que había desplazamientos muy importantes, y evacuaron el pueblo dos días antes de una enorme riada”. En los Alpes hay recursos para controlar estas masas de hielo, pero en países en desarrollo como Nepal, India o Pakistán es más complicado. “Hay más zonas potencialmente peligrosas y desniveles más amplios, por lo que es difícil monitorizar todas las montañas. Pero al menos habría que tener acotadas e identificadas las zonas que pueden ser susceptibles de este tipo de deslizamientos, así como los valles donde pueden desembocar”, concluye.

World.title: Las familias egipcias se quedan sin colchón financiero
World.content:
Para mercados emergentes como Egipto, disponer de una tasa de ahorro elevada es crucial para financiar la inversión interna que necesitan sus economías y poder crecer a largo plazo de forma sostenible y sin depender de deuda externa. Más allá de ofrecer una red de seguridad más conveniente y barata ante posibles shocks económicos, todo lo que se ahorre puede dirigirse a inyectar fondos en servicios públicos, infraestructuras o industrias.

En el caso del gigante árabe, banqueros han señalado al medio económico local Enterprise que la horquilla ideal sería una tasa de ahorro en relación con el producto interior bruto (PIB) de entre el 20% y el 30%. Pero nada más alejado de la realidad. En el año fiscal 2024-2025, este índice se desplomó en Egipto hasta el 1,2% respecto al 6,1% del curso anterior; una caída del 80% que lo colocó en su nivel más bajo desde que se comenzó a calcular en los años sesenta del pasado siglo.

Según un estudio del think tank cairota Instituto Nacional de Planificación, vinculado al Ministerio de Planificación y Desarrollo Económico, esta severa limitación se ve agravada por el hecho de que más del 60% de los egipcios permanecen fuera del sistema bancario formal, lo que limita el trasvase de capital (si lo hubiese). Además, casi el 70% del crédito bancario actual del país se dedica a financiar su abultado déficit fiscal, lo que drena sus escasos fondos.

La drástica caída de la tasa de ahorro no se atribuye, sin embargo, a ninguna falta generalizada de planificación, sino que se lee como una nueva señal de que gran parte de las familias egipcias sencillamente no pueden ahorrar nada. Y el gran culpable de ello es la rápida erosión del poder adquisitivo que sufre el país a raíz, sobre todo, de un prolongado ciclo de inflación, que no cae por debajo del 10% desde enero de 2022 y que acarició el 34% en 2023.

Para la mayoría de egipcios, esta abrumadora inflación (y la vertiginosa caída de los ahorros) refleja una situación económica límite. En los últimos años, varios estudios ya han observado que muchas familias se han visto obligadas a comer menos y peor y a recortar su gasto en partidas fundamentales como educación y sanidad debido a una persistentemente alta subida de precios. Ahorrar se ha convertido para muchos en poco más que un sueño.

Por ello, numerosas voces han vuelto a apuntar a este círculo vicioso como otra señal de la distancia cada vez más abismal entre los análisis complacientes acerca de la economía egipcia, a menudo muy centrados en indicadores macroeconómicos como su crecimiento (de entorno al 5% este año), y la realidad cotidiana de millones de egipcios, mucho más adversa.

Bum del crédito

La fuerte reducción de la capacidad de ahorro de la mayoría de familias egipcias ha ido de la mano de otro proceso paralelo que también genera inquietud: la proliferación en el país de plataformas que ofrecen servicios de financiación para realizar compras a plazos. Un bum del clásico compra ahora y paga después que se está traduciendo en un consumo cada vez más centrado en el endeudamiento. Este cambio de patrón no se está produciendo para adquirir ni productos de lujo ni bienes como viviendas, sino que muchos ciudadanos recurren al crédito para cubrir necesidades más bien básicas, como la compra de electrodomésticos. En el último lustro, la cartera total de financiación al consumo no bancaria en Egipto se ha multiplicado por cinco y hay medios que señalan que, en los dos últimos años, el importe medio de los préstamos por prestatario ha disminuido, lo que indica un mayor endeudamiento destinado a compras de menor valor.

Aunque la mayoría de gente vaya con el agua al cuello, la subida de precios precipita compras a corto plazo, incluso si implica endeudarse, para evitar pagar más en el futuro. Y más allá de frenar un ahorro que permita alimentar la economía doméstica, el riesgo es evidente desde hace un tiempo: una encuesta de finales de 2022 del Instituto Internacional de Investigación sobre Políticas Alimentarias (IFPRI) ya alertó de que, a raíz de la crisis desatada por la invasión rusa de Ucrania, hasta un 84% de familias egipcias habían dejado de pagar algunas deudas.
