World.title: Por el Rouletenburg de Dostoievski: un viaje a Baden-Baden, Wiesbaden y Bad Homburg
World.content:
El escritor ruso desplegó pasión, literatura y su adicción a la ruleta en estas tres ciudades de Alemania que le sirvieron de inspiración para ‘El jugador’

Roulettenburg es la ciudad ficticia de juego y aguas termales que Fiódor Dostoievski creó para El jugador (1866) con su memoria de las ciudades de Baden-Baden, Wiesbaden y Bad Homburg, en Alemania. Anna Dostoievskaia, su joven esposa y taquígrafa de la novela, taquigrafió en agosto de 1867 cómo fue el regreso del genio a Baden-Baden, donde empeñó incluso su anillo de bodas (el de ella) para seguir jugando. Sudaba, temblaba, perdía casi todo otra vez soñando con el dinero que traería la ruleta. Pero se recuperó con la genialidad de ella, que se convertiría en su editora y librera, y en quien logró consolidar su obra globalmente.

En el centro de Baden-Baden, al suroeste del país y una de las tres ciudades que inspiran el lugar donde transcurre El jugador, está el paseo Lichtentaler, con decenas de tipos de rosas, dalias, castaños, azaleas, ginkos y robles junto al Museo Frieder Burda de arte contemporáneo. Más o menos al final de los más de dos kilómetros junto al río Oos, a los pies de la Selva Negra, el viajero observa un edificio neoclásico con columnas y la maestría de las pinturas mural: es el Trinkhalle. El edificio se construyó en la primera mitad del siglo XIX y Jakob Götzenberger pintó los murales que representan mitos autóctonos y adornan su fachada. Llama la atención el de la sirena enamorada —¡pobre!— de un cazador al que fue enriqueciendo con joyas sacadas de un palacio submarino. Pero él quería siempre más joyas; hasta exigir a su amada que robara la corona de oro del rey de las profundidades. Tras morir a manos del rey, la sangre de la sirena tiñó el agua. El cazador, arrepentido, deambuló por siempre. Jamás pudo perdonarse haber sacrificado a su gran amor.

Más información Las mejores terrazas de los cafés históricos de Viena

Estatua de Fiódor Dostoievski, del artista Nikolai Karlychanow, en un parque de la ciudad alemana de Bad Homburg. Joerg Hackemann ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Los viajeros que buscan las huellas del escritor ruso en Baden-Baden descubren que en el verano de 1867 Anna y su genial esposo debieron ver los frescos cada tarde y reparar, de entre todos, en el de la sirena del lago. Dostoievski siempre pedía dinero, joyas, ropa lujosa para empeñar. Él temblaba a veces. Ella lloró al conocer las pérdidas. Esta era la ruta de su paseo vespertino, cuando él salía del casino. El lugar no ha cambiado mucho desde entonces. Hotelitos y restaurantes limitan con el paseo. Estamos en la zona joya del Estado de Baden-Wurtemberg, en una ciudad de cerca de 60.000 habitantes donde se citaban en verano los aristócratas y burgueses en el siglo XIX que durante el invierno se iban a París. Aunque en agosto la ciudad, que en el estío se llena de música, sufre temperaturas inusuales y tormentas eléctricas.

Exterior del Museo Frieder Burda de arte contemporáneo, en Baden-Baden. Peter Schickert ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Anna Dostoievskaia taquigrafió en su diario la cara más inusual del genio y el lugar, la del jugador y su trampa. Harto de deudas, Dostoievski firmó un contrato mortal con su editor: entregaría en tiempo récord El jugador o perdería los derechos de todas sus obras. Y ella llegó a su vida con el reto de taquigrafiar la obra en 26 días. Él, viudo y 25 años mayor, le pidió que se casaran. En el verano de 1867, Anna estaba embarazada y escribía en su diario la odisea paralela a El jugador. Taquigrafió: “Sus jardines son perfectos, sus fuentes cantan, pero cada rincón huele a dinero perdido”. También: “Las calles están llenas de rusos que pasean con sonrisas falsas ocultando que por la noche han empeñado sus abrigos”. Además: “Me desesperaba que Fedja siguiera convencido de que podía ganar miles”. Ese agosto también anotaba: “Llevamos cuatro días comiendo sin pagar (…) no nos quedará más remedio que empeñar mi vestido morado, el único que queda para empeñar”. “Fedja se abalanzó sobre mí (…) y confesó llorando que lo había perdido todo…”, dejó escrito el 21 de agosto de 1867.

La pareja vivía en dos habitaciones en una casa humilde de la calle BäderstraBe, junto al balneario de Caracalla —piscinas abajo, arriba zona nudista con aguas de contraste, baño turco y un restaurante sencillo para comer—. En la calle adoquinada y en la casa que se alza donde ambos vivieron hoy el genio permanece con un busto, libro e inscripción en la fachada en su honor. Nada aquí recuerda que ese tiempo no fue fácil.

Baden-Baden es joya de la Unesco y hoy, como debió ocurrir siempre, tiene su propio plan de sostenibilidad en, por ejemplo, transporte y aguas termales. Según la actriz Marlene Dietrich, tiene también el casino más bello del mundo. El lujoso casino, en el edificio Kurhaus, está decorado imitando el estilo del palacio de Versalles. Frente a las ruletas, los y las crupiers piden que se haga juego, cortan el aire con la palma de la mano y hacen girar la rueda. “He visto de todo aquí”, dice un crupier de ascendencia española. “Es un buen lugar. Hay gente que pierde. O gana. Es bonito el sitio y la ciudad. ¿Qué es lo que siempre sale? No podría decirte”. Un jugador, frente a él, apunta en un rústico cuaderno dónde pone cada ficha. Parece probar un método de juego, comprobar una ley. Dostoievski también creyó haber encontrado la fórmula para ganar. Taquigrafiaba en su diario Anna: “Él regresó a casa. Entonces teníamos 55 taleros. Se los di. (…) Nos quedamos con cuatro taleros porque el quinto estaba reservado para el almuerzo”.

Interior del casino Baden-Baden. JLGuti ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Él se había enganchado a la ruleta en Wiesbaden, capital del Estado federal de Hesse —y también inspiración para Roulettenburg—. Wiesbaden, junto al Rin, es tan tranquila, ordenada y armónica que, pese a sus casi 300.000 habitantes, el viajero siente el lugar como hogar.

Una de las calles en el centro histórico de Baden-Baden. carla65 ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Rodeado de jardines, recuerda mucho a Baden-Baden, incluso por sus termas, las aguas que manan de fuentes en la calle, el juego y su atracción. “Creía tener el método para ganar. Tenía poco más de 20 años. Trabajaba. Me arreglaba. Iba al casino. Apostaba. Mi método de juego no podía fallar, pero en poco tiempo perdí todo. Así descubrí que dentro de mí había un jugador. Corté con las apuestas y dejé de ir al casino, pero el jugador sigue ahí”, dice Thomas, de pie junto a la Kurhaus de Wisbaden. Él tiene 59 años, nació en Wisbaden y el juego y el dinero forman parte de su ADN. Y también forma parte de su memoria la paz que hay a los pies de los montes Taunus. En 1865, Dostoievski comenzó aquí Crimen y castigo, y tramó El jugador. “Todo en la ciudad es una trampa. Las aguas te curan el cuerpo y matan el alma”, escribió en El jugador. “El parque era magnífico, con castaños centenarios y fuentes que cantaban. Pero yo no veía nada de eso, solo veía el casino, que me llamaba como un abismo”. Su esposa, que, según escribió en sus memorias, taquigrafiaba 200 palabras por minuto cuando conoció al escritor, pronto tomó el timón administrativo de la familia. A orillas del Rin, en Wiesbaden, él la escribía: “Lo he vuelto a perder todo. (…). Envía dinero para ir”.

Interior del Kurhaus de la ciudad de Wiesbaden. ZImages / Alamy / CORDON PRESS

En verano, hoy la Luisenplatz de Wiesbaden se llena de terrazas con comida de todos los continentes junto a la catedral. En invierno aquí huele al vino caliente del mercado de Navidad. El busto de Dostoievski está en la Nizzaplätzchen, en el Kurpark, pero no describen sus gestos la relación casi mística con la ruleta, ni su obsesión. Todo el foco estaba en el juego —“De las maravillas de la naturaleza solo he visto el Rin con sus orillas. Eso sí es una maravilla”, escribiría—. También en Bad Homburg, ciudad balneario que los reyes prusianos y emperadores alemanes utilizaron como residencia de verano habitual en el siglo XIX, atrayendo a la alta sociedad europea.

El Kaiser-Wilhelms-Bad, un histórico edificio balneario en la ciudad de Bad Homburg. Luise Berg-Ehlers ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

En esta ciudad alemana, la Torre Blanca despunta en el horizonte y se siente el vivificante aire de los Taunus. A partir del siglo XX esta ciudad de poco más de 50.000 habitantes se convirtió en la predilecta de los más adinerados de Fráncfort, en especial tras la devastación de la guerra. La ciudad, que nació sobre más de veinte manantiales, este año ha eliminado de los festejos estivales los fuegos artificiales, las hogueras y cualquier tipo de fogatas. Aquí Dostoievski acabó de construir su Roulettenburg.

La torre blanca del castillo de Bad Homburg. Sina Ettmer ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

El genio pareció encontrar la cura tras jugar tres días seguidos y perder: “Anya, ángel de mi guarda. Me ha ocurrido algo grande: me he librado de la abominable ilusión que me ha atormentado durante casi 10 años. (…) soñaba con ganar dinero. Soñaba con ello en serio, con pasión. ¡Pero ahora se acabó! Esta fue verdaderamente la última vez. (…) ahora dedicaré mi mente a cosas de provecho (…) Y así mi trabajo será mejor y más rentable, (…) sigamos juntos nuestro camino, ¡y me encargaré de que seas feliz!”. Era 1971. Pocos meses después, la joven Anna editaba y enviaba los libros de su marido al extranjero. Convertida en editora y librera, cumplió el sueño de él de atraer dinero.

World.title: Por la Comarca de la Sidra de Asturias entre historia, naturaleza, pueblos y cultura
World.content:
Una de las calles de la localidad asturiana de Villaviciosa, uno de los municipios que forman parte de la Comarca de la Sidra.

El Principado es un paraíso natural, gastronómico y artístico cada día más apreciado como privilegiado destino turístico. Y la sidra, la bebida más popular y su símbolo identitario más universal

Emprendemos un viaje por la Comarca de la Sidra de Asturias, para, entre culín y culín, descubrir algunos de los grandes atractivos de esta emblemática tierra y todos los secretos de esta bebida milenaria. La comarca o mancomunidad sidrera asturiana es un territorio al que dan vida seis municipios del centro-oriente asturiano: Colunga, Nava, Cabranes, Villaviciosa, Bimenes y Sariegu. Tomaremos como punto de partida Nava, población popularmente conocida como “El Corazón de la Sidra”, y que cuenta con un interesante e interactivo Museo de la Sidra, así como con el Festival de la Sidra, declarado de Interés Turístico Nacional y que cada año se celebra la segunda semana de julio.

Para aprovechar el tiempo, lo ideal es visitar el museo a primera hora (durante su horario de verano, hasta el 15 de octubre, abre a las 11.00; lunes cerrado). De esta forma, encontraremos poca gente y la visita será más agradable. En el museo tendremos ocasión de conocer el origen e historia de la sidra, así como el proceso que debe tener lugar antes de poder disfrutar de esta chispeante bebida. También conoceremos cómo se elaboran las distintas variedades —natural, espumosa, filtrada, y de hielo—, el porqué y el cómo hay que escanciar la sidra. Todo ello ilustrado con amenas explicaciones, vídeos, herramientas, prensas o llagares, envasadoras… Después de la visita y de conocer lo laborioso que resulta hacerla, entenderemos la mucha razón que tiene Luis Benito, director de la Cátedra Universitaria de la Sidra de Asturias, al afirmar: “La sidra es un producto de lujo, a precios populares”. Benito fue, además, la persona que más contribuyó a que la Unesco proclamase en 2024 patrimonio cultural inmaterial de la humanidad a la sidra asturiana.

Más información Las mejores terrazas de los cafés históricos de Viena

En cuanto al origen de la sidra, pese a que existen registros históricos que hablan de que los egipcios ya fermentaban manzanas, y que griegos y romanos disponían de una bebida parecida a la sidra, es a través del geógrafo griego Estrabón —siglo I a.C.—y del historiador romano Plinio el Viejo —siglo I— cuando tenemos noticia de que, en los pueblos del norte de la Península, existía una bebida elaborada a partir de las manzanas. Pero no es hasta el siglo XVI cuando hay evidencia escrita de que ya se producían en Asturias 35.000 litros de sidra. No obstante, es posible que un primer acontecimiento decisivo en el auge y difusión de la bebida fuera la creación en el siglo IX, por parte del rey Alfonso II, del Primitivo Camino de Santiago, que partía desde Oviedo y que fue la primera ruta de peregrinación de la historia. A partir de entonces, aunque con algún altibajo histórico, el consumo de la sidra no dejó de crecer y apreciarse. Por eso, y porque la sidra asturiana terminó por viajar a los confines del mundo con la gran emigración del pueblo asturiano, podría afirmarse que el viaje y la sidra han ido siempre de la mano.

Villa Maximina, una de las casas indianas que se pueden ver en la localidad asturiana de Nava. Alamy / CORDON PRESS

Después de la sidra y la fabada, lo mejor es una excursión

Lo que se impone después de visitar el Museo de la Sidra es dar una vuelta por Nava y su casco histórico, y quizás acercarse a conocer la pintoresca villa rural de Ceceda, que conserva viejos hórreos y paneras; algunas casas indianas de estilo colonial y una pequeña capilla con frescos. Tampoco hay que dejar de ver en la cercana pedanía de Fuensanta el palacio de La Ferrería; una imponente casa fuerte medieval del siglo XIV, declarada Monumento Histórico Artístico, donde vivió Doña Jimena —mujer de El Cid—. Como todo está muy próximo, probablemente dé tiempo de regresar a Nava para tomarse un vermut en el bar de La Naveta y comer en alguna de sus muchas sidrerías, por ejemplo, en La Plaza.

Vista aérea del palacio de La Ferrería, en la pedanía de Fuensanta. GETTY IMAGES

Como en los meses de verano el día cunde mucho, después de comer, y para bajar los fabes, el pixín y la sidrina, podemos aprovechar y practicar senderismo haciendo alguna ruta que recorra cualquiera de los imponentes entornos naturales de la zona. Las opciones son numerosas. Se puede hacer la ruta de las Foces del Río Pendón (PR-AS 45); un recorrido circular que se inicia al lado de un antiguo balneario y se adentra en un espectacular desfiladero flanqueado por densas masas de hayas y castaños. Es de dificultad media-baja, de algo más de ocho kilómetros, y se realiza más o menos en tres horas. Otra alternativa, aunque más retirada —ya en el concejo de Bimenes—, es la Senda de Los Molinos (PR-AS 141), también circular y de dificultad moderada, que discurre a la vera del río Pra, recorriendo un valle exuberantemente verde, entre castaños, arces, alisos… y cinco antiguos molinos que crean estampas imborrables. La distancia de esta excursión es de poco más de seis kilómetros y su duración aproximada de tres o cuatro horas.

Un senderista por la Senda de Los Molinos. WHPics / Alamy / CORDON PRESS

Si lo de andar no te apasiona, puedes sustituir el senderismo por acercarte a conocer Santa María de Narzana —en el concejo de Sariego—, una interesante iglesia románica del siglo XII, que conserva portada y ábsides decorados con curiosos motivos zooantropomórficos.

Un pueblo encantador y un conocido ‘llagar’

Partiendo de Nava en dirección a Villaviciosa, un lugar de obligada parada es el pueblo de Torazu, perteneciente al concejo de Cabranes. Se localiza en un pequeño altiplano desde el que se tienen unas privilegiadas vistas del campo y las montañas astures. Reconocido como uno de Los Pueblos más Bonitos de España y distinguido con Premio Príncipe de Asturias al Pueblo Ejemplar en 2008, es un destacado ejemplo de la arquitectura popular asturiana. Conserva numerosos hórreos, la capilla porticada de Nuestra Señora de la Sienra y la iglesia de San Martín el Real; un templo barroco del siglo XVII, situado en la parte más elevada de esta pequeña y coqueta localidad de no más de 100 habitantes. Dispone también de un estupendo establecimiento para alojarse; se trata de La Hostería de Torazo, un lugar con spa y piscina acristalada con inmejorables vistas al más genuino paisaje interior asturiano.

Después de hacer noche en Torazu y volviendo al hilo conductor de este viaje, resulta obligado visitar un llagar (en castellano lagar), que no es otra cosa que la prensa con la que se extrae el mosto de la manzana y, por extensión, también el nombre que recibe el lugar, o bodega, en la que se elabora la sidra. Una buena opción puede ser acercarse al llagar e instalaciones de Viuda de Angelón, casa fundada en 1947 y uno de los 34 únicos llagares que trabaja en el Principado según los estrictos criterios del Consejo Regulador de la Denominación de Origen Protegida, que establece que en la elaboración de la sidra solo se pueden utilizar 76 variedades de manzana, de las más de 550 que se cultivan en Asturias.

Según la época en que se vaya, se podrán presenciar todas las fases del proceso de elaboración de la sidra. Nos explicarán las dos fermentaciones que tiene que experimentar el mosto de la manzana para convertirse en sidra natural: la alcohólica, para transformar los azúcares en alcohol y gas carbónico; y la maloláctica para convertir el acido málico, en láctico y así suavizar la acidez de la bebida. También nos hablarán de lo que dura el proceso en los toneles —de una a tres semanas la primera fermentación, y de tres a cinco meses la segunda—. Te ilustrarán también sobre los tipos de sidra existentes. O te contarán que, al principio, la sidra se servía directamente desde el barril, a través de la espicha (un pequeño grifo que hace salir a presión la sidra del tonel), hasta que hace 150 años empezó a embotellarse y a escanciarse, para así liberar el gas carbónico y resaltar los aromas de la sidra.

Del románico más genuino a los pueblos más bellos del Cantábrico

La siguiente etapa del viaje se centra en recorrer la que probablemente sea la mayor concentración de templos prerrománicos y románicos de Asturias y una de las mayores densidades de arquitectura medieval de toda Europa. La lista es casi inabarcable. Entre las iglesias más destacadas están San Salvador de Priesca, iglesia originaria del siglo X y monumento nacional desde 1913; Santa María de Llugás, un conjunto de singular belleza, que, después de Covadonga, es el principal santuario mariano de Asturias y Bien de Interés Cultural desde 1994; y San Juan de Amandi, reconocida construcción románica con un esbelto ábside semicircular y una fantástica colección de capiteles, reconocida como monumento nacional desde 1931. Bien de Interés Cultural, igualmente, es San Julián de Viñón, iglesia construida en el siglo XII y uno de los mejores ejemplos de románico rural de la zona, que, además, está muy cerca del Museo de la Escuela Rural de Asturias que también merece una visita; ambos en el concejo de Cabranes.

La iglesia de Santa María de la Oliva, en Villaviciosa. Aliaksandr Mazurkevich ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Pero si tuviéramos que resaltar un ejemplo especialmente sobresaliente de arte prerrománico y románico asturiano de la zona, ese, sin duda, sería el conjunto de Valdediós, con la iglesia y el monasterio de Santa María (fundado en 1200 y declarado Monumento Nacional en 1931), y, sobre todo, la iglesia de San Salvador, uno de los más hermosos monumentos del Principado y obra cumbre de la última etapa del arte prerrománico; conocido como el Conventín. Esta iglesia de tres naves fue consagrada en el año 893 y tiene notables influencias mozárabes, tanto en su estructura como en sus pinturas, además se encuentra situada en un paraje lleno de encanto y serenidad.

La iglesia de San Salvador de Valdediós, conocida popularmente como el Conventín. Alexei Fateev ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Pese a abarcar un espacio muy limitado, este formidable circuito de arte prerrománico y románico de la Comarca de la Sidra es prácticamente imposible de visitarse en un solo día. Como en algún momento habrá que comer y pensar en alojarse en algún sitio, una buena idea podría ser hacerlo en Narbasu, un hotel y restaurante que la familia Manzano ha montado en el antiguo palacio de Rubianes; una histórica construcción iniciada en el siglo XIV, enclavada en un paraje privilegiado en las inmediaciones de un río y con las montañas asturianas como imponente telón de fondo. La filosofía del lugar es integrarse y ser respetuoso con su entorno, haciendo, por ejemplo, que los productos vegetales utilizados sean de sus propios huertos y el resto, de pequeños productores de las inmediaciones. El lugar respira sosiego y hospitalidad y el restaurante tiene toda la calidad de una carta de cocina tradicional inspirada y avalada técnicamente por Nacho Manzano, reconocido chef —tres estrellas Michelin—, de Casa Marcial. Si comes allí, y lo pides, te maridarán la comida con los diferentes tipos de sidra.

Continuando con nuestro periplo turístico y sidrero, nos encaminamos hacia el litoral; la Comarca de la Sidra ofrece kilómetros de una costa con multitud de espléndidas playas y acantilados que disfrutar, así como algunos de los pueblos más bonitos de Asturias y de la cornisa cantábrica. Pero antes de llegar al mar, si tenemos tiempo, podemos desviarnos a Sietes para ver uno de los conjuntos de hórreos y paneras mejor conservados de todo el Principado. También podemos hacer un alto en Gobientes para conocer la iglesia románica de Santiago —Monumento Histórico-Artístico—, cuya construcción se remonta al siglo X y desde la que parte una pequeña senda, de un par de kilómetros, hacia la cascada de Obaya; un paraje natural que también merece la pena conocer.

Una calle de Sietes, donde espera uno los conjuntos de hórreos y paneras mejor conservados de todo el Principado. FedevPhoto ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Ya oliendo la sal, veremos las populosas playas de Isla —con sus llamativos bosques de eucaliptos— y, especialmente, la preciosa playa de Rodiles, en Villaviciosa, rodeada de vegetación y famosa entre los surfistas por tener un singular tipo de ola. La otra playa que no puede dejar de disfrutarse es la de La Griega, en Colunga, magnífico arenal en el que desemboca el río Libardón. Cerca de su extremo derecho se pueden ver imponentes ignitas (huellas fosilizadas) de dinosaurios, descubiertas en los años noventa. Hablando de dinosaurios, muy cerca de allí se encuentra el Museo del Jurásico de Asturias, con monumentales reproducciones de estos gigantes del pasado.

Las ignitas (huellas fosilizadas) de dinosaurios junto a la playa de La Griega, en Colunga. Alba Boix ( Alamy /CORDON PRESS )

Antes de abandonar la costa para dirigirnos a Villaviciosa, merecen una parada Lastres y Tazones, ambos reconocidos entre los Pueblos más Bonitos de España. El primero, creciendo escalonada y vistosamente desde el puerto hacia los acantilados que dominan la población, y el segundo, exhibiendo sus coloridas casas de pescadores y sus calles empedradas, y teniendo la singular significación histórica de haber sido la primera tierra española que pisó Carlos V a su llegada a la península Ibérica. En los dos se puede comer bien en cualquiera de sus restaurantes, aunque si se quiere disfrutar de unas vistas espectaculares, el restaurante El Mirador de Lastres regala un impresionante panorama de toda la bahía.

Calle en la localidad asturiana de Lastres. Politi Markovina ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Ría, piedras medievales y sidra viajera

La siguiente y prácticamente última etapa es Villaviciosa, conocida como “Capital Manzanera de España”, y famosa tanto por su ría y magnífico casco histórico como por ser la sede de la sidra El Gaitero. El concejo de Villaviciosa tiene el mayor número de pumaradas (plantaciones de manzanos) de Asturias, lo cual hace que su campo sea una explosión de color con la floración de los manzanos en primavera y, a finales del verano o principios de otoño, un espectáculo de árboles cargados de fruta.

La sidrería El Gaitero, en Villaviciosa. Ingenui ( GETTY IMAGES )

Villaviciosa tiene muchas historias que contar y una de las más importantes está relacionada con la sidra, porque fueron las industrias sidreras de la población las que popularizaron en todo el mundo la sidra espumosa o achampañada, que fue creada por el productor gijonés Tomás Zarracina en 1857, como respuesta a la añoranza que sentía la enorme colonia de emigrantes asturianos —más de medio millón— repartida por México, Argentina, Cuba… de poder celebrar sus fiestas con la bebida típica de su tierra; algo que antes resultaba imposible, porque la sidra natural no resistía el viaje y se estropeaba, y que no sucedería después con la sidra sometida al método champenoise (segunda fermentación en botella). La empresa que mejor supo producir y comercializar la sidra espumosa y viajera fue sidra El Gaitero, entre otras cosas, con su popular eslogan publicitario: “Sidra El Gaitero, famosa en el mundo entero”. Esta compañía sigue produciendo en Villaviciosa y organiza visitas guiadas por sus instalaciones, en las que muestran sus antiguos llagares o bodegas, que son como el interior de enormes y hermosas catedrales, al tiempo que explican todo el proceso de elaboración de su producto estrella.

Antes o después de visitar las bodegas hay que dar un paseo por el monumental casco histórico de Villaviciosa, que sorprende con sus numerosas casas blasonadas y con sus iglesias; especialmente Santa María de la Oliva, un templo románico-gótico del siglo XII, con artística portada principal. Otros edificios de gran interés son la iglesia parroquial de San Francisco, construcción del siglo XVII, y la capilla de la Concepción. Además de todo lo dicho, la mayor singularidad de la villa quizá sea que está a la vera de la ría que lleva su nombre y que tiene la consideración de Reserva Natural, por su característico ecosistema marítimo-fluvial y por ser un importante refugio de aves.

Una sugerencia que puede ser del gusto de adultos y, sobre todo, para los más pequeños, es la visita —a la salida de Villaviciosa— de la finca Los Caserinos, una granja ecológica familiar muy conocida en la zona, que elabora productos naturales de gran calidad (quesos, yogures bio, y arroz con leche, helados…) y que para los niños puede resultar un plan perfecto, porque la granja tiene cabras, vacas, ovejas, gallinas, caballos… a los que poder ver y tocar; además de aprender a hacer queso.

Como alguien dijo: “La sidra es una bebida ligera, anima a hablar y compartir, pone de buen humor, es diurética y buena para la salud, alegra el corazón y, por su baja graduación, es una buena compañera de viaje”. Pues eso.

World.title: Italia quiere poner orden en el caos de sus 12.000 playas privadas: más transparencia y nuevas tasas
World.content:
Entre el 33% y el 42% de los arenales del país son de pago. El Gobierno de Meloni, presionado por Bruselas, abrirá a concurso su gestión

Italia presume de sus 8.000 kilómetros de costa, pero disfrutar de ellos no siempre es gratis. Mientras que en otras partes ir a la playa significa buscar un hueco en la arena, en Italia la experiencia suele ser muy distinta. Encontrar un espacio donde plantar la sombrilla sin pagar puede convertirse en toda una aventura. En amplios tramos del litoral, el acceso al mar está gestionado por empresas privadas, mediante concesiones públicas, que han transformado las playas en un negocio multimillonario. El resultado es una de las estampas más características del verano italiano: bosques interminables de sombrillas perfectamente alineadas, acompañadas de sus respectivas tumbonas, esperando a ser alquiladas por precios que pueden superar los 35 euros al día.

Este modelo, muy arraigado en el país y marcado por una gestión plagada de irregularidades, afronta una reforma que lleva años aplazándose a pesar de la presión de Bruselas para poner orden. Las playas gestionadas por concesionarios privados no han dejado de ganar terreno. Según la asociación ecologista italiana Legambiente, ocupan ya más del 42% de los arenales del país. El Ministerio de Infraestructuras rebaja esa cifra al 33%, una diferencia que se explica por el criterio utilizado para el cálculo: el Gobierno utiliza para sus cuentas toda la línea costera italiana y no únicamente las zonas aptas para el baño.

Desde hace décadas, las empresas, casi siempre familiares —las concesiones suelen heredarse—, pagan cánones relativamente bajos al Estado por explotar espacios públicos, mientras los precios para los usuarios han aumentado de forma exponencial. Las concesionarias gestionan los servicios como los baños, las duchas, los vestuarios, los aparcamientos, además del alquiler de sombrillas y tumbonas. También controlan los chiringuitos y cafeterías y se encargan de las labores de salvamento. Mientras que las zonas públicas suelen estar descuidadas, a menudo sucias, y desprovistas de servicios públicos.

Se trata de un asunto sensible que divide a la opinión pública italiana. Para unos, las playas de pago garantizan orden, limpieza y comodidad; para otros, representan la privatización de un bien público que debería ser accesible para todos. La principal crítica al sistema es la enorme diferencia entre lo que pagan las concesionarias por explotar las playas y los beneficios que obtienen. El Estado recauda entre 80 y 100 millones de euros al año por las concesiones, mientras que el sector, marcado por la opacidad, mueve más de 2.000 millones de euros anuales, según distintas estimaciones. El propio Tribunal de Cuentas italiano ha advertido de que los cánones abonados por los empresarios no suelen ser proporcionales a los ingresos que obtienen.

Uno de los aspectos más controvertidos del modelo italiano es que las concesiones se han renovado durante años casi por inercia. Sin concursos abiertos ni una competencia efectiva y sin controles ni transparencia, los mismos operadores han conservado la explotación de amplios tramos del litoral público durante generaciones, consolidando un sistema difícil de encontrar en otros países europeos.

Un paso adelante

Bruselas lleva años reclamando cambios. La Comisión considera que Italia incumple la directiva Bolkestein de 2009, que obliga a garantizar la libre competencia en la adjudicación de este tipo de concesiones, y ha presionado repetidamente a Roma. Tras décadas de aplazamientos y enfrentamientos, el Gobierno de Giorgia Meloni ha abordado la cuestión. La reforma aprobada prevé que para el 30 de septiembre de 2027 salgan a concurso público todas las playas de pago, unas 12.000 repartidas por todo el país. Además, las concesiones tendrán una duración limitada, de entre cinco y 20 años, y habrá compensaciones económicas para los actuales titulares por las inversiones y obras que hayan realizado.

La perspectiva de abrir el mercado ha despertado, sin embargo, inquietud entre muchos empresarios del sector, que temen que los concursos favorezcan la entrada de grandes grupos turísticos o fondos de inversión capaces de desplazar a los negocios familiares que tradicionalmente han dominado las costas italianas.

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Dutch men’s hockey team have missed out on a home World Cup final, losing their semi-final to Spain in Amstelveen on Friday, the day before the Dutch women play for the title.

Spain, coached by the former Netherlands manager Max Caldas, won 4-3 at the Wagener Stadium.

The game turned in the final quarter, with the score at 1-1, when striker Duco Telgenkamp was sent to the sin bin for 10 minutes for pushing a Spanish defender to the ground.

With Telgenkamp off the pitch, Spain scored three times to go 4-1 ahead, José Basterra completing a hat-trick. Jip Janssen and Joep de Mol pulled two goals back late on, but Spain held the lead.

The result ended the Dutch men’s hopes of a first world title since 1998. They will play Argentina for bronze on Sunday in Wavre, Belgium, where Spain will meet defending champions Germany in the final.

The Dutch women, meanwhile, reached the final with a 1-0 win over Belgium and will face Argentina at the Wagener Stadium at 4pm on Saturday. Victory would give them a fourth successive world title, a feat no country has achieved.

World.title: Forget Belgian roads, we need to talk about Dutch drivers
World.content:
Our regular columnist Molly Quell drove through Belgium and France on her holiday and has developed some strong feelings about road design.

I’ve just returned from the most sacred of Dutch annual traditions. No, not early Sinterklaas festivities or a kring party for my mother-in-law’s birthday.

The yearly pilgrimage to France.

Don’t tell the authorities, as they may well take my passport, but this was my first year making the summer trek south to soak up the sun, drink plenty of wine and contribute to the wear and tear on Belgian roads.

In fact, as a childless adult, I don’t often take a proper summer holiday. Who wants to pay three times more to have your vacation infested with irritable parents and their inevitably sticky children?

I usually have my vacation during the school year when the temperatures are better and teenagers are locked up in educational institutions rather than blasting an unending roll of TikToks at full volume at the table next to mine while their parents order more drinks and pretend everyone is enjoying the perfect summer getaway.

But due to a series of unfortunate events, (namely, being at the mercy of the schedules of people who do have children) I took part in the annual ritual of packing up a car and driving many, many hours to spend time complaining about the French in France.

As I rarely have the opportunity to drive around rural Belgium and France, my husband and I decided to make the most of it and tick off a series of “places we’d like to see but aren’t worth planning an entire weekend around.”

Dunkirk. Omaha Beach. Jules Verne’s grave (very cool). Jardins d’Étretat (also cool). Mont-Saint-Michel (less cool and more like the temperature of Satan’s sauna in August).

We saw a lot of things and thus we did a lot of driving. Therefore, I now consider myself an expert on the ins and outs of Western European roadway infrastructure.

It is classist and problematic to mock the Belgians for their accents. It is simply stating objective and true facts when you mock their roads. It isn’t merely the quality of the roads (which can have a sort of deep tissue massage effect) that is bad but how they are designed.

It is as though Belgian road engineers are required to sample every single variety of local Trappist beer before planning an interchange.

Belgian drivers are also unhinged, but in fairness if I had to commute over Mad Max-style infrastructure every day, I would also operate a motor vehicle like I had no regard for human life.

The French are much better drivers. There is plenty to disparage about the French as a nation and a people, but the overall quality of their driving is very good. They do have the tendency to drive a bit close to the bumper, which my Dutch husband suggests they could improve by “having more than six minutes of driving lessons.”

What is confusing about French roads is the liberal use of the term “round about” for any jumble of intersecting roads without a stop light. Roundabouts have a shape. It’s literally in the name. French roundabouts are what happens when the children of drunk Belgian road engineers scribble on the design plans.

At least the French are largely forgiving of cars with foreign plates driving through their convoluted roundabouts Mario Kart style.

Given these experiences, you would think returning back over the border at the end of the journey would be a welcome relief. It was certainly a relief for my jaw, which I no longer had to clench to keep my molars from bashing together, but the Dutch are not without their own problems.

South of the border, there was a general regard for the speed limit. The occasional outlier (nearly always in a BMW) would fly past you in Belgium or France, but mostly people minded the rules.

The second we crossed the border, yellow plates began zooming past us as though everyone had been informed there was only one plate of bitterballen for the party and it would be distributed on a first-come, first-serve basis.

Maybe it is the smoothness of the roads, but Dutch drivers react to the border marker like a cow does to seeing grass for the first time in the spring.

It was very obvious that these drivers had insider information about the country’s wealth of speed cameras as you would see a car zip past on the left, only to brake a few kilometers later to avoid racking up fines.

Hell isn’t a place where the chefs are British and the police are German. It’s where the intersections are French and the drivers are Dutch. And the Belgians waste hours lost on poorly marked roads instead of brewing beer.

World.title: Oldebroek council executive apologises for Kalashnikov photo
World.content:
A member of the executive on Oldebroek council in Gelderland has apologised for posting a photograph of himself posing with a Kalashnikov in front of a pro-Russian flag. Standing next to him in the photo is a former Almere council candidate for the far-right FvD party, according to the Volkskrant.

Tom de Nooijer, of the local Christelijk Verbond Oldebroek party, shared the image on Instagram after visiting Transnistria, a self-declared, unrecognised pro-Russian region that broke away from Moldova after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

De Nooijer said he had been on holiday in Moldova and travelled to the region out of a “historical interest in the Soviet past”, and went to a shooting range there. He said the trip was private and not meant as a political statement. He is a former presenter of the right-wing broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland.

He initially declined to comment or apologise, prompting anger from opposition councillors. “They fled the violence he is glorifying by posing for a pro-Russian flag,” said Frank van ’t Ende, referring to the 200 Ukrainian refugees the council houses. A ChristenUnie councillor called the photo “shocking”.

Mayor Tanja Haseloop-Amsing told Omroep Gelderland that the council’s executive had been “unpleasantly surprised” by the image.

In a written statement on Wednesday, De Nooijer distanced himself from the hammer-and-sickle flag in the photo, called the visit unwise and apologised to anyone who might have been insulted.

World.title: Dutch spy agencies to get more powers against foreign enemies
World.content:
The Netherlands’ two intelligence agencies are to gain new powers to track and disrupt “obvious adversaries” such as Russian hackers, Chinese spies and Iranian operatives without asking permission in advance, under a draft law published by the cabinet.

The domestic intelligence service AIVD and military intelligence service MIVD would no longer need prior sign-off to follow an individual hacker online. “By then they have already gone,” said defence minister Dilan Yesilgöz.

Once a foreign service is formally designated an adversary, the agencies could pursue anyone thought to be working for it, with a watchdog checking afterwards whether their actions were lawful and able to halt operations it considers inappropriate.

The plans have raised concerns about the privacy of Dutch citizens. Yesilgöz said oversight would remain in place. “Putin and his cronies do not deserve our privacy, but the people of the Netherlands do,” she said.

The bill would also let the agencies work more closely with Dutch banks, universities and online platforms, warn them of risks and, in some cases, demand information from them. Interior minister Pieter Heerma, who is responsible for the AIVD, declined to name specific organisations.

It follows the previous cabinet’s abandoned plan to screen 8,000 foreign researchers and students for espionage risks, which was judged unworkable. Oversight of the two agencies would be merged into a single body.

The draft is open for public consultation before it goes to parliament.

World.title: “We have to stop this man”: mass sperm donor fathered 121 kids
World.content:
A Dutch man has fathered at least 121 children as a sperm donor and is still active, according to an investigation by current affairs programme Nieuwsuur – the latest in a line of mass donors who exploit a gap in the legal rules by working outside licensed clinics.

The man, who is 43 and from the Groningen region, donated to several sperm banks but operates mainly online, approaching women directly. Investigators spoke to dozens of affected mothers, and said the true figure is probably far higher.

They also found that the man sat on a government commission that evaluated the Dutch donor law in 2019. It is unclear how or why he was appointed.

Dutch clinics may not use a single donor for more than 12 families. But donors and would-be parents who arrange conception privately are bound by no legal maximum, a gap that lets a determined donor father dozens or hundreds of children unchecked. Nieuwsuur revealed last year that clinics had produced at least 85 mass donors.

The health and youth care inspectorate IGJ, part of the health ministry, said it did not know the man and called the case “very undesirable”. But a spokesperson said the inspectorate oversees care provided in clinics, not conception arranged in the private sphere.

Evasive behaviour

The donor children’s foundation Stichting Donorkind and several of the mothers want him to stop. “We have to stop this man,” they told the programme.

The mothers say he lies about how many children he has fathered, growing evasive or hinting he will break off contact when pressed – leverage that matters to women who want their child to be able to know their biological father one day.

Some of the women told Nieuwsuur he sent them sexually suggestive messages, offering to help conceive via the “natural method.” One mother from the Randstad who tried to report him said the police were no help. “The police just stared at me blankly,” she said.

Traces abroad

There are also signs that the same man has fathered children abroad. One mother traced several children in Germany through an online DNA database, and the man has donated at a Danish sperm bank.

The man declined to be interviewed, saying he wanted any contact to run anonymously through the mothers or official bodies. He asked for privacy for himself and the families, and would not confirm how many children he has conceived.

The most notorious Dutch case remains that of Jonathan Meijer, who fathered some 550 children worldwide and was ordered by a court to stop in 2023.

World.title: Majority of student rooms priced well over the legal limit
World.content:
The majority of student rooms on the Netherlands’ biggest rental platform, Kamernet, are being advertised at prices well over the legal limit – an average of €239 a month, and more than €400 in Amsterdam – investigative outlet Argos has found. Local councils are not intervening and say they have no power to do so.

Argos compared rent on 2,637 ads against the maximum each room is legally allowed to charge. Six in ten rooms were priced above the legal maximum over July and August, with landlords of overpriced rooms asking an average of €239 a month more than the rules permit.

In some cities, like Amsterdam, where the average room costs nearly €1,000 a month, 97% of the rooms Argos sampled were above the cap, by an average of €421 a month. In Utrecht the figure was 72%.

Utrecht and Nijmegen issued no fines and lowered no rents last year, while Rotterdam and The Hague were the exceptions, acting far more often.

Amsterdam council reaction

Since the Affordable Rent Act 2025 was introduced, which caps prices by a points system based on a room’s size and features, councils have been required to intervene – something the investigation found is not being done in many cities.

A spokesperson for Amsterdam council housing executive Zita Pels told DutchNews that the council cannot take legal action on advertising alone – an illegal rent must already be in force before it can do something. So students must first get into an illegally high rental contract before they can be helped.

The spokesperson also said the council “strongly opposes” the way people “shamelessly” exploit the housing crisis in Amsterdam, but that it unfortunately cannot do more about the advertising problem.

They also said the council itself advertises on rental platforms, attends student events, and visits tenants at home, because many people are reluctant to report overcharging for fear of losing their room.

In March, Amsterdam council also imposed a €45,000 penalty on the manager of a student complex in Amsterdam’s Zuidoost district for a range of violations, the council highlighted, including excessive rents. The landlord can still object.

There is a tenant advice foundation called !Woon that the council subsidises. Its 2025 report records more than 19,000 contacts about rent or service charges and 575 reports of serious landlord misconduct, and lists cases it has won, including 21 rulings against a single landlord, one of which cut a rent from €1,076 to €280.

The council’s own enforcement report to councillors, published in May, shows direct action on rents is a small part of the picture. Of 726 complaints under the new rental laws in 2025, 96 concerned rent levels; 167 were passed to !Woon and 102 fell outside the rules. The bulk of the council’s 1,836 enforcement outcomes last year involved empty or misused homes, not overcharging.

World.title: It ain’t pretty: botched Botox on the rise in country’s youth
World.content:
Just as the new school year gets underway, the Dutch Health and Youth Care Inspectorate (IGJ) has warned about a five-fold increase in complaints resulting from failed cosmetic treatments involving Botox and other dermal fillers.

The IGC received 175 reports of failed treatments, up from some 35 per year in the preceding years. The skyrocketing numbers, they say, are largely due to increased demand for the procedures among youth looking for fuller lips and less wrinkles and a surge in places providing them.

Young people, IGJ inspector Rosemarie Jansen told broadcaster NOS, were especially vulnerable to cutthroat rates among providers who often lack the mandatory qualifications to provide them. That “lowers the threshold for young people, precisely because they do not have much to spend,” she said.

Some 67% of the complaints involved a practitioner who was not legally qualified or lacked the necessary medical competence.

In the Netherlands, a doctor is required to be present when a patient receives such cosmetic treatments, something which is lacking in the proliferation of places offering them.

The botched procedures have led to swelling and drooping eyelids, lip inflammation and allergic reactions. The ICJ says the number of complaints is likely unreported due to the shame many young people feel about getting cosmetic work.

Fillercheck.nl

To help combat the problem, the IGC, along with Tilburg University and the consumer platform wiemooiwilzijn, have created fillercheck.nl, a website where those seeking cosmetic treatments can go down a four-part checklist that gets them thinking about the treatment, lets them find out if their provider is qualified and, says the IGC, help them recognize red flags.

The Inspectorate is taking their message via pop-up clinics disguised as cosmetic treatment centres to students in Amsterdam, Nijmegen, Zwolle and Breda this week and next – just in time for university introduction weeks.

World.title: Polish government sets out draft 2027 budget with deficit remaining at 7.1% of GDP
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has approved a draft budget for 2027 that keeps defence, healthcare and the energy transition among its spending priorities, while projecting another year of heavy borrowing. The deficit is forecast at 7.1% of GDP, unchanged from 2026 but well above the level of 3.7% the government had committed to reach by 2027 after Poland was placed under the European Union’s excessive deficit procedure in 2024. Rada Ministrów przyjęła projekt ustawy budżetowej na 2027 rok. Projekt odpowiedzialnie łączy finansowanie bieżących potrzeb państwa i przedsięwzięć wzmacniających jego bezpieczeństwo oraz potencjał rozwojowy.#BudżetPolaków 🔗 https://t.co/SjWyBUwi8U pic.twitter.com/X9ue6cw5ns — Ministerstwo Finansów (@MF_GOV_PL) August 28, 2026 The budget – which must still be consulted with business and trade union representatives before being approved by parliament and then signed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki – sets total expenditure at 977.6 billion zloty (€225.4 billion), 58 billion zloty more than this year. Revenues are projected to rise by 68.4 billion zloty to 695 billion zloty, leaving a nominal budget deficit of 282.6 billion zloty, the highest on record and 10 billion zloty more than this year. Defence spending will remain high, at 198.1 billion zloty, equivalent to 4.5% of GDP, one of the highest levels in NATO. The healthcare budget will reach 274.1 billion zloty, up 26.3 billion zloty from 2026. Spending on energy security and transformation will rise 8.3% year-on-year to reach 19.7 billion zloty. The government expects GDP growth to remain strong, at 3% in 2027, while average inflation is forecast at 2.8%, within the central bank’s target of 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point. Average wages are expected to rise by 5.9% next year in nominal terms, slightly slower than the 6.4% forecast for this year. The government expects that unemployment, measured according to the national methodology, will stand at 6% at the end of 2027, broadly unchanged from its current level. Poland’s gross borrowing needs are projected at 565 billion zloty in 2027, below the 688 billion zloty budgeted for this year. Debt-servicing costs, however, are expected to rise to 107 billion zloty, up 17 billion zloty from this year. Finance minister Andrzej Domański said that the rise in debt-servicing costs is driven by an increase in the overall volume of debt and the need to refinance bonds issued in 2020 and 2021 at very low interest rates. Poland's debt has been growing at the second-fastest rate in the EU this year, and is set to continue rising. What is behind this trend – and should we be worried – asks Alicja Ptak in the latest of her series of articles and podcasts on Poland’s economy https://t.co/1pvnb2ZxoY — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 30, 2025 The projected deficit leaves Poland under continued pressure to bring its public finances into line with EU fiscal rules. In 2024, the country was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure after its deficit exceeded the bloc’s limit of 3%. Warsaw pledged at the time to bring the deficit below 3% by 2028. However, last year the deficit actually rose, from 6.4% of GDP in 2024 to 7.3% in 2025, which was the second-highest level among all EU member states. This year, Poland’s public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time on record. “The 2027 budget represents a continuation of expansionary fiscal policy, and Poland is making no progress in correcting its excessive deficit and is taking no action to bring it below 3% of GDP,” wrote analysts at ING Bank Śląski today. “The result is a further increase in public debt.” Poland’s public debt has passed 60% of GDP for the first time, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. The country is already under the EU's excessive deficit procedure, requiring it to take steps to bring public finances under greater control https://t.co/LNJ0YrP2Ge — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2026 Efforts to reduce the deficit have also been complicated by political stalemate between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who has vetoed several fiscal measures, including tax increases. Nawrocki did, however, approve a new levy on banks that came into force this year. The situation has led two of the big three rating agencies, Fitch and Moody’s, to shift Poland’s credit outlook to negative. This year, Fitch warned that the political gridlock between Nawrocki and the government was making tackling the deficit and debt more difficult. However, speaking today, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that the 2027 budget reflects Poland’s position at a time when war is being waged across its eastern border and other conflicts are weighing on the country’s finances. Meanwhile, 2027 will also see pivotal parliamentary elections, at which Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, will seek a second term while the right-wing opposition, supported by Nawrocki, will attempt to win power. World.title: Polish “vampire” burial sheds light on 17th-century efforts to keep the dead in their graves
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Researchers investigating an unusual 17th-century burial in northern Poland, in which the remains of a teenage girl were found with a padlock fastened to her toe and a sickle placed across her neck, believe the measures may have been intended to stop her returning from the dead. The burial, discovered in 2022 at an unmarked cemetery in the village of Pień, is an example of what archaeologists describe as “anti-vampiric” or “anti-demonic” burial, in which precautions were taken to protect the living from a deceased person believed to pose a danger. In a newly published academic paper, a team of researchers led by Dariusz Poliński, an archaeologist at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, say that the girl, whom they have named “Zosia”, may have been blamed by her contemporaries for misfortunes such as disease and famine. The unusual combination of objects that Zosia was buried with – a triangular padlock attached to her left big toe and an iron sickle laid across her throat, with the blade facing towards her neck – immediately attracted archaeologists’ attention when they were discovered. Poliński and his colleagues have used radiocarbon dating, DNA sequencing, isotope analysis and X-ray and microscopic imaging to investigate the burial. Their findings have now been published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. The researchers have established that Zosia, who was aged between 17 and 19, died around the mid-17th century, most likely between 1620 and 1674. Her grave appears to have been secured in two stages, with analysis of soil layers showing that it was reopened after the initial burial and the sickle added later. “It was unusual that there were two precautions, two methods of showing that this skeleton should be kept in the grave – so the fear of the body coming back to life was greater,” Poliński told CNN. The researchers say the padlock had several possible meanings in funerary symbolism. It could mark the end of earthly life and the transition to the world of the dead, prevent contact between the living and the dead, break a run of bad luck, or protect the community from the deceased returning. “In some interpretations, it was also believed to help halt the spread of epidemics,” Poliński told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The sickle had a more direct purpose: if the deceased tried to rise from the grave, it was positioned to sever the head or slit the throat, preventing her from returning to the world of the living. However, the latest findings suggest there may have been a third protective element. Researchers found “a distinct green discolouration” in the oral cavity, suggesting that an object containing a high proportion of copper had been placed in the girl’s mouth. Given the extent of the discolouration, they have largely ruled out the possibility that it was simply a coin. “The protective measures taken at the time of the original burial and subsequently after the grave was opened clearly demonstrate the immense fear of Zosia,” said Poliński, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. The grave of a "vampire child" – who was turned face down and secured with a padlock to ensure he could not rise from the grave – has been discovered in Poland Researchers believe the site was a cemetery for those excluded or feared by the local community https://t.co/Ez2QgvMnuX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2023 Poliński believes that the woman may have been ill or had a physical or mental disability, leading her neighbours to treat her badly while she was alive and fear that she would haunt them after her death. However, the researchers found no skeletal evidence of trauma, violence or disease that might explain her treatment, and her cause of death remains unknown. The Pień cemetery, which has not been marked on maps, contains several other unusual burials, including a child buried face down with a padlock beneath the foot and skeletons weighed down with rocks. This has led researchers to suggest that the cemetery may have been located on unconsecrated ground, away from a church or chapel, and used for people who were poor, disgraced, feared, or otherwise excluded from the community. Zosia’s burial, however, appears to have been unusual in another respect. Analysis suggests she was of relatively high social status. Traces of silk and gold-and-silver thread near her skull suggest she wore an expensive cap, a luxury item generally associated with nobility or wealth. Two years ago, sculptor and artist Oscar D. Nilsson unveiled a 3D facial reconstruction of Zosia, based on measurements of her skull and skeletal clues about her age, weight and health. The reconstruction shows a young woman with blue eyes, light brown hair and a broad nose. “It’s really ironic, in a way,” Nilsson told Reuters at the time. “These people burying her, they did everything they could in order to prevent her from coming back from the dead…We have done everything we can in order to bring her back to life.” A team of scientists has reconstructed the face of a 400-year-old woman, once believed by her neighbors to be a vampire, revealing the human story buried by supernatural beliefs https://t.co/Q6sipo7h4O pic.twitter.com/0gLVIEfaZi — Reuters (@Reuters) October 30, 2024 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. A dispute has emerged between Poland’s government and the office of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over whether Poland would be willing to host allied nuclear weapons. Deputy defence minister Paweł Zalewski announced on Thursday that Poland wants to participate in the US-led NATO nuclear sharing programme, but without actually hosting warheads. That prompted criticism from Nawrocki’s senior foreign policy aide, Marcin Przydacz, who says Poland should host such weapons. Jedno zdanie wiceszefa MON wystarczyło, by wywołać polityczną burzę wokół kwestii broni jądrowej w Polsce. Paweł Zalewski stwierdził w Kwaterze Głównej NATO w Brukseli, że Polska nie chce głowic nuklearnych na swoim terytorium. Kilka godzin później zareagował szef MON Władysław… pic.twitter.com/EqjTPKqidg — OficjalneZero (@OficjalneZero) August 28, 2026 Zalewski met on Thursday with Elbridge Colby, US under secretary of defence for policy, at NATO’s headquarters in Brussels. Afterwards, he was asked by reporters if an expanded future US military presence in Poland might include nuclear weapons. “No. I would like to say this very clearly and openly: Poland does not want nuclear warheads on its territory,” replied Zalewski, quoted by broadcaster TVN. The minister added that Poland still wants to be part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence programme. However, he said that this could be achieved without hosting the weapons themselves. Those remarks triggered criticism from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party. Former PiS defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak said that refusing to host warheads “in practice means renouncing participation in nuclear sharing”. “Poland should strive for full participation in nuclear sharing,” added Błaszczak. “This is not a matter of Poland possessing its own nuclear weapons, but of strengthening NATO’s nuclear deterrence on the eastern flank.” Criticism also came from other sources, including retired Brigadier General Stanisław Koziej, who served as head of the National Security Bureau (BBN) of former President Bronisław Komorowski, who is an ally of the current government. Koziej called Zalewski’s announcement “an incomprehensible strategic mistake in the field of deterrence”. He said that, to deter Russia, Vladimir Putin must know that there is the possibility Poland could host nuclear weapons. Chęci nie odstraszają. Odstraszają realne zdolności – własne i sojusznicze. A przede wszystkim takie, o jakich użyciu sami decydujemy. To elementarz, który warto przypomnieć https://t.co/Nc3xXnA7bU — Paweł Zalewski (@ZalewskiPawel) August 27, 2026 Late on Thursday, Zalewski commented on the controversy. He rejected Błaszczak’s claim that refusing to host warheads would effectively exclude Poland from nuclear sharing. “We want to participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence programme without wanting the stationing of nuclear weapons in Poland,” he wrote. “Thanks to our efforts, NATO has opened up precisely such a possibility.” In response to Koziej, Zalewski argued that “intentions do not deter, real capabilities do…above all, those whose use we ourselves decide upon”. Meanwhile, defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz also weighed in, declaring that “Poland remains strongly interested in participating in the NATO nuclear sharing programme” and is also “conducting talks regarding the proposal for participation in a European nuclear protective umbrella”. Kosiniak-Kamysz did not, however, comment on the issue of Poland potentially hosting warheads. Rozwiewając wszelkie wątpliwości: Polska jest niezmiennie zainteresowana udziałem w programie NATO Nuclear Sharing. Prowadzimy także rozmowy na temat propozycji uczestnictwa w europejskim nuklearnym parasolu ochronnym. Stanowisko naszego rządu jest w tych kwestiach… — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) August 27, 2026 On Friday morning, Przydacz, who is the head of President Nawrocki’s International Policy Bureau (BPM), joined the criticism of Zalewski, calling his comments “bizarre, absurd and completely inconsistent with what Poland has been saying so far and what the policy of the Polish state is”. “Both the presidential palace and the executive branch of the government have so far supported Poland joining the nuclear sharing programme as part of its deterrence policy,” he continued. Przydacz added that “it is not true” the country wants to participate without actually hosting warheads. “Poland also wants to have warheads on its territory,” he said. Nawrocki, who is a close ally of President Donald Trump, has made clear his support for Poland seeking a nuclear sharing arrangement with the United States. But it remains unclear exactly what the government’s plans are. Earlier this year, Poland entered discussions with France over the extension of the French “nuclear umbrella” over Europe. Later, however, Prime Minister Donald Tusk indicated that Poland would not want to actually host French nuclear-armed aircraft. Both last year and this year, Tusk has also hinted that Poland could seek to develop its own independent nuclear deterrent. However, Colby made clear that the US would “strenuously oppose” European countries such as Poland, Germany or the Scandinavian states seeking to develop their own nuclear weapons. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has regularly clashed with the government, including vetoing a record number of laws. However, the two sides have sought to present a more united front on issues of national security. The United States would “strenuously oppose” Poland, Germany or the Scandinavian countries seeking to develop their own nuclear weapons, says a senior Pentagon official. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A ban on the use of fireworks that was introduced last year by Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has been withdrawn after the local authorities decided not to appeal against a court decision revoking it. Kraków had argued that the ban would boost the safety and health of both humans and animals. However, opponents of the measures, including the provincial governor, who launched the legal challenge against it, argued that it was excessive and undermined constitutional freedoms. Kraków bez zakazu fajerwerków. Miasto nie zaskarży wyroku WSAhttps://t.co/rPEYNhEMAQ — Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) August 25, 2026 In November 2025, Kraków’s city council adopted a resolution banning fireworks, firecrackers, sparklers and other pyrotechnic materials being set off “for entertainment purposes”. The ban, which carried an exemption for last year’s New Year’s celebrations, applied in public spaces as well as private properties where the use of fireworks was deemed to impact public places. The city said the ban aimed to “protect the life, health and peace of residents” and “ensure public safety”, adding that the discharge of pyrotechnics created noise and air pollution and could pose a threat to the health and life of humans and animals. Some councillors also argued that a ban would benefit residents suffering from trauma, including World War Two veterans and Ukrainian refugees. The city’s then mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, cited a city poll finding that 67.5% of respondents supported a year-round ban on fireworks and 31.2% opposed it. However, the measures were criticised by the head of the Association of Pyrotechnic Importers and Distributors, Marta Smolińska, who told news service Puls Krakowa that the ban was an “extreme solution” that would hurt local businesses. She called instead for “promoting the responsible use of pyrotechnics”. In December, Krzysztof Klęczar, the government-appointed governor of the Małopolska province, of which Kraków is the capital, announced that he would challenge the ban in the Provincial Administrative Court. Klęczar argued that the measures may “violate the principle of proportionality of limiting constitutional freedoms and rights as well as the freedom…to conduct business activity”. National parks in Poland have appealed to revellers to refrain from using fireworks this New Year’s Eve to avoid awakening wild animals from their winter slumber. A number of cities have also called on residents to abandon the tradition to protect petshttps://t.co/T6RQHdsF9P — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 29, 2022 His arguments were endorsed by the court, which, in a ruling in late June, deemed the resolution introducing the ban “invalid” and ordered that the city of Kraków pay legal costs. The court said the ban “went beyond the competence of the city council” and “violated the principle of proportionality of the protection of constitutional freedoms and rights”. It added that it “was not necessary to protect health, life or public order”. While Kraków could have appealed against the ruling at the Supreme Administrative Court, it has decided not to take that step. An appeal “would probably have little chance of upholding the resolution,” spokeswoman Dominika Jaźwiecka-Bujalska told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Poland's largest opposition group has proposed a law banning fireworks, arguing that they cause distress, and even death, among domestic pets and wild animals https://t.co/UVzFMv3IEn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 23, 2021 At the national level, in 2021, Civic Coalition (KO) – which was then the largest opposition party and is now Poland’s main ruling party – proposed a law that would have banned the use of most fireworks and firecrackers to protect domestic and wild animals. While that legislation did not proceed beyond a parliamentary commission, two further bills seeking to limit the use of fireworks to protect animals are currently proceeding in parliament, reports local news service Portal Samorządowy. Several Polish cities have introduced their own restrictions, which in some cases have also faced legal challenges. Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, also introduced a ban in January, which was likewise revoked in an administrative court after facing opposition from the provincial governor, reports PAP. Year-round bans remain in place in the Baltic resort town of Sopot, where there is an exemption for 31 December and 1 January, and the southern mountain resort town of Zakopane, a popular destination for New Year’s revellers, where the New Year period is included. The president of the Polish Olympic Committee (PKOl), Radosław Piesiewicz, has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a cryptocurrency firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland’s Olympic team. The development comes a day after Waldemar Żurek, Poland’s justice minister and prosecutor general, revealed that prosecutors are investigating possible crimes relating to Zondacrypto’s financing of various individuals and organisations, including PKOl, Piesiewicz, and figures from Poland’s right-wing opposition. Dziś w ramach śledztwa w sprawie ZondaCrypto zatrzymany został Radosław P. Prokuratura będzie przekazywała dalsze informacje po zakończeniu czynności z jego udziałem, prowadzonych w Śląskim Wydziale PZ PK. — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) August 27, 2026 On Thursday afternoon, Żurek announced that Piesiewicz had been detained and would be charged. He said he was unable to reveal what the charges would be, but confirmed that prosecutors are investigating a €40,000 watch reportedly given to Piesiewicz by the former head of Zondacrypto, Przemysław Kral. Under Piesiewicz’s leadership, PKOl signed an agreement in 2025 with Zondacrypto that made the crypto firm the main sponsor of the Polish team at this year’s Winter Olympics in Italy. However, in April, Zondacrypto began to come under scrutiny after customers began reporting being unable to access their funds. The firm subsequently collapsed and Kral went into hiding abroad. Prosecutors estimate losses to its clients of at least 350 million zloty (€81.4 million). At a press conference today, Żurek confirmed that Piesiewicz had been detained in connection with the investigation into Zondacrypto, which concerns suspected large-scale fraud and other criminal activity. The development comes days after two leading media outlets, Wirtualna Polska and TVN, published a joint investigation in which they alleged that Piesiewicz received a watch worth €40,000 and other gifts from Kral. The gifts were allegedly given in exchange for Piesiewicz intervening on behalf of Zondacrypto with Poland’s consumer protection authority, UOKiK. Piesiewicz denies the allegations and says he bought the watch with his own money, with Kral simply helping facilitate the purchase. 🔴Szef Zondacrypto, prezes PKOl i złoty zegarek za 40 tysięcy euro Prezes Polskiego Komitetu Olimpijskiego Radosław Piesiewicz dostał od szefa Zondacrypto Przemysława Krala zegarek Patek Philippe wart 40 tysięcy euro oraz inne prezenty – wynika z ustaleń wspólnego śledztwa… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) August 24, 2026 Piesiewicz, who became head of PKOl in 2023 under Poland’s former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, has long been a controversial figure. In 2024, after PiS had lost power, he publicly clashed with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s new government following Poland’s poor performance at the Paris Olympics, where the Polish team finished with its lowest medal haul since 1956. This year, as Zondocrypto fell into crisis, it emerged that the company had failed to provide promised bonuses to Polish athletes following the Winter Olympics. In May, 82 of the 106 members of the Polish Olympic Committee supported a motion calling for an extraordinary meeting at which the sole item on the agenda was the dismissal of Piesiewicz from his position. He has so far refused to convene the meeting. Poland has finished @Paris2024 with just one gold and 10 medals in total – its worst result since 1956. The prime minister has suggested there are failings in how Polish sport is managed. But the head of the Olympic committee has blamed the government https://t.co/iS9OqF1RuB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2024 On Wednesday, Piesiewicz and PKOl were among a list of individuals and organisations Żurek announced were being investigated by prosecutors over potential crimes relating to financing they had received from Zondacrypo. Most of them are linked to Poland’s right-wing opposition. They included the foundations of Zbigniew Ziobro, a deputy leader of PiS, and Przemysław Wipler, a former PiS politician now associated with the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja); conservative broadcaster Republika and its head, Tomasz Sakiewicz; and the Polish version of the American CPAC conference. Earlier this year, Tusk claimed that Zondacrypto’s financial success was “rooted not only in Russian money linked to…one of Russia’s most powerful mafia groups, but also to the Russian security services”. His ruling coalition has three times passed a bill to introduce tougher regulation of the crypto market. However, each time, it has been vetoed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, who argues that the measures are too restrictive. Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026 On Wednesday, Tusk wrote on social media that “we now know why Nawrocki and PiS have blocked the cryptocurrency bill like maniacs”. “Cash for watches worth €40,000 euros, [financing] for media, election parties, foundations of right-wing politicians,” he continued. “And the ‘Zonda’ show is just getting started.” PiS figures have, however, denied any wrongdoing in relation to Zondacrypto. “I’m outraged by the suggestion that PiS was involved in anything illegal,” one of the party’s MPs, Piotr Kaleta, told news website Interia. He noted that no evidence had been presented and no indictments made against PiS politicians. “Instead, we have ministers threatening to hold others accountable, and nothing has happened. This is simply meant to cover up the incompetence of the current government.” Teraz już wiemy, dlaczego z uporem maniaka @NawrockiKn i PiS blokowali ustawę o kryptowalutach. World.title: Poland asks EU to fine Meta €250m over scam Facebook ads
