World.title: Serbian President Vucic Says UN Court ‘Wanted Mladic to Die Behind Bars’
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said on Friday that “The Hague wanted [Ratko] Mladic to die behind bars, not in a hospital” because the UN court declined to release the former Bosnian Serb military chief for palliative care in Belgrade ahead of his death.

“We have seen that they did not want to allow the general to die in Serbia, where he wanted to die. That is uncivilised behaviour, behaviour without precedent and without justification,” Vucic said in his first public statement after the death of Mladic on Thursday.

He added that he had been in close contact with Mladic’s family, and that Serbia would ensure that the former Bosnian Serb military leader’s funeral would be “done in a dignified and proper manner”.

On Thursday, Serbia’s Justice Minister Nenad Vujic said that Mladic would be buried with state honours in Serbia. Vucic introduced a note of doubt, however, saying that everything published in the press had been inaccurate.

Vucic also claimed that “the West” had only found Serbs guilty of war crimes from the 1990s.

“Do I believe in justice from The Hague? I never have, and I still do not,” he said.

“All those who took part in crimes against Serbs in the former Yugoslavia were always either acquitted or given token sentences, only for those decisions to later be changed on appeal and the defendants ultimately released,” he added.

Vucic’s statement, slamming the Hague court, echoes Thursday’s reactions to Mladic’s death in pro-government media, among members of the governing Serbian Progressive Party, from hardline nationalist politicians Vojislav Seselj and Aleksandar Vulin and from Bosnian Serb political leader Milorad Dodik.

Serbia is an EU candidate state, and on Friday, the European Commission told Radio Free Europe that it was up to the Belgrade authorities to decide what role they would play in the funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic.

However, the Commission warned: “The European Commission considers any glorification of war criminals to be contrary to the most fundamental European values and to have no place either in the EU or in countries that are candidates for EU membership.”

World.title: Montenegro President Summons Security Council Over ‘Destabilisation Threats’
World.content:
President Jakov Milatovic’s office said on Friday that he has called the heads of the country’s security sector Defence and Security Council after allegations by Prime Minister Milojko Spajic that the country faces “hybrid threats” from two of its neighbours.

Spajic claimed that officials from at least two countries in the region are involved in coordinated activity aimed at destabilising Montenegro and undermining its path towards European Union membership.

Milatovic’s office said the security chiefs will be asked to provide precise information on Spajic’s allegations, as well as a comprehensive assessment of the country’s security situation.

Spajic said on Thursday that Montenegro had “serious operational security information” that threats would accompany the country’s expected progress in opening new EU negotiating chapters. Montenegro is currently seen as the frontrunner among Balkan states to become the next EU member.

“According to our information, such activities are aimed at destabilising Montenegro, with the expected support of certain political actors and part of the media scene in our country,” Spajic posted on X.

On Friday, Montenegrin newspaper Vijesti reported that Serbia and Albania are the two countries referred to by Spajic.

Vijesti quoted an unnamed source who said that some key players in the region were unhappy with Montenegro’s rapid progress toward European integration and wanted to slow it down.

Another anonymous source quoted by the newspaper claimed that a senior government official was vulnerable because of compromising information that could be used by foreign powers. The source suggested that the official’s political party might leave the ruling coalition as a result.

Milatovic’s office said that the president was concerned by the reports, and that “the public has the right to know which official this is”. But it added that serious security issues should not be used to score political points.

“Issues concerning the security and stability of the state must be addressed responsibly, based on facts and through the institutions of the system,” it said.

The warning did not stop some prominent figures connecting the security issue to responses to the death on Thursday of the Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic.

After parliamentary speaker Andrija Mandic stated that he had sent condolences to the former general’s family, the head of Montenegro’s Islamic Community, Rifat Fejzic, asked if politicians who “mourn war criminals [are] in collusion with this hybrid war?”

Albania’s Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Ferit Hoxha has rejected the suggestion that his country was part of any “destabilising scenario” in Montenegro. Posting on X, Hoxha insisted that the allegations could not “artificially create problems between our two countries”.

“Although no formal accusations have been articulated against Albania, I wish to state clearly and strongly that Albania is not, and cannot be, part of any destabilising scenario, whether in Montenegro – a neighbour, friend, partner, and NATO ally with whom we share the same EU membership goal – or anywhere else,” he wrote.

World.title: Week in Review: Hopes and Dilemmas
World.content:
The question of who owns Bosnia and Herzegovina’s state property is a major point of dispute and an unresolved issue on the country’s path away from supervision by the Office of the High Representative and towards membership of the EU. Not surprising, perhaps, in a country where the core issue of sovereignty is contested.

Intractable though the issue may seem, might there be movement towards resolving it? Washington’s newly-discovered interest in energy, mining and infrastructure projects in the country is putting the spotlight on this issue. Now the question is whether Bosnia will solve the issue of state property on Washington’s terms or its own.

World.title: Mladic is Dead, and My Serb Grandfather Was Right About His Fate
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

“You will answer for this disgrace and make the entire Serbian people bear the blame,” my grandfather said, punctuating the sentence with a curse as he walked out of the house to calm himself down in the yard. On the television screen, Ratko Mladic was handing out sweets to children gathered in Srebrenica as cameras from the wartime Serb television station SRNA filmed him.

I could not quite understand what the problem was. I had just turned 15. I had grown up in a Serb family and a predominantly Serb community. Mladic was a hero and a liberator. A source of national pride. Fortunately, I had grown up with a grandfather for whom truth and facts mattered more than any other identity. Especially the national one.

At the beginning of the war, my grandfather was subject to military conscription. He did everything he could to avoid taking part in the aggression. We lived in the hills above Sarajevo, and every day and every night we watched shells falling on the city.

My grandfather kept repeating that they would be held to account. I did not give it much thought. Not until I turned 20, returned to Sarajevo, enrolled at the Media Plan School of Journalism and saw footage of Eduard Limonov, the Russian poet, and Radovan Karadzic, the Bosnian Serb leader, firing a machine gun from Zlatiste, near Mount Trebevic. During pauses, they passed a bottle of rakija from hand to hand, sharing it with the soldiers and taking swigs.

World.title: Tribute Gatherings for Ratko Mladic Held Across Bosnia’s Republika Srpska
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp



Bosnian Serb political leader Milorad Dodik (C) attending a church service for Mladic in Banja Luka. Photo: SNSD/Facebook.

Crowds of Serbs gathered in towns and cities across Republika Srpska on Thursday evening to pay tribute to convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic after his death, with hundreds marching through Zvornik chanting his name and senior entity officials attending a memorial service in Banja Luka.

Mladic, the former commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, died on Thursday aged 84 at the UN Detention Centre in The Hague, where he was serving a life sentence for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes.

The gatherings were attended by members of the public, war veterans and government officials, while some of the events featured open glorification of Mladic and his wartime role.

In Republika Srpska’s administrative centre, Banja Luka, Milorad Dodik, the president of the ruling Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, SNSD, and Republika Srpska prime minister Savo Minic attended a memorial service at the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour, where they lit candles for Mladic.

The service was also attended by representatives of the entity authorities, veterans’ organisations and many members of the public.

Dodik said Mladic had and demonstrated “how to defend one’s people” in what he described as “an unstable, difficult period”.

“Some want this [Serb] people not to remember him, but people have feelings. You cannot ban them, you cannot erase feelings,” Dodik said.

Similar gatherings were held in Trebinje, Bijeljina, Prijedor, Srbac, East Ilidza and elsewhere. In Trebinje, former Bosnian Serb Army members, families of deceased soldiers and local officials lit candles in front of the town’s memorial room and monument to its defenders.

In Bijeljina, Bosnian Serb Army veterans, veterans’ organisations and members of the public gathered, while a memorial service was held in Prijedor.

The head of East Ilidza municipality, Marinko Bozovic, Banja Luka mayor Drasko Stanivukovic, Republika Srpska National Assembly MP Jelena Trivic and Bosnian Serb delegate to the House of Peoples of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina Zelimir Nes­kovic attended a memorial service for convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic at the Monastery of St Nicholas on Mount Ozren.

In a social media post, Bozovic wrote of the convicted war criminal: “Eternal remembrance, General, and may you enter the Kingdom of Heaven.”

The memorial service was attended by a significant number of local residents, as well as Branko Blanusa, president of the opposition Serb Democratic Party.

The attendance of ruling party and opposition politicians marked a shared approach between them to commemorating Mladic, despite his convictions for wartime atrocities.

However, scenes from Zvornik in eastern Bosnia drew particular attention. Several hundred people, including a large number of young people, gathered and marched through the town chanting Mladic’s name. According to footage circulating online, participants also carried flags and symbols associated with the Army of Republika Srpska.

Republika Srpska vice president Camil Durakovic condemned the gathering, recalling that Zvornik was the site of mass persecution and killings of Bosniaks during the war.

“This is Zvornik – this is the town where Mladic’s dogs of war carried out his orders. This is the town of mass graves of my people. This is the town from which tens of thousands of Bosniaks were expelled,” Durakovic said.

He questioned whether state institutions existed that would respond to such scenes, warning that, in his words, this represented the “final stage of genocide”.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the public glorification of convicted war criminals is prohibited under the state-level Criminal Code, following amendments imposed in 2021 by then-High Representative Valentin Inzko after domestic authorities failed to adopt legislation addressing genocide denial and the glorification of war criminals.

Mladic was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2021 under a final verdict, as the UN war crimes court upheld his responsibility for genocide in Srebrenica, persecution, extermination, murder, deportation, forcible transfer and terrorising civilians during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

World.title: Serbia to Organise Genocide Convict Ratko Mladic’s Funeral with State Honours
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Serbian Justice Minister Nenad Vujic told Republika Srpska’s Alternativna Television on Thursday evening that Bosnian Serb genocide and war crimes convict Ratko Mladic will be buried with state honours in Serbia.

“General Mladic is a general, and there are protocols that apply. His role is known, as is what is due to General Mladic, and that will certainly be respected,” Vujic said.

He added the location of Mladic’s burial will depend on the family’s decision.

Mladic was a general of the Yugoslav People’s Army at the start of the Yugoslav wars, and then became a general with the Bosnian Serb Army and the commander of its Main Staff, waging a campaign of ethnic cleansing that ultimately led to his indictment by the Hague Tribunal.

When he died on Thursday in detention in The Hague, aged 84, Mladic was serving a life sentence for committing genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes during the 1992-95 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Vujic’s statement is one of the only signs of the Serbian government’s position on Mladic so far. After the news on his death on Thursday, Serbian officials remained silent, although pro-government media mourned his death and accused the Hague Tribunal of neglecting his health.

Vujic told Republika Srpska’s public broadcaster RTRS that he spoke with Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic on Thursday and that they agreed Serbia would provide any assistance needed to organise the transportation of Mladic’s body and arrange to fly it to Belgrade on a “special aircraft”.

“I will probably also travel with the family so that we can complete the formalities related to the transfer of the body,” Vujic said.

“This is sad news for all of us, for the entire Serbian people,” he told RTRS, stressing that Serbian authorities had done everything in their power to urge the early release of Mladic due to his illness.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Crypto Scandal Returns to Haunt Poland’s Right Ahead of Election Year
World.content:
Slovakia foils arson plot on Ukrainian drone factory; Fico pulls plug on transaction tax

Slovak police foiled an alleged arson attack on a Ukrainian drone factory located near Presov, in what appears to be one of the first serious sabotage plots targeting Slovakia’s growing defence industry. The target was Skyeton, which produces sophisticated surveillance and reconnaissance drones at its plant in eastern Slovakia; Skyeton’s Slovak plant does not export its drones eastwards. Police, acting on information from the civilian SIS and Military Intelligence, arrested three men – reportedly two Latvians and a Ukrainian – who they say were preparing the attack “on commission”. One was detained in Germany. The suspects had allegedly gathered petrol mixed with polystyrene, commonly known as napalm, as well as tools, phones, an action camera and a hand-drawn plan. Some 70 employees could have been inside the plant, where equipment is worth tens of millions of euros. Who commissioned the attack remains the big unanswered question. An anti-war group whose name references George Orwell’s novel 1984 purportedly claimed responsibility for the planned attack in a letter sent to Dennik N. Skyeton itself pointed towards Russia, saying Moscow had repeatedly tried to destroy its facilities in Ukraine and damage its reputation. The company said the Slovak plot showed Ukrainian defence manufacturers had become “a real thorn in their side”. The Russian connection has not been established by investigators, however. Slovak police have so far made no public attribution. The case is sensitive given mounting concerns over suspected Russian sabotage operations elsewhere in Europe. A Slovak pro-Russian influencer had filmed himself outside the Skyeton plant weeks earlier and called it a “legitimate target of the Russian army”. There is no evidence his video was connected to the alleged plot. Deputy Speaker Tibor Gaspar of the ruling Smer party echoed the influencer’s view in a recent interview.

In other news, PM Robert Fico announced that Slovakia would scrap its controversial transaction tax from January 2027, reversing course on one of his government’s main measures to restore the public finances. Fico said he had instructed Finance Minister Ladislav Kamenicky to prepare the necessary legislation. The announcement came as something of a surprise. Only last year, Fico described the tax as effectively impossible to abolish because the government needed the revenue for its fiscal consolidation. The tax, introduced in April 2025 and inspired by a similar levy in Hungary, quickly became a headache for the government. Businesses complained that it penalised ordinary payments to suppliers and employees, encouraged a return to cash and made Slovakia a less attractive place to do business. Criticism eventually spread to Fico’s own coalition. Andrej Danko’s nationalist SNS party, which originally voted for the tax, later pushed to water it down, while politicians from the other coalition party, Hlas, also began calling for changes. The bigger problem was that the tax did not bring in as much money as Kamenicky had hoped. Initial estimates spoke of around 700 million euros a year. In its first year, the state collected only 340 million euros, and official forecasts suggest this year’s target will also be missed. That leaves one rather important question unanswered: where will the government find the missing hundreds of millions? Fico did not say. Instead, he predicted that abolishing the tax would lead to unusually strong economic growth. Slovakia’s independent fiscal watchdog is more cautious, estimating the benefit at 0.1-0.15 percentage point.

World.title: Every Fifth Woman in Montenegro Has Suffered Domestic Violence: Report
World.content:
Protest march in Podgorica marking International Women’s Day. Photo: BIRN/Samir Kajosevic.

One in five women in Montenegro has experienced some form of intimate partner violence, and more than half of them victims have not sought help, according to an analysis published by the Ministry of Social Welfare, Family Care and Demography.

“One in five women surveyed (19.7 per cent) reported experiencing some form of violence from their partner or spouse, which, given methodological limitations and the tendency of non-reporting, suggests that the real percentage is significantly higher,” the ministry said in the report

“About 58.6 per cent of victims who experienced violence did not seek help from anyone. Of those who sought help, only 35 per cent contacted the relevant institutions,” it added.

Analysts say that victims often remain silent due to fear of retribution from their partner, economic dependence or concern about stigmatisation.

The ministry’s report was based on a survey of attitudes and perceptions of violence against women and girls in the family and intimate relationships. The survey was conducted last August but the report released by the ministry this month.

In other findings likely to cause alarm, 76.8 per cent of respondents agreed with the statement that “a man should be the head of the family”.

Twenty-two per cent of respondents said they believe that sexual intercourse within marriage cannot be rape, while 44 per cent were willing to justify men who “lose control because of women’s behaviour”.

The ministry’s analysis highlights the need for better protection for women from Montenegro’s Roma and Egyptian minorities, women with disabilities, and those living in rural areas.

It also points to the need for specialised services for victims and mandatory training for professionals who come into contact with them.

According to data from the Police Directorate, 968 criminal offenses related to domestic violence were committed in Montenegro last year, the report states.

World.title: Ploče: The Croatian Town That Changed its Name 4 Times in 45 Years
World.content:
August the 29th, 2026 – There’s a coastal Croatian town now called Ploče that changed its name 4 times in 45 years, being named after the same man twice.

A resident born in 1945 in what is now Ploče would have had to change his address as many as four times by 1990. Putni kofer writes that the former Ploča first became Kardeljevo, then Ploče, then Kardeljevo again, and finally Ploče once more. All of this happened in a period of just 45 years, while one of the youngest towns on the Croatian coast was rapidly developing at the mouth of the Neretva.

turning the clock back to 1387…

The name Ploča was first mentioned back in 1387 in documents of Dubrovnik provenance. However, in those years there was no proper, organised settlement in the area of today’s town. It was a small port, or rather a sea landing place located right next to the mouth of the Neretva River. Ideas about building a large port had existed for centuries, but more serious works only began in the first half of the 20th century. The port was heavily damaged towards the end of the Second World War. After 1945 its reconstruction began, and on the previously mostly empty, rocky and marshy area a new town gradually emerged. Its original name Ploča, in the singular, was restored to it.

speeding much further forward to 1950

Silvio John, Elsterwerda

The first post-war change took place on the 1st of May 1950. Ploča was then renamed Kardeljevo, after the Slovenian politician Edvard Kardelj, who was one of the closest associates of Josip Broz Tito and one of the leading ideologues of the then Yugoslavia. The name Kardeljevo, however, didn’t really last long. The town existed under that name for only four years, until 1954. Interestingly, even while the town bore the name Kardeljevo, the port retained the name Port of Ploče. During those years the town began to develop rapidly. Instead of the wooden barracks in which port and transport workers lived, the first residential buildings started to appear. The settlement got electricity and a water supply, a cinema and a school were opened, and in 1952 it became a municipal centre.

a plural name change came in 1954…

During 1954, Kardeljevo ceased to exist and the town was given the name Ploče. This was the first time that the plural form of the historical name Ploča was officially introduced, a form that can still be heard among some of the local population today. The new name remained for the next 26 years, during the period of the town’s and the port’s greatest development. After the construction of the Adriatic Highway, the road towards Mostar and the railway line that connected Sarajevo, Mostar and Ploče, the town became one of the most important transport and port centres on the southern Adriatic. It seemed that the story of changes to its name was over, but in 1980 political circumstances once again decided the fate of the town’s plaques, documents and the addresses of its residents.

a name change occurred in 1980, back to a former name…

Edvard Kardelj died in February 1979, and the very next year Ploče was once again given his name. On the 2nd of February 1980 the town became Kardeljevo for the second time. As such, residents who only a few decades earlier had lived in Ploča, then in the first Kardeljevo and in Ploče, once again found themselves in Kardeljevo. The second period under that name lasted significantly longer than the first, a full ten years. At the end of the 1980s, with political changes in Yugoslavia and the strengthening of processes that would lead to Croatian independence, thoughts began to turn to restoring the previous name.

a name restoration in 1990

At the local level the decision to return the name Ploče was made on the 10th of October 1990. The Croatian Parliament then, on the 9th of November, passed the Act on Amendments to the Act on the Areas of Municipalities, which stipulated that the word “Kardeljevo” be replaced by the word “Ploče”. The Act was published in the Official Gazette (Narodne novine) on the 14th of November and entered into force on the eighth day after publication, on the 22nd of November 1990. This was the fourth time since 1950 that the name of the town had been changed.

World.title: The Croatian Island Settlement Once Called the Village of Millionaires
World.content:
August the 29th, 2026 – There’s a very old Croatian island settlement that was once often referred to as the village of millionaires, but today a mere 20 people remain there.

On the beautiful central Dalmatian island of Hvar there are an incredible 936 monuments, six of which are protected by UNESCO. It’s home to the oldest public theatre in all of Europe, one of the larger town squares in the entire Mediterranean, beautiful churches, fortresses and summer residences… As Putni kofer writes, listing all of Hvar’s beauty and attractions would take hours, and for most people, there’s never quite enough time to see them all.

Many people therefore only focus only on the coast and miss the picturesque interior and the fascinating areas it is home to. One of them is the old, now eerily quiet Velo Grablje, once known as the village of millionaires.

ancient stone homes locked in another time

Hidden among the hills, vineyards and dry-stone walls, Velo Grablje at first glance looks as if it has remained frozen in another time. Narrow stone streets, old houses with wooden shutters and an almost unreal silence only reinforce that impression. Today, according to the latest census, the village has only 20 inhabitants, but a hundred years ago there were as many as 500. That means that in one century the place lost 96 percent of its former population.

Today tourists visit the village for its authentic Dalmatian atmosphere, but the reason for its prosperity a hundred years ago was not tourism. There were never luxury villas, swimming pools or wealthy foreigners here, but there was something far more valuable at the time: lavender. The story begins in the late 1920s, when Hvar’s vineyards were going through a difficult period because of downy mildew. Looking for a new crop that could thrive on the rocky and dry soil, local resident Bartul Tomičić was the first to start growing lavender and producing essential oil.

Lavender had existed on the island earlier, but it was he who, at the end of the 1920s, began cultivating it as a commercial crop and producing oil from it. It was not an easy decision. After the problems with the vineyards, the island’s inhabitants had to look for new crops that could succeed on the stony soil and bring in income. Tomičić became convinced about lavender after a lecture by two experts from Split. At first his neighbours found the idea strange. Planting flowers instead of the usual crops? Many thought it frivolous. However, it turned out that Hvar’s climate is ideal for this plant, and production soon began to spread across the entire island.

every household was involved in the harvest

The centre of production was precisely Velo Grablje. In the middle of the 20th century lavender brought such good income that the villagers were among the wealthiest on the island, and their village earned the nickname “village of millionaires.” For a time Velo Grablje was the largest producer of lavender oil in Dalmatia. For decades, lavender shaped the life of the local people. Almost every family took part in the harvest, distillation and sale of the oil, and the scent of the purple fields became the trademark of the whole island. Until the 1970s, the island of Hvar was among the most important lavender-growing areas in the entire Mediterranean.

Naturally, the glorious age of lavender did not last that long. Purchase prices fell, young people left for the mainland or abroad, some plantations were destroyed by fires, and the old village gradually emptied. In the hardest times only seven permanent residents remained in Velo Grablje.

only around 20 people remain in velo grablje today

Although the number of inhabitants is smaller than ever, the village still lives, but at a slower and quieter pace. That emptiness, peace and old stone architecture are exactly what delights tourists who arrive from the busy and noisy coast into its narrow stone lanes. In recent years Velo Grablje has even been experiencing a kind of revival, precisely thanks to the preservation of tradition and cultural heritage. The golden age of lavender has been turned into a brand of the small place, whose highlight is the Lavender Festival held at the beginning of July.

This year, the festival took place on the 3rd and 4th of July. The story of lavender on Hvar is wider than Velo Grablje. Lavender fields are also found around Brusje and in the area of the Stari Grad Plain, and since 2015 almost a hectare of plantations has been grown near Jelsa. Individual lavender bushes can be seen in other parts of the island as well, along roads and on old terraces.

World.title: Mate Rimac Talks Super Cars, Bugatti and Tech
World.content:
August the 29th, 2026 – Bugatti CEO Mate Rimac has discussed the future of super cars, the situation at Bugatti and the technology current and future buyers are turning towards.

“The automotive industry is a bit like the watch industry. Digital and smart watches have taken over most of the market, while expensive Swiss mechanical watches remain popular among the wealthy” explained Mate Rimac, CEO of Bugatti. He added that the super car market is entering its “Swiss watch phase.” Poslovni reports that he claims that the wealthiest buyers are turning their backs on high technology and electric vehicles in favour of precision mechanics and handcrafted details.

Rimac, who took over Bugatti back in 2021, said that the car market is splitting into two parts: the main global car market is beginning to be dominated by cheaper electric vehicles, many from China, while the very top of the car market will be led by wealthy buyers who prefer “old” cars with loud internal combustion engines and emotional appeal, according to CNBC.

“For normal cars, for normal people, the vast majority will be electric,” Rimac said. “The upper segment, like sports cars and above, will ‘burn’ for a long time, just like watches. Only about 5 percent of watches are produced in Switzerland, but 90 percent of the profit is made there. An Apple Watch or any kind of smartwatch can do many more things. But no one will pay 200,000 dollars for that.”

a totally new vehicle

The hybrid Tourbillon has an 8.3-litre V16 engine that delivers 1,000 horsepower, combined with electric motors for a total of 1,800 horsepower. When the Rimac Group took control of Bugatti from Porsche and Volkswagen in 2021, many expected the newly formed Bugatti Rimac Group to launch an electric Bugatti. Instead, Rimac built a completely new car powered by one of the largest internal combustion engines ever made for a production car. The hybrid Tourbillon has an 8.3-litre V16 engine that delivers 1,000 horsepower, combined with electric motors for a total of 1,800 horsepower.

“It’s a bit ironic that I’m now making the largest internal combustion engine in the world,” he said. “Now you have a crazy situation in our plant in Croatia. On the same production line, you have the most powerful electric car in the world being built right next to the world’s largest internal combustion engine. Life is sometimes strange.” Bugatti will produce only 250 Tourbillons, which are sold out at a starting price of around $4.5 million. Rimac said that the average Tourbillon buyer adds an extra $600,000 to $700,000 in personalisation options, such as special colours, leather, stitching, and other design features.

The rise of personalisation and customisation has become one of the biggest profit drivers for super car companies like Bugatti, Ferrari, and Lamborghini. Super car companies are also launching special one-off cars for their customers that can cost tens of millions of dollars. At Monterey Car Week, Bugatti presented its latest model called Destrier. Rimac said that customisations and unique examples reflect the desire of today’s wealthy to have objects that show their identity. A staggering two billion dollars is the price for which Porsche AG sold its 45 percent stake in Bugatti Rimac back in April.

maintaining exclusivity

“Those clients want something that is truly theirs, that is connected to them, that tells their story, their personality, their preferences, not just as a car. There’s a whole story behind it.” Mate Rimac said that his goal for Bugatti is to continue increasing production, quality, and profit while maintaining exclusivity. He said production will never be higher than “low three-digit numbers.” The company made 200 million euros in profit before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation last year and will continue to grow, Rimac said.

Porsche AG agreed to sell its 45 percent stake in Bugatti Rimac back in April to a global consortium led by HOF Capital. While some reports put the valuation of Bugatti at over 1.1 billion dollars, Rimac said the price was “significantly higher” than 2 billion dollars. “What I want to do is produce the best cars in the world, the most exciting cars in the world, and have the most profitable car company in the world on a percentage basis,” he concluded.

World.title: New Health Tourism Hotel Opened in Zagorje in 17.6 Million Euro Investment
World.content:
August the 29th, 2026 – A brand new health tourism hotel has opened its doors in beautiful Zagorje as part of a 17.6 million euro investment made with EU cash.

The final conference was recently held in Stubičke Toplice regarding a project called “Construction of the pool and hotel of the Special Hospital for Medical Rehabilitation Stubičke Toplice”. Zagorje.com reports that that took place alongside the opening of the Thermal Hotel Wrello.

With the opening of the Thermal Hotel Wrello, the Special Hospital Stubičke Toplice begins a new chapter in its development. The project, worth more than 17.6 million euros, included the construction of a brand new four-star hotel and the covering of the pool complex with wellness and accompanying facilities, which will now be available year-round. The new health resort and hotel in the green heart of Zagorje boasts 36 rooms and two apartments (approximately 70 beds) and a restaurant with 100 seats. It’s connected to the existing hospital premises, uniting medical rehabilitation, thermal facilities, and hotel accommodation into a functional whole.

a step forward for continental croatian health tourism

Director of the Special Hospital Stubičke Toplice, Zorica Capar, emphasised that this facility is not only a combination of modern design and top technology, but also a symbol of vision, perseverance, and joint work.

“This project represents a historic step forward for our hospital and for the entire Krapina-Zagorje County. Stubičke Toplice has been known for centuries for its sources of healing thermal water and its tradition of treatment. With this hotel, we are combining that rich tradition with the highest standards of modern medicine, rehabilitation, and hospitality. We can now offer our patients and guests the care and comfort they truly deserve,” the director said, reflecting on the development path. The investment journey began back in May 2021 with the opening of the outdoor pool, the first phase worth 3.5 million euros. The hotel construction and outdoor pool covering project officially started in September 2024 and took 23 months to complete. The total value of this capital investment is 17,426,263 euros. From the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, 16,564,159 euros was secured, of which 16,452,978 euros are non-repayable EU funds. The 99.32% support intensity testifies to the sheer excellence of the project.

“Through extensive construction work, a four-star hotel was built, the existing pool was covered, and a new wellness centre was constructed, covering a total area of 6,500 square metres. A connecting corridor was also built that enables direct indoor communication between the hotel and the hospital, which is crucial for patients. On the ground floor, the Thermal Hotel offers top-quality hospitality facilities with a kitchen and restaurant, while the first and second floors house accommodation capacities with 37 rooms and two apartments with loggias. On the first floor there is a completely new physiotherapy department equipped with the most modern equipment, and the third floor offers a rooftop terrace and a social space. All works have been successfully completed, the occupancy permit has been obtained, and the hotel has received a four-star categorisation,” the director said.

an employment boost for krapina-zagorje

“Through this investment, 34 people from the Krapina-Zagorje County area have been newly employed, thereby directly strengthening the local community. The new tourist infrastructure will operate all 12 months of the year, and all additional hotel facilities will also be available to citizens, tourists, and visitors, ensuring the full potential of year-round health tourism. Special thematic wellness service packages have been designed to provide top-quality spa and wellness tourism services. The spaces of the new covered pool are equipped with the most modern water exercise equipment, including special bikes, treadmills, and elliptical trainers, raising medical recreation and rehabilitation to a new level,” Capar emphasised.

The authenticity of the offer is further enriched by a special food corner within the complex, where local products will be offered through cooperation with local family farms (OPGs). “This project raises standards for hospital staff, ensures top-quality care for users of health services, and creates a new experience for all users of spa and wellness tourism services,” the director noted, expressing gratitude to everyone who participated in the project.

“May this spa hotel be a place of recovery, rest, and shared success,” Capar concluded.

the largest project in the history of the municipality

Mayor of the Municipality of Stubičke Toplice, Josip Beljak, stressed that this day will remain written in golden letters in the history of the municipality.

“This is individually the largest project in the history of the municipality. The opening of the Thermal Hotel Wrello and the new pools is not just the opening of a new facility. It is the beginning of a new centre of health, rehabilitation, and tourism. Every quality investment that takes place in our municipality, regardless of who the investor is, means the development of Stubičke Toplice, a better offer, new jobs, new guests, greater recognition of the place, and also opportunities for all our people and our entrepreneurs. And when we put today’s project into the broader picture of everything currently happening in Stubičke Toplice, I think only then can we see the scale of what we are witnessing. Another historic moment awaits us soon, and that’s the completion of the extension of our primary school and the completion of the school gymnasium. The hotel and pools, the school and sports hall — different projects with different investors, but they have one thing in common: our Stubičke Toplice and the people who live here.

When we add up these two major investments, we’re talking about more than 23 million euros invested in the municipality area in the last two years alone. For such a small municipality, these are exceptionally large figures, an exceptional investment cycle, and I think we can all be proud of that together. Stubičke Toplice has a long and valuable tradition. Generations before us recognised the value of our thermal springs and built the identity of our place on them. Our task is not only to preserve that tradition, but also to develop it. We want modern Stubičke Toplice that will remain recognisable as a place of health, but we also want to be a place of quality living, sport, tourism, quality education, and pleasant life. We want to be a place where our young people will have a reason to stay, where families will want to live, and where our guests will always return. That is why I do not see today’s day only as the completion of one large project; I see it as the beginning of the direction in which Stubičke Toplice is heading,” Beljak emphasised.

health in the palm of your hand

County Prefect Željko Kolar pointed out that this project is the result of a long-term vision and continuous investment in health tourism, with the goal of positioning Zagorje as the leading region in rehabilitation and health services, highlighting the “Health in the Palm of Your Hand” project.

He emphasised that this is the realisation of a long-term vision started back in 2017, aimed at uniting all health institutions to provide top-quality services. Kolar stressed that the key to success is the excellent people in healthcare and the rich tradition of rehabilitation in Stubičke and Krapinske Toplice. The project was realised in five phases, the first of which, with an investment of 3.5 million euros, was completed back in 2021.

“With this, the government enabled us to combine the second, third, and fourth phases, which we would objectively have done over the next ten years or so without this European funding call,” Kolar explained. He expressed particular pride that domestic designers and contractors participated in the realisation.

The saga doesn’t end with the opening of the new health resort in Zagorje. Kolar announced further investments until 2030. As early as next spring, the adaptation of the Antonina facility, worth around 6 million euros and financed by the County, will begin. A project for the energy renovation of the old hotel of the Special Hospital for Medical Rehabilitation, worth 5 million euros and co-financed from the Environmental Protection Fund, has also been submitted. This will mean almost 10 million euros invested in Stubičke Toplice over the last decade.

World.title: New York TImes, Forbes, Conde Nast Discover New Hvar Sirena Resort
World.content:
August 28, 2026 – It has been open less than a month, but the new Hvar Sirena Resort, set an idyllic secluded bay, is already attracting impressive international column inches of praise.

It only opened on August 4, a soft opening in peak season, but it did not take long for a new rising star of Croatian tourism to attract international headlines, with news of the latest renovation by Suncani Hvar Hotels reaching as far away as New York, with the influential New York Times including Hvar Sirena Resort in its article 5 New Hotels for One Last Sun-Drenched Getaway, from Cape Cod to Croatia.

New York, of course, is very much on the minds of Hvar tourism providers, with the inaugural New York to Split direct flight being an unqualified success this year, reducing the travel time from the Big Apple to Hvar Paradise to just 10 hours, including an impressive speedboat transfer to the island. According to various sources I have come across, this direct flight will be more frequent and last longer in 2027, which is great news for American tourists, who are now the undisputed number one visitors to Croatia’s Premier Island.

While there is no such thing as a private bay or private beach in Croatia, Hvar Sirena Resort come pretty close, located in isolation in a forested bay 1.5 miles north of the town, with hourly shuttle transfer to the vibe of Hvar Town, meaning that guests can have the best of both worlds – the transquillity of Hvar, the island, and the internationally famous vibe of Hvar Town, something noted by the Times:

“While Hvar has long been a favourite of boldface names and partygoers, Sirena, set in a cover, says the emphasis is on tranquillity, where a guest can unfurl on the beach or by the pool. The hotel offers ‘silent sailing excursions’ to serene beaches, and each evening a bell signals a ’15-minute’ pause on the hotel terrace during which guests are guided through breathing exercises. The hotel also has a spa and yoga deck and offers weekly cultural activities, like a sunset tasting of honeys and sparkling wine with a local beekeeper.”

The honey theme was picked up by Forbes, which explores an intriguing new trend of bee conservation and honey tasting in luxury hotels around the world in Apitourism Is Buzzing—Is Honey Tasting The New Wine Tasting?, with honey tasting experiences in luxury hotels from Hawaii to New York City and Australia, to Rwanda, Tuscany and Hvar Sirena Resort:

Sunset Honey Ritual, Sirena, Hvar, Croatia

“On an island where bees reportedly outnumber residents 9,000 to 1, Sirena—Hvar’s newest boutique hotel—partners with the multigenerational, family-run Mikletovi Apiary, now in its third generation, dating back to a great-grandmother who supported her family through honey alone. At full summer harvest, the apiary’s 130 hives can produce more than 4,400 pounds of honey in a single week, worked under a zero-waste philosophy that uses everything from the honey to the pollen to the propolis. Guests join a sunset tasting of Hvar’s wild rosemary, sage, and lavender honeys as part of Sirena’s weekly Serene Sessions, with the beekeepers themselves on hand to talk through the island’s ecology.”

And no international tourism media comment on Hvar would be complete without Conde Nast Traveler, the influential American publication which regularly features Hvar among its top destinations in Europe (indeed, its famous Conde Nast Traveler Readers Awards is responsible for the oft-quoted statement that Hvar is among the 10 most beautiful islands in the world).

Sirena: First In – Located on one of Croatia’s prettiest swimming coves, this Havar island newcomer is just right for long summer days

Best for: Solo travelers, groups, or a romantic getaway

Solo travelers, groups, or a romantic getaway Location: Mala Garška Bay, just 1.5 miles from Hvar Town

Mala Garška Bay, just 1.5 miles from Hvar Town Can’t-miss feature: The small turquoise-hued cove is one of Croatia’s most beautiful and a quiet alternative to busy Hvar Town.

The small turquoise-hued cove is one of Croatia’s most beautiful and a quiet alternative to busy Hvar Town. In a nutshell: New 154-room boutique hotel in a secluded, turquoise-hued sea cove, just 10-minutes drive from busy Hvar Town on the hotel’s free shuttle, but a world apart. The dreamy setting is an ideal spot to drop anchor for a relaxing swim, snorkel, and linger over a bottle of local wine under umbrella pine trees buzzing with cicadas.

A really impressive start for this, the latest renovation in the Suncani Hvar Hotels portfolio, which has also added several stars to its hotels in the last 10 years. In addition to the Hvar Sirena Resort upgrade, Pharos, Hvar Bayhill Hotel has upgraded from a 2-star to 4-star hotel since 2016, which Palace Elisabeth upgraded from a 2-star hotel to the first 5-star hotel on a Dalmatian island back in 2019.

I have not stayed there, but I did visit last week, and, although Hvar Sirena Resort had only been open a few days, it was clear that this is a phenomenal addition to the Hvar tourism scene, offering something a little bit different to the other hotels on the island, with the accessibility of the Hvar Town vibe, but a boutique serenity a whole world away, just 10 minutes by shuttle transfer. One of the best uses of Hvar’s many incredible bays that I have seen in a long time, and I predict a bumper season for 2027 – but do sneak in this autumn to be among the first.

You can learn more about the complete Suncani Hvar portfolio on the official website.

World.title: Ratko Mladić Dead: Before Srebrenica there was Škabrnja
World.content:
August the 28th, 2026 – Ratko Mladic, the butcher of Bosnia and one of the worst monsters of the 20th century is finally dead, but before the infamous Srebrenica massacre, there was Croatia’s Škabrnja.

War criminal Ratko Mladić died yesterday without ever answering for the crimes committed in Škabrnja, even though documents and testimonies presented before the Hague Tribunal point to his role in the attack of the 18th of November, 1991. Index reports that Mladić will primarily be remembered as the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska who was finally sentenced to life imprisonment for the genocide in Srebrenica, the terrorising of the population of Sarajevo, persecution, thousands of murders and other repugnant crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He left a trail of blood wherever he went.

Despite it being the most infamous, his wartime path did not actually begin in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Before Sarajevo and Srebrenica he was one of the key commanders of the JNA in operations based in Croatia, especially in northern Dalmatia. His forces attacked Kijevo, the area of Šibenik, Zadar and Sinj, and he also played an important role in the attack on Škabrnja, after which one of the gravest crimes of the Homeland War was committed.

his role in the crimes against humanity committed in croatia

At the time of the attack, Ratko Mladić was not yet formally the commander of the 9th Corps of the JNA based in Knin, as is often stated. He was actually the chief of its staff and deputy commander, while the corps was commanded by General Vladimir Vuković. Mladić was officially appointed corps commander on the 30th December 1991. Nevertheless, already in November he was one of the most influential people in the chain of command and took part in the preparation of operations.

Škabrnja was located in the zone of responsibility of the 180th Motorised Brigade of the JNA from Benkovac, which was part of the 9th Corps. Alongside the JNA, units of the Territorial Defence and police of the so-called SAO Krajina, as well as volunteer and paramilitary groups from Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, operated in the Zadar area. Documents and statements presented before the Hague Tribunal link Mladić to the preparation of the attack. In the war diary from a meeting held the day before the attack it was recorded that the 180th Brigade was to move an armoured battalion towards Škabrnja and Nadin, with the formulation “that it be wiped out”. A witness who was present at the meeting told the court that this task was issued by Ratko Mladić.

The attack began on the 18th of November at around 07:30 and was carried out from two directions. One column of tanks, armoured personnel carriers and infantry came via Zemunik Gornji, and the other from the direction of Biljane. The JNA used tanks, artillery and aircraft, while members of the Territorial Defence and other Serbian units advanced behind the armoured forces.

“if you withdraw, i’ll shoot you”

Marko Miljanić, the then commander of the defence of Škabrnja, testified before the Hague Tribunal about Mladić’s horrendous behaviour during the attack. Miljanić said that over an open radio channel he heard a conversation between Mladić and the commander of the forces attacking the village. According to his testimony, the commander reported that his ammunition supply had exploded and that he could not continue the attack. Mladić replied: “Continue the attack, you’ll get a reserve of ammunition. If you withdraw, I’ll shoot you.”

After breaking through the Croatian defence the attackers entered the village. Murders of civilians, the abuse of prisoners, looting and the systematic destruction of houses followed. Civilians, among them women, children and elderly people, were dragged out of basements and murdered in houses, courtyards and on the streets. Rape and sexual violence was also committed.

the use of human shields

Captured civilians and defenders were driven in front of tanks as human shields. More than a hundred civilians, mostly women and children, were captured and taken to Benkovac. Adult men were separated from the women and children, and some of them ended up in the Knin camps. According to official Croatian data, on the 18th of November, 43 civilians and 15 Croatian defenders were listed as having been killed in Škabrnja. The crimes continued during the occupation, and the place was looted, burned and almost completely destroyed. During the Homeland War a total of 56 Škabrnja civilians died, and 25 defenders from that place were also killed. After the war another six residents were killed by leftover mines.

why was Škabrnja not included in the hague tribunal?

In the case against Milan Martić, the Hague Tribunal established that units of the JNA, Territorial Defence and SAO Krajina police took part in the attack. Martić was sentenced to 35 years in prison for a wider series of crimes in Croatia, among which were the crimes in Škabrnja and Nadin. The infamous Slobodan Milošević was also indicted for the crimes committed in Škabrnja. His indictment stated that forces composed of the JNA, Territorial Defence and Martić’s police went from house to house murdering civilians. Milošević died before the end of the trial, so no verdict was ever formally delivered against him.

The crime in Škabrnja, however, was not covered by the indictment against the monstrous Ratko Mladić. His Hague case was limited to crimes committed across Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1992 to 1995. There was no legal obstacle to trying him for crimes in Croatia as well. The Hague Tribunal had jurisdiction over them, as confirmed by the proceedings against Martić, Milošević and other accused persons. There is no publicly published official explanation of why the Hague prosecution did not include Škabrnja in Mladić’s indictment. When he was finally arrested back in 2011, the court was already implementing a completion strategy, and the case against him was further narrowed.

The number of individual crimes for which the prosecution intended to present evidence was reduced from 196 to 106, and the number of covered Bosnian-Herzegovinian municipalities from 23 to 15. Nor did the Croatian judiciary complete proceedings against Ratko Mladić for his role in the unimaginable horror that took place in Škabrnja.

The District Court in Šibenik had already sentenced him in absentia in 1992 to 20 years in prison for the attack on Kijevo and the areas of Sinj, Vrlika and Šibenik. Proceedings were also initiated against him for Peruča, the shelling of Zadar and other attacks. Documentation from the Croatian cases was forwarded to the Hague prosecution in 2002. However, in the DORH review of proceedings against Mladić published in 2017, Škabrnja is not formally mentioned.

most of those convicted never did their time

The frequently repeated claim that only one person was convicted for the crime in Škabrnja is also incorrect. The County Court in Zadar in 1995 convicted 18 people: sixteen to 20 years in prison each, one person to 15 years, and Jovan Badžoka to ten years. Most were tried in absentia. Badžoka served his ten-year sentence. Zoran Banić, initially convicted in absentia, after arrest in Switzerland and extradition to Croatia was granted the right to a retrial and was finally sentenced to six years in prison. In some retrials the original verdicts were later quashed and the accused acquitted for lack of evidence. Most of those convicted were never available to the Croatian judiciary nor served the sentences imposed, and numerous direct perpetrators and commanders remained unpunished.

the children growing up today are the greatest victory against this genocidal war criminal

After the news of Ratko Mladić’s death there was no celebration in Škabrnja. Danka Dražina, who was a nurse during the attack, told RTL Danas that she did not feel relief. Instead of Mladić, she said, she wants to think about the fallen comrades and innocent civilians. Dražina believes that “Croatian institutions failed”, especially Croatian politics and the judiciary, because Mladić was not prosecuted for Škabrnja. She said that the children growing up happily today in a free place are “the greatest victory” over the man whom the people of Škabrnja consider one of the main creators of the evil that cloaked their area back in 1991.

World.title: Dominik Livaković Completes Move to Barcelona on Four-Year Deal
World.content:
Croatia’s number one goalkeeper Dominik Livaković has put pen to paper on a four-year contract with Spanish champions Barcelona, the Catalan club confirmed on Thursday. Livaković arrives at Barcelona as a Fenerbahçe player, having spent the second half of last season on loan at Dinamo Zagreb. The deal runs through the end of the 2029/30 season, with Fenerbahçe set to receive a fixed fee of two million euros, plus the possibility of a further two million euros in add-ons.

Announcing the signing, Barcelona posted a photo of the Croatian keeper with the message: “Ready when needed.”

What’s still unclear is exactly how Livaković’s first season in Catalonia will play out. According to reporting from Fabrizio Romano, picked up by outlets worldwide, Barcelona had initially planned to sign Livaković as a long-term option without immediately bringing him into the first-team squad, with the idea being that he’d spend the 2026/27 season out on loan, most likely back at Fenerbahçe, before moving to Camp Nou for good in June 2027 to become primary backup to number one Joan García, once Wojciech Szczęsny’s contract expires. However, a well-connected Barcelona radio programme on Cadena SER has since suggested that plan may have changed, with the club reportedly now leaning toward keeping him with the squad immediately.

Asked about his immediate future upon arriving in Catalonia, Livaković kept it brief: “We’ll see.”

Barcelona used the unveiling to look back on his career path, coming through the youth ranks at Zadar and Zagreb, breaking into NK Zagreb’s first team in 2012/13, before moving to Dinamo Zagreb in the summer of 2016. Over seven seasons in Zagreb, he established himself as one of the side’s most important players, making 295 appearances, conceding 249 goals and keeping 137 clean sheets, while winning seven Croatian league titles among other honors. Those performances earned him a move to Fenerbahçe in the summer of 2023.

Livaković has been a regular for Croatia’s national team since 2017, with his biggest moment on the world stage coming at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, where his heroics in the penalty shootouts against Japan and Brazil helped Croatia to a bronze medal. Four years earlier, he was part of the squad that won silver in Russia. He has featured at the last three World Cups — 2018, 2022 and 2026 — as well as the European Championships in 2021 and 2024.

The move to Barcelona represents the biggest club transfer of his career. The only question now is whether he’ll be fighting for minutes between the posts straight away, or whether another loan spell awaits before his chance at Camp Nou arrives.

World.title: Croatian Pensions to Increase Following Latest Adjustments
World.content:
August the 28th, 2026 – Croatian pensions are set to increase once again following the latest adjustments, with differences set to be paid for July 2026.

The Croatian Pension Insurance Institute (HZMO) has announced that at the recently held 26th session of the Management Board a Decision was adopted on the current value of the pension (AVM) from the 1st of July 2026, which amounts to 15.64 euros. Poslovni reports that it was calculated on the basis of the published official data of the Croatian Bureau of Statistics. “Since the AVM from the 1st of January 2026 amounted to 14.84 euros, and the rate of increase of the AVM from the 1st of July 2026 is 5.40%, the new AVM amounts to 15.64 euros,” HZMO states.

They explain that the rate of adjustment of the current value of the pension, which is applied on the 1st of January and the 1st of July of every calendar year, is determined by adding the rate of change of the average consumer price index in the previous half-year relative to the half-year preceding it and the rate of change of the average gross wage of all employees in the Republic of Croatia in the previous half-year relative to the half-year preceding it.

If the share of the rate of change of the average consumer price index in the sum of the rates is less than or equal to 50 percent, the pension adjustment rate is determined by adding 15% of the rate of change of the average consumer price index and 85% of the rate of change of the average gross wage. If the share of the rate of change of the average consumer price index in the sum of the rates is greater than 50%, the pension adjustment rate is determined by adding 85% of the rate of change of the average consumer price index and 15% of the rate of change of the average gross wage.

The share of the rate of change of the consumer price index in the sum of the rates of change is less than 50 percent, which means that the annual pension growth rate is determined by adding 15% of the rate of change of the average consumer price index and 85% of the rate of change of the average gross wage, so that the adjustment rate from the 1st of July 2026 amounts to 5.40%. “Pensions increased according to the new current value will be paid in September (with the pension for August), together with the difference for July 2026,” they emphasised.

At the session, a Decision was also adopted on the lowest pension for one year of pensionable service from the 1st of July 2026, according to which the lowest pension for one year of pensionable service from the 1st of July 2026 amounts to 16.58 euros, as well as a Decision on the base for determining compensation due to physical impairment and on the adjustment of cash benefits due to physical impairment from the 1st of July 2026, according to which the base for determining compensation due to physical impairment arising from a work injury or occupational disease amounts to 358.48 euros.

World.title: Ancient Bonfires organizer: Three fires registered in America this year
World.content:
Mairold Vaik, organizer of the Night of Ancient Bonfires, told Vikerraadio that, interestingly, it has rained on the event only twice in the past 18 years.

"The Night of Ancient Bonfires tradition began in the early 1990s when two friends — one on the Tahkuna Peninsula on Hiiumaa and the other near Turku in Finland — agreed to light bonfires together and send good thoughts to each other across the sea," Mairold Vaik explained. He added that when he learned about the tradition a few years later, he was particularly drawn to the sense of unity it created. "That feeling is what keeps me taking part in the tradition."

Vaik, who compiles information about different bonfires on a shared map on the Night of Ancient Bonfires website, said he began collecting reports of bonfires from people he knew in 2009. "At first it was a simple Google Maps map, but for years now there has been a separate website."

"When I look at the list right now, there aren't that many bonfires listed. There are around 50 public bonfires and another 45 to 50 private ones, so a little over 100 in total. But what I can say is that the map isn't as popular anymore as the event itself," he stressed, adding that there are probably 10 times as many bonfires as are shown on the map.

"We've even received three bonfire reports from the United States. Estonians there have also gotten together and will be enjoying the evening. We've also received some reports from around the Baltic Sea — from Latvia, Sweden and Finland — and there's even one from the eastern shore of the Gulf of Finland."

According to Vaik, no one dictates how the Night of Ancient Bonfires should be celebrated. "No one tells you the right way to celebrate Midsummer Day either. But from my own experience, I can say that the best bonfire site is your own, with a small group of your own people."

"Bonfire events haven't been canceled because of rain, but it really is remarkable that, by my estimate, on the evening when the bonfires are lit, rain has fallen in parts of Estonia only twice in the past 18 years," he said, adding that there could be a brief shower on the islands of western Estonia during this year's Night of Ancient Bonfires. "Fortunately, no rain is forecast for mainland Estonia."

The fires are lit on the last Saturday of August, which this year is August 29, at sunset.

World.title: Gallery: Siim Kallas sent off with state honors
World.content:
Former Prime Minister Siim Kallas will be laid to rest with state honors on Saturday.

The hearse began its journey in Viimsi, from where traveled through Tallinn and via Toompea to the Estonia Concert Hall.

The first memorial stop was at the Viimsi municipal government building where representatives of the Viimsi municipal government and council had gathered. Siim Kallas lived in Viimsi and served as mayor of Viimsi Municipality from 2017 to 2019.

Tunne Kelam and Mari-Ann Kelam arrive for Siim Kallas' farewell ceremony at the Viimsi municipal government building. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

In Tallinn, the hearse stopped outside the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Bank of Estonia, Ministry of Finance, Riigikogu and Stenbock House.

The hearse then arrived at the Estonia Concert Hall. The coffin was received with military honors by the Guard Battalion's honor guard and the military band of the Estonian Defense Forces.

Inside the Estonia Concert Hall, representatives of Viimsi Municipality, the Reform Party, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Finance, Bank of Estonia and Riigikogu stood guard of honor beside the coffin.

The hearse carrying Siim Kallas' remains also stopped outside the Bank of Estonia. Source: Iris Tähema/ERR

President Alar Karis said in a speech at Siim Kallas' memorial ceremony that Kallas was never afraid of bold ideas for advancing life in Estonia and knew that ideas also had to be put into practice, because otherwise there was a risk of remaining invisible in a small and distant corner of the world.

"That is precisely how he helped Estonia grow into a modern country that values freedom and did everything in his power to bring us back into Europe," Karis said.

Following Karis' remarks, the current and former prime ministers placed a parliamentary gavel on the coffin.

Prime Minister and Reform Party Chair Kristen Michal said in his eulogy that the measure of a statesman lies not only in making decisions at the right time, but also in those decisions proving to be right decades later. "Siim Kallas had that fortunate touch, coupled with a sharp mind, courage and perseverance!"

Farewell to Siim Kallas at the Estonia Concert Hall. Source: Iris Tähema/ERR

Siim Kallas died on August 22 at the age of 77. He served as Estonia's prime minister, foreign minister and finance minister, governor of the Bank of Estonia, vice president of the European Commission and a member of the Riigikogu on several occasions. Kallas was one of the authors of the Self-Managing Estonia (IME) proposal, one of the leaders of the 1992 monetary reform and one of the founders of the Reform Party.

World.title: Education minister: Parental and pedagogical responsibility off-balance in Western society
World.content:
Education and Research Minister Kristina Kallas believes schools and teachers today are being saddled with an unrealistically heavy burden, while parents should take greater responsibility.

Speaking on Raadio 2's morning show, Kallas said all adults have a responsibility to support children and young people throughout their education. She said responsibility for raising a child is shared by parents, teachers and specialists from local governments, the Ministry of Education and Research and support services.

"There really is an imbalance, not only in Estonia but more broadly in Western society, between parental responsibility and teachers' responsibility," the minister said.

Kallas acknowledged that the responsibilities involved in supporting children currently fall primarily on teachers.

"Teachers today are expected to make sure children get enough sleep to be able to concentrate on their schoolwork, that they eat properly and have healthy habits. They also have to make sure children get enough exercise, are not addicted to social media and do not play too many computer games. Teachers have to check whether they have brought their notebooks and have their clothes for physical education," Kallas explained.

Kallas compared the current situation with her own school days when parents would be called to the school over such problems and expected to take responsibility.

"Today, all of this is the responsibility of the school and the teacher. Teachers are effectively expected to be both parents and teachers at the same time. In my view, that boundary is out of balance as well and parents' expectations of teachers are unrealistic," she said.

Kallas said that boundary needs to be shifted.

"A teacher's job is to teach children their subject and certain skills and competencies, but it is not their job to be responsible for raising a child 24/7," Kallas said.

There are currently around 1,600 students in Estonia who still do not know which school they will attend this fall. Kallas said around half of them have a school place but have not yet been entered into the system.

"Let's imagine that 800 of those children across Estonia are children whom no adult has ever taken an interest in. No one has wanted to deal with them — neither their parents nor the other adults around them," Kallas said.

"Today, they are in a situation where we are all tossing them around like a hot potato and looking for someone to blame: whether it is the City of Tallinn, the Ministry of Education and Research or the education minister personally," she added.

Kallas said looking for someone to blame would not resolve the situation.

"As a society, we have to acknowledge that we have been failing these children for quite some time. Now, they have finally come onto our radar, we are talking about them and trying to address their situation," she added.

Minister: Some children do not even know they have to attend school in the fall

Kallas stressed that it is the responsibility of local governments to identify and locate children who do not know where they will be studying this fall.

"Out of curiosity, I personally called 10 local governments yesterday and asked whether they had been looking for these children. Most of them had. They have called them and know where these children are," she said.

Kallas highlighted several issues affecting efforts to provide school places.

"For example, there are Ukrainian children whose names are on the list, but when they answer the phone, they say they are in Ukraine and are not sure whether they will return," she said.

At the same time, Kallas said there are children whom officials have been unable to reach at all, as well as those who answer the phone but are unaware that they are supposed to attend school this fall.

"For example, in one smaller town, the city government has said, 'Come and see us tomorrow and we'll discuss together what the child wants to do, what their grades are and how they can continue their education,'" Kallas said.

She said officials have encountered a wide range of circumstances involving these children and this is the first time their situations are actually being addressed.

"Perhaps the lesson for next year is that before we hand children their basic school graduation certificates and send them on their way, we should check whether they have actually applied anywhere to continue their education," Kallas said.

Kallas stressed that adults should pay closer attention to children's plans for the future, as many may be uncertain about what to do next. She said there are also children who have never even been asked what they want to do next.

"We should be providing career counseling and discussing children's futures with them while they are still in basic school, rather than waiting until they have walked out the school doors and then starting to look for them in the fall after summer vacation," Kallas said.

World.title: Ain Hanschmidt: The economy's glass is half full
World.content:
Not long ago it seemed that the economic downturn and high cost of living had no intention of easing, and that the most painful and bleak records in the economy would soon be set. Now, fresh statistics inject a measure of optimism, writes Ain Hanschmidt in a commentary originally published in the Employers' Manifesto 2026.

The economy grew faster in the first half of 2026 than the euro area average, inflation is calming, and investors have become more confident than before — they are no longer quick to sell their businesses and leave. For the first time in a long while, dialogue has re‑emerged between the government and entrepreneurs.

Thus, several proposals formulated four years ago in the Estonian Employers' Confederation manifesto have already been implemented or are in the process of being implemented.

For example, the state is rapidly reducing bureaucracy that suffocates entrepreneurship; the shortage of workers with necessary skills is being eased by more flexible employment relationships and simpler hiring of foreign workers. There is now a responsible party for ensuring a competitive electricity price — crucial for business — and the state has accelerated planning procedures. These are critically important and commendable changes for economic development.

It is equally true that government spending continues to grow faster than the economy. There is no alternative: the state must bring its expenditures under control as quickly as possible and declare a period of tax peace — no new taxes or increases in the tax burden for the next four years. Tax hikes made during a shrinking economy produced the opposite result: they raised prices and reduced the competitiveness of our companies.

We need a longer view and greater ambition: Estonia's economic policy must be as bold, radical, and pragmatic as it was in the 1990s. Fine‑tuning will not take us forward, and in recent years we have lost much of the success and competitive advantages we once gained.

The state's long‑term strategy Estonia 2035 sets the goal of raising productivity to 110 percent of the EU average. As employers, we support this, because Estonia's future success depends on productivity growth. But to achieve this goal, we must begin developing twice as fast — what has been done so far, and simply continuing it, will not get us there. We must set a clear target and begin working toward it both in business and in government, and cooperate effectively.

At the same time, we must improve our position in the international investor community. It may sound unbelievable, but for investors Estonia still sits in the lowest category — a frontier market. This means that a large share of global investment capital never reaches us.

Although the country's credit rating is good — A+ — our aim must be the highest rating, AAA, and a place among developed markets. This sends a signal that it is safe to operate here long‑term, makes borrowing cheaper for companies and individuals, and as the economy grows, wages rise as well.

These issues are not merely economic questions, because only a successful, growing, and competitive economic environment can fulfill the main purpose of the Constitution — to ensure the preservation of the Estonian nation, language, and culture.

Eighty‑five percent of the state's revenues come from consumption and labor taxes. The collection of these taxes into the state budget depends on how high the wages paid by Estonian companies can be. That, in turn, depends on how competitive our companies and economic environment are.

On 7 March 2027, Estonians will again elect members of parliament whose choices and decisions will determine our future success. Leaders who will bear responsibility for setting direction and driving bold change.

We expect the newly mandated politicians to answer questions such as: What is the plan for fixing the state's finances? How will we solve the labor shortage crisis in a society with an aging and shrinking working‑age population? How can we turn educational knowledge into business competitiveness? How can we fund healthcare in a way that is affordable for society and increases healthy life years? How can we support companies' innovation leap? And what conditions can we offer in Estonia to create a competitive environment that drives economic growth?

The Employers' Manifesto helps answer these questions through the views of Estonia's top economic leaders and specialists, outlining not only the challenges ahead but also a set of solutions and proposals.

Their goal is singular: to improve the well‑being of Estonian people through a better economic environment.

Decisive choices lie ahead, and action must be taken with statesmanship. The Employers' Confederation is ready for this — in both words and deeds.

We await a new government and parliament that understand the importance of the decisions to be made in the coming years and are ready to take responsibility for putting Estonia's economy and people's well‑being on a firm path of growth. Employers stand ready for cooperation and joint effort.
