World.title: Underground No More: China’s ‘History Fangirls’ Stand Up
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018940/Underground No More: China’s ‘History Fangirls’ Stand Up
World.content:
“Serve the dead as one serves the living.”

This principle has shaped Chinese funeral and ancestral rites for over two millennia. Traditionally, it meant visiting tombs with food and wine and burning joss paper or paper effigies to honor the deceased. In recent years, however, some rather unexpected offerings have started appearing at the burial sites of famous historical figures.

For example, visitors to the tomb of Guo Rong, also known as Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou (r. 951–960), have left offerings of Beijing soil. A copy of a book on child psychology was discovered at the grave of Zhang Juzheng, a high official during the Ming dynasty (1368–1644). And custodians of the tomb of Cao Cao, a warlord during the Three Kingdoms period (220–280), have been inundated with ibuprofen packets — one of which was accompanied by a heartfelt instruction: “General Cao, these are to help with your migraines. Take half a tablet when the pain strikes.”

These unconventional offerings may seem absurd, but each one has a story behind it. For example, it is well known in China that Cao Cao suffered from persistent headaches. And Guo Rong fell ill and died during an expedition north to reclaim lost territory, so well-wishers now bring the north to him. Meanwhile, the book on children’s psychology left for Zhang Juzheng was a more tongue-in-cheek offering. After serving for 10 years as a stern tutor and father figure to a young emperor, Zhang was posthumously stripped of all titles, ranks, and property by the ruler he’d helped raise. Perhaps a more modern approach could have helped him navigate their power imbalance.

In every case, however, the offerings centered on some aspect of the deceased’s life — a well-known habit, a historical anecdote, or an unfulfilled ambition. And they were all carried out by members of an unlikely, yet increasingly popular subculture in China: shitong nü, or “history fangirls.”

The shitong nü movement has its roots in fanfiction — specifically Japanese doujin — but with a focus on history instead of pop culture. But unlike historical fiction, which tends to ask what historical figures did or might have done, history fangirls are often more interested in who they were: who they loved, how they behaved, what they might have said to a friend, or what it would have been like to know them.

The result is something that closely resembles modern fandom culture, but instead of young singers or movie stars, fans fixate on people who’ve been dead for centuries, if not longer.

Members of the community are not blind to these parallels. Indeed, they will sometimes jokingly describe themselves as fans of “underground idols” — a term taken from the Japanese “chika aidoru,” referring to idol groups that have yet to break into the mainstream. This Japanese loanword has taken on an additional layer of meaning in China: Since the people being admired are six feet under, they are quite literally underground idols.

The ways in which these enthusiasts relate to historical figures generally fall into two categories. The first are “solo stans,” who focus all their time and energy on a single celebrity. Some even become what is known as a “dream girl,” imagining romantic relationships with their favorite historical figure through various kinds of fan-made works.

The other major type are “shippers,” who invent emotional relationships between two or more historical figures.

These two categories are not exclusive. For example, a history fangirl might have a favorite emperor, while also being deeply invested in imagining his close relationship with one of his generals.

As for why, to many history fangirls, historical figures are the ideal subjects for the emotional investment required by contemporary fandom. Loving a living celebrity comes with a certain amount of risk, since there will inevitably be a gap between the carefully curated public image and the real individual. Even fictional characters are at the mercy of their creators, who may do or say something that fans find unacceptable.

Historical figures, however, are different. Their lives have already been extensively documented, and there are few surprises in store. There is little risk at this point that the deceased will fall from grace, for example, or betray their fans or disappoint them by revealing some hidden side.

Moreover, the sparseness of the historical record leaves plenty of space for imagination. Official histories rarely describe how someone walked, sat, or conversed with a close friend. As such, history fangirls are free to fill in the blanks, attach their own understandings, and invest themselves emotionally. Importantly, since the deceased can never contradict them, there is no one to reject fans’ interpretations or deny their emotional projection, making them unusually safe objects of affection.

Deciding which historical figure to stan and how to express one’s affection varies from person to person. However, the practice generally follows a similar pattern: reading historical materials, creating fan works, and making pilgrimages to historical sites.

When you care deeply about someone, it is natural to want to learn everything you can about them, and so history fangirls typically spend a lot of time reading up on their underground idols. In some cases, publishers of obscure old books have been surprised by sudden sales spikes, with some works even selling out the moment they are put on sale. On platforms like Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, fans swap tips for how to buy rare books like the “Complete Collected Works of Cao Pi,” Cao Cao’s son and a particularly popular underground idol.

In addition to reading up on history, fans mark special occasions such as Tomb-sweeping Day and the Dragon Boat Festival, as well as birthdays and death anniversaries, with collaborative online creative projects or offline pilgrimages. Even the most secluded tombs and little-known ruins can now be found using guides posted on social media. Many leave handwritten notes or gifts connected to the figure’s life as a way of making the visit feel more personal, as if the deceased were capable of “receiving” this kindness.

Because their focus is history — a serious and important field of knowledge — the fandom enjoys cultural legitimacy that other forms of celebrity obsession don’t receive. Its economic potential has also encouraged wider acceptance. Various cemeteries have gradually adapted to and encouraged the subculture, while museums and cultural institutions have started producing related merchandise and collaborating with games aimed at fans. Even state media outlets have lauded enthusiasts for “strengthening cultural confidence” and “promoting national heritage.”

Critics, however, worry that fandom is turning history into entertainment. The most common concern is the “fandomization” of history, with critics worrying that fan-made creations will ultimately distort the public’s understanding of the past.

Yet both sides risk missing the fandom’s essence. History fangirls are not trying to produce historical knowledge or advance a social agenda. They are enthusiasts practicing a personal hobby, with the simple goal of enjoying themselves.

Take, for example, the popularity of “underworld couples” — pairings understood to be toxic, or which romanticize violent or unequal relationships. One well-known example is between Cao Pi and one of his wives, Lady Zhen, whom he later had killed. Some fan-made works imagine the deep, tragic love between the pair, while others attempt to give Lady Zhen — whose personal name is not recorded in the historical records — greater subjectivity, or even place her in a parallel universe where she can choose her own fate. The fandom has no single, central discourse. Morality is not the primary standard; chemistry is.

Ultimately, the subculture’s power lies precisely in these intimate, personal acts of imagination that grand historical narratives cannot co-opt. As the 16th-century poet-official Yang Shen once wrote: “The history books contain but a handful of names, while the hills are strewn with countless forgotten tombs.” Yet, through the imaginations of the living, these historical figures continue to walk among us.

Translator: David Ball; portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: A woman takes a photo of a display dedicated to Cao Cao at the Cao Cao Mausoleum Site Museum in Anyang, Henan province, May 2026. VCG)

World.title: Tracing the Route of ‘Cathay’
World.content:
Eighty years ago, Roy Farrell and Sydney de Kantzow — two ex-air force pilots who had supported China’s War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression during World War II — purchased a Douglas DC-3 twin-engine propeller airplane. After establishing an import-export company in Shanghai, they soon relocated to Hong Kong and officially registered their new venture: Cathay Pacific Airways.

Today, Cathay Pacific is ranked as a 5-star airline and flies to 60 countries worldwide. Less recognized is the origin of “Cathay” as a common term. Chosen by the founders as a nod to their China connection alongside “Pacific” to capture their ambition for their enterprise to one day cross the world’s largest ocean, the word itself tells a story of communication and misunderstanding between ancient China and the West.

Indeed, for centuries, the name “Cathay” haunted the European imagination. It conjured visions of a distant, mythical realm of silk and spices beyond China — even as European merchants and missionaries quietly traded with the immense state. The great irony is that for nearly 300 years, Europe operated under the profound delusion that these two magnificent empires were separate neighbors, and perhaps even rivals.

This mismatch in geographical understanding can be traced back to a difference in terminology, itself a byproduct of accounts from travelers who visited different parts of the region amid shifting names for the north and south. According to the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), “Cathay” can be traced back to “Khitan,” the name of the nomadic people who established the Liao dynasty in the north from the 10th to the early 12th century. The Khitan name was then absorbed by the powerful Kara-Khanid Khanate to the west along the Silk Road, which subtly altered its pronunciation. As the word flowed westward into Persian (as Katā), then post-classical Latin (Cataia or Cathaia), and in Marco Polo’s accounts as Catai, “Cathay” came into being.

And yet, a linguistic rift began to appear as Europeans who landed on China’s southern coast found themselves dealing with a country named “China,” an older word derived from Sanskrit. On 16th-century maps, “China” was thus often depicted as a mere coastal strip known to Portuguese sailors, while “Cathay” loomed as a vast, mysterious inland empire to the north.

This was no mere academic error; it had monumental, real-world consequences. In fact, this geographical schism served as the very engine of the Age of Discovery. When Christopher Columbus and John Cabot set sail for the New World — with a heavily annotated copy of Marco Polo’s book of travels — they were convinced they were heading toward Cathay. Driven by the desperate hope of finding this elusive northern empire, Humphrey Gilbert penned his 1576 treatise, “A Discourse of a Discoverie for a New Passage to Cataia.”

Yet, the human drive to uncover the truth is a powerful instinct. The reconciliation of “Cathay” and “China” belongs not to kings or cartographers, but to the walkers — specifically, the missionaries who refused to accept that the map was complete. When Matteo Ricci arrived in China in the late 16th century, he noticed that the “Cathay” described by Polo perfectly matched the empire of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644). To settle any lingering doubts, the Portuguese Jesuit missionary Bento de Góis then embarked on a grueling overland expedition from India. Crossing the unforgiving Pamir Mountains and the Gobi Desert, he searched for the legendary kingdom of Cathay. Though he died waiting for permission to enter Beijing, his ultimate sacrifice proved that the Silk Road led directly to the seat of the Ming’s rule, not the separate land of “Cathay.”

By the early 17th century, Western travelers like Ricci, de Góis, and Martín de Rada had conclusively established that the China reached by sea could be accessed by following Marco Polo’s land route across Central Asia. When their letters finally reached Europe, the phantom of “Cathay” vanished from the maps, leaving behind only the tangible reality of China.

One might expect the word “Cathay” to have perished alongside that geographical revelation. Instead, it transformed. As the OED notes, from the beginning of the 17th century, “Cathay” was gradually superseded by “China,” and by the century’s end, the process was complete. Stripped of its geographical necessity, the word was reborn as an archaic, highly connotative strand of poetic use. In the early 18th century, poet James Thomson wrote of caravans bending “to the golden coast of rich Cathay/With news of human-kind.” By 1823, Lord Byron was similarly invoking “far Cathay” alongside Ceylon and Inde in “Don Juan.” In 1859, Harper’s Magazine placed Cathay alongside Atlantis and El Dorado as a land now “peopled with beings of flesh and blood.” By 1871, Joaquin Miller mused, “Where the winds come in from the far Cathay/With odor of spices and balm and bay.” Through these verses, the word had become a timeless vessel for exotic mystery and richness.

Perhaps most fascinating is the OED’s entry for the phrase “cycle of Cathay,” defined as “a period of time which is long-lasting but during which little changes.” Popularized by Lord Tennyson’s poem “Locksley Hall” (“Better fifty years of Europe than a cycle of Cathay”), the phrase reflects a complex, heavily Eurocentric Western gaze assuming cultural superiority. This cultural bias was further cemented in an 1886 issue of the North American Review, which claimed that “the world has made more progress in that time [...] than in many cycles of Cathay.”

The name then found a romantic revival in the bustling commercial heart of the East. In the cosmopolitan Shanghai of the 1930s, “Cathay” was embraced as a symbol of ultimate luxury and modernity. The legendary Cathay Theatre and the grand Cathay Hotel (now the Fairmont Peace Hotel) adopted the ancient name to evoke timeless elegance and prestige. When the theater’s name was localized into the Chinese characters pronounced Guotai, evoking an auspicious idiom meaning “peace and prosperity,” it marked a brilliant fusion of Western phonetics and Eastern cultural values. Here, Cathay was no longer just a distant Western fantasy, but a glamorous reality woven into the very fabric of the city’s urban memory.

Decades later, this evocative name took flight, finding its most enduring manifestation in the clouds. By reusing the beloved “Guotai” moniker, Cathay Pacific’s founders seamlessly carried that century-old promise of peace and prosperity into the jet age.

The story of Cathay teaches us that names are far more than mere labels; they are the enduring vessels of our shared history. The long journey from “Cathay” to “China” charted a passage from fragmentation to wholeness, from distant myth to tangible reality. It serves as a poignant reminder that while maps and misunderstandings may carve the world into “us” and “them,” the human spirit — propelled by the footsteps of explorers and the verses of poets — can’t help but try to blur such divides. In the end, we are all, in some way, still searching for Cathay, hoping to discover that behind the ancient myth lies a shared humanity.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: China’s Beloved Beef Noodles Are Getting a Rebrand
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018933/China’s Beloved Beef Noodles Are Getting a Rebrand
World.content:
China’s signature local specialty Lanzhou lamian, or Lanzhou pulled noodles — named after the capital city of the northwestern Gansu province — are undergoing a rebranding. At many noodle shops across the country, the dish will now be known as “Qinghai lamian,” as the northwestern Qinghai province strives to build its own regional brand.

More than 1,000 noodle shops nationwide have made the shift, state broadcaster CCTV reported on Saturday. In June, 72 noodle shops in the northern port city of Tianjin first changed their names to bear the words “Qinghai lamian,” followed by hundreds of shops in several other provinces in the months since.

Composed of hand-pulled noodles in a clear broth, sliced beef and radish, and chili oil, the dish traces its history back to the turn of the 19th century in the central Henan province. After being brought west, they took on the name of Gansu’s capital, a stop on the old Silk Road — where the halal noodles first became a hit in part owing to its significant Muslim Hui population. They were further popularized as a local specialty by Hui noodle maker Ma Baozi in the 1910s.

Later, as China opened up in the 1980s, entrepreneurs from poverty-stricken counties in Qinghai, such as Hualong, began capitalizing on the noodles’ popularity, opening small, mom-and-pop restaurants across the country.

“There was little brand awareness back then, and hardly anyone had heard of Hualong, Qinghai. However, Lanzhou is close by, so (noodle shop owners) thought they’d just call them ‘Lanzhou noodles,’ because everyone knows Lanzhou,” Ma Liping, president of the Qinghai Noodles Industry Association, told local media.

The shops have become a familiar sight nationwide. As of the end of February 2026, there were 31,000 noodle restaurants operated by owners from Qinghai in more than 330 cities across China, generating more than 24 billion yuan ($3.5 billion) in annual revenue, according to data from the Qinghai Noodle Industry Association.

But tensions over the use of the dish’s name have grown among Lanzhou and Qinghai residents, as people from Lanzhou call it “Lanzhou niurou mian” — Lanzhou beef noodles — while people from Qinghai call it “Lanzhou lamian,” or “Lanzhou pulled noodles.”

The dish has also evolved two differing preparation methods among Gansu and Qinghai restaurant owners, fueling debate. Lanzhou noodle makers have made efforts to preserve its traditional flavors, while Qinghai shop owners have adapted to local tastes — for instance by using less oil and salt in Guangdong, or adding more pepper in the southwestern Sichuan province.

To distinguish their wares from the noodles sold by people from Qinghai, local authorities in Lanzhou registered a trademark featuring a bull’s head for “Lanzhou Beef Noodles” in 2007, marking the city’s first step toward building a formal regional brand.

The recent rebrandings are part of Qinghai’s broader effort to build a provincial brand. About one-fifth of the rebranded shops have adopted a “three-in-one” model, adding in-restaurant sales of local specialties such as yak jerky and highland barley products, as well as tourism promotion, as new revenue streams.

Online, users voiced their support for the change. “After all, the two noodle dishes differ significantly in taste and texture, so distinguishing them clearly will help consumers make informed choices,” one user wrote on microblogging platform Weibo.

In a commentary, state-backed Haibao news wrote that “the rebranding reflects the growing push to standardize China’s grassroots food industry.”

The push is evidenced by multiple regions recently moving to standardize the production of local dishes. Gansu began regulating Lanzhou lamian in 2023, while a vocational college in the southern Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region launched a course dedicated to standardizing and promoting its river snail rice noodles in 2020. In July, the catering industry association of the eastern Zhejiang province also introduced a standard for preparing duck heads, a Quzhou city specialty.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A Lanzhou lamian shop in Yichang, Hubei province, Aug. 11, 2026. VCG)

World.title: FULL INTERVIEW: Mike Dizon on drumming for 3 bands, love for food
World.content:
Dizon sits down with Rappler to talk about his beginnings in music, what it's like for him to move from genre to genre as the drummer of TEETH, Sandwich, and Pedicab, and how he discovered his love for documenting the restaurants he comes across

MANILA, Philippines – It’s not every day that an artist finds himself being a part of three of the Philippines’ most influential bands at the same time, until you meet Mike Dizon.

Dizon co-founded the alternative rock and grunge outfit TEETH in 1993. Years later, he also began playing the drums for rock band Sandwich and electronic rock band Pedicab. He is also a prolific songwriter, and is the mind behind hit songs like “Laklak” and “Prinsesa” by TEETH.

Outside of music, though, Dizon runs a successful YouTube channel, where he visits local eateries to try out the best dishes on the menu.

Ahead of TEETH’s reunion concert tour in celebration of their 33 years as a band, Dizon sits down with Rappler to talk about his beginnings in music, what it’s like for him to move from genre to genre, and how he discovered his love for documenting the restaurants he comes across.

Catch the full interview at 7 pm on Saturday, August 29, by bookmarking this page or heading to Rappler’s YouTube! – Rappler.com

World.title: Judicial and Bar Council opens application for next Supreme Court chief justice
World.content:
HIGH COURT. In this file photo, the Supreme Court is holding oral arguments on the national budget and unprogrammed funds on April 7, 2026.

Marcos will get to pick the next chief justice after Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo's retirement in November

MANILA, Philippines – The Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) on Saturday, August 29, announced the opening of application for the next Supreme Court (SC) chief justice due to the upcoming retirement of Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo.

The new chief magistrate, who will be chosen by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., will replace Gesmundo who will retire on November 6. Under the rule, justices are mandated to retire from the judiciary when they reach the age of 70.

The Judicial and Bar Council (@JBC_Ph) has announced the opening, for application, the position of #SupremeCourtPH Chief Justice (vice Hon. Alexander G. Gesmundo, who will compulsorily retire on November 6, 2026).



Read the full text of the Announcement and the guidelines on… pic.twitter.com/OlxIxSyI2X — Philippine Supreme Court Public Information Office (@SCPh_PIO) August 29, 2026

The next chief magistrate will be the country’s 28th Chief Justice and will sit at the SC’s top post. The High Court oversees all courts in the country, including high level courts like the Sandiganbayan, Court of Appeals, and the Court of Tax Appeals.

Gesmundo has been the chief justice since April 2021 upon the appointment of former president Rodrigo Duterte. Sources and court people alike often refer to Gesmundo as the High Court’s “stabilizing force” for introducing a concept of collegiality among the justices and reforms inside the SC.

Meanwhile, Gesmundo’s replacement will be chosen by Marcos after a screening process to be led by JBC. Public interviews will be held as well as part of this process.

Apart from Gesmundo, Associate Justice Amy Lazaro Javier is also retiring in November.

This gives Marcos two new appointments to the High Court after his first pick in 2025, Associate Justice Raul Villanueva. (READ: IN NUMBERS: Things to know about the Philippine Supreme Court and its justices)

Once Gesmundo and Lazaro Javier retire, the Duterte appointees inside the SC will drop to 10; Marcos might have three, while former president Benigno Aquino III has two. – Rappler.com

World.title: Monsoon rain due to enhanced southwest monsoon affecting 12 areas in Luzon
World.content:
WEATHER. A low pressure area and the southwest monsoon affecting Luzon as of August 29, 2026, 5:10 pm.

The enhanced southwest monsoon or habagat is bringing monsoon rain to Metro Manila, Ilocos Sur, Pangasinan, La Union, Benguet, Bataan, Zambales, Tarlac, Pampanga, Bulacan, Rizal, and Cavite

MANILA, Philippines – At least 12 areas in Luzon are experiencing monsoon rain on Saturday afternoon, August 29, as the enhanced southwest monsoon or habagat continues to affect the island.

On Saturday morning, the low pressure area (LPA) previously inside the Philippine Area of Responsibility was already located outside PAR. It was last located 640 kilometers north northeast of Itbayat, Batanes, with a “low” chance of developing into a tropical depression.

Another LPA being monitored outside PAR, which has a “high” chance of developing into a tropical depression, was last located 1,545 km east of extreme Northern Luzon. Once it enters PAR and strengthens, it will be called the local name Pilandok.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) reported monsoon rain due to the enhanced southwest monsoon in Metro Manila, Ilocos Sur, Pangasinan, La Union, Benguet, Bataan, Zambales, Tarlac, Pampanga, Bulacan, Rizal, and Cavite.

The southwest monsoon is also bringing occasional rain to Ilocos Norte, Abra, Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, Nueva Vizcaya, Nueva Ecija, Laguna, Batangas, Occidental Mindoro, and Oriental Mindoro, scattered rain and thunderstorms to the rest of Luzon, Western Visayas, and Negros Island Region, and isolated rain showers or thunderstorms to the rest of Visayas.

PAGASA Weather Specialist Daniel James Villamil said heavy rain will continue to affect Metro Manila, most of Central Luzon, and portions of Southern Luzon over the weekend and until Monday. By Monday, there will be a shift in rainfall distribution, with heavy rain affecting Northern Luzon.

Below is PAGASA’s latest heavy rainfall outlook due to the southwest monsoon in the next three days:

Saturday afternoon, August 29, to Sunday afternoon, August 30:

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 millimeters): Ilocos Sur, Pangasinan, La Union, Benguet, Bataan, Zambales, Tarlac, Pampanga, Bulacan, Metro Manila, Rizal, and Cavite

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Ilocos Norte, Abra, Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, Nueva Vizcaya, Nueva Ecija, Laguna, Batangas, Occidental Mindoro, and Oriental Mindoro

Sunday afternoon, August 30, to Monday afternoon, August 31:

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Abra, Benguet, Zambales, and Bataan

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, Nueva Vizcaya, Tarlac, Nueva Ecija, Pampanga, Bulacan, Metro Manila, Rizal, Cavite, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro

Monday afternoon, August 31, to Tuesday afternoon, September 1

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Abra, Benguet, and Zambales

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Batanes, Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, Nueva Vizcaya, Tarlac, Nueva Ecija, Bataan, Pampanga, Bulacan, Metro Manila, Rizal, and Cavite

PAGASA warned those living in low-lying and susceptible areas under a red heavy rainfall warning to be vigilant against floods and landslides. – Rappler.com

World.title: [OPINION] Faith in the Footprints: How the youth today see religion, values, morality
World.content:
Comparative global findings demonstrate that while secularization is present — predominantly in Western contexts — religious faith and spiritual yearning remain robust forces shaping youth personhood worldwide

What’s the tea about today’s youth’s beliefs and attitudes towards God, morality, and religion?

The Footprints Project, a multi-phase, multiyear, comprehensive research initiative coordinated by the Pontifical University of the Holy Cross in Rome, seeks to answer this question. Our team employed a method of “continuous listening” to better understand young people’s values, hopes, and expectations regarding their faith.

Grounded in relational sociology, our study operates on a core conviction: that relationships are central to identity formation, and that religion — understood as a relationship to one’s origin — is key to building personal identity and community cohesion.

To map this landscape for the first phase of the project, which focused on youth attitudes to religion and faith, our team conducted an international survey and gathered data from 4,889 young people aged 18-29 across eight countries from five continents: Argentina, Brazil, Italy, Kenya, Mexico, the Philippines, Spain, and the UK.

The findings offer a nuanced look at global youth religiosity. They challenge the long-held assumption popularized by sociologists that modern societies are bound for total secularization.

In fact, when the entire survey population is considered as a whole, 73% of youth identify as believers in God. The study also shows that in the last five years, 50% of respondents claimed an increase in their spirituality compared to only 15% reporting a decrease. This finding suggests that spirituality among youth has increased globally.

Among the eight countries in the survey, interesting patterns and trends emerged:

Countries with strong religious identity: Brazil, Kenya, and the Philippines share a strong religious identity. Even if predominant religious denominations differ for each country — evangelicalism for Brazil, Catholicism for the Philippines, and other religions for Kenya — they all exhibit similar moral and social values, which reflect the deep influence of religion in their societies.

Secularizing countries with a relevant Christian presence: Argentina, Italy, and Spain still have a not insignificant Christian presence, but they are in a rather advanced stage of secularization. While religion still plays an evident role in public life, and those who do identify as believers exhibit deeper faith through practices like more frequent daily prayer, it is clear that the nation’s once-strong Catholic influence is diminishing.

A country in between: Mexico appears to be between the above two categories. It represents a transitional stage that shows the country in general retaining a notable religious identity while also showing trends pointing towards secularization.

Unique case: The United Kingdom stands out as a distinct case, in which only 15% of youth identify with a specific faith tradition, yet 48% express belief in God. As well, a surprisingly high percentage engage in frequent prayer and service attendance.

‘Ironic contradictions’

Across all groups, religious perspectives strongly influence social issues. For example, attitudes diverge on topics like surrogacy, prostitution, and sexual ethics: non-believers make no bones about these issues in contrast to their religious counterparts.

Interestingly, both believers and atheists agree on their opposition to war, political corruption, and abuse of the environment. On the whole, however, believers were still shown to be more civic-minded.

At the same time, the study uncovered intriguing “ironic contradictions” among both non-believers and Catholic youth.

Among self-described non-believers, nearly half engage in prayer during times of difficulty or out of gratitude, 42% believe in life after death, and 37% actually ask believers to pray for them.

Conversely, while many Catholic youth actively attend Mass and pray, significant numbers reject Church teachings on sexual morality, preferring personal conscience as their ultimate authority — views that mirror non-believers more than Church doctrine.

These comparative global findings demonstrate that while secularization is present — predominantly in Western contexts — religious faith and spiritual yearning remain robust forces shaping youth personhood worldwide. – Rappler.com

Robert Z. Cortes is assistant professor III in the School of Media and Marketing of the University of Asia and the Pacific (UA&P), with a PhD in social communication. His areas of study and teaching include communication/media ethics; the dynamics of entertainment, cultures, and societies; philosophy of technology; youth media habits and values. The original article on which this article is based was published in the journal Church, Communication, and Culture and was written by Norberto González Gaitano, José María Díaz-Dorronsoro, John Olukuru, and Robert Z. Cortes. It can be read or downloaded here.

World.title: Kai Sotto overcomes comeback jitters in Gilas Pilipinas win
World.content:
Kai Sotto embraces the pressure and steps up when needed the most as he steers Gilas Pilipinas back on track in the FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers

MANILA, Philippines – Kai Sotto erupted in a thunderous roar after his block sealed Gilas Pilipinas’ win over Jordan in the FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers.

It was the culmination of two years of waiting and pent-up emotions, all released in one defining moment as the 7-foot-3 big man proved to be just what the doctor ordered in his national team return.

“Before the game, I had a lot on my mind. There was a mix of excitement and the realization that it had been such a long time since I last played for the national team,” said Sotto in a mix of Filipino and English.

“I knew I was carrying a lot of pressure, and I’m just really happy that was able to translate into my performance on the court what I had been waiting so long to do — play for the national team again.”

Play Video

Sotto finished with team highs of 18 points, 14 rebounds, and 2 blocks as the Philippines escaped with an 82-81 overtime win on Friday, August 28, to get its World Cup bid back on track after losing its last four games in the Asian Qualifiers.

Jordan stayed on the Philippines’ heels until the final second before Sotto swatted away a point-blank layup by Abdullah Olajuwon to secure the victory, much to the delight of a packed crowd at the Mall of Asia Arena.

The block completed the Filipinos’ comeback from 18 points down as they defended their turf even without injured naturalized player Justin Brownlee, with the likes of CJ Perez (16 points), Kevin Quiambao (14 points), and Dwight Ramos (14 points) rising to the occasion.

“I’m really happy that everyone contributed. We had a slow start, but as you saw, we fought our way back. I’m extremely proud of the team,” said Sotto.

Sotto last saw action for the national team in 2024 before an injury in early 2025 sidelined him, but there was little sign of rust as he seamlessly fit back into the squad.

For head coach Tim Cone, that adaptability makes Sotto special.

“He’s really that smart and intelligent. And that makes the people around him better. Everybody’s better when he’s on the floor,” Cone said of Sotto.

“Whether it be passing or screening or rolling, the attention he grabs, he just makes everybody around him better.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Why Bicol theater revived a century-old epic
World.content:
DEFEND IBALONG. In a scene from ‘Ibalong Z: A New Bikol Musical,’ Baltog lfigures in a bone-crushing struggle against the 'tandayag,' a monstrous, tusked terror laying waste to the farmers' sacred taro fields.

The playwright behind ‘Ibalong Z: A New Bikol Musical’ hopes the younger generation will ‘fall in love with the story and feel inspired to read’ the epic

ALBAY, Philippines — Far from a simple adaptation, Ibalong Z: A New Bikol Musical gives the classic epic a fresh life on stage. It honors the roots of Bicolano culture while also taking a closer look at how the region’s stories have nearly been forgotten.

Drawn from the 60 surviving stanzas of the Ibalong epic, which chronicles the tales of ancient Bicol, the musical explores a growing disconnect between the younger generation and the region’s cultural heritage. These challenges have made it more difficult for traditional and cultural stories to be remembered and staged for public viewing.

DYING TRADITION. As old Kadunung takes his final breath, the heartbeat of the ancient past slips away. His passing mirrors the tragic fading of the epic itself, leaving the legendary tale of’ Ibalong’ a stranger in the very homeland it helped shape. All photos by Reinnard Balonzo/Rappler

Playwright and Bicol University theater instructor Jobert Gray Landeza shared that while the musical offers audiences a fresh theatrical experience, its ultimate goal is to introduce audiences to the original material, inspiring more readers and advocates to help preserve these regional stories.

“My best hope is that when the audience watches the play, they will fall in love with the story and feel inspired to read the original material,” Landeza said.

“I wanted to show them how great and powerful the epic is and how it deserves to be read and talked about in our age.”

Landeza also noted that transforming the epic into a play gives the younger generation an opportunity to appreciate Ibalong, especially since most of them are not inclined to read and understand ancient literature.

This reluctance to read has been documented, with Bicol ranking fourth among the regions in the country struggling most with reading. In August 2026, the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) reported that at least 42,000 learners in the region struggle with reading, based on a comprehensive rapid literacy assessment.

FADING MEMORY. As the epic slips from the minds and books of the locals, the forgotten characters of Isla Memorya begin to dissolve, slowly fading out of existence as their stories are erased by time.

“With the looming literacy drought in the region, it’s very hard to make the younger generation read and understand Ibalong. Through theater and by using the language they are most familiar with, they were able to understand the cultural significance of Ibalong,” Landeza said.

“Of course, theater is our best hope to cultivate the most important values and lessons from the epic for our younger audiences.”

With at least 12,500 attendees across six show schedules — the majority of whom were students and younger viewers — Landeza said the play successfully inspired many learners to read ancient and local literature. He added that this engagement helps in their journey to develop literacy skills while honoring the culture of the region.

DESPERATE MEASURES. With the ancient line of storytellers broken and no modern ‘kadunungs’ left to keep the flame alive, the vanishing inhabitants of Isla Memorya turn to an unlikely savior: a tech-savvy “Generation Z” kadunung, tasked with resurrecting an ancient myth for a digital age.

Artistic hurdles

Ibalong originally bears influences from Indian Hindu epics like the Ramayana and Mahabharata, and was traditionally narrated by a local poet known as a kadunung.

In Bicol, the root word dunong means wisdom, portraying the kadunung as a wise bard safeguarding the survival of the ancient epic.

The story follows the three hero-warriors of Bicol: Baltog, Handyong, and Bantong. These heroes face various challengers and evil creatures that aim to destroy the land and people of Ibalong.

Despite inspiring its own festival, previous Ibalong runs suffered from a low audience turnout, largely due to a lack of public funding and support for the local theater community and the scarcity of modern kadunungs who can retell the story.

EPIC IN RAP. Bridging ancient myth and modern culture, the mythical creatures from Isla Memorya step up to the mic in a fierce rap battle, transforming traditional verse into a viral digital showdown.

Ibalong Z production manager Julie DM Vega noted that the costs entailed for such a production demand a larger budget, but local theater companies are left with minimal funding and restrictions on venues where they can rehearse.

“The budget allocated for Ibalong Z was too small for the demands of the production, leaving the team with so little resources for the preparations, given that the venue for practice was also very hard to find and outsource. We even had our rehearsals in the venue sometimes with the air conditioning shut down,” Vega said.

Because of this, Vega said that much of the younger generation has a very limited and surface-level knowledge and appreciation for Ibalong and other local epics. She believes that through this musical, audiences will not only discover the story but also learn more about the region and themselves.

“We want our audience to have their own experience and appreciation of Ibalong. Despite the hurdles, we saw how the audience embraced the play and the story of Ibalong, making the show boom,” she said.

HANDYONG’S LOVE. Given a second chance at fate, the legendary hero Handyong and the half-serpent, half-goddess Oryol defy the odds once more — igniting a forbidden romance while defending the wild, monster-haunted land of Ibalong.

Modern ‘kadunungs’

Izel Manata, who watched the play with her family and friends, shared that the play taught her about her Bicolano roots through the lens of a Gen Z kadunung.

“Watching Ibalong Z was very grounding and expansive because of how it made us realize the global and contemporary resonance of an epic that was first told centuries ago” she said. “The play was able to transform the historical relic into a humanizing methodology that deeply touched me.”

Manata added that in a fast-evolving world, it is crucial that Bicolano folktales be preserved through vigorous and expansive storytelling, much like what was achieved with Ibalong Z.

GEN Z KADUNONG. Armed with beats and rhyme, an aspiring young rapper flips the century-old myth into a high-energy anthem, infusing the ancient tale of Ibalong with fresh flavor to hook internet viewers.

With the rest of the unrecovered original parts of the epic forever lost, Bicolanos must now take on the role of modern kadunungs.

Landeza emphasized that it is vital for them to help preserve the story of Ibalong and make it more meaningful. He noted that audiences should retell their experiences, grounding the epic in their contemporary realities of living in and loving the land of Ibalong.

“It is very important that we document and write our reviews of the play and of the story of Ibalong because it can help us reach more people,” he said. “That can greatly help not only the theater scene to thrive, but also promote our cultural identity as Bicolanos.”

SONG OF HOPE. Voices rising as one, the entire cast of Ibalong joins in a powerful, unifying anthem, inviting the audience to embrace, celebrate, and honor the timeless culture and traditions of the region.

–Rappler.com

World.title: DELF 2026: Hong Kong Advances AI Integration Across Arts and Entertainment
World.content:
HONG KONG – The Hong Kong SAR government is moving from AI strategy planning to active execution focusing on infrastructure expansion and application-driven development. This was announced by Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry, Professor Sun Dong, at the Digital Entertainment Leadership Forum (DELF 2026) on Aug. 28.

“The committee on AI+ and Industry Development Strategy is established to empower industrial transformation through AI, with an initial focus on health technologies and embodied AI, extending to transportation, cultural and creative industries, and more. The Hong Kong AI Research and Development Institute will also come into operation later this year to translate upstream research into real-world applications,” said Professor Dong in his opening remarks.

Key initiatives also include a risk-based ethical AI framework, AI adoption in 100 public procedures and a growth in computing power at Hong Kong’s IT hub Cyberport.

“AI is transforming the digital entertainment industry, turning imagination into unprecedented experience,” emphasized Professor Dong. “And technology only serves its purpose when everyone can participate in it. That is why we launched the $50 million AI for All Inclusive Program – Cyberport, the Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks, and the Hong Kong Productivity Council will roll out awareness-raising programs and practical training targeting at different sectors of the community to promote AI awareness and enhance professional skills as well as competitiveness through AI.”

The creative industry has already observed the impact of these changes, according to Terry Lam, Dean of the School of Film and Television at The Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts.

“In the old days, if you went to any university in Hong Kong, they would not talk about the creative industry. Now, even if you go to the most famous or high-ranking university in Hong Kong, in an engineering course or scientific course, they will still have a sub-topic called the creative industry,” he said.

Terry Lam also expressed strong interest in collaborating with arts institutions across Central Asia noting substantial opportunities for cross-cultural exchange.

This vision aligns with growing ties between Hong Kong and Eurasia. This June, Cyberport agreed on cooperation with Central Asian’s largest innovation clusters Astana Hub and IT Park Uzbekistan during a visit of Hong Kong business delegation to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, led by Chief Executive John Lee. The partnership focuses on technology transfer, supporting tech companies in areas such as AI, fintech, smart city solutions and Web 3, and facilitating overseas expansion and global market access for innovation and technology companies from both regions.

Held under the theme “Dreamtic Circus,” the three-day forum featured four themed experience zones: digital entertainment, culture and arts, smart living and business, and robotics and drones. Major showcases were the immersive interactive art exhibition titled “Gudo: Another World,” Harbour dreams VR/XR simulator guided by AI panda An An flying over Hong Kong sights and an eVTOL, the city’s first passenger drone test flight.

The event also hosted AI interactive workshops, film screenings, drone performances and competitions.

World.title: China Consolidates Position as Kazakhstan’s Top Trading Partner
World.content:
ASTANA – China is strengthening its position as Kazakhstan’s largest trading partner, overtaking Russia in the country’s foreign trade structure.

In January-June, China accounted for 23.2% of Kazakhstan’s foreign trade turnover, compared with 18.4% for Russia. Bilateral trade with China reached $16.65 billion, while trade with Russia stood at $13.22 billion, according to the Bureau of National Statistics.

The shift matters not only for trade volumes but also for the structure of bilateral trade.

According to an analysis by Tengenomika published on Aug. 27, Kazakhstan imported around $9.14 billion worth of goods from China in the first half of this year, compared with approximately $9.74 billion from Russia. However, the composition differs considerably. China is increasingly supplying machinery, equipment, electrical goods and other investment products, while Russia remains a broader source of fuel, food and industrial inputs.

The export structure is also different. Kazakhstan exported around $7.51 billion to China, compared with nearly $3.49 billion to Russia. Exports to China are dominated by ores and concentrates, copper, oil and other raw materials, while exports to Russia are more diversified and include metals, chemicals, machinery and equipment.

China’s growing role is particularly significant as Kazakhstan enters a new investment cycle. The government forecasts that goods imports will rise to $88.4 billion by 2029, while exports are projected at $88.5 billion.

Tengenomika highlights that the shift represents more than a change in Kazakhstan’s largest trading partner.

“China is increasingly becoming a supplier of the machinery, equipment and components needed for new production and infrastructure, while Russia continues to play a major role in supplying the goods and inputs needed by Kazakhstan’s economy today,” Tengenomika said in its analysis.

This emerging division of roles highlights how Kazakhstan’s trade ties with the two countries are evolving, with China playing a growing role in investment-driven demand and Russia retaining a broad position across the domestic supply chain.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Global Ties, Economic Outlook, Abai’s Legacy and More
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest covers Singapore-Kazakhstan relations, political and economic developments, energy expansion, cultural cooperation with Vietnam and more.

Singapore keen to build on goodwill, deepen ties with Kazakhstan: SM Lee

Singapore wants to build on the goodwill it enjoys in Kazakhstan and deepen ties in areas ranging from business to connectivity, Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong said as he wrapped up his first visit to the Central Asian country, reported The Straits Times on Aug. 28.

Lee said on Aug. 27 that Singapore’s relationship with Kazakhstan was “an account well worth cultivating”, with Singapore companies showing growing interest in the country and trade and investments increasing significantly in recent years

“We enjoy a lot of goodwill,” he told Singapore media in a doorstop interview at the St. Regis Astana Hotel, noting that Kazakhstan remembers warmly founding prime minister Lee Kuan Yew’s first visit in September 1991, three months before the country became an independent republic.

The Goethe of the Steppe: How Kazakhstan’s national philosopher shapes the bridge to the global economy

News Mark released an article on Aug. 10 exploring how Abai Kunanbayev’s philosophy, literary legacy and emphasis on education, honest work and openness to other cultures can help international investors understand Kazakhstan’s modern business culture and economic ambitions.

“Anyone wanting to invest in Central Asia’s dynamic market today cannot ignore one name: Abai Kunanbayev. What Johann Wolfgang von Goethe is to Germans, Abai (1845-1904) is to Kazakhs. He is not only the undisputed national poet, but also the ethical foundation of a country rapidly transforming from a former nomadic state into a global economic player. For international decision-makers, his work offers the key to understanding the mentality, business culture, and economic ambitions of modern Kazakhstan,” reads the article.

Kazakhstan after Kurultai elections: Expanding opportunities for co-operation with the European Union

EU Reporter published an article on Aug. 25 about parliamentary elections on Aug. 23 that completed the formation of Kazakhstan’s new legislature – the Kurultai – the central element of the country’s renewed political system following constitutional reform. Seven political parties took part in the vote. Turnout stood at 74%.

“The first convocation of the Kurultai has cemented the completion of the institutional transition and marked the country’s entry into a new political cycle.

The Aug. 23 elections have concluded the phase of institutional renewal in Kazakhstan and opened the period of practical implementation of reforms. For the European Union, this means a more predictable foundation for cooperation with Kazakhstan in the key spheres of energy, raw materials, and transport infrastructure. Kazakhstan enters a new political cycle with an updated institutional system, reinforcing its position as a strategic partner of the EU in Eurasia,” reads the article.

Astana Finance Days 2026 to bring global investors and financial leaders to Kazakhstan

More than 5,500 participants from over 80 countries are expected to gather in Kazakhstan’s capital on Sept. 9-10 for the ninth Astana Finance Days (AFD) 2026 forum, hosted by the Astana International Financial Center (AIFC), reads an EU Reporter article on Aug. 24.

The forum will bring together investors, representatives of the financial and technology sectors, regulators, government and quasi-state institutions, and international businesses.

Since its launch in 2018, Astana Finance Days has developed into one of the region’s major financial forums, providing a platform for discussions on capital markets, investment and financial cooperation. The 2026 program will focus on capital markets and investment products, regulation and market confidence, institutional innovation, financing the real economy, and regional and cross-border capital cooperation.

After ending power shortages, Kazakhstan can become electricity exporter

An EU Reporter article published on Aug. 25 covered Kazakhstan’s planned expansion of electricity generation in 2026-2027, the growing role of gas and renewable energy, and the government’s goal of moving from an electricity deficit to a surplus while building a reserve for the national grid.

“The expected 1.3 billion kilowatt-hour surplus by the end of 2027 marks an important shift in the government’s projections. The objective is no longer limited to covering immediate electricity consumption but also includes creating a reserve that could strengthen the reliability of the national grid. However, installed generation capacity and actual electricity output are not identical. The amount of electricity ultimately available to the system will depend on factors including the operating performance of new plants, fuel supply, grid infrastructure and, in the case of wind and solar projects, weather conditions,” reads the article.

Vietnam, Kazakhstan boost experience sharing in cultural industry development

Vietnam Pictorial released an article on Aug. 27 about Vietnam and Kazakhstan strengthening cooperation in cultural industries, tourism, education and other sectors while using cultural exchange as a tool to deepen bilateral ties and diversify economic relations.

During the meeting with Aida Balayeva, deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Culture and Information of Kazakhstan, Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister Pham Thi Thanh Tra called for stronger people-to-people exchanges, local cooperation and tourism, noting that nearly 200,000 Kazakh tourists visited Vietnam in 2025 following the visa exemption policy for ordinary passport holders, according to the article.

Kazakhstan’s expanded Korea: A cultural legacy

The Chosun Daily published an article on Aug. 26 about Kazakhstan’s large Koryoin community and how Korea’s historical diaspora, cultural influence and growing popularity among Kazakh youth connect the two countries across generations.

“The ties between Kazakhstan and Korea date back much further than these cultural interactions. In 1937, the Stalinist regime forcibly relocated approximately 170,000 Koryoin from the Primorsky Krai region to Central Asia, citing fears they could become Japanese spies. Many of those transported by cargo trains settled in Kazakhstan, where around 120,000 of their descendants still live today. Kazakhstan is the country with the second-largest Koryoin population in the world, following Uzbekistan,” reads the article.

World.title: Experts Say Kazakhstan’s New Kurultai Leadership Reflects Diversity, Faces Heavy Legislative Agenda
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s new unicameral legislature, the Kurultai, elected its leadership and heads of eight standing committees during the first session of its first convocation on Aug. 28. Experts say the newly elected leadership reflects political and gender diversity and will face a significant legislative workload from the outset.

Aibek Dadebai, chairman of the Adilet party and former head of the Presidential Administration, was elected Kurultai Chairman. He thanked President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev for nominating him and deputies for supporting his candidacy, describing the position as a “great honor and responsibility.”

Adilet deputy and former Senator Nurlan Beknazarov, who represented Shymkent in the Senate from 2018 to 2026 and most recently chaired its Committee on Constitutional Legislation, Judicial System and Law Enforcement, and Ak Zhol party chairwoman and former Mazhilis Deputy Chair Daniya Yesspayeva were elected Deputy Chairs. Former Commissioner for Children’s Rights Dinara Zakiyeva, who served as a Mazhilis deputy from the Amanat party from 2021 to 2023, became the third Deputy Chair.

Political scientist Gaziz Abishev said the composition of the Kurultai’s leadership reflects broad political and gender representation.

“In other words, the composition of the Kurultai’s leadership is diverse with respect to both party affiliation and gender,” he said.

In an earlier interview with The Astana Times, Zhandos Aktayev, chairman of the Esti Bol Qory public foundation and Doctor of Law, said the new legislature would face a substantial workload from the outset.

“Although the Kurultai is a new institution, it will inherit legislation left unfinished by the previous Parliament, giving deputies an immediate and substantial workload,” Aktayev said.

Deputies also elected the chairs of the Kurultai’s eight standing committees. Serik Yegizbayev of the Auyl party was elected to head the Committee on Agrarian Affairs. Askhat Aimagambetov will chair the Committee on Social and Cultural Development, Unzila Shapak the Committee on Constitutional Legislation, Judicial System and Law Enforcement, Olga Perepechina the Committee on Finance and Budget, Amirbek Ospanbekov the Committee on Regional and Infrastructure Development, Marat Kozhayev the Committee on International Relations, Defense and Security, Darkhan Akhmediyev the Committee on Digitalization, Innovation and Science, and Natalia Godunova the Committee on Economic Policy, Energy and Industry.

The standing committees will review draft legislation before the full chamber considers it, making them central to the Kurultai’s legislative work.

Seven of the eight committees are headed by deputies from Adilet, the majority party. The new legislature has eight standing committees, compared with seven in the former Mazhilis and six in the Senate.

All 145 deputies took an oath to the people of Kazakhstan during the inaugural session, marking the formal start of the new legislature under the constitutional framework that took effect on July 1.

Speaking after his election, Dadebai said the scale of reforms requires “well-balanced decisions, professionalism and dedicated work,” adding that the Kurultai should contribute to the country’s modernization and constructive public dialogue.

“A lot of work lies ahead. I am confident that we will go through this responsible path together,” he said.
