World.title: Georgian minister quits politics shortly after ex-PM’s accusations
World.content:
Georgian minister quits politics

Georgia’s Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze is stepping down from his post and leaving politics. He announced the decision at a briefing at the government administration, saying he wanted to devote more time to his family.

Until April 2026, Mamuka Mdinaradze served as head of the State Security Service. On 21 April, he was appointed deputy prime minister and state minister for the coordination of law enforcement agencies. On 29 July, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that Mdinaradze would take up the post of state minister for regional policy. The new position was due to be created in September, and until then Mdinaradze was appointed regional development minister.

Mdinaradze said his 10 years in politics had been marked by hard work, service to his country and cooperation with the team of the ruling Georgian Dream party. At the briefing, he thanked party members and leaders, including its founder and honorary chairman, Bidzina Ivanishvili.

Mdinaradze said he had been considering leaving politics for the past several weeks and had made the decision on his own initiative before discussing it with Irakli Kobakhidze and Bidzina Ivanishvili. He said they initially disagreed with his decision, but he ultimately managed to convince both that it would be better for him.

Mdinaradze explained his decision to leave politics by saying he wanted to spend more time with his family. According to him, his children, aged nine and 13, had grown up with him largely absent.

The former minister stressed that his decision had not been prompted by any political or personal crisis. He also said there was no need for him to remain involved in regional development, as the ruling team had other leaders capable of overseeing the area.

Mdinaradze did not rule out returning to politics one day, but said he would do so only if necessary.

“I will return only if the team really needs me and there is no other option,” he said.

Mamuka Mdinaradze

As for his future plans, Mdinaradze said he might try his hand in the private sector, including business, although he does not yet have any specific plans.

“Believe it or not, I haven’t thought about it. Perhaps I’ll try my hand in business,” Mdinaradze said.

Reflecting on his 10-year political career, Mdinaradze said its intensity and the level of responsibility had not been easy for him, and that he now wanted to focus on the part of his life that he had put on the back burner for years.

Mamuka Mdinaradze’s announcement that he was leaving politics came after his name was mentioned in connection with serious allegations made by former Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili. Garibashvili, who is currently serving a prison sentence, alleged that he had been pressured “on Bidzina Ivanishvili’s orders”, with Mdinaradze acting as an intermediary, to confess to a corruption offence in order to prevent him from returning to politics in the future.

On 24 August, Garibashvili was charged with a new corruption offence. The charge carries a prison sentence of 11 to 15 years.

According to investigators, key testimony in the case was provided by former Defence Minister Juansher Burchuladze, who has also been convicted of a corruption offence. According to his testimony, of the 1.5m lari (around $555,000)received as a bribe from businessman Zurab Tukvadze, who won a tender for the Gori Military Hospital, Burchuladze personally handed 750,000 lari (around $277,000) in cash to Irakli Garibashvili in several instalments.

Garibashvili denies the allegations. He says the demand that he admit guilt was politically motivated and intended to limit his ability to return to politics in the future. It was in this context that he mentioned Mamuka Mdinaradze as an intermediary and alleged that the demand had been made on Bidzina Ivanishvili’s orders.

Mdinaradze did not address the allegations against him when explaining his decision to step down.

World.title: ‘No to occupation and de facto annexation’: Anti-annexation platform launched in Georgia
World.content:
Anti-annexation platform launched in Georgia

A new public association, the Anti-Annexation Platform, has been established in Georgia.

Its founders say the group will be non-partisan and apolitical, with its main goal being to oppose Russia‘s occupation and de facto annexation of Georgian territories through legal and peaceful means.

At the platform’s launch at the Tbilisi Marriott hotel, a declaration entitled “No to occupation and de facto annexation – yes to justice, peace and Georgia’s territorial integrity” was adopted.

According to the declaration, the platform brings together Georgian citizens who regard the country’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, the principles of international law, freedom and human dignity as core values.

The founders say that Russia’s occupation in any form, the de facto annexation of the Abkhazia and Tskhinvali regions, support for separatism and forced demographic changes in the occupied territories constitute violations of international law and fundamental human rights.

The declaration also states that the organisation is ready to cooperate with members of any political party, regardless of their political affiliation.

Among the platform’s main objectives are supporting Georgia’s territorial integrity and sovereignty and promoting a legal assessment of Russia’s continuing occupation and de facto annexation.

The group plans to work to protect the rights of internally displaced people and refugees from the occupied territories, prepare legal research and analytical papers, and raise public awareness of developments in the occupied regions.

The platform also intends to cooperate with international partners, think tanks and diplomatic missions. Its activities will include organising conferences, discussions and educational events, as well as helping to protect the rights of people affected by the occupation and de facto annexation.

The platform supports targeted international sanctions against the leaders of the de facto regimes in the occupied regions and individuals involved in the annexation process. The declaration also calls for efforts to initiate international criminal proceedings.

The document stresses that the group’s activities will not be limited to the political agenda.

“We believe that the struggle against occupation and de facto annexation by the Russian Federation is not only a political issue. It is a struggle for justice, human dignity, historical truth and the security of future generations,” the declaration says.

According to its founders, the platform is based on the peaceful and legal resolution of conflicts, respect for international law and the protection of human rights.

“Russia’s de facto or de jure annexation will never become a legal reality, and borders changed by force will never acquire moral or legal legitimacy,” the declaration says.

The declaration was signed by the founders of the Anti-Annexation Platform:

World.title: Kyrgyz President inspects Manas airport’s readiness to receive SCO summit delegations
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 29. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov visited Manas International Airport on August 29 to check its readiness to receive foreign delegations arriving for upcoming international events.

According to the Kyrgyz president’s press service, Sadyr Japarov inspected the airport grounds as well as the halls designated for receiving Kyrgyz citizens and foreign delegations.

"President of the Kyrgyz Republic Sadyr Japarov made an unscheduled visit to Manas International Airport today, August 29, to inspect its condition following a major reconstruction," the statement said.

Sadyr Japarov also reviewed the airport complex’s readiness to receive high-ranking guests arriving in Kyrgyzstan to participate in the meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), the World Nomad Games and other events.

The president instructed the relevant officials to ensure the full readiness of the airport and adjacent areas, with particular attention to order and security, the proper organization of protocol procedures and the quality of services provided to arriving delegations.

Sadyr Japarov also stressed the need to ensure a high level of preparation for the upcoming international events.

Meanwhile, the SCO was established in 2001 and initially comprised China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Over the past 25 years, its membership has expanded to 10 countries. The 26th SCO summit will be held in Bishkek on August 31-September 1, 2026, under Kyrgyzstan’s chairmanship.

The meeting will focus on the organization’s further development, strengthening economic and transport cooperation, and security cooperation.

Following the summit, the leaders are expected to consider a number of documents related to the development of the SCO’s financial and economic mechanisms, including initiatives to expand settlements in national currencies and establish new cooperation institutions.

World.title: Xi Jinping calls for deeper trade and transport ties with Kyrgyzstan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 29. China and Kyrgyzstan should continue deepening bilateral relations, with a focus on trade, transport connectivity, infrastructure and new technologies.

This was stated in an article by Chinese President Xi Jinping published on August 28 on the official website of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the People’s Republic of China ahead of his state visit to Kyrgyzstan, where he will also attend the 26th meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO).

"Cooperation should be strengthened in traditional areas such as trade and investment, infrastructure connectivity and green minerals, while cooperation in emerging sectors, particularly the digital economy, clean energy and artificial intelligence, should be expanded," Xi Jinping said.

According to Xi Jinping, the two sides should step up the alignment of development strategies and deepen exchanges of experience in state governance, creating conditions for further economic cooperation.

He placed particular emphasis on transport connectivity. The construction of the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway is underway in Kyrgyzstan, while transport links between the two countries are also expanding.

"It is important, with a long-term perspective, to make high-quality Belt and Road cooperation the main direction and promote practical cooperation in terms of both scope and level," Xi Jinping noted.

He called for stronger cooperation in trade and investment, infrastructure connectivity and green minerals, as well as expanded cooperation in the digital economy, clean energy and artificial intelligence.

The Chinese president also stressed the need to accelerate implementation of the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway project and modernization of border checkpoints.

"Meanwhile, connectivity should be enhanced not only in terms of infrastructure, but also in terms of rules and standards, so as to create favorable conditions for the smooth movement of people and goods," he said.

According to Xi Jinping, the development of humanitarian ties remains an important area of cooperation. China and Kyrgyzstan should expand cooperation in culture, tourism, arts, education, healthcare and archaeology, as well as interaction between media outlets, think tanks and youth organizations.

Xi Jinping noted that humanitarian exchanges between the two countries have increased in recent years. In particular, the number of mutual visits by citizens of China and Kyrgyzstan exceeded 400,000 last year.

He also highlighted the importance of multilateral cooperation between the two countries within the UN and SCO, noting the need for joint efforts on regional security and international cooperation.

Speaking about bilateral relations, Xi Jinping noted that China and Kyrgyzstan have progressed from establishing diplomatic relations to a comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era.

According to him, in February 2025, the two sides reached agreements on further deepening their comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era and building a China-Kyrgyzstan community with a shared future.

Xi Jinping’s upcoming visit will be his third visit to Kyrgyzstan. During the visit, he will meet with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov and attend the meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the SCO, which will be held in Bishkek on September 1.

Kyrgyzstan is celebrating the 35th anniversary of its independence this year. Xi Jinping conveyed his congratulations and best wishes to the Kyrgyz people on the occasion.

World.title: SCO summit could give fresh impetus to Kyrgyzstan-Azerbaijan transport links – expert (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 29. The upcoming summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) could give fresh impetus to transport cooperation involving Kyrgyzstan, Temirlan Razbaev, chief expert at the Analytics and Coordination Department of the National Institute for Strategic Initiatives under the President of the Kyrgyz Republic, told Trend.

According to him this includes the integration of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway with the Middle Corridor via the Caspian Sea and Azerbaijan. “The first promising area is logistics. It would be advisable to link the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway with the Middle Corridor via the Caspian Sea and Azerbaijan. According to official Azerbaijani data, the capacity of the Alat Port is planned to be increased from 15 million to 25 million tons per year, while cargo volumes along the Middle Corridor via Azerbaijan have increased by nearly 90% since 2022. For Kyrgyzstan, the practical benefit will come not from the route simply being mapped out, but from a regular container service, a single electronic document and a competitive end-to-end tariff,” he said.

The expert added that investment was another promising area. In particular, in July 2026, the capital of the Azerbaijan-Kyrgyzstan Development Fund was increased from $100 million to $200 million. At the same time, three joint projects were opened and eight initiatives were launched. “The next stage should involve moving toward measurable production projects in agro-processing, logistics, green energy and digital services. These are areas with potential rather than sectors in which agreements have already been finalized for specific projects,” he added.

At the same time, Razbaev said tourism and people-to-people ties represented a third area of potential cooperation. “On July 31 this year, the five-star Baku Resort & Spa complex, built by the Azerbaijani side, opened in the village of Kara-Oy on Lake Issyk-Kul. According to the official announcement, the complex covers more than 17 hectares, includes 111 rooms and 10 cottages, and can accommodate 330 guests. At the initial stage, it is expected to provide employment for 255 people. This is a concrete example of a project whose impact can be assessed in terms of the facility itself, employment and the quality of its infrastructure. Overall, the success of cooperation should be measured not by the number of memorandums signed, but by cargo volumes, investment, operational enterprises and jobs created,” the chief expert said.

Razbaev also emphasized that Kyrgyzstan’s role in the SCO is currently determined primarily by its ability to advance Central Asian interests within the broader Eurasian organization. “The SCO comprises 10 countries with a combined population of more than 3.4 billion people, accounting for about a quarter of global GDP and more than 15% of international trade. By comparison, when Kyrgyzstan held the SCO chairmanship in 2019, the organization had eight members – Iran and Belarus joined later. Therefore, the current chairmanship is taking place within a larger and more complex organization.

Over 2025-2026, Bishkek has identified specific priorities, including streamlining trade procedures, developing the digital economy and transit potential, expanding renewable energy, and improving security mechanisms. A practical indicator was the SCO Investment and Business Forum held on June 24, 2026, which brought together more than 600 participants. The Universal SCO Center currently being established is also set to include a Center for Combating Transnational Organized Crime in Bishkek.

It is therefore more accurate to say that over the past year, the country has strengthened its role as a coordinator and initiator of the Central Asian agenda. The final assessment will be determined by the package of decisions adopted at the Bishkek summit,” he concluded.

The SCO was established in 2001 and initially comprised China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Over the past 25 years, its membership has expanded to 10 countries. The 26th SCO summit will be held in Bishkek on August 31-September 1, 2026, under Kyrgyzstan’s chairmanship. The meeting will focus on the organization’s further development, strengthening economic and transport cooperation, and security cooperation. Following the summit, the leaders are expected to consider a number of documents related to the development of the SCO’s financial and economic mechanisms, including initiatives to expand settlements in national currencies and establish new cooperation institutions.

World.title: Turkmenistan moves to increase railway system capacity
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 29. Turkmenistan is taking measures to strengthen the material and technical base of its railway transport system and increase its capacity.

This was reflected in the statement of the Turkmen government, published following a regular Cabinet of Ministers meeting chaired by President Serdar Berdimuhamedov via digital system.

Deputy Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers B. Annaev reported on ongoing work in the railway sector, with particular attention being paid to cooperation with leading foreign companies.

"The measures being implemented are expected to significantly increase the capacity of Turkmenistan’s railway system and improve the safety of passenger and freight transportation," he said.

Annaev submitted a relevant proposal to the president for consideration. Berdimuhamedov stressed the importance of measures aimed at developing domestic railway transport and strengthening its material and technical base. The president approved the proposal aimed at increasing the sector’s capacity and instructed the deputy prime minister to carry out the necessary work in this direction.

Turkmenistan’s railway network spans approximately 5,000–5,100 km of 1,520 mm gauge track and is operated by the state company Türkmendemirýollary. The system plays a key role in both domestic transport and international corridors linking Central Asia with Iran, Afghanistan, Kazakhstan and the Caspian region. Major modernization efforts are underway, including plans to upgrade the Ashgabat–Turkmenbashi line to allow passenger trains to reach speeds of up to 160 km/h and freight trains up to 90 km/h. The country maintains long-standing cooperation with Chinese manufacturers, which have supplied a significant portion of its locomotive and rolling-stock fleet, and is advancing projects with support from international partners to expand capacity and improve operational efficiency.

World.title: President Ilham Aliyev sends congratulatory letter to President of Uzbekistan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 29. President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev has sent a congratulatory letter to Shavkat Mirziyoyev, President of the Republic of Uzbekistan.

This was reported by the press service of the President of Azerbaijan.

"Dear Shavkat Miromonovich,

Dear Brother,

On this landmark occasion—the 35th anniversary of the Independence of the Republic of Uzbekistan—I am pleased to extend my sincere congratulations and best wishes to you and, through you, to your brotherly people, on my own behalf and on behalf of the people of Azerbaijan.

Since gaining independence, brotherly Uzbekistan has followed a path of comprehensive and dynamic development, achieving remarkable success and earning high authority and respect both regionally and internationally. Under your wise leadership and guided by your strategic vision, large-scale reforms and construction projects have been successfully implemented across all areas, significant economic progress has been achieved, and the social welfare of the population has been ensured.

Your tireless efforts, together with the profound trust and support of your people for the state policy you firmly pursue, lie at the heart of all the achievements Uzbekistan has made and the goals it has attained. As a brotherly country and ally, we consider every success of Uzbekistan our own and take immense pride in it. Every time I visit your unique and hospitable country, I witness firsthand its significant accomplishments. I fondly recall my recent state visit to the brotherly country and my meeting with you.

Built upon shared historical and cultural roots, unwavering friendship, and brotherhood, Azerbaijan-Uzbekistan relations today stand at their highest level. The further comprehensive development and strengthening of our bilateral relations with Uzbekistan remain among our top priorities. I am pleased that, through our joint efforts, our interstate relations and alliance are growing stronger day by day, while our multifaceted cooperation is enriched with new practical substance.

I am confident that, through our joint efforts, we will continue to successfully fulfill the honorable mission entrusted to us to preserve our greatest asset—the Azerbaijan-Uzbekistan unity—to develop our comprehensive cooperation, and to constantly strengthen our alliance.

Dear Shavkat Miromonovich,

On this historic day, sharing in your joy and that of the brotherly people of Uzbekistan, I wish you robust health, happiness, and success in your high state activities, and wish the Republic of Uzbekistan continuous prosperity, well-being, and progress," the letter reads.

World.title: Turkmenistan to showcase economic achievements at independence exhibition
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 29. Turkmenistan is preparing an exhibition showcasing the country’s economic achievements to mark the 35th anniversary of independence.

This was reflected in the statement of the Turkmen government, published following a regular Cabinet of Ministers meeting chaired by President Serdar Berdimuhamedov via digital system.

Deputy Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers N. Atagulyyev reported on preparations for the large-scale exhibition. According to the report, the exhibition will showcase Turkmenistan’s achievements and progress made during the years of independence, as well as major transformations taking place across all areas of the state and society.

"The event is intended to highlight the country’s development and achievements aimed at strengthening Turkmenistan’s standing and improving the well-being of its people," the statement reads.

A relevant proposal was submitted to the president for consideration. Following the report, Berdimuhamedov stressed the importance of reflecting the country’s major activities and achievements in the exhibition’s displays. The president instructed the relevant authorities to properly prepare for the exhibition and ensure that it is held at a high level.

Turkmenistan declared independence on 27 October 1991. The 35th anniversary in 2026 is expected to feature a series of official events, including large-scale exhibitions that traditionally present progress in the oil and gas sector, textiles, agriculture, construction, transport infrastructure, and social development. Similar exhibitions held in previous anniversary years have served as platforms to display industrial output, new technologies, and state programs aimed at economic diversification and improving living standards.

World.title: Turkmenistan takes measures to expand power generation capacity
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 29. Turkmenistan is taking measures to increase power generation capacity and ensure uninterrupted electricity supplies to consumers, the country's government says.

According to the Turkmen government, this was announced by the Deputy Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers B. Annamammedov during a regular meeting of the Cabinet of Ministers chaired by President Serdar Berdimuhamedov via digital system.

According to the report, relevant work is underway at power plants, combined heat and power plants and other facilities of the energy sector. "Particular attention is being paid to cooperation with foreign companies to significantly increase the sector’s production capacity and ensure reliable electricity supplies to consumers," the statement notes.

A relevant draft document was submitted to the president for consideration. After hearing the report, Berdimuhamedov noted the effectiveness of measures being taken to develop the energy sector and strengthen its material and technical base. The president signed the relevant resolution and instructed the authorities to carry out the necessary work.

Turkmenistan’s power system is based almost entirely on natural gas and has an installed generating capacity of approximately 6,500–7,000 MW. The largest facility is the Mary State Power Station (nearly 3,000 MW), which includes a 1,574 MW combined-cycle unit. A second large combined-cycle plant of the same capacity is under construction at Kiyanly in Balkan province, with commissioning targeted for around 2027 and involvement of Turkish company Çalık Enerji. The country generates a surplus of electricity that supports exports to neighboring states, while ongoing modernization programs focus on converting existing gas-turbine plants to more efficient combined-cycle operation and expanding transmission infrastructure.

World.title: Jai Arrow makes emotional return for South Sydney
World.content:
Jai Arrow has made an emotional return for South Sydney, leading the side out and officially playing his 99th match for the club against Gold Coast.

Arrow, who was diagnosed with MND earlier this year, has received special dispensation from the NRL to play the opening seconds of the Rabbitohs' final two matches for the year.

He was substituted before kick-off for Cameron Murray and left the field at Skilled Park to a standing ovation.

Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett and former stalwart Jason Clark helped Arrow put his boots on before the match.

The Titans wore a commemorative jersey with Arrow's face on the front.

He played 56 matches for the club from 2018 to 2020.

Arrow will lead South Sydney out again next week in their final game of the regular season against the Sydney Roosters.

Arrow was in tears as he left the field. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

It will mark his 100th game for the club and the 180th and final match of his career.

Arrow was in the room when elated Souths players were told about the plan during their team review session on Monday morning.

"We all play a tough sport and we all mean so much to so many people, but it's so special to see what players mean to other players when things are going tough," said Rabbitohs fullback Matt Dufty.

"[Jai] brings a smile to everyone's face. Whatever we can do to give back to him, even if it's a little bit, it's just what we need to do. We're all behind him."

The NRL world has rallied around Arrow since his shock diagnosis and immediate retirement in May.

Murray replaced Arrow before kick off. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde )

The league threw Arrow "the world's biggest birthday party" on the day Souths beat Newcastle in July, rolling out a birthday cake in the shape of his jersey and presenting him with a commemorative jersey.

Fundraising efforts have already passed $1 million in support of Arrow, who is the father of a young daughter.

Players from all clubs showed their support by marking tries with 'arrow' celebrations during July.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Nepali families' desperate search for news of missing loved ones
World.content:
Photographs of unidentified dead plaster the walls of a major hospital in Kathmandu.

The pictures are printed on A4 paper, displayed in the hope someone will recognise them.

But the rain regularly arrives before a loved one can — streaking and washing away the faces, forcing them to be reprinted.

Rescuers in the areas hardest hit in Nepal's catastrophic flash flooding have to prioritise survivors. They cannot bring all the bodies back, so photos are taken instead.

Nepal flash floods updates: Follow this story as it unfolds with our live blog.

A woman searches for information about her family members at the Maharajgunj Medical Campus in Kathmandu. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Hanging alongside the pictures of the lost is a noticeboard with lists of survivors and the injured.

Crowds of people gather at the gates of the Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital desperately hoping they will find their loved ones on the latter.

Almost 2,500 people are now missing in Nepal after a glacial collapse sent a wall of water, mud and debris tearing through the valley on the border with Tibet, wiping out communities.

Some 517 bodies have been recovered on the Nepali side.

Family members are posting their own pictures rather than relying on authorities. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Hung next to the pictures of the deceased are smiling photos of those who are missing — remnants of better days.

Friends and family are taking matters into their own hands, posting pictures of the people they are searching for.

Police and volunteers are set up at desks taking the names and numbers of those who have missing relatives.

Some people come here multiple times a day in the desperate hope they will receive good news.

'His phone is not connecting'

Mud-covered properties following a flash flood at Trishuli in Nepal. (Reuters: Navesh Chitrakar)

Among the crowd at the hospital is Tilmaya Gurung. She has been visiting hospitals and morgues in the city searching for news of her sister's husband.

Meg Bahadur was working at a hydropower plant in Rasuwa when the flood hit. The 49-year-old has two children.

"We tried his phone several times but his phone is not connecting," she wept.

" We came here to hospital to check the list pasted here but not found his name on the list. "

A missing person's QR code is scanned at the Maharajgunj Medical Campus. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Her husband Jai Bahadur Gurung explained that the relatives split into groups to go to different sites to search for information.

He is trying to remain hopeful, but as the days stretch on the fear is building.

"We are here at hospital looking among dead," he said.

New methods for treatment developed

Doctors are treating survivors who were covered from head to toe after being buried in mud. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

More than 400 injured people, airlifted from the disaster area, have been brought here.

Chief of the emergency medicine department Ramesh Kumar Maharjan said most of those patients had been buried in mud.

"People were buried from head to toe and they have chest injuries and limb injuries, fractures, as well as head injuries and aspiration," he said.

" They were crushed. Their chests were crushed. They had become trapped. "

This QR code directs families to information about unidentified and unclaimed bodies. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

He said some of the people that had recovered from suffocation had "mud trapped inside them".

Staff have never treated patients like this before and are having to develop new methods, including a "decontamination shower" to remove the mud.

People adding missing person details to lists at the Maharajgunj Medical Campus. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

One of his patients is a five-year-old girl who had lost all of her family members. She is in critical care with a head injury.

This region is prone to natural disasters. It's been hit with earthquakes and more standard flooding before. But Dr Maharjan said this was a "different type of natural disaster" altogether.

Difficulty in accessing key locations

The flooding has destroyed roads and bridges, meaning the worst hit areas are only accessible by helicopter.

It is not only making it difficult to get injured people out, it is also making it difficult to get aid in.

Some young survivors have lost all their family members. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Less than 10 kilometres from the hospital, at a specialist hub, people are loading trucks with supplies like hygiene kits, food, water, and protective equipment.

Hangers are lined up, filled with donations from all over the world.

The humanitarian staging area was already set up, built on experiences with previous natural disasters, and in some areas allowed supplies to arrive within five hours of the emergency being declared.

Almost 3,000 people are still unaccounted for in Nepal and Tibet. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

But getting aid to those most in need is incredibly difficult.

UN World Food Programme country director Riaz Lodhi said road access being cut to the worst hit areas was "very restrictive" and made it difficult to assess the situation.

"We still don't know what the needs are out there," he said.

Some 93,000 people are believed to have been impacted by the disaster. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Aid supplies are currently being trucked a certain distance before being transferred to helicopter to be flown in.

"It's an enormous challenge given the magnitude of the disaster," he said.

World.title: Child stars say fame gives a 'wound' regulation has failed to prevent
World.content:
At just 16, Hayden Panettiere was handed a pill that would propel her "downfall of addiction".

The US star — who died last week aged 36 — wrote she was given the drug as a teen to boost her energy ahead of a red carpet appearance.

It was just one of the candid disclosures she made in the weeks before her death, in a memoir that laid bare the challenges of child stardom, substance abuse and postpartum depression.

Early coronial reports from Panettiere's death say she suffered a cardiac arrest, while police dispatchers said they were resuscitating the star after a possible "overdose".

The US Drug Enforcement Agency has also reportedly joined the investigation.

And while it's still unknown if drugs or alcohol played a factor in her death, Panettiere has joined the tragic roll call of former child stars who have died prematurely over the last year or so.

Hayden Panettiere (centre) wrote of how the traumatic storylines she portrayed led her to associate "catastrophe with adoration". (AP: Kevork Djansezian/File)

Her Ice-Princess co-star Michelle Tratchenberg died aged 39 last February, as a result of complications from diabetes — with co-star Rosie O'Donnell later alleging Tratchenberg struggled with addiction before her death.

Daveigh Chase, of The Ring and Lilo & Stitch fame, died in June aged 35 of AIDS, after suffering from drug abuse and homelessness.

Ice Princess director Tim Fywell paid tribute to his dual leads, Hayden Panettiere and Michelle Trachtenberg, saying he would remember them as "two shining talents, gone far too soon". (Getty Images: Alli Harvey/Stuart Weitzman)

Child stars have long been a vital facet of Hollywood, but this latest triad of deaths has reignited calls for better protections.

Anna Paquin, who was 11 when she won her Oscar, has joined the calls for better support for child actors. (Reuters: File)

In an essay following Panettiere's death, Even Stevens star Christy Carlson Romano said stars like herself powered "one of the most profitable storytelling machines in the world, while their mental needs are treated as inconvenient or irrelevant".

"Those of us who make it are given the adoration of saints — and then, if we don't climb to A-list fast enough, we're torn down as if we've committed some unspeakable mortal sin. All before our frontal lobes have fully formed," she wrote for Elle.

"Is it any wonder so many of us struggle with addiction?

" The industry gives us the wound and then acts surprised when we reach for something to treat it. "

Anna Paquin, who was 11 when she won her Oscar for The Piano, said the deaths were more than coincidence, in a separate statement about Panettiere's death.

"We are not as protected by the 'systems' that look great on paper, as we are supposed to be," she wrote on Instagram.

The first child star who almost lost it all

There is one key piece of US law that enshrines the rights of child stars — and it is nearing 100 years old.

The 1939 Coogan Law is named after Jackie 'The Kid' Coogan, arguably Hollywood's first child star.

At age four, he was foisted onto the screen by Charlie Chaplin to star 1921's The Kid.

Coogan became a hit, making millions but still only received a weekly allowance of $6.25 from his family.

Hours after Coogan (right) filed his lawsuit, the child star act was rushed through legislation. (Wikimedia Commons: Unknown photographer)

Then when he turned 21, he found his mother and manager-turned-stepfather would not give him a cent more.

Coogan eventually won the subsequent lawsuit he waged, albeit recovering only a small portions of his earnings.

As Coogan Law currently stands, it ensures 15 per cent of a child actor's earnings are set aside in a blocked trust, and also codifies issues such as schooling, work hours, and time off.

In her final months, Hayden Panettiere chose to be 'brutally honest' The actress, who died on Sunday aged 36, spoke openly about the hardships she experienced throughout her decades in the spotlight.

Yet despite decades of regulation, the extent of Hollywood's alleged 2000s lawlessness has been made fully apparent.

The child stars from Nickelodeon's heyday have grown up, and now they're speaking out against the machine and long-time producer Dan Schneider.

The 2024 documentary Quiet on Set delved into how dialogue coach Brian Peck was brought onto Disney's The Suite Life of Zack & Cody after previous convictions for the sexual abuse of Nickelodeon stars.

Meanwhile, Disney star Alyson Stoner says unsafe working conditions left her malnourished and chronically stressed, despite the labour laws in place.

And just this week, former child star Raquel Lee Bolleau has sued Disney, alleging a middle-aged employee repeatedly raped her on a 2001 set while other visible adults failed to intervene.

These are the same spaces Panettiere grew up in.

And now, some fear a new era of child stars could face similar problems with even less oversight.

Hayden Panettiere said her mother was a "momager" more often than not. (Reuters: Mario Anzuoni)

Fame arrives from 'the first ultrasound'

In 2024, former Disney star Demi Lovato shone a light on a new child star industry, booming and unregulated.

She was ushering in two new Californian bills that brought kidfluencers in line with the financial restraints of Coogan Law.

Risks of promoting children as influencers remain largely unregulated around the world, including in Australia where there is no specific legislation around kidfluencing, despite being a multi-million industry.

Demi Lovato lamented how her young fame had made her the family "breadwinner". (Supplied: Gavin Newsom )

Social media communication researcher Catherine Archer says she has seen how some kids are famous "from the first ultrasound".

What follows can be enormous pressure to gather large followings that may result in thousands of dollars in earnings for the family — with no guardrails.

"If it's your source of income and you're also their parent, there's a bit of a conflict of interest there, isn't it?" Dr Archer notes.

"It's going to be that pressure to continue, particularly if (your child is) getting the likes, the shares and the comments."

Jerome is a four-year-old model who makes thousands. But his fame has a dark side Children are gathering large followings and earning thousands of dollars through social media influencing — but some warn it comes with a dark side.

No case is a better example of the risks of unregulated family vloggers than Utah mother Ruby Franke, who created a "concentration camp-like setting" for two of her four children.

Her daughter Shari Franke later testified to politicians as a "victim of family vlogging".

"If I could go back and do it all again, I'd rather have an empty bank account now and not have my childhood plastered all over the internet," she said.

" No amount of money I received has made what I've experienced worth it. "

Complicating the issue is a general "reluctance to regulate what goes on in people's homes" Dr Archer adds, while acknowledging the entertainment relies on that very access.

"You see the kids in their bathrooms getting ready for bed. You'll see them in their bedrooms getting ready," she says.

"There's this lack of privacy."

Ruby Franke (centre) was arrested after her 12-year-old son escaped through a window, malnourished and badly bruised. (Washington County Attorney's Office via AP)

Saving stars from 'a lawless area'

France now regulates the hours under-16s can work online, their earnings — and their right to be removed from online platforms at their wish.

MP Bruno Studer said the bill was France's duty to protect children from the internet "which must not be a lawless area".

Disturbing rumours have followed Dan Schneider for years. Now people are speaking out The child stars from Nickelodeon's heyday have grown up, and now they're speaking out against the machine and long-time producer Dan Schneider.

Panettiere's death and those of Tratchenberg and Chase have reignited a debate about the treatment of children on movie sets.

Yet the rise of the kidfluencer shows the new and insidious ways child entertainers continue to face harm.

These are children who often just started with a dream to be creative, as Dr Archer says.

"I don't want to say it is 100 per cent all bad because there are things to enjoy," she says.

"But there's definitely another dark side to it too."

As Anna Paquin says, it can be "possible to holistically look after the kids on set and tell complex and upsetting stories".

World.title: Three teenagers arrested over alleged burglary spree in Melbourne
World.content:
Three teenage boys have been arrested following an alleged crime spree in Melbourne's north-eastern suburbs yesterday morning.

A 17-year-old from the Greater Shepparton area, and a 15-year-old and a 17-year-old, both from the Manningham area, were arrested by detectives at an address in Darebin.

The 17-year-old from the Greater Shepparton area was charged with four counts of aggravated burglary, two counts of burglary, an attempted theft from a motor vehicle, among other charges.

The 15-year-old and the 17-year-old from Manningham were both charged with four counts of aggravated burglary, attempted theft from a motor vehicle and theft of a motor vehicle, among other charges.

Youth crime has been a key election topic ahead of Victoria's November state election. (AAP: James Ross)

Victoria Police said the charges followed several alleged incidents in the early hours of August 28, including two separate aggravated burglaries in Balwyn North; an attempted theft from a motor vehicle in Templestowe; and aggravated burglaries in Bulleen and Templestowe.

The trio were remanded to appear before a children's court today.

It comes as crime, particularly youth crime, dominates debate between the Labor government and Coalition opposition ahead of Victoria's November state election.

Stepping into the top job after Jacinta Allan was ousted in late July, Premier Ben Carroll vowed to "continue the same hardline approach to tackling crime."

Last month, the Coalition pledged to add new offences to the state's Adult Crime, Adult Time laws if elected, including car theft and attempted carjacking.

According to the most recent statistics, youth crime fell last year in Victoria for the first time in four years, but adult crime rose by more than 10 per cent over the same time frame.

The Crime Statistics Agency (CSA) released its figures for the 12 months to March 2026, showing Victoria's overall crime rate fell by just under 2 per cent.

The CSA said the figures showed youth crime falling for the first time since the COVID pandemic.

There were 22,654 alleged offences involving young people, which was a fall of 6 per cent on the previous year.

However, adult crime rose by 10 per cent, which the CSA attributed to increases in breaches of bail, retail theft and breaches of family violence orders.

World.title: Qld Labor MP confirms she will recontest seat after electoral redraw
World.content:
Queensland Labor frontbencher Meaghan Scanlon has confirmed she will recontest her Gold Coast seat after speculation she may move to a safer electorate after a substantial redraw.

There will be significant changes to the boundaries of her Gaven electorate for the 2028 state election following a review by the Queensland Redistribution Commission released in June.

The redraw raised questions about whether Ms Scanlon, who reclaimed it at the last state election with a margin of less than one per cent.

The seat of Gaven, on the Gold Coast, will be substantially redrawn for the next state election. (Supplied: Queensland Redistribution Commission)

Opposition Leader Steven Miles announced Ms Scanlon would stand again in Gaven in his speech at the Labor state conference on Saturday, noting there had been "a lot of speculation".

"I know there has been many in Meaghan's ear trying to encourage her to look to a safer seat elsewhere, but to be honest I don't think Meaghan ever really entertained that idea," he said.

"I am very confident, not only can she win but she will win."

Ms Scanlon, who many consider a future party leader, is Labor's only MP on the Gold Coast, with all the other seats held by the LNP.

Two Qld state electorates to be axed after review A Brisbane Labor-held seat and a north Queensland electorate held by the Katter's Australian Party (KAP) have been abolished, under a review of the state's electoral boundaries.

She was first elected to Gaven in 2017 and served in the Palaszczuk and Miles governments as environment minister and housing minister.

The commission noted in its report it was required to make significant changes to Gaven because it was below quota and projected to fall further under quota.

Ms Scanlon said she was committed to remaining in the seat where she grew up.

"I've been underestimated every time I've run," she said. "My focus is getting the support of Gold Coasters to win.

" I don't give up when things get tough, I'm going to stay and fight. "

Meaghan Scanlon was first elected to Gaven in 2017. (ABC News: Mackenzie Colahan.)

Ms Scanlon narrowly defeated LNP candidate and former television journalist Bianca Stone at the 2024 election.

Now chief of staff in police minister Dan Purdie’s office, Ms Stone said she had not turned her mind to the next poll, and was happy in her current role.

When questioned whether he could guarantee he would lead the party to the 2028 election, Mr Miles said: "Of course".

Former Labor MP and political analyst John Mickel said if Ms Scalon had abandoned her seat, the LNP's "enormous advantage" on both the Gold and Sunshine Coasts would have grown.

"If she had abandoned that, the maths for Labor to win a state election are simply enormous," he said.

"It is sending a signal that Labor is serious about the Gold Coast, particularly that northern end."

World.title: Interest rates, fish and Donald Trump on Icelanders' minds as nation goes to referendum on EU
World.content:
High interest rates and inflation, a fishing industry under threat and the shadow of Donald Trump are on the minds of Icelanders as the country goes to a referendum this weekend to decide whether it should restart negotiations on joining the European Union.

If this tiny island nation of almost 400,000 people chooses 'yes', they would have a second vote later to seal the deal reached between Reykjavik and Brussels.

Or the people could reject it and keep the status quo.

Iceland's picturesque capital, Reykjavik. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

A Gallup poll this month found voters split on restarting talks with the EU: 46 per cent said they would vote yes and 46 per cent no, with 8 per cent undecided.

Other polls show a majority against actually joining the bloc.

For Icelanders who support the 'yes' side the most compelling argument is around creating economic opportunities and improving cost of living.

Living standards and wages are high, but so are inflation and interest rates.

Economics student Óðinn Freyr Baldursson, 21, is saving up to buy his first home.

Óðinn Freyr Baldursson believes interest rates will eventually go down if Iceland joins the EU. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

"The interest rates for mortgages, regular mortgages for homes, are around 9 per cent here in Iceland," Mr Baldursson said.

"Which is more than two times higher than most other places in Europe, and that's the main reason why owning a house here in Iceland is so, so tough."

He said he believed that if Iceland joined the EU and replaced the volatile krona with the euro, interest rates and inflation would come down.

"Just based off of the experience of other countries joining the EU, we can expect that interest rates will decrease by 3 to 4, maybe 5 per cent," he said.

" We need more stability if we want to continue to develop as a country and an economy, and I think the euro is the way to do that. "

The 'no' side fervently disagrees that joining the EU would solve this.

Tourists at Kirkjufellsfoss in Iceland's east. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

"Telling people 'we just need to go into the EU because we have so high interest rates, because we have so high inflation' [is wrong], because we have to deal with inflation and the interest rates either way," 'no' campaigner Steinar Ingi Kolbeins, 29, told 7.30.

"For me, that's just that the government is not doing their job."

He said even if Iceland were to have a seat at the table in Brussels, he doubted his country's officials would have much impact because it would have fewer seats than the larger nations.

"We have to think about what does the seat at the table look like? What's the size of the chair? And what's the trade-off? What are we letting go of for that seat at the table?" Mr Kolbeins said.

His colleague Magnea Gná Jóhannsdóttir, also 29, said she was motivated to vote 'no' because she wanted "decisions to be made in Iceland by Icelanders".

Steinar Ingi Kolbeins and Magnea Gná Jóhannsdóttir are both planning to vote 'no' in the referendum. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

"I don't want to sell the EU the right of our natural resources or fisheries or farming and all the other things that are part of the European Union," she said.

"And [having negotiations] is not a journey that's free. It costs money. It costs the time of the government."

The government, though, argues the time and investment would be worth it and provide more opportunities for the people.

Fears for fishing industry

On the west coast of Iceland, the Snaefellsnes Peninsula is famous for its appearance in the hit TV show Game of Thrones, but it is also home to a thriving fishing industry.

Sustainable fishing is central to Iceland's identity and economy — only Icelandic ships can fish within the 200 nautical miles (321 kilometres) of the island, and foreign companies can't own fish processing facilities.

Some hope Iceland would get exemptions to protect its fishing industry if it joined the EU. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

If Iceland joins the EU, those in the fishing industry fear the bloc's Common Fisheries Policy will mean these exclusive waters will become a free-for-all.

Arnar Kristjánsson's family business, G.RUN, has been fishing in them for more than 70 years.

G.RUN is the biggest employer in the small town of Grundarfjörður — 80 of the roughly 800 residents work for the company.

Arnar Kristjánsson fears what would happen to Iceland's fishing industry if it joins the EU. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett )

Mr Kristjánsson is firmly against joining the EU.

"The big companies in Europe will swallow up all these small companies, and for small towns like this, there will be no more fish production," the third-generation owner said.

"Iceland tries to use our fish stocks in a way that they can keep producing, [but] Europe has not done that. Many of their fish stocks are in a very bad shape, and we don't like to have that here."

Sustainable fishing is central to Iceland's identity. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

Prominent 'yes' supporter and Reykjavik MP Dagur B Eggertsson said fishing history "matters very much" and Icelandic officials would fight for exemptions so the industry could be protected.

"The kind of detailed plans of how to handle this have been met with the kind of words of flexibility and openness on the EU's behalf," Mr Eggertsson told 7.30.

Reykjavik MP Dagur B Eggertsson supports a 'yes' vote. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

"Some people say [exemptions] are out of the question, but one of the arguments for a 'yes' in this referendum is exactly to go into negotiations."

Former president of Iceland from 1996 to 2016, Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, said he believed exemptions would not happen.

"The core element in the whole EU existence is the commonality of the rules applying to everyone, every country, every economy, so you can't perhaps say, 'Let's try to see what we can get,' no," Mr Grímsson told 7.30.

He said he feared Iceland would be taking a huge step backwards if it was to eventually join the EU.

Former president of Iceland, Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, is against joining the EU. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

"It took the generation of my parents and grandparents 100 years to gain independence [from Denmark], full control over our powers, the right to negotiate with other countries, to be a sovereign state," the former president said.

" Whatever people say, this is fundamentally about transfer of power [from Iceland] over to EU institutions. "

'No' campaigners see multiple threats

Iceland has been proudly independent since it broke away from Denmark in 1944.

Iceland's referendum will be closely watched by the EU this weekend. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

It first looked at EU entry 17 years ago after the global financial crisis and the collapse of Iceland's banking sector, but walked away after disagreements on several policies, including fishing.

But the world has changed a lot since then.

Iceland sits opposite Greenland, just beside the Arctic Circle, a region the US, Russia and China all want to exploit for resources and new shipping channels as the polar ice melts due to climate change.

US President Donald Trump's ongoing campaign to slap tariffs on allies, and his threats to annex Greenland, before confusing it with Iceland multiple times in a speech at January's Davos Economic Forum, have startled people here.

These developments have prompted some Icelandic policymakers to seek deeper security and economic cooperation with European partners.

A recent poll found the country was evenly divided over whether to rejoin EU talks. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

Iceland is already a member of the defence alliance NATO and some European trade agreements, but now the coalition government wants extra reinforcement with EU membership as well.

"I think all countries, especially small and middle-sized countries, have to rethink their position and take in how the world has changed," Mr Eggertsson said.

"Wars are not just wars fought with weapons. We also see trade wars going on and threats of tariffs being used. Tariffs are being weaponised.

"So where should we, as Icelanders, seek tighter bonds? I see that within the EU."

The EU will be watching Saturday's referendum closely.

Iceland is famous for its puffins. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

Given how peaceful, prosperous and well-positioned Iceland is, this Nordic nation would be seen by many in Brussels as a very good get.

But if the 'yes' vote gets up, the path forward will be tricky — negotiations will require delicate diplomacy and calculated compromise.

For the Icelandic people, though, the vote is not about what is in it for the EU, but all about what is in it for them.

World.title: Power, privilege, protection: Society has come to this
World.content:
NationalNSWLetters Power, privilege, protection: Society has come to this August 29, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

So, integrity is about doing what is right or following strong moral rules even when no one is watching. Jacqueline Maley (“How wealth, privilege protect boys and men accused of sexual violence”, August 23) channels the reminder that “If you have integrity, nothing else matters. If you don’t have integrity, nothing else matters”. Steve Ngeow, Chatswood Jacqueline Maley shines a light on gendered violence Steven Siewert Jacqueline Maley powerfully analyses the world of privilege and its impact on the attitudes that males emerging from that world have towards women. She unfortunately was blinded by a simple truth – each of those boys was also raised by a mother, who needs to take the same responsibility for the attitudes their sons now have towards women. Or maybe they presented that to them – submissive, focused on personal grooming, attracted to power and money, incapable of calling out wrong from right and prepared to turn a blind eye to their own partner’s inappropriate behaviours. That’s the world we need to be unpacking for this to have any chance of stopping. Brian Barrett, Padstow Jacqueline Maley makes a good case against victim blaming and, while correct, she misses two vital points: one is that a 14-year-old, by law, cannot consent (even if they do); second, who was responsible for the other 14-year-old drinking with 17-year-olds (mind you, all underage)? Maybe we need education around the law. Jenny Greenwood, Hunters Hill Jacqueline Maley is rightly outraged by “the men and boys who commit violence against women, or enable it”. Recent instances of sexual violence by snobbish blokes with misplaced notions of superiority because of their privileged upbringing, and boof-headed yobbos with little self-control and even less sensitivity, are a disgrace. And I certainly don’t want people like that, or their enablers, in any positions of authority or public adulation. I hope Maley and other women don’t assume that all men are like that, or that they think it’s OK or even just shrug their shoulders at it. I’m just as revolted by it as they are. Adrian Connelly, Springwood



Park the perfectionism The Greens have the devil of a dilemma to deal with (“New forest proposal to dwarf Koala Park”, August 23). The National Parks Association’s proposal to create a Great Southern National Park based on the state government’s Improved Native Forest Management (INFM) method, allowing the use of carbon credits, appears to have much in its favour. Like its counterpart, the Great Koala National Park, it promises the end of native forest logging and the protection of habitat for endangered species. It has the support of some Indigenous groups and the Nature Conservation Council, but is opposed by the Nationals and Greens’ luminaries Bob Brown and Christine Milne. The fact that the INFM was devised by a harsh critic of dodgy offsets, Professor Andrew Macintosh, gives the park proposal credibility. On the face of it, it would be a great pity if the Greens put conservation perfection ahead of the immense practical good of this scheme. They will need to consider carefully what its rejection could entail. Tom Knowles, Parkville (Vic) Cap rent rises Shane Wright (“Rents spike up to 80% as housing crisis bites”, August 23) sets out the various hotspots where rents are spiking and ends with a brief note that Canberra is again the “outlier”, recording the smallest increase in the country. Absent from this short observation is the very important reminder that the ACT is the only state/territory that explicitly and legally caps the percentage amount a landlord can increase rent by (with a process for a landlord to get approval to exceed this threshold). Notwithstanding the admirable efforts of other state governments to make renting fairer in Australia, most have baulked at mandating the capping approach. It seems to be working in the ACT. Is it worth a try in NSW? Cathryn Callaghan, Croydon Far down in this story was the line: “The pace of growth in rents has slowed this year”. Surely that should have been the headline? Brendan Jones, Annandale



Outspoken Abbott Tony Abbott just can’t keep his mouth shut (“Abbott backs Hanson’s challenge to High Court racial vilification ruling”, August 23). He is the president of the Liberal Party, not its leader. He should take a look at One Nation’s Free Speech policy – it is a doozy. It calls for absolute free speech, which would result in the repeal of any legislation that now controlled it. If it had been in place for the past three years, then the racial and religious hate we have seen would be permissible, even stopping the police from acting. No need for a royal commission; anarchy and violence would be the order of the day. Well done, Tony, who failed drastically at being a prime minister. John Rome, Mount Lawley In Tony Abbott’s latest example of his bizarre brand of logic, he claims that his decade-long fight to overturn section 18C is because it is a “risk to free speech”. He says that “leadership is about preserving national unity on the essentials, and this is why I have taken this position”. So, to preserve “national unity”, we should all be able to “offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate another person or group because of race or ethnicity”? Go figure. Alan Marel, North Curl Curl Sit down, Tony. You are not a party. Anne Eagar, Epping To submit a letter to The Sun-Herald, email letters@smh.com.au. Click here for tips on how to submit letters. World.title: ‘Blessed’ to be Australian: Survivor of Nepalese floods speaks out
World.content:
Cara Severino, an Australian thought to have been missing in the Nepalese floods, has spoken for the first time since her rescue, thanking embassy officials and the crew she had been hiking with when the disaster struck. The 26-year-old had been listed as missing prior to making contact with her parents on Friday morning. Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong confirmed on Saturday night that Severino has since been located by consular officials in Nepal. Australian consular officials have made contact with Cara Severino, previously listed as missing. Facebook In a statement released alongside comments from Wong, Severino said she felt “blessed” to be Australian. “I’m so grateful for the crew we formed on that first day when we entered the national park on the tractor. Sudha, Lucas, Samir and Saugat. It’s thanks to these amazing people I got out safely,” she said.



“I feel for the families of those still missing – I know how much my family and friends went through. “Blessed to be from Australia and have the embassy and Australian government giving so much support.” Wong said Australian consular officials maintained regular contact with Severino on Saturday and were able to eventually identify her location and drive out to meet her from Kathmandu. “They are now transporting her to a safe location and will continue to check on her welfare and provide assistance to her and her family as needed,” Wong said. “While this is a welcome development, there remain grave concerns for the other Australians who are still unaccounted for, given the tremendous scale of the flooding and its impact.”



View post on X The number of Australians officially missing in the floods now stands at 41 in what could be the worst loss of Australian life on foreign soil since the Bali bombings. Bharat Mangwani, Karan Bhardwaj, Arpan Kothari, Bhavin Raval, Michael Ryan Keats and Gopi Agastya were all identified among the list of Australians after family members for each either reached out to this masthead or posted on social media about the search for their loved ones. Bharat Mangwani with his wife Neha and son Anjaneya. Mangwani was confirmed missing in the Nepal floods. Facebook Harsh Maheshwari, a friend of Sydneysider Mangwani, said they held out hope that some Australians were still alive and were stuck in a building, under the mud.



“We are all still hoping. His family have travelled there to search for him. They could have stayed in the building or maybe they went out. We don’t know, but we have hope,” he said. Mangwani’s last known location was at the Gyirong Immigration Facility, which was inundated with floodwater in the early stages of the disaster. Like many Australians caught in the tragedy, he was taking part in a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar as part of the Kailash Manasarovar Yatra. Bhardwaj (centre) was travelling with his friends Arpan Mithalal Kothari (left) and Bhavinkumar Rajnikant Raval (right). The family of Royal Australian Air Force member Karan Bhardwaj is pleading for information after losing contact with the Brisbane father, who was travelling with tour group Kailash Journeys when the flash floods hit. Bhardwaj was travelling with friends Kothari, 40, and Raval, 41. The Brisbane-based trio have not been heard from since and are among six Australians currently missing from the Kailash Journeys tour group.



Keats, from NSW, was understood to be returning from a journey to Mount Kailash in Tibet, and had reached the border crossing into Nepal when the floods struck. The 37-year-old had been due to arrive home on Thursday night. Michael Ryan Keats is one of the Australians missing in Nepal. Facebook Details surrounding 45-year-old Gopi Agastya are still scarce, but his brother-in-law confirmed he was missing. Venkatesh Bittu said his family were “waiting for him to return safe”. Nepal’s disaster agency revised the overall death toll to 626 on Saturday; 2426 people are officially listed as missing. More than 3700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. China’s state media said 554 people were missing on the Chinese side. Search and rescue efforts are continuing at several locations in Nepal and Tibet, a Chinese territory, including the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project in Nepal’s Rasuwa district and the severely damaged Gyirong border crossing on the Chinese side.



Loading Poor weather temporarily hampered aerial rescue operations in Nepal as the search for thousands of missing people entered its fourth day. Nepali Army spokesperson Brigadier General Raja Ram Basnet said rescue efforts would continue at the hydropower construction site, where authorities believe more than 100 people are trapped in a tunnel filled with thick mud. Basnet said rescuers had used baskets and ropes to reach some people, but the operation remained difficult because of the mud up to 1.5 metres thick and the limited number of places where helicopters could land. Rescuers remain on high alert for more flooding from a new lake that formed high up in the Himalayan mountains after the initial floods on Wednesday. Experts had warned that the lake, created after the glacier collapse that triggered the floods, was at risk of overflowing.



However, monitoring data from the Chinese Ministry of Water Resources showed late on Friday that the lake had dwindled in size. The water level dropped by 10 metres from the high point on Thursday morning, Chinese broadcaster CCTV said. Related Article Updated

Floods The 41 Australians missing in the Nepal-Tibet floods, and what we know about them Rescuers have reached Gyirong Port, the border crossing with Nepal obliterated by a wave of water. It was not immediately known how many people were at the border checkpoint building when the floods hit. The cost of rebuilding once the rescue operations are complete for Nepal could stretch into billions of dollars. Finance minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters the country may need up to $US5 billion ($6.9 billion), a bill equal to nearly a tenth of the economy. “The initial estimate is between $4 to $5 billion. Just an estimate,” Wagle said. “We will require much less than what we needed for the 2015 earthquake. Loss and damage is being assessed.”



Wagle did not elaborate on why the reconstruction bill was expected to be less than the $US9 billion spent after the 2015 magnitude-7.8 quake, Nepal’s worst recorded disaster. It killed nearly 9000 people, destroyed more than half a million homes and caused losses estimated at around a third of Nepal’s economy. Buildings are damaged and partially buried in mud and debris in the Devighat area of the Nuwakot district in Nepal. NYT Wednesday’s floods will be a major blow to an economy reliant on remittances, tourism and hydropower, damaging power projects that account for more than 12 per cent of national generating capacity. Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs said it had fielded more than 450 consular calls in relation to the disaster, with communities across the country reeling from the news. The department revised the list of missing Australians to 41 on Saturday, up from 38 on Friday. It has the potential to be the worst loss of life overseas since the 2002 Bali bombings, which killed 88 Australians.



Assistant Immigration Minister Matt Thistlethwaite said the Nepalese and Tibetan communities were desperate for news after holding two online forums on Friday. An aerial view shows debris and mud covering an area in Devighat village, Nepal. Getty Images “Obviously, we’re working with people who are in the region, the Australians that we know, the roads are cut off, about 10,000 homes have been destroyed,” he told the ABC’s News Breakfast program. He said there were no telecommunications infrastructure to the region and power has been cut off.



Related Article Floods ‘I must look for my sons’: A farmer’s extraordinary survival in Nepal “I also attended a vigil last night, with the Nepalese community in Strathfield, and obviously, there was quite a bit of despair and anxiety, in that community, but we’re doing our best to support the Tibetan and Nepalese communities here in Australia.” He confirmed that Nepalese authorities had requested support from Australia and that eight officials had been sent, including “four crisis response team members and four consular members”. NSW Premier Chris Minns said the state government is prepared to send emergency crews to help rescue efforts, while adding that he wanted to add to the “chorus of concern and sorrow” across Australia and the world for the “terrible scenes” in the Nepal flood zone. “Our hearts bleed for them. I imagine their families back in Australia are incredibly worried.

World.title: Roosters sweat on Walker scans after damaging defeat to Dolphins
World.content:
The Roosters’ season continues to unravel after halfback Sam Walker suffered an ankle injury in the 26-12 loss to the Dolphins on Saturday night.

A week after a shock defeat to Wests Tigers cost the Tricolours their chance of winning the minor premiership, the star playmaker went down clutching his lower leg in the 52nd minute following a tackle from Dolphins No.12 Kulikefu Finefeuiaki, and played no further part in the match

Walker was sent for scans on Saturday night, with Roosters coach Trent Robinson unsure of the seriousness of the injury.

Sam Walker goes down injured in the Roosters loss to the Dolphins. Getty Images

“Only saw him briefly there before he went for scans,” Robinson said. “We’ll deal with that when we get to it.”

It was initially thought Walker had been the victim of a hip-drop tackle, but replays did not show Finefeuiaki landing on the back of Walker’s legs, although his knee did slide into the back of Walker’s ankle.

Returning Roosters captain James Tedesco said it had a disappointing night all round.

“We don’t know how severe [Walker’s injury] is yet, so hopefully it’s not too bad,” Tedesco said. “It’s one of those ones [where] you get caught in the tackle. I had a similar one as well. It’s tough, hopefully it’s not too long. We’ll see how it is.

“But again, I think everyone’s disappointed with our performance and the injury as well.”

Sam Walker comes from the field injured. Getty Images

Walker’s agony was compounded by an injury to hooker Reece Robson, who was taken off in the final minute, but Robinson said the hooker had just been caught in an awkward tackle.

“He put his head down to get it [the ball], and they came in to tackle, and he just got his head crunched,” Robinson said.

“He just got some pins and needles once the head sort of went into his neck there. He’s OK, it was just an awkward one.”

Reece Robson leaves the field in the final minute. Getty Images

It was a case of history repeating for Walker, who ruptured his ACL at the same point of the season – round 26 – two years ago.

Playmaker-turned-centre Hugo Savala shifted back into the halves alongside Daly Cherry-Evans in Walker’s absence.

The Roosters were already 20 points down when Walker left the field, but sensed a glimmer of hope when Tom Flegler was sent to the sin bin for repeat infringements before Morgan Knowles was also marched for 10 minutes for dangerous contact on Robert Toia.

The Roosters managed to score in the two minutes the Dolphins had 10 men on the field, with Salesi Foketi charging across, but could not make up the 14-point gap before referee Todd Smith blew the final whistle.

Daly Cherry-Evans in action against the Dolphins. Getty Images

Now the Roosters must wait to see if Walker – who is yet to re-sign with the Tricolours past 2027 – will be fit enough to make it back before finals.

If Cronulla beat Parramatta on Sunday, the Roosters must win their final round match against the Rabbitohs next Friday night to guarantee a top-four finish. A defeat in that match coupled with a Sharks win over Melbourne in the final round would then see Cronulla pinch fourth spot.

The Dolphins’ victory sees them leapfrog the Roosters to third on the NRL ladder, while the Roosters slip to fourth.

Kristian Woolf’s men have already beaten the Warriors this year, pushed Penrith to golden point and flogged the Roosters during the Origin period.

But this was by far their best performance, and a top-two finish with two home finals is now a mathematical possibility ahead of next week’s clash with Gold Coast.
