World.title: ‘Blessed’ to be Australian: Survivor of Nepalese floods speaks out
World.content:
Cara Severino, an Australian thought to have been missing in the Nepalese floods, has spoken for the first time since her rescue, thanking embassy officials and the crew she had been hiking with when the disaster struck. The 26-year-old had been listed as missing prior to making contact with her parents on Friday morning. Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong confirmed on Saturday night that Severino has since been located by consular officials in Nepal. Australian consular officials have made contact with Cara Severino, previously listed as missing. Facebook In a statement released alongside comments from Wong, Severino said she felt “blessed” to be Australian. “I’m so grateful for the crew we formed on that first day when we entered the national park on the tractor. Sudha, Lucas, Samir and Saugat. It’s thanks to these amazing people I got out safely,” she said.



“I feel for the families of those still missing – I know how much my family and friends went through. “Blessed to be from Australia and have the embassy and Australian government giving so much support.” Wong said Australian consular officials maintained regular contact with Severino on Saturday and were able to eventually identify her location and drive out to meet her from Kathmandu. “They are now transporting her to a safe location and will continue to check on her welfare and provide assistance to her and her family as needed,” Wong said. “While this is a welcome development, there remain grave concerns for the other Australians who are still unaccounted for, given the tremendous scale of the flooding and its impact.”



View post on X The number of Australians officially missing in the floods now stands at 41 in what could be the worst loss of Australian life on foreign soil since the Bali bombings. Bharat Mangwani, Karan Bhardwaj, Arpan Kothari, Bhavin Raval, Michael Ryan Keats and Gopi Agastya were all identified among the list of Australians after family members for each either reached out to this masthead or posted on social media about the search for their loved ones. Bharat Mangwani with his wife Neha and son Anjaneya. Mangwani was confirmed missing in the Nepal floods. Facebook Harsh Maheshwari, a friend of Sydneysider Mangwani, said they held out hope that some Australians were still alive and were stuck in a building, under the mud.



“We are all still hoping. His family have travelled there to search for him. They could have stayed in the building or maybe they went out. We don’t know, but we have hope,” he said. Mangwani’s last known location was at the Gyirong Immigration Facility, which was inundated with floodwater in the early stages of the disaster. Like many Australians caught in the tragedy, he was taking part in a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar as part of the Kailash Manasarovar Yatra. Bhardwaj (centre) was travelling with his friends Arpan Mithalal Kothari (left) and Bhavinkumar Rajnikant Raval (right). The family of Royal Australian Air Force member Karan Bhardwaj is pleading for information after losing contact with the Brisbane father, who was travelling with tour group Kailash Journeys when the flash floods hit. Bhardwaj was travelling with friends Kothari, 40, and Raval, 41. The Brisbane-based trio have not been heard from since and are among six Australians currently missing from the Kailash Journeys tour group.



Keats, from NSW, was understood to be returning from a journey to Mount Kailash in Tibet, and had reached the border crossing into Nepal when the floods struck. The 37-year-old had been due to arrive home on Thursday night. Michael Ryan Keats is one of the Australians missing in Nepal. Facebook Details surrounding 45-year-old Gopi Agastya are still scarce, but his brother-in-law confirmed he was missing. Venkatesh Bittu said his family were “waiting for him to return safe”. Nepal’s disaster agency revised the overall death toll to 626 on Saturday; 2426 people are officially listed as missing. More than 3700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. China’s state media said 554 people were missing on the Chinese side. Search and rescue efforts are continuing at several locations in Nepal and Tibet, a Chinese territory, including the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project in Nepal’s Rasuwa district and the severely damaged Gyirong border crossing on the Chinese side.



Loading Poor weather temporarily hampered aerial rescue operations in Nepal as the search for thousands of missing people entered its fourth day. Nepali Army spokesperson Brigadier General Raja Ram Basnet said rescue efforts would continue at the hydropower construction site, where authorities believe more than 100 people are trapped in a tunnel filled with thick mud. Basnet said rescuers had used baskets and ropes to reach some people, but the operation remained difficult because of the mud up to 1.5 metres thick and the limited number of places where helicopters could land. Rescuers remain on high alert for more flooding from a new lake that formed high up in the Himalayan mountains after the initial floods on Wednesday. Experts had warned that the lake, created after the glacier collapse that triggered the floods, was at risk of overflowing.



However, monitoring data from the Chinese Ministry of Water Resources showed late on Friday that the lake had dwindled in size. The water level dropped by 10 metres from the high point on Thursday morning, Chinese broadcaster CCTV said. Related Article Updated

Floods The 41 Australians missing in the Nepal-Tibet floods, and what we know about them Rescuers have reached Gyirong Port, the border crossing with Nepal obliterated by a wave of water. It was not immediately known how many people were at the border checkpoint building when the floods hit. The cost of rebuilding once the rescue operations are complete for Nepal could stretch into billions of dollars. Finance minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters the country may need up to $US5 billion ($6.9 billion), a bill equal to nearly a tenth of the economy. “The initial estimate is between $4 to $5 billion. Just an estimate,” Wagle said. “We will require much less than what we needed for the 2015 earthquake. Loss and damage is being assessed.”



Wagle did not elaborate on why the reconstruction bill was expected to be less than the $US9 billion spent after the 2015 magnitude-7.8 quake, Nepal’s worst recorded disaster. It killed nearly 9000 people, destroyed more than half a million homes and caused losses estimated at around a third of Nepal’s economy. Buildings are damaged and partially buried in mud and debris in the Devighat area of the Nuwakot district in Nepal. NYT Wednesday’s floods will be a major blow to an economy reliant on remittances, tourism and hydropower, damaging power projects that account for more than 12 per cent of national generating capacity. Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs said it had fielded more than 450 consular calls in relation to the disaster, with communities across the country reeling from the news. The department revised the list of missing Australians to 41 on Saturday, up from 38 on Friday. It has the potential to be the worst loss of life overseas since the 2002 Bali bombings, which killed 88 Australians.



Assistant Immigration Minister Matt Thistlethwaite said the Nepalese and Tibetan communities were desperate for news after holding two online forums on Friday. An aerial view shows debris and mud covering an area in Devighat village, Nepal. Getty Images “Obviously, we’re working with people who are in the region, the Australians that we know, the roads are cut off, about 10,000 homes have been destroyed,” he told the ABC’s News Breakfast program. He said there were no telecommunications infrastructure to the region and power has been cut off.



Related Article Floods ‘I must look for my sons’: A farmer’s extraordinary survival in Nepal “I also attended a vigil last night, with the Nepalese community in Strathfield, and obviously, there was quite a bit of despair and anxiety, in that community, but we’re doing our best to support the Tibetan and Nepalese communities here in Australia.” He confirmed that Nepalese authorities had requested support from Australia and that eight officials had been sent, including “four crisis response team members and four consular members”. NSW Premier Chris Minns said the state government is prepared to send emergency crews to help rescue efforts, while adding that he wanted to add to the “chorus of concern and sorrow” across Australia and the world for the “terrible scenes” in the Nepal flood zone. “Our hearts bleed for them. I imagine their families back in Australia are incredibly worried.

World.title: Hopeful signs on AI regulation and social media
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Hopeful signs on AI regulation and social media August 29, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Hopeful signs

The government’s proposed and already legislated actions against AI and social media platforms have been powerfully vindicated by two developments. First, Bill Gates, while acknowledging the enormous potential of AI (“Gates warns global leaders on risks of AI to humanity”, 28/8), identifies many potential dangers due to its “mind blowing” rate of advance. He acts as an industry whistleblower declaring that big business will actively resist government actions to slow or rein in its advance, due to “economic incentives”. He also suggests some innovative guard rails: preserve certain jobs and responsibilities for humans and taxing the “tokens and robots” that replace humans.

Second, the financial penalty agreed to by Meta (“Meta to pay $24b in addiction case”, 28/8) and the controls it now says it can and will build into its platforms to protect teenagers and limit their usage, justifies the government’s social media controls. Both developments strengthen its negotiating position with big business.

Peter Thomson, Brunswick Energy necessity

The only requirement the government needs to make of new data centres is that they choose the most cost effective source of energy and that they supply themselves with that in the fastest possible time. That’s it. Let’s see what then emerges.

Carolyn Ingvarson, Canterbury Robot peril

The proper response to the Chinese robot games is not laughter or ridicule but fear. Remember ″⁣tank man″⁣ near Tiananmen Square? Robots, with suitable improvements in control, will soon be out on the streets in countries with authoritarian governments (realistically all governments, because the temptation will be too great to resist) and used for crowd control.

No tanks or armoured vehicles will be needed. Armed or not, humanoid robots will be unstoppable and capable of causing great harm to people, including killing us. If they are stopped, they can immediately be replaced. No morality or conscience will be involved in their actions. At the current pace of development of robots (and data centres) I fear they will be used within a few years and, given the lack of resistance by us humans to the other humans who are responsible for what is happening, I don’t see much of a future for the majority of us. I weep for my grandkids.

Don Jordan, Mount Waverley



White board for Hanson

I think it might be time to get out the whiteboard at One Nation headquarters and in big, bold letters put down a definition, and differences between, net overseas migration (NOM), true NOM, net zero migration, net negative migration, the different categories of visas and permanent residency. After 30 years in politics Pauline Hanson is struggling, as witnessed by her answers at the Bush Summit.

Invite all their current MP’s and senators along, together with candidates for election because the vilification of migrants is the attraction of many of One Nation’s supporters. Surely they must want to know who the migrants are, where they come from, and how many they are blaming for all woes. Maybe not, as it’s easier to use a broad brush and blame all migrants without answering questions on future numbers or categories.

Doug Shaw, Sunbury Glad to be out of it

Melbourne a megacity of 10 million – are we totally mad? (″⁣Megacity, how will it cope?″⁣, 28/8). Where is the water coming from? The food? The emergency services when the hyperfires of 2050, fed by 3-5 degrees of global warming, burn deep into the sprawling outer suburbs? The bayside suburbs forced to move uphill when sealevel rises half a metre or more? The police to try to quell the periodic uprisings of the out-of-work and the never-worked, squeezed out of society and the economy by AI? Now 75, living in the lotus land of the bush and not having to go to this nightmare city any more, I am glad I will miss all this.

Mick Webster, Chiltern Show some humanity

Imagine if the boot was on the other foot and Australia suffered a disaster or a war and other countries said, ″⁣Sorry, we have a limit on the number of refugees.″⁣ We would be crying out in disgust at the complete lack of humanity.Would we graciously accept being told, ″⁣Go back to where you came from.″⁣ We would argue that we are people too, with feelings and the need to be treated with dignity and respect, regardless of the colour of our skin, our religious beliefs, our ethnicity and even of our gender.

If we can’t see the need to help others who are suffering, why should we expect others to see the need if we are suffering? There will be some who play the system, but stats don’t show that is a very low number. Policy makers, if you have any humanity, then put yourself in someone else’s shoes.

Greg Tuck, Warragul Very little sense

The federal government will provide $5 million in humanitarian assistance to Nepal. That’s 18 cents per Australian.

Peter Seligman, Brunswick West Rein in lobbyists

While I support the push to increase the transparency of the interactions between decision makers and lobbyists, why don’t we also restrict the access of lobbyists for non-corporate interests to ministers? Corporate interests should be restricted to engaging with the public service and public servants should be banned for at least five years from lobbying roles or representing corporate interests to government.

Rosemary Marcon, Hawthorn



Drew a picture of world

Cathy Wilcox had the unerring skill with a brushstroke to eviscerate and expose the hypocrisy, evil, narcissism, self-importance and sadness in the world to make us pause and nod collectively in a way words alone never could.

Peter Russo, West Brunswick Annual calendar, please

I had to re-read Cathy Wilcox’s commentary a few times to fully realise what “taking a break” really meant, and it made me sad. Wilcox has always been so refreshingly insightful, intelligent and direct without any hint of malice or meanness. Could she be invited to consider preparing a yearly calendar for us to buy? I would love to continue to enjoy her work as each new month arrives.

Helen Clements, Mount Waverley As good as it gets

To your correspondent (Letters, 29/8) we all need to face the fact that Australia is incapable of building roads. Built for price, on the cheap and a ″⁣she’ll-be right″⁣ attitude, this is as good as it gets.

Gregory Head, Ararat The kids are all right

Recently on the train I saw and heard a group of teens talking and laughing with each other. Not a device in sight. Still annoying, but fun watching them interacting with each other instead of heads down looking at phones.

James Lane, Hampton East Great start to finals

I was not a fan of the AFL finals 10 with wildcard rounds. The Bulldogs v Collingwood game changed my opinion. An edge-of-the-seat match that delivered a fantastic game to start the finals.

Ross Kroger, Barwon Heads



... for some

Pies lose with a kick on the siren. Pendlebury leaves for the Suns. A total eclipse of the heart!

Glenda Johnston, Queenscliff ... solace, of sorts

Q. Why do Collingwood supporters never end up in hell? A. Because they have received more than enough punishment here on Earth!

Philip Anthony, Hawthorn East

World.title: Thousands of youths to lose access to unemployment benefits after welfare law change
World.content:
Thousands of youths across the country are set to lose access to unemployment benefits, after a welfare bill passed into law under urgency on Friday night.

From November 2026, the government will end Jobseeker payments to 18-19-year-olds whose parents earn more than $67,225.

The limit was originally just over $65,000 when the policy was announced, but has since been adjusted.

In October last year, it was estimated that about 4300 young people would become ineligible for support as a result.

Social Development and Employment Minister Louise Upston said the legislation reflected the government's commitment to reduce benefit dependency and encourage people into work.

"This legislation reinforces the expectation that young people who are not in employment, education or training should be financially supported by their parents, not by taxpayers through the welfare system," she said.

"New Zealanders deserve a welfare system that is firm, fair and simple."

The bill also makes changes to how accommodation supplements are calculated.

Upston said the changes would "better target that support to those who need it most".

"Importantly, it does not apply to homeowners who are receiving New Zealand superannuation, veteran's pension, supported living payment, or the emergency benefit that is the equivalent to the supported living payment.
